a0701: Course home / Phase 7 · Inside the Transformer Why RNNs ran out of road Lesson 7.1 45 min Learn Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 3 (Neural Networks, Inside Out), Phase 5 · 09 (Sequence-to-Sequence), Phase 5 · 10 (Attention Mechanism) Type : Learn. Time : about 45 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line RNNs process tokens one at a time. Transformers process all tokens at once. That single architectural bet changed every scaling curve in deep learning after 2017. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Recurrence "RNNs are sequential" Computation where step t depends on step t-1 , forcing serial execution along the time axis. Serial depth "How deep the graph is" Longest chain of dependent ops; bounds wall-clock even on infinite hardware. Attention "Let tokens look at each other" Weighted sum $\sum_j a_{ij} v_j$ where $a_{ij}$ comes from a similarity score between positions $i$ and $j$. Context window "How much the model sees" Number of positions an attention layer can take as input; quadratic memory cost scales here. Inductive bias "Assumptions baked into the architecture" Prior about what the data looks like; CNNs assume translation invariance, RNNs assume recency. State-space model "RNN with algebra behind it" Recurrence parameterized for parallel training via structured state-space matrices. Quadratic bottleneck "Why context costs so much" Attention memory = $O(N^2)$ in sequence length; Flash Attention hides the constants, not the scaling. The problem In plain words first A recurrent network reads a sentence the way you read with a finger under the words: one word at a time, carrying a running summary forward. That has two costs. The work cannot be split up, because word 10 waits for word 9, so a chip built to do thousands of things at once sits mostly idle. And anything the network learned about word 1 must survive being rewritten at every later step, so its influence fades. A transformer instead lets every word look at every other word directly, all at once; the price is that the number of word pairs grows with the square of the length. This lesson measures all three effects on this page's CPU with real PyTorch layers: the same arithmetic done as a chain versus in one batch, how much the last output still depends on early words, and how running time grows with length for a GRU and a self-attention layer. Nothing is trained. Before 2017, every state-of-the-art sequence model on the planet — language, translation, speech — was a recurrent neural network. LSTMs and GRUs won ImageNet-equivalent translation benchmarks for half a decade. They were the only tool anyone had. They had three fatal weaknesses. Sequential computation meant you could not parallelize along the time axis: token t+1 needs the hidden state from token t . A 1,024-token sequence meant 1,024 serial steps on a GPU that can do hundreds of thousands of floating-point operations per clock cycle. Training wall-clock time scaled linearly with sequence length on hardware designed for parallelism. Vanishing gradients meant information 50 tokens back was already compressed through 50 non-linearities. Gated recurrent units (LSTM, GRU) softened the crush but never eliminated it. Long-range dependencies — "the book I read last summer on a plane to Kyoto was…" — routinely failed. Fixed-width hidden states meant the encoder squeezed the entire source sequence into a single vector before the decoder saw anything. Doesn't matter if the source is 5 tokens or 500; the bottleneck is the same shape. The 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need" proposed something radical: drop recurrence entirely. Let every position attend to every other position in parallel. Train in one big matrix multiplication instead of 1,024 sequential ones. The result dominates every modality by 2026. Language (the GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama and Qwen families), vision (ViT, DINOv3, SAM 3), audio (Whisper), biology (AlphaFold 3), robotics (vision-language-action models). Same block, different inputs. The idea Recurrence as a bottleneck. An RNN computes ​ = f ( h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ) . Each step depends on the previous. You cannot compute ​ before ​ . On modern GPUs with 10,000+ parallel cores, this wastes 99% of the silicon on a long sequence. Attention as a broadcast. Self-attention computes output_i = sum_j(a_ij * v_j) for every pair simultaneously. The whole N×N attention matrix fills in one batched matmul. No step depends on another. GPUs love it. The speedup is not a constant. It is the difference between serial depth and serial depth. In the original paper, the big Transformer beat the best recurrent translation models while training for 3.5 days on 8 GPUs, a fraction of their training cost; the advantage grows with sequence length until you hit the ) cost of attention (which FlashAttention makes manageable in memory, though not in compute — see Lesson 7.12 ). What transformers cost. Attention memory scales as ) . For 2K context, fine. For 128K context, you need sliding windows, RoPE extrapolation, Flash Attention tiling, or linear attention variants. Recurrence was in both time and memory; transformers trade time for memory and then win the time back through parallelism. The inductive bias shift. RNNs assume locality and recency. Transformers assume nothing — every pair is a candidate for attention. That is why transformers need more data to train well but scale further once they have it. Kaplan et al. (2020) measured it: as models grow, transformers keep improving and make use of far more of their context than LSTMs of the same size. (Chinchilla, 2022, is about something else: how to split a compute budget between parameters and training tokens; see Lesson 7.13 .) Worked example Counting depth and memory by hand Depth. A 12-layer LSTM over 4,096 tokens has a dependency chain of about steps (each layer can start once the one below has produced its first output); a 12-layer transformer has 12 layers of a few batched products each. Attention memory. One head at stores = 16.8 million scores: 64 MiB in fp32, 32 MiB in bf16. With 32 heads and a batch of 8, a naive implementation needs GiB for one layer's scores, which is why FlashAttention never stores the full matrix. RNN memory at inference. An LSTM with width 1,024 keeps numbers per sequence (hidden and cell state), whatever the length; a transformer's KV cache grows with every token (Lesson 7.12). Check your mental model ✗ "Transformers do less arithmetic than RNNs." ✓ They do more, d ) for the scores alone; they win because the arithmetic has no chain of dependencies, so parallel hardware can do it at once. ✗ "Attention removes the vanishing-gradient problem everywhere." ✓ It gives every position a one-step path to every other within a layer; deep stacks still need residual connections and normalisation to train. ✗ "RNNs are obsolete." ✓ Their constant memory per step is why state-space layers appear in production hybrid models. In the attention layer, every earlier position sits one weighted sum away from the last output, so its dependence stays at roughly the same level (around ) whether the input is 1 or 255 tokens back; only the token itself, through the residual connection, stands out. Step 1 · measure serial depth No neural network here — we simulate the core bottleneck numerically so you feel the gap on your laptop. See code/main.py . We build two functions. One encodes a sequence as a chain of additions (serial, like an RNN). One encodes it as a parallel reduction (broadcast, like attention). Same math, different dependency graph. Copy We time both on sequences up to 100,000 elements. The RNN version is and a single CPU pipeline. Even in pure Python, the attention-style reduction beats it at length ≥ 1,000 because Python's sum() is implemented in C and iterates without interpreter overhead per step. Step 2 · count theoretical operations Both algorithms do N adds. The difference is dependency depth : how many operations must happen sequentially before the next can start. RNN depth = N. Attention depth = log(N) with a tree reduction, or 1 with a parallel scan. Depth, not op count, decides GPU time. Step 3 · empirical scaling on long sequences We print a timing table that makes the gap visible. On a 2026 Mac laptop, sequences under 1,000 elements are too fast to measure. Sequences of 100,000 show a clean linear scan. Scale that to a 16,384-token transformer with a 12-layer LSTM equivalent and you see why training wall-clock was a blocker in 2016. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output With identical arithmetic, the batched version is 6 to 9 times faster on two CPU cores, and the gap is about the same at every length: the chain pays a fixed cost per step (a small matrix-vector product cannot keep the cores and vector units busy, and each step waits for the previous one), while one large product gives the matrix library big blocks it can split across cores. A GPU, with thousands of cores, widens the gap to tens or hundreds of times; that is the hardware argument for transformers. Use it: the same idea with real libraries When to still pick an RNN in 2026: Situation Pick Streaming inference, one token at a time, constant memory RNN or state-space model (Mamba, RWKV) Very long sequences (>1M tokens) where attention memory explodes Linear attention, Mamba 2, Hyena Tiny always-on device (wake word, sensor stream) Small RNN or state-space model: constant memory per step Anything else (training, batched inference, context up to 128K) Transformer State-space models (SSMs) like Mamba are essentially RNNs with structured parameterization that gives them the best of both: scan memory, parallel training via selective scan. Pure SSMs still trail transformers on tasks that need exact recall from far back in the context, which is why the production versions are hybrids that keep a few attention layers: AI21's Jamba, NVIDIA's Nemotron-H, IBM's Granite 4.0 and Qwen3-Next. Recurrence is not dead; it is a component. Timings vary a little between runs. Two CPU cores cannot exploit the parallelism that makes attention fast on a GPU, so here the quadratic term dominates, just as the formula box predicts for lengths beyond the width (256). That is the trade: attention buys parallel training with ) work, and long contexts on any hardware need the efficient-attention methods of Lessons 7.12 and 7.15. Break it on purpose In the gradient experiment, replace the random read-out (y[0, -1] @ r) with y[0, -1].sum() for the attention layer. Every gradient becomes almost zero. Why? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Transformers are the production default for language, vision, speech and multimodal models; the remaining engineering is about attention's cost: FlashAttention kernels, grouped-query attention and KV-cache compression (Lessons 7.12 and 7.15) in every serving engine (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM). Hybrids bring recurrence back. NVIDIA's Nemotron-H, IBM's Granite 4.0 (October 2025), AI21's Jamba and Qwen3-Next replace most attention layers with Mamba or linear-attention layers to cut memory and speed up long contexts, keeping some attention layers for exact recall. Small RNNs ship on devices for wake words, keyboards and sensor streams, where constant memory per step matters more than parallel training. Sources: FlashAttention-3 , Nemotron-H , IBM Granite 4.0 , Jamba , Qwen3-Next , Kaplan et al. 2020 . Recap What to keep from this lesson Recurrence forces dependent steps; attention computes every position at once. Same arithmetic is much faster when it has no chain of dependencies (the run under Step 3). Attention gives every position a one-step path to every other; recurrence passes signals through every step in between. Attention's price is the score matrix: quadratic time and, without FlashAttention, quadratic memory. Production models are transformers, with recurrent layers returning inside hybrids. Solution B1 · LayerNorm makes the sum constant The encoder layer ends with LayerNorm, whose output has mean zero across the feature dimension before its learned scale and shift. Summing the features therefore gives (almost) a constant, the sum of the shift parameters, and a constant has zero gradient with respect to the input. The LSTM has no final normalisation, so its sum still depends on the input. Reading the output through a random direction measures the dependence fairly for both. Time : about 90 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Attention is a lookup table where every word asks "who matters to me?" - and learns the answer. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Query (Q) "The question vector" A learned projection of the input that represents what information this token is looking for Key (K) "The label vector" A learned projection that represents what information this token contains, matched against queries Value (V) "The content vector" A learned projection carrying the actual information that gets aggregated based on attention scores Scaled dot-product attention "The attention formula" $\mathop{\mathrm{softmax}}(QK^T / \sqrt{d_k}) V$ - scaling prevents softmax saturation in high dimensions Self-attention "The token looks at itself and others" Attention where Q, K, V all come from the same sequence, letting every position attend to every other position Attention weights "How much focus" A probability distribution over positions, produced by softmax over scaled dot products Multi-head attention "Parallel attention" Running multiple attention functions with different projections, then concatenating results for richer representations The problem In plain words first Self-attention lets every word in a sentence build its new meaning from the other words. Each word makes three vectors from its embedding with three learned matrices: a query (what it is looking for), a key (how it describes itself to others) and a value (what it passes on if chosen). A word's query is compared with every key by a dot product, the scores become weights that add up to 1, and the word's output is the weighted average of the values. In a language model that writes left to right, a causal mask stops each word from looking at words that come after it. This lesson builds that from NumPy, then checks it against a real model: it rebuilds the attention weights of GPT-2's first layer from GPT-2's own weights with the lesson's functions, looks at what GPT-2's 144 heads actually attend to, and compares the code with PyTorch's fused attention kernel. Nothing is trained. RNNs process sequences one token at a time. By the time you reach token 50, the information from token 1 has been squeezed through 50 compression steps. Long-range dependencies get crushed into a fixed-size hidden state - a bottleneck that no amount of LSTM gating fully solves. The 2014 Bahdanau attention paper showed the fix: let the decoder look back at every encoder position and decide which ones matter for the current step. But it was still bolted onto an RNN. The 2017 "Attention Is All You Need" paper asked a sharper question: what if attention is the only mechanism? No recurrence. No convolution. Just attention. Self-attention lets every position in a sequence attend to every other position in a single parallel step. That is what makes transformers fast, scalable, and dominant. The dot product between a query and all keys produces attention scores. High score means "this key matches my query." Those scores weight the values. The output is a weighted sum of values. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) One function call in production. PyTorch's scaled_dot_product_attention dispatches to FlashAttention or memory-efficient kernels, and Hugging Face models select it by default ( attn_implementation="sdpa" ); serving engines (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM) use FlashAttention and FlashInfer kernels with paged KV caches. Custom masks without custom kernels. PyTorch's FlexAttention (2024) compiles mask and score modifications (sliding windows, document masks for packed sequences, ALiBi) into fused kernels, which training stacks use for packed pretraining batches. Grouped-query attention is the default in open LLMs (Llama 3, Qwen3, Gemma 3, Mistral): several query heads share one key-value head to shrink the cache (Lesson 7.3). Sources: scaled_dot_product_attention , Transformers attention backends , FlexAttention , FlashInfer , Llama 3 paper . Hints open one at a time; the reference solution opens when every check passes. medium 25 min implement Attention lets each query token collect information from a set of key and value tokens. Every transformer layer in the course uses this operation. A decoder adds a causal mask, so that a token cannot see the tokens that come after it. Task Write two functions. causal_mask(T) returns the causal mask for a sequence of T tokens. scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V, mask=None) returns the attention output and the attention weights. The scores are / d k ​ ​ , where ​ is the size of the last axis of Q . The weights are the softmax of each row of , over the key axis. The output is the weights times V . The mask is a boolean array. True means blocked. A blocked query and key pair gets a weight of exactly 0. The other weights in the row are a softmax over the allowed keys only, so each row of weights sums to 1. The causal mask has True at row i and column j when j > i . Token i can see token i and every token before it. Constraints 1 <= T, Tq, Tk <= 64 and 1 <= d_k, d_v <= 64 . Each row of the mask has at least one allowed key. Scores can be larger than 1000. The output must stay finite. Transpose only the last two axes of K . The leading axes are batch axes. Do not change the input arrays. Use numpy only. Builds the causal mask with k=0, so each token also blocks itself and the first row has no allowed key. Sets the blocked weights to 0 after the softmax, so the rows do not sum to 1. Calls np.exp on the raw scores, so large scores overflow to infinity. Forgets to divide the scores by sqrt(d_k). Divides the scores by d_k, not by sqrt(d_k). Hint 1 Write a softmax over the last axis first. Use axis=-1 and keepdims=True , so that it works for any number of leading axes. Hint 2 K.T reverses every axis of a 3D array. Use np.swapaxes(K, -1, -2) to transpose only the last two axes. The @ operator then treats the leading axes as a batch. Hint 3 Apply the mask to the scores before the softmax. Put minus infinity at each blocked position with np.where . The exponential of minus infinity is exactly 0. Hint 4 Subtract the maximum of each row before np.exp . Each row has at least one allowed key, so the maximum is finite. np.triu with k=1 gives the causal mask. Reference solution and notes Copy Why divide by the square root of d_k Each score is a sum of ​ products. When the entries of and have variance 1, the score has variance ​ . Large scores push the softmax toward a one-hot vector, and the gradient of a one-hot softmax is almost 0. Division by ​ ​ sets the variance of the scores back to 1. Why the mask goes before the softmax The softmax divides by the sum over the row. When you set a weight to 0 after the softmax, the row sum is less than 1. When you put minus infinity in the score, the softmax gives that key a weight of exactly 0, and the other weights still sum to 1. The numerical trap Masked rows and large scores need the same fix: subtract the row maximum before np.exp . A row with no allowed key has a maximum of minus infinity, and the result is NaN. Real models avoid such rows. Some implementations use a large negative number such as -1e9 in place of minus infinity for this reason. Where this goes next Multi-head attention runs this function once for each head. The KV cache runs it for one new query at a time. In the lessons on BERT and GPT, the only difference between the two models is the mask. What changes? What stays the same? Solutions Solution P1 · More than half More than half. In layers 5 to 10, 63–78% of all attention goes to the first token, and one head (layer 7, head 2) puts 96% there. This is the "attention sink": softmax must give each row weights that sum to 1, so a head with nothing useful to read parks the weight on a token every position can see. In a 21-token sentence part of the effect is that there are few tokens to choose from, but the same pattern appears in long texts, which is why streaming LLMs keep the first tokens in their cache. Solution B1 · It learns to copy the answer Without the mask, position can read token , which is exactly the token it is trained to predict. The model learns to copy it from the input, so the training loss drops close to zero, but at generation time the next token does not exist yet and the model has learned nothing useful. Rebuilding GPT-2 without the mask also no longer matches GPT-2's weights: every row except the last changes, because the softmax now spreads over later positions too. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Read the code A decoder's attention returns a zero vector in the first row of every sequence. The mask code is: python def causal_mask(T): return np.triu(np.ones((T, T), dtype=bool), k=0) weights = softmax(scores) weights[mask] = 0 out = weights @ V Two things are wrong. Find both and explain what each one does to the output. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The mask uses a diagonal offset of zero, so every token blocks itself and the first token has no allowed key, which leaves an empty row. The mask is also applied after the softmax, so the rows no longer sum to one. Build the mask with an offset of one, and set the blocked scores to a very negative value before the softmax. Bug one: the diagonal. A causal mask lets position i see positions zero through i , itself included. np.triu with k=0 keeps the diagonal in the blocked set. For the first query every key is blocked, so this code sets the whole first row of weights to zero and the first output row is zero. If you only move the mask before the softmax and fill with negative infinity, that row has nothing to normalize and the division produces NaN. Use k=1 so the diagonal stays visible. Bug two: masking after the softmax. Setting weights to zero after normalization leaves each row summing to less than one, by exactly the mass that the future keys received. The output then shrinks and the model trains against a moving scale. The mask must act on the scores before the softmax, by setting blocked entries to a very negative value, so that their exponentials are zero and the remaining entries renormalize. The corrected code. Copy Why both bugs can pass a shape test. Neither bug changes a shape. Only a check of the weights, or a check that the first output row is not zero, exposes them. The practice task checks the causal weights against a reference and includes the first row. Plausible wrong answers. "Set the blocked weights to zero and renormalize the rows." It works numerically but doubles the work; masking the scores before the softmax does the renormalization for free. "The first token should attend to nothing." The first token must attend to itself; an empty row has no valid distribution. "Use a lower-triangular ones matrix as the mask." A ones matrix marks the allowed entries, so it must be inverted before it is used as a blocked-entry mask. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why a very negative number and not negative infinity? Expected: infinity works in most frameworks, but a fully masked row then produces NaN, while a finite value keeps the arithmetic defined. (level 2) How does the mask interact with the batch dimension? Expected: the mask is tokens by tokens and broadcasts across batches and heads; it is built once per sequence length. (level 3) The same model is used for prefill and then one token at a time. Does the mask change? Expected: at decode time the single query sees every cached key, so no mask is needed for that step; the causal rule was already applied when those keys were produced. (level 3) A padding mask and a causal mask must both apply. How do you combine them? Expected: combine the boolean masks with a logical or before the scores are masked, so a padded key is blocked for every query. Where it is taught. The self-attention lesson asks for the mask as its first exercise, and the attention practice tests the first row of the masked weights. Read the code Here is an attention function from a take-home submission: python def attention(Q, K, V): scores = Q @ K.T / Q.shape[-1] return softmax(scores) @ V The tests for shape pass and the tests for the attention weights fail. Find the bug and explain what the correct factor protects against. Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The scores are divided by the key dimension instead of its square root. Dot products of random vectors grow with the dimension, so without the square root the softmax input is either too large, which saturates it and kills the gradient, or too small, which flattens every row toward uniform. The correct line divides by the square root of the last dimension of the keys. The fix. Copy Why the square root. When the entries of a query and a key have unit variance, their dot product has a variance equal to the dimension. Its typical size is therefore the square root of the dimension. Dividing by that size brings the scores back to unit scale, where the softmax has useful gradients. Dividing by the dimension itself over-corrects and makes every row close to uniform, so the output is almost the mean of the values regardless of the query. Two neighbors of this bug. No scale at all: at a head size of 64 the raw scores reach the tens and the softmax saturates to one hot rows. K.T on a batched tensor: .T reverses every axis, so a shape of batch by tokens by features becomes features by tokens by batch. With distinct sizes the matmul raises a shape error, and when the sizes happen to line up it mixes batches without an error. Swap only the last two axes. How the practice checks it. The practice task compares the weights, not only the output shape. A wrong scale changes every weight, so a reference weight matrix catches it at once. Plausible wrong answers. "Any constant works, the model learns around it." The learned projections can compensate in training, but the practice checks a fixed reference, and in a trained model the wrong factor changes every head. "Divide by the sequence length." The growth comes from the feature dimension, not from the number of tokens. "Scaling is only for numerical overflow." The max shift inside softmax handles overflow; the scale keeps the softmax out of its saturated and flat regions. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) What is the shape of the scores for one sequence? Expected: tokens by tokens, one row per query over all keys. (level 2) Why do shape tests pass with the wrong factor? Expected: scaling does not change shapes; only the values move. (level 2) How do you transpose the keys for a batched input? Expected: swap the last two axes only, for example with swapaxes(-1, -2) . Where it is taught. The self-attention lesson explains the square-root scale factor, and the attention practice checks the weights against a reference. Read the code A candidate writes this softmax for a batch of logits and the tests pass on small inputs but return NaN on a real attention row: python def softmax(x): e = np.exp(x) return e / e.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) What is wrong, how do you fix it, and why does the fix not change the result? Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A large logit overflows the exponential to infinity, and infinity divided by infinity is NaN. Subtract the maximum of each row before the exponential. The softmax of a row is unchanged when the same constant is subtracted from every entry, because the constant cancels between the numerator and the denominator. The failure. Attention scores and language model logits can reach values in the tens or hundreds. The exponential of such a value does not fit in a float, so the row becomes infinite and the division gives NaN. Small test inputs never show it. The fix. Copy After the shift the largest entry of each row is zero, so the largest exponential is one and nothing overflows. Entries far below the maximum underflow to zero, which is the correct limit. Why the result is the same. Softmax of a row divides each exponential by the sum of all exponentials in that row. Subtracting a constant multiplies every exponential by the same factor, and that factor cancels in the ratio. The shift must be per row, over the last axis. A single maximum taken across the entire batch changes nothing about correctness but lets one hot row push every other row into underflow. Two more details that bite. Keep the dimension with keepdims=True so the subtraction broadcasts along the row and not along the batch. Do not subtract in place when the caller still needs the logits. Plausible wrong answers. "Clip the logits to a safe range." Clipping changes the distribution; the shift does not. "Use float64 and the problem goes away." It moves the threshold, and attention scores still overflow in long rows. "Subtract the mean instead of the maximum." The mean does not bound the largest entry, so a row can still overflow. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Where does this same shift appear inside attention? Expected: in the softmax over the scaled scores, which is why the attention lesson writes the shifted version first. (level 2) Why is a global maximum over the whole batch a bug? Expected: one row with a very large logit shifts every other row far below zero, so those rows underflow to all zeros and divide by zero. (level 2) The practice task also asks for the gradient of the mean cross-entropy. What is it? Expected: the softmax minus the one-hot target, divided by the batch size. Where it is taught. The self-attention lesson builds the shifted softmax as its first step, and the softmax and cross-entropy practice checks it with large logits. Debug a failure An attention module between an encoder and a decoder runs without any exception, but the model's accuracy slowly falls behind the reference implementation. When you print the context tensor, its second dimension is the encoder length instead of the decoder length. Walk me through the diagnosis. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A module that runs and still produces the wrong shape is a broadcast bug, and a silent broadcast is the worst attention bug because it degrades accuracy instead of crashing. Write the expected shapes first: scores and weights are batch by decoder length by encoder length, and the context is batch by decoder length by the encoder state width. Then find the matmul whose operands were swapped or not transposed, fix it with one transpose or reshape, and add asserts on the shapes and on the weights summing to one. The shape table. Tensor Shape Encoder states H (T_enc, d_h); d_h is twice the hidden size for a bidirectional encoder Decoder state s (d_s,) Score for one encoder position scalar Weights after the softmax (T_enc,) for one decoder step Context vector (d_h,), the same shape as one encoder state Batched over decoder steps, the weights are (batch, T_dec, T_enc) and the context is (batch, T_dec, d_h) . How the wrong shape appears. The context is weights @ H . If the code built the scores as H @ H.T because the query tensor was replaced by the encoder states, the shapes still multiply and the result has the encoder length where the decoder length belongs. Nothing raises. Downstream layers broadcast or reshape the tensor and the loss keeps falling, just more slowly. The diagnosis steps. Print the shape of every intermediate tensor and compare with the table. Check the score formula. For the additive form the projection vector collapses an attention-dimension vector to a scalar; for the dot form the query and the key must have the same width, and a bidirectional encoder doubles the key width, so the dot form fails unless a matrix W sits between them. Check which decoder state feeds the query. One classic formulation uses the state before the current step and the other uses the state after it. Mixing them gives subtly wrong gradients that are very hard to see. Fix with one transpose, reshape or projection. Refuse any fix that only silences the mismatch by broadcasting. The regression test. Copy The third line catches a softmax taken over the wrong axis, which is the other silent bug in this layer. Plausible wrong answers. "Reshape the output to the expected shape and continue." The values inside are wrong; a reshape only hides the mismatch. "Lower the learning rate; the model is just unstable." The run is not unstable; it is computing the wrong quantity. "Add a mask to fix the shape." A mask changes which positions get weight, not the layout of the tensor. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Which single test catches most attention bugs? Expected: the weights have shape batch by decoder length by encoder length and sum to one along the last axis. (level 2) The score matrix comes out square in the encoder dimension. What happened? Expected: the keys were scored against themselves; the query tensor was replaced by the encoder states. (level 3) Why does the plain dot score fail with a bidirectional encoder? Expected: the encoder state is twice the hidden width, so it no longer matches the decoder state; use the general form with a matrix between them. (level 3) Why is the state convention a gradient problem and not a shape problem? Expected: both states have the same shape, so nothing fails; the gradient flows to the wrong step and the model learns a slightly wrong alignment. Where it is taught. The attention mechanism lesson gives the shape table and the shape-debugging prompt, and the self-attention lesson gives the projections. Explain the mechanism A new teammate has read the word "attention" a hundred times and still cannot say what a query, a key or a value is. Explain the three to them in one minute. Then tell me what changed between the 2014 encoder-decoder version and the version inside a transformer. Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Attention is a soft lookup. Each token produces a query that asks for information, a key that says what the token holds, and a value that the token hands over when it is picked. The query is scored against every key, the scores go through a softmax, and the output is the weighted sum of the values. In the 2014 version the query was the decoder state and the keys and the values were the same encoder states; a transformer takes all three from one sequence through three learned projections. The three projections. For a sequence X of n tokens with d dimensions each: Copy Row i of the score matrix is one token's view of the whole sequence. The softmax turns the row into weights that sum to one. The output for token i is the weighted sum of all value vectors. The database picture. A real database matches a query to one key and returns one value. Attention matches a query to every key with a similarity score and returns a blend of every value. The blend is what lets the model combine information from several positions in one step. What the 2014 version had. The encoder-decoder attention of 2014 used the previous decoder state as the query and scored it against every encoder hidden state. The context vector was the weighted average of those same encoder states. In that design the keys and the values were the same thing. Two score functions were common: an additive score that passes the pair through a tanh and a learned vector, and a multiplicative score that takes a dot product. The three-line fix broke the fixed-size bottleneck of the encoder-decoder. What a transformer changed. Self-attention queries a sequence against itself, and it separates keys from values with different learned projections. Multi-head attention runs several of these in parallel. The weighted sum of values is the same idea. The score function changes: the additive tanh score and the plain dot product give way to a dot product divided by the square root of the key width. Plausible wrong answers. "The key and the value must be the same vector." They were in the classic version, but a transformer learns separate projections for them. "Attention picks the single best matching token." The softmax gives a weight to every position, and the output blends all of the values. "The query comes from the encoder." In encoder-decoder attention the query comes from the decoder and the keys and the values come from the encoder. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) What shape does the output have for one token? Expected: the value dimension, because the output is a weighted sum of value vectors. (level 2) Why give keys and values separate projections? Expected: a token can be matched on one kind of information and return another kind. (level 2) Why does the plain dot-product score need the query and the key to have the same dimension? Expected: a dot product is only defined for vectors of equal length; the general form inserts a matrix W to remove that constraint. (level 3) Name the convention trap between the two classic score functions. Expected: one uses the decoder state before the current step and the other uses the state after it; mixing them produces subtly wrong gradients. Where it is taught. The attention mechanism lesson builds the classic version and the self-attention lesson builds the projections. Explain the mechanism In the attention formula the raw scores go through a division before the softmax. A new engineer calls the division a convention and removes it to save one multiply. What happens to training, and how would you show the effect in ten minutes? Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A dot product of two vectors grows with their length, so without the division the scores grow with the key dimension. Large scores push the softmax into a region where one key takes almost all of the weight and the gradient to every other key is close to zero, so learning stalls. The division by sqrt(d_k) keeps the variance of the scores about constant for any head size. Show it with random Q and K at d_k = 64 : print the score range and the softmax weights with and without the division. The size of a score. A score is the sum of d_k products. When the components of Q and K have unit variance, the sum has variance d_k , so a typical score is about sqrt(d_k) in size. At d_k = 64 the raw scores sit in the range of tens. A softmax over scores in the tens puts almost all of its mass on the largest entry. Why the model stops learning. The gradient of the softmax with respect to a score is small when one weight is near one and the others are near zero. The attention layer then behaves like a fixed lookup. The loss plateaus, and nothing fails loudly. The lesson calls this regime one where "one entry has almost all the mass and the others are vanishingly small". The fix and its range. Divide the scores by sqrt(d_k) before the softmax: Copy In multi-head attention the dimension under the root is the head width, d_head = d_model / n_heads , not the model width. Production models land d_head at 64 or 128. The scaling keeps the score variance constant at any width. The lesson's rule of thumb keeps heads at 32 or wider, because a narrower head sees too few dimensions, and below 256, because wider heads lose the benefit of many small specialists. The ten-minute demonstration. Draw Q and K from a standard normal with d_k = 64 . Print (Q @ K.T).max() with and without the division. Print the largest softmax weight in one row for both cases. Without the division it sits near one. Plausible wrong answers. "The division keeps the attention weights summing to one." The softmax normalizes any scores to sum to one; the division controls their spread, not their sum. "A larger learning rate recovers the lost gradient." When the softmax is saturated the gradient carries almost no information about the other keys, and a larger step does not create information. "Scale the values instead of the scores." The values are summed after the weights are fixed, so their scale does not touch the softmax. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) What is the shape of the score matrix for a sequence of n tokens? Expected: (n, n), one row per query and one column per key. (level 2) Why does the missing division cause a silent failure instead of an exception? Expected: the softmax saturates, the gradients become tiny, and the loss plateaus with no error. (level 2) Does the division change what the layer can represent? Expected: no, the projections can absorb a constant; it changes the scale of the scores at initialization, which is where training happens or stalls. (level 3) With eight heads of width 64 in a model of width 512, which number goes under the root? Expected: 64, the head width, because each head computes its own softmax over its own scores. Where it is taught. The self-attention lesson explains the saturation, the multi-head lesson gives the head widths, and the capstone attention block applies the scaling inside the batched block. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Head "A single attention circuit" One Q/K/V projection of dimension $d_{\text{head}} = d_{\text{model}} / n_{\text{heads}}$ with its own attention matrix. d_head "Head dimension" Per-head hidden width; almost always 64 or 128 in production. Split / combine "Reshape tricks" (N, d_model) ↔ (n_heads, N, d_head) reshape+transpose around attention. Induction head "The circuit behind in-context learning" A pair of heads that detect previous occurrences and copy what followed them. The problem In plain words first One attention head produces one set of weights per word, so it can follow one kind of relationship at a time: the previous word, or the subject of the verb, or an earlier mention of the same name. Multi-head attention runs several smaller heads side by side, each with its own query, key and value projections over a slice of the embedding, then joins their outputs and mixes them with one more matrix. It costs no more arithmetic than one big head. The variants that matter in practice change only the keys and values: grouped-query attention lets several query heads share one key-value head, so the memory a chatbot keeps per token (the KV cache) shrinks several times. This lesson builds the split and merge, checks PyTorch's grouped-query call, reads the real head counts and cache sizes from six production models' configuration files, and finds the "induction heads" inside GPT-2 that let it continue a pattern it has just seen, then switches them off. Nothing is trained. A single self-attention head computes one attention matrix. That matrix captures one kind of relationship — usually the one that minimizes loss on whatever the training signal is. If your data has subject-verb agreement, co-reference, long-range discourse, and syntactic chunking all tangled together, a single head smears them into a single soft-max distribution and loses half the signal. The fix from the 2017 Vaswani paper: run several attention functions in parallel, each with its own Q, K, V projections, and concatenate the outputs. Each head operates in a smaller subspace of dimension ​ / n heads ​ . Total parameters stay the same. Expressive power goes up. Multi-head attention is the default every transformer in 2026 ships with. The only argument is about how many heads and whether keys and values share projections (Grouped-Query Attention, Multi-Query Attention, Multi-head Latent Attention). The idea Split. Take X of shape (N, d_model) . Project to Q, K, V each of shape (N, d_model) . Reshape to (N, n_heads, d_head) where ​ = d model ​ / n heads ​ . Transpose to (n_heads, N, d_head) . Attend in parallel. Run scaled dot-product attention inside each head. Each head produces (N, d_head) . The heads operate on different subspaces of the embedding and never talk during the attention computation itself. Concatenate and project. Stack heads back to (N, d_model) and multiply by a learned output matrix W_o of shape (d_model, d_model) . W_o is where heads get to mix. Why it works. Each head can specialize without competing with the others for representational budget. Probing studies from 2019–2024 show distinct head roles: positional heads, head that attends to the previous token, copy heads, named-entity heads, induction heads (which underlie in-context learning). Reference solution and notes Copy Why GQA saves memory At inference, the model keeps the keys and values of every earlier token in a cache. The size of the cache is proportional to the number of key and value heads. GQA keeps heads in place of , so the cache is times smaller. Llama 3 70B uses 64 query heads and 8 groups, so its cache is 8 times smaller than the cache of the same model with full multi-head attention. Why not always one group Multi-query attention ( ) gives the smallest cache. The paper shows that it also loses quality and can make training less stable. A small number of groups gives most of the speed of multi-query attention and a quality near that of multi-head attention. Uptraining The paper does not train GQA models from the start. It takes a multi-head checkpoint, mean-pools the key and value heads of each group, and trains for about 5 percent of the original steps. The paper compares mean pooling with other methods, such as the first head of each group, and mean pooling works best. Estimate it You have a trained model with 64 query heads and 64 key and value heads, and you want to serve it with 8 key and value heads to shrink the cache. Write the function that pools the key projection of the checkpoint into groups, say by what factor the cache memory for keys and values falls, and explain why the pooled model needs more training before it is usable. Level 4 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Group g of the new projection is the mean of the consecutive heads g r to g r + r - 1 , where r is the number of query heads per group, taken over the columns of the projection matrix. The cache holds keys and values for 8 heads instead of 64, so that memory falls by a factor of eight. The mean of several heads is not a head the model was trained with, so quality drops until a short continued training run adapts the query heads to their shared group. The pooling. Copy The reshape puts the groups first and the heads inside a group next, because the heads of one group are consecutive blocks of columns. Reshaping as (D, r, G, d_head) pools heads that are G apart, which gives a correct shape with the wrong groups. The mean, not the sum, keeps the scale of the projected keys close to the original, so the attention scores stay in range. The memory factor. The cache stores one key and one value vector per layer, per head, per token. The number of query heads does not enter. Going from 64 to 8 key and value heads divides the stored bytes per token by eight, which is the example the multi-head lesson gives for a large open model. Weights fall much less, because the query and output projections are unchanged and only the key and value projections shrink. Why it needs training. The query heads were trained against their own key heads. After pooling, eight query heads read one averaged key head that none of them saw in training. The lesson's lineage describes converting multi-head checkpoints to grouped-query checkpoints as a recipe with a continued training step; the pooling gives a starting point close to the original, and the uptraining recovers most of the quality. Serving the pooled weights directly works, but the eval must be rerun before shipping. What does not change. The head size, the query projection, the output projection and the attention function itself are the same. Only the key and value projections and the repeat inside attention change, so the rest of the loader and the block are untouched. Plausible wrong answers. "Pooling is lossless since the mean preserves the average key." The individual heads are lost; the queries were trained against them, so quality drops until the model is adapted. "The cache shrinks by the ratio of query heads to total heads." Only key and value heads live in the cache; the factor is the old count of key and value heads over the new count. "Sum the heads so no information is lost." The sum scales the keys by the group size and pushes the scores out of the range the softmax was trained for. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why pool consecutive heads and not every eighth head? Expected: the attention reads group h floor-divided by r for query head h , so the pooled heads must be the ones that will share a group. (level 4) How does the cache saving change when the model is served with a longer context? Expected: it does not change as a factor; the saving is per token, so the absolute bytes saved grow with the number of tokens held. (level 4) The multi-head latent variant compresses keys and values into a low-rank latent. What does it trade for the extra saving? Expected: compute, because the latent must be projected back to full keys and values at attention time. Where it is taught. The multi-head attention lesson gives the grouped-query lineage and the cache factor, and the grouped-query practice implements the pooling of a multi-head checkpoint. Read the code A GQA implementation repeats the key and value heads up to the query head count with this line, where kv has shape batch, groups, tokens, head size: python kv_full = np.tile(kv, (1, n_heads // n_kv_heads, 1, 1)) The shapes match and the outputs are wrong for every configuration with more than one group. Explain which query head ends up with which group, and write the correct expansion. Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Tiling repeats the whole block of groups, so query head h reads group h modulo the number of groups. The convention is that consecutive query heads share a group: head h reads group h floor-divided by the repeat factor. Repeat each group in place along the head axis instead of tiling the block. The two layouts. With four query heads and two groups the repeat factor is two. The correct expansion gives the sequence of groups 0, 0, 1, 1 : the first two query heads share group zero and the next two share group one. Tiling gives 0, 1, 0, 1 , so heads one and two swap partners. Every head still has a key and value tensor of the right shape, which is why no shape check fails, but half the heads attend with the wrong keys. The fix. Copy np.repeat along the group axis copies each group r times next to itself, which produces the floor-division mapping. The divisibility check belongs here, because a non-integer repeat factor silently truncates and drops heads. Why the mapping is a convention and not a choice. The projection weights of a trained checkpoint were learned under one mapping. The multi-head lesson describes the lineage: multi-head attention with one group per head, multi-query attention with a single shared group, and the grouped form in between with the first r heads on group zero. A model converted from multi-head weights by pooling consecutive heads only works if attention reads the groups in the same consecutive order. Why it exists. Only G key and value heads live in the cache instead of H , so the cache shrinks by the factor H / G while quality stays close to standard multi-head attention. The lesson's example is a large open model that pairs 64 query heads against only 8 shared groups. Plausible wrong answers. "Tile and repeat give the same result when the shapes match." They give different head-to-group assignments; only one matches the trained weights. "Average the groups and use one key tensor for all heads." That turns the model into multi-query attention with weights it was not trained for. "The mapping does not matter because attention is permutation invariant." Attention is invariant over keys within a head, not over which key head a query head reads. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) With one group, what does the function compute? Expected: multi-query attention; every query head shares the single key and value head. (level 3) Where does the scale factor come from after the repeat? Expected: the square root of the head size, the same as in multi-head attention; dividing by the square root of the full width is a separate common bug. (level 4) How does a framework avoid materializing the repeated copies? Expected: it broadcasts the group axis inside the attention kernel, or the attention call accepts fewer key and value heads directly, so memory holds only the groups. Where it is taught.
