Debug a failure A multi-head attention forward passes the split and merge tests but fails the end-to-end test against a reference, and a trained checkpoint loaded into it generates nonsense: python def multi_head_attention(x, w_q, w_k, w_v, w_o, n_heads): Q, K, V = split_heads(x @ w_q, n_heads), split_heads(x @ w_k, n_heads), split_heads(x @ w_v, n_heads) d_head = Q.shape[-1] scores = Q @ K.swapaxes(-1, -2) / np.sqrt(d_head) weights = softmax(scores, axis=-2) return merge_heads(weights @ V), weights Find both defects and explain what each one does to the model. Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The softmax normalizes over the query axis instead of the key axis, so each column sums to one and a query's weights no longer form a distribution over the keys. The output projection is also missing: the merged heads are returned without the multiplication by w_o , which is the only place where heads exchange information. Normalize over the last axis and multiply the merged result by the output matrix. Defect one: the softmax axis. Scores have shape batch, heads, queries, keys. Each query row must become a distribution over the keys, so the softmax runs over the last axis. Over the second-to-last axis each key column sums to one across queries instead, and the weighted sum of values no longer means "what this token attends to". Defect two: the output projection. Each head computes attention in its own subspace and the heads never interact during the attention computation itself. The concatenation followed by the output matrix is where the heads mix. Without it, the model's output is a stack of independent per-head results, the next layer sees a different function than the one the weights were trained for, and a loaded checkpoint produces noise. The corrected function. Copy Why the reshape tests passed. Both defects live after the split and before the merge, or after the merge. The reshape helpers are correct, and the shapes of the final output match the reference because w_o is square. Only a value comparison against a reference, or a real checkpoint, exposes them. Why the scale is still right. The division uses the head size, not the full width. That part of the submission is correct; dividing by the square root of the full width is a third common error that the practice also tests. Plausible wrong answers. "The softmax axis does not matter because the scores are symmetric." Scores are query by key and not symmetric; the two normalizations differ for every real input. "Skip the output projection to save parameters; the merge already recombines the heads." The merge only concatenates; without the projection the heads never interact. "Use the identity for the output projection when a checkpoint lacks one." A trained checkpoint always has one; a missing tensor means the name map is wrong. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why does the output projection have shape full width by full width? Expected: it maps the concatenation of all heads, which has the full width, back to the model width, and it is the one matrix that reads from every head. (level 3) Which test would you add to catch the missing projection early? Expected: a case where w_o is not the identity, so the projected and unprojected outputs differ. (level 4) A probing study finds one head attends to the previous token. Where in this code does that head's result reach the residual stream? Expected: only through its block of columns in the concatenation and the rows of w_o that read it; w_o decides how much of that head the next layer sees. Where it is taught. The multi-head attention lesson explains that heads only mix through the output projection, and the split and merge practice checks the softmax axis and the projection. Read the code A submission splits a tensor of shape batch, tokens, features into heads with one call: python def split_heads(x, n_heads): B, T, D = x.shape return x.reshape(B, n_heads, T, D // n_heads) The shape test passes and every attention test fails. Explain what the function actually did to the data and write the correct version. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The reshape alone reinterprets memory. It keeps the bytes in order and relabels them, so the head axis cuts across tokens and features instead of slicing the feature axis. The correct split reshapes to batch, tokens, heads, head size and then transposes the token and head axes, so that head h holds a contiguous block of d_head neighbor columns for every token. What the bug does. Row-major memory lists features of token zero, then features of token one, and so on. Reshaping straight to batch, heads, tokens, head size slices that flat list into equal pieces. The first "head" then holds the first T times d_head numbers, which are the complete feature vectors of the first few tokens, not a slice of every token. Shapes agree. Numbers are scrambled. The fix. Copy Reshape to batch, tokens, heads, head size first, which only splits the last axis. Then transpose so the head axis comes before the token axis. The merge is the same two operations in reverse. One reshape and one transpose, no loop; that is also what the framework version does under the hood. The strided variant of the bug. A second wrong version gives head h the columns h , h + H , h + 2H and so on. That slices the feature axis, so the per-head attention runs, but it does not match the convention that a head owns one contiguous block of columns, and a checkpoint trained with the standard layout no longer loads into it. How to test it. merge_heads(split_heads(x, H)) must return x exactly, and split_heads(x, H)[b, h, t, j] must equal x[b, t, h * d_head + j] . The second check is the one that fails for both wrong versions. Plausible wrong answers. "Reshape is the same as transpose for equal sizes." Reshape relabels memory in place; transpose reorders it. "Any split works as long as merge undoes it." The attention tests and any loaded checkpoint depend on each head owning one block of neighbor columns. "Loop over heads and slice columns." It is correct but slow; the reshape and transpose give the same result in two operations. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does the round-trip test catch the plain reshape bug? Expected: merge_heads transposes the head and token axes before it reshapes, so it does not undo a plain reshape and the features come back in a different order; only a merge written as a plain reshape would hide the bug. (level 2) What does the scale factor become after the split? Expected: the square root of the head size, not of the full feature dimension. (level 3) After the split, how does attention run for all heads at once? Expected: as one batched matmul over the leading batch and head axes, so adding heads costs no extra kernel launches. Where it is taught. The multi-head attention lesson gives the split and combine pair as a reshape followed by a transpose, and the split and merge practice checks each element of the split. Defend a design Design the attention stack of a new 70B-class decoder that must serve 128K-token contexts on a single 80 GB accelerator at batch size one. Cover the head layout, the positional scheme, the kernel, and the memory arithmetic that ties them together. Level 4 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Start from the memory, because it decides the rest. With 8 key-value heads, 80 layers and a head size of 128 in a 16-bit type, the stored keys and values cost 4096 bytes per token per layer, about 10 GiB at 32K and 40 GiB at 128K before a single weight is loaded. So the head layout is grouped-query or latent attention, the stored type is reduced to FP8 to halve those bytes, the positional scheme is rotation with base scaling so that the model reaches 128K without a position table, and the kernel is a tiled one so that the N by N scores never touch main memory. Then count again: at 16 bits the weights of a 70B-class model alone are larger than the 80 GB card, so the weights also need a 4-bit type before the cache and the activations can fit beside them. Head layout. Plain multi-head attention with 64 key-value heads at this scale would hold about 8 times more, about 80 GiB at 32K, which is the whole card. Grouped-query with 8 key-value heads is the production default and keeps nearly full quality. If the memory still does not close, latent attention compresses the keys and values to a low-rank vector and pays FLOPs at each step to decompress. The query heads stay at 64 with a head size of 128 in either case. The memory table. Copy Halve the bytes per value with an FP8 cache and the 128K figure halves. Then add the weights. At 16 bits a 70B-class model needs two bytes per parameter, which is more than the whole 80 GB card before any cache is stored. At 8 bits the weights still fill most of the card. Only a 4-bit weight type leaves room for the FP8 cache at 128K and for the activations. Batch size one is the stated requirement; every additional concurrent request adds another cache. Positional scheme. Rotation of the queries and keys, with a base scaled for the target length through NTK-aware scaling or YaRN. It adds no parameters, encodes relative distance, and the lesson's reference family reached 128K from 8K this way. A learned table would need 128K rows and would stop there. Linear-bias attention is a valid training-time alternative with strong extrapolation, but rotation gives a cleaner knob and matches the ecosystem. Kernel. Attention is memory-bound from about 2K tokens, so a tiled kernel is not optional at 128K. Use the current tiled implementation for the hardware, with FP8 where the generation supports it, and keep the training kernel on the version that has a backward pass. What to measure before committing. Perplexity at the target length and at the original short length after the long-context fine-tune. Peak memory at 128K with the quantized weights, the cache and the activations on the card, and the quality loss from the 4-bit weights. Time per token at 128K against 8K, to confirm the kernel and the cache behave linearly. Plausible wrong answers. "Use full multi-head attention for quality; memory is cheap." At 128K the full cache alone exceeds the card. "The sinusoid handles any length, so the position scheme is solved." The formula extends but the model never saw those phases; rotation with base scaling is what reached 128K in practice. "Skip the tiled kernel on a quality model because it changes the output." It is exact up to 16-bit reordering and it is what makes long context affordable. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why not pick linear-bias attention for its extrapolation? Expected: it is a fair choice for a new model, but rotation has the long-context tooling and a base to scale, and neither can be swapped after training. (level 4) The product later asks for batch size 8 at 128K. What changes? Expected: the cache multiplies by 8, so latent attention, a smaller stored type, a shorter maximum length or more cards; the weights do not change. (level 4) Grouped-query from scratch or convert a multi-head checkpoint? Expected: from scratch for a new model; conversion with a fine-tune is for existing checkpoints and needs a quality check. (level 4) Where does Flash Attention stop helping? Expected: it removes the N by N traffic; it does not shrink the cache, which still grows linearly with the context, so the cache math dominates at 128K. Where it is taught. The multi-head attention lesson gives the head variants, the positional encoding lesson gives the scaling tricks, and the KV cache and Flash Attention lesson does the memory arithmetic. Explain the mechanism A paper draft shows attention heatmaps as proof that the model "reasons over the right tokens". You are the reviewer. What do you say about the heatmaps, and what would convince you that a given head does something specific? Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Attention weights are a distribution over positions, and on their own they are not an explanation: for some tasks they can be permuted or replaced by arbitrary alternatives without changing the prediction, so a heatmap shows where mass went, not that it mattered. Ask for an ablation or a counterfactual, zero or shuffle the head and show that the prediction moves. The head roles that have survived probing are specific and testable: heads that attend to the previous token, copy heads, and induction heads that find an earlier occurrence of the current token and copy what followed it. The caveat from the literature. A 2019 study showed that on some tasks the attention distribution can be permuted, or swapped for an adversarial alternative, while the output stays the same. The lesson's rule follows: never report attention weights as evidence of reasoning without an ablation or a counterfactual check. Reviewers like heatmaps because they are easy to read; that is a reason to be careful, not a reason to accept them. What a head can show you. The inspection hook in the lesson's block returns the per-head weights of shape (B, H, T, T) . In a trained model the patterns differ by head: some attend to the token just before, some to the start of the sequence, some spread almost uniformly. Those are descriptions. Turning a description into a claim takes an intervention. The evidence that convinces. Ablation. Zero the head's output or replace its weights with a uniform row and measure the change in loss or in the specific prediction. A head that matters moves the number. Counterfactual input. Change the token the heatmap points at and show that the output changes in the direction the story predicts. A behavioral test for the claimed role. For an induction head, feed a random token sequence repeated twice and show that the head attends from each token to the token that followed its first occurrence, and that ablating the head removes the copying. Replication across seeds and prompts. One heatmap on one example is an anecdote. What to write in the review. Ask the authors to keep the heatmaps as illustration and to add the intervention results as the evidence. If the ablation does not move the prediction, the heatmap was decoration. Plausible wrong answers. "A high weight means the token caused the output." Weight shows where the lookup went; causation needs an intervention. "Average the heads to get the model's attention." Heads do different things; the average hides the roles and still is not evidence. "If the heatmap matches human intuition, the model reasons like a human." Agreement with intuition is not a test; the permutation result shows intuitive maps can be irrelevant to the output. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) A head attends almost uniformly across positions. What does that tell you? Expected: little on its own; it may carry an average or nothing, and only an ablation says which. (level 3) Describe a test for an induction head in one sentence. Expected: repeat a random token sequence and check that the head attends from each token to the token after its earlier occurrence, with ablation removing the copy behavior. (level 4) Why can the weights be permuted without changing the output? Expected: the values at the attended positions may carry near-identical information, other heads may be redundant, and later layers can compensate. (level 4) What replaces the heatmap as the headline figure? Expected: the change in loss or in the target probability under ablation and counterfactual edits, with a band across seeds. Where it is taught. The attention mechanism lesson states the explanation trap, the multi-head lesson lists the probed head roles, and the attention capstone exposes the weights for inspection. Weigh a trade-off You are choosing the attention variant for a new 70B-class decoder: full multi-head, multi-query, grouped-query, or MLA with its compressed latent. What does each one do to the memory that decoding holds per token, and what do you give up with each? Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. All four keep the same number of query heads; they differ in how many key and value heads exist, and only the keys and values are stored during decoding. Multi-query shares one key-value head across every query head, the smallest cache and some quality loss. Grouped-query uses a group of key-value heads, cuts the cache by n_heads / n_kv_heads and keeps nearly full quality, which is why it is the default. Latent attention compresses keys and values to a low-rank vector and decompresses at attention time, so it saves even more memory and pays extra FLOPs. The lineage. Variant Query heads Key-value heads Cache cost Multi-head N N full Multi-query N 1 smallest, quality loss Grouped-query N G, for example N / 8 shrinks by N / G Multi-head latent N compressed to a low-rank latent smaller still, more compute What the cache holds. Per layer and per token, the stored bytes are 2 * n_kv_heads * d_head * dtype_size , where the 2 counts the key and the value. The query of a past token is never needed again, so it is not stored. A 70B-class model with 80 layers, a head size of 128 and 8 key-value heads in a 16-bit type holds 4096 bytes per token per layer, about 10 GiB for a 32K context and 40 GiB at 128K. The same model with 64 key-value heads would hold 8 times more, about 80 GiB at 32K. That is the whole memory of a large accelerator spent on one request. The quality side. Grouped-query keeps the query heads, so each head still asks its own question; it only shares the answers it can look up. The published work converts trained multi-head checkpoints to grouped-query with a fine-tune and reports nearly full quality. Multi-query shares a single answer set across all heads and loses more. Latent attention trades compute for memory: the latent must be projected back to keys and values on every step. Grouped-query in code. Only the key and value projections change. They produce n_kv_heads heads, and each is repeated to match the query heads: Copy At inference only the n_kv_heads copies live in the cache, not the repeated ones. The pick. For a 70B decoder with long contexts to serve, grouped-query with a small group is the safe default. Latent attention is the choice when memory is the binding constraint and you accept the compute cost and the engineering. Plausible wrong answers. "Grouped-query reduces the compute of attention." The scores are still computed for every query head; the saving is in the stored keys and values. "Multi-query is free." It shares one answer set across all heads and the lesson records a quality loss. "The cache size follows the parameter count." It follows the key-value heads, the layers, the head size and the data type. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Which numbers set the stored bytes per token? Expected: layers, key-value heads, head size and bytes per value, times 2 for the key and the value; the parameter count does not enter. (level 3) Why does latent attention cost more compute per step? Expected: the stored latent has to be projected back to full keys and values at every decode step before the scores are computed. (level 3) Can you move an existing multi-head checkpoint to grouped-query? Expected: yes, the grouped-query paper converts trained checkpoints and fine-tunes; measure quality on your own eval before you ship. (level 4) The product wants 128K contexts at batch size one on a 40 GB card. Which variant and what else? Expected: grouped-query alone already fills the card at 128K, so latent attention or a smaller key-value type, and the weights still need their own memory. Where it is taught. The multi-head attention lesson gives the variants and the grouped-query code, and the KV cache lesson does the memory arithmetic. Explain the mechanism You change an attention layer from one head to eight heads and keep the model width fixed. What happens to the parameter count, to the compute, and to what the layer can represent? And why do practitioners refuse to make heads narrower than about 32? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The parameters do not change: the four projections are still d_model by d_model , and the heads are only a reshape of the same matrices into slices of width d_model / n_heads . The compute stays about the same because the per-head attention runs as one batched matmul over the head axis. Each head can specialize on its own relation, and the output projection is where the heads mix. The lesson's rule of thumb keeps a head at a width of 32 or more, because a narrower head sees too few dimensions, and above 256 you lose the benefit of many small specialists, while the sqrt scaling itself keeps the score variance constant at any width. Split, attend, combine. Copy Project X to Q, K and V, split each into heads, run scaled dot-product attention per head, stack the heads back and multiply by the output matrix W_o . The GPU sees the per-head scores as a single batched matmul of shape (heads, N, d_head) times (heads, d_head, N) . Adding heads adds batch entries, not weights. Why the output projection matters. The heads never talk during the attention step itself; they work on different subspaces. W_o , of shape (d_model, d_model) , is where their outputs mix. Without it the heads could only recombine through later layers and the block would be artificially constrained. What heads learn. Probing work from 2019 to 2024 found distinct roles: heads that attend to the previous token, copy heads, heads that track named entities, and induction heads, the pairs that detect an earlier occurrence of the current token and copy what followed it, which underlie in-context learning. One head would have to smear all of these into one softmax. Picking the head width. Model size d_model n_heads d_head Small (about 125M) 768 12 64 Base (about 350M) 1024 16 64 Large (about 1B) 2048 16 128 Frontier (about 70B) 8192 64 128 The head width lands at 64 or 128 almost every time. It is the unit of how much one head can see. The production implementation. One linear layer maps D to 3D and is sliced into Q, K and V. Three separate layers compute the same thing, because three matmuls by (D, D) weights equal one matmul by a stacked (3D, D) weight, but the fused layer launches one kernel instead of three. Plausible wrong answers. "More heads mean more parameters." The projections keep their size; the heads are a reshape of the same matrices. "Heads exchange information while they attend." They work on separate subspaces; mixing happens only in the output projection and in later layers. "Use as many heads as the width allows." Heads narrower than the lesson's rule of thumb of 32 see too little; the common widths are 64 and 128. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why is the fused QKV projection faster if the math is identical? Expected: one kernel launch and one matmul instead of three; the stacked weight gives the same result. (level 3) What goes wrong if you remove the output projection? Expected: the heads can only mix through later layers, so the block loses expressive power even though the shapes still work. (level 3) What is an induction head? Expected: a pair of heads that finds a previous occurrence of the current token and copies the token that followed it; the circuit behind in-context learning. (level 4) Grouped-query attention keeps the query heads and shrinks something else. What and why? Expected: the key and value heads, because only they live in the decode-time cache; fewer of them cut cache memory while the query heads keep quality. Where it is taught. The multi-head attention lesson builds the split and the width table, and the attention capstone fuses the projection and explains the output matrix. Read the code Two versions of a head split landed in review. X has shape (n, d) with n tokens and d features. python def split_a(X, n_heads): n, d = X.shape d_head = d // n_heads return X.reshape(n, n_heads, d_head).transpose(1, 0, 2) def split_b(X, n_heads): n, d = X.shape d_head = d // n_heads return X.reshape(n_heads, n, d_head) Both return a tensor of shape (n_heads, n, d_head) and both run without error. Which one is right, what does the other one do to the data, and what test would have caught it? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The first version is the right one: split_a groups the d features of each token into n_heads slices of width d_head and then moves the head axis to the front. split_b reads the same memory in the wrong order: it cuts the flat buffer into n_heads equal chunks and calls each chunk a head, so one head now holds runs of consecutive tokens, a chunk can end inside a token, and the columns no longer line up with the projection that produced them. The test is the round trip: combining the split must return X exactly, and head h must equal the column slice X[:, h * d_head:(h + 1) * d_head] . What the shapes mean. After the projection, each token's d features are the concatenation of n_heads groups of d_head features. A head is a column slice across every token. The reshape (n, n_heads, d_head) keeps each token's row intact and only regroups its columns; the transpose then puts the head axis first so that the per-head attention becomes a batched operation over heads. Why the wrong version still runs. Both tensors have n * d elements, so NumPy and PyTorch are happy to reinterpret the memory. A reshape of a contiguous array does not move data; it only changes how the flat buffer is indexed. split_b therefore cuts the buffer into n_heads equal chunks. When n is divisible by n_heads , head zero holds the first n / n_heads tokens with all of their features; otherwise a chunk ends inside a token. The scores inside that head compare the wrong vectors, and the model trains to something, which is why this bug can survive for weeks. The combine must be the exact inverse. Copy Transpose back first, then reshape. Reshaping directly from (h, n, d_head) to (n, h * d_head) makes the same mistake in reverse, and the output projection sees scrambled features. The production shape contract. With a batch dimension the intermediate tensors are (B, H, T, d_head) . The head dimension sits next to the batch so that the accelerator treats the per-head attention as B * H independent problems, and d_head stays last so that Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1) contracts it. The constraint is D % H == 0 . Tests that catch it. combine_heads(split_heads(X)) == X . split_heads(X)[h] == X[:, h * d_head:(h + 1) * d_head] for every head. Single-head attention on the slice equals the head's output from the batched path. Plausible wrong answers. "Reshape and transpose are interchangeable when the shapes match." A reshape reinterprets memory and a transpose moves axes; the order decides which elements land together. "If it runs and the loss falls, it is correct." The loss falls for the wrong layout too; only the round-trip and slice tests prove the layout. "Each head needs its own weight matrix, so the split is irrelevant." The heads are slices of one projection; the split is what defines them. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does a reshape never raise here? Expected: it only reinterprets a buffer with the same number of elements; the data is not checked for meaning. (level 2) Why must d_head stay the last axis? Expected: the score matmul contracts the last axis of Q with the second-to-last of the transposed K. (level 3) How does grouped-query attention reuse this code? Expected: split K and V into n_kv_heads heads and repeat each along the head axis n_heads // n_kv_heads times to match Q. (level 3) A model trained with the wrong split reaches a decent loss. Why does that not clear the bug? Expected: the projections learned to work with the scrambled layout, but the heads no longer correspond to subspaces of the input and any pretrained weights or exported checkpoints will be wrong. Where it is taught. The multi-head attention lesson gives the split and combine pair, and the attention capstone sets the batched shape contract. Sources and further reading Vaswani et al. (2017). GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints — how to convert MHA to GQA after training. DeepSeek-AI (2024). DeepSeek-V2 Technical Report — MLA and why it beats MHA/GQA on cache memory. Olsson et al. (2022). In-context Learning and Induction Heads — mechanistic look at what heads actually do. Time : about 45 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Attention is permutation-invariant. "The cat sat on the mat" and "mat the on sat cat the" produce the same output without positional signal. Three algorithms fix it — each with a different bet on what "position" means. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Positional encoding "Tells attention about order" Any signal added to embeddings or attention that encodes position. Sinusoidal "The original one" sin/cos at geometric frequencies added to embeddings; doesn't extrapolate. RoPE "Rotary embeddings" Rotate Q, K by position-dependent angle; dot product encodes relative distance. ALiBi "Linear bias trick" Add $-m \cdot \lvert i-j \rvert$ to attention scores; no embedding needed, great extrapolation. base "RoPE's knob" The frequency scaler in RoPE; increase to extend context at inference. NTK-aware "A RoPE scaling trick" Rescale base so high-frequency dims aren't squeezed when context expands. YaRN "The fancy one" Per-dimension interpolation+extrapolation that preserves attention entropy. Extrapolation "Works beyond trained length" Can the position scheme serve correct output past max_len seen in training? The problem In plain words first Attention compares every word with every other word, but nothing in that comparison says which word came first, so "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" look alike to it. Position has to be added. The original transformer added a fixed pattern of sine waves to each word's vector. Almost every current open model instead uses RoPE: it turns each query and key by an angle that grows with the word's position, so that when two of them are compared, only the distance between them matters. A third method, ALiBi, simply subtracts a penalty that grows with distance. The choice decides how a model copes with texts longer than any it was trained on. This lesson shows that attention without positions really is order-blind, reads the real RoPE settings of Llama, Qwen, gpt-oss and DeepSeek from their configuration files, and runs a small RoPE model on text twice as long as its training length, with and without the stretching methods production models use. Nothing is trained. Scaled dot-product attention is order-blind. The attention matrix softmax(Q K^T / √d) V is computed from pairwise similarities. Shuffle the rows of X , get the rows of the output shuffled the same way. Nothing inside attention cares about position. That is not a bug in a bag-of-words model. For language, code, audio, video — anything where order carries meaning — it is fatal. The fix is to inject position into the embeddings somehow. Three eras of answers: Absolute sinusoidal (Vaswani 2017). Add sin/cos of position to the embedding. Simple, learnable-free, extrapolates poorly beyond trained lengths. RoPE — Rotary Position Embeddings (Su 2021). Rotate Q and K vectors by an angle proportional to position. Encodes relative position directly in the dot product. Dominant in 2026. ALiBi — Attention with Linear Biases (Press 2022). Skip embeddings entirely; add a per-head linear penalty to attention scores based on distance. Excellent length extrapolation. As of 2026, essentially every frontier open model uses RoPE: Llama 2/3/4, Qwen 2/3, Mistral, Mixtral, DeepSeek-V3, Kimi. A handful of long-context models use ALiBi or its modern variants. Absolute sinusoidal is historical. See it drawn Order-blindness, measured A two-head attention layer with no positional information, given six random token vectors and the same vectors shuffled. That is why decoder-only models trained with no positional encoding at all ("NoPE") still learn some sense of order; encoders get none without one. What property is lost, and what would a trained model see? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) RoPE is the production default. Llama 3, Qwen2.5 and Qwen3, Mistral, Gemma 3, DeepSeek-V3, Kimi K2 and gpt-oss all use it, usually with a large base (500,000 for Llama 3, 1,000,000 for Qwen2.5) and a frequency-scaling scheme for 128K-plus contexts. Scaling schemes in configs. YaRN (DeepSeek-V3, gpt-oss, Qwen's long-context releases) and Llama's "llama3" scaling are set in config.json and applied by transformers , vLLM and llama.cpp; serving a longer context than the release supports usually means setting rope_scaling explicitly. Mixed layers. Some models leave RoPE out of a few layers (Llama 4's interleaved "NoPE" layers) or use different bases for local and global layers (Gemma 3), to help long-context recall. Sources: RoFormer , YaRN , transformers RoPE utilities , Gemma 3 report , Llama 4 announcement , vLLM supported models . Recap What to keep from this lesson Attention alone is order-blind (a causal mask leaks some order). RoPE rotates queries and keys so scores depend only on distance; its pairs turn at speeds from a few tokens to millions. Past the training length, unseen angles break the model; interpolation, NTK, YaRN and llama3 scaling stretch the slow pairs, and long-context releases also continue training. The position scheme is part of the config: read it before serving a model. It turns each pair of coordinates by an angle that grows with the position. Then the attention score of a query and a key depends only on the distance between their positions. Most open language models use RoPE. The copy keeps the last coordinate when d is odd. Reference solution and notes Copy Why the score depends on the gap only Each pair is a point in a plane. RoPE turns the query pair by ​ and the key pair by ​ . The dot product of two points in a plane depends on their lengths and on the angle between them. The angle between the turned points changes by ​ . So the score sees only the gap . The model gets relative positions, but each token needs only its own absolute position. Why the norm stays the same A rotation matrix is orthogonal. It keeps the length of every pair. So RoPE does not change the size of the scores. It changes only their direction. The pairing convention This lesson pairs adjacent coordinates (2i, 2i+1) . Some libraries pair coordinate i with i + d/2 . Both conventions give the relative property. But the weights of a trained model expect one convention. If you load weights with the other convention, the model gives wrong outputs and no error appears. The original transformer adds a fixed table of sines and cosines to the token embeddings. Each row of the table is the code of one position, and each pair of columns turns at its own frequency. This turn is the same for every . So a linear map can move from the code of position to the code of position . The model can learn relative offsets from absolute codes. Why many frequencies The first pair turns once in about 6 positions. The last pairs turn very slowly. The fast pairs separate neighbours. The slow pairs separate positions that are far apart. Together the columns give each position a different code. The limit The table is fixed and the model sees only the positions of its training data. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Defend a design A model was trained with a context of 8K tokens. The product now needs 128K. You have a modest fine-tuning budget and no budget to pretrain again. Lay out the options by the way the model encodes position, and give me the plan you would run. Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The answer depends on the positional scheme, so read the config first. A learned absolute table has no row past the trained length and cannot be extended without new parameters. With rotary embeddings you scale the base or interpolate the positions, with NTK-aware scaling, YaRN or LongRoPE, and fine-tune on long sequences; the lesson's reference is a model family that went from 8K to 128K this way. Linear-bias attention extrapolates by construction, but you cannot switch a trained model to it for free. Option by scheme. Scheme in the checkpoint Can it reach 128K? How Learned absolute table Not without new rows Add rows and train them, or retrain Fixed sinusoid The formula extends, the model does not The model never saw those phases; expect poor quality Rotary Yes Scale the base or interpolate positions, then fine-tune Linear bias Yes by design Already extrapolates; a training-time choice The rotary toolbox. Position interpolation plus fine-tuning. Shrink the positions by the extension factor so the angles stay inside the trained range, then fine-tune for 1 to 5B tokens. Simple and effective. NTK-aware scaling. Rescale the base to base * scale_factor ** (d / (d - 2)) when going from 4K to 16K and beyond, so the high-frequency pairs are not squeezed. YaRN. A per-dimension mix of interpolation and extrapolation that preserves the entropy of attention on long contexts; it needs a fine-tuning stage. LongRoPE. A search over per-dimension scale factors; used for very long contexts. The plan. Confirm the scheme from the model config and read the current rope scaling block. Pick YaRN or position interpolation, set the factor for 128K, and build a long-sequence fine-tuning set. Before training, measure perplexity on sequences longer than the trained length with and without the scaling, the way the lesson's exercise does at lengths 256 and 1024. Fine-tune, then measure again at the target length and at the original length, so that a win on long inputs does not hide a regression on short ones. Budget the memory. The cache of keys and values grows linearly with the context, and 128K is sixteen times 8K. What to tell the product team. The positional scheme is the gate. A rotary model gives you a clean knob and a short fine-tuning job. A model with a learned table or a sinusoid needs a retrain or a different model. Plausible wrong answers. "Set the maximum position in the config higher and ship." A learned table has no row for the new positions, and a rotary model needs its base scaled and a fine-tune. "The sinusoid extends to any length, so the model works." The formula extends; the model was never trained to read those phases and its quality drops. "Position interpolation needs no training." The lesson's recipe is to shrink the positions and then fine-tune for 1 to 5B tokens. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why does a rotary model fail when you just run it at 128K with no change? Expected: the fast-turning coordinate pairs reach angles the model never saw, so the scores at long distance are noise. (level 3) What two measurements do you insist on before shipping? Expected: perplexity or task quality at the new length, and the same at the original length to catch a regression. (level 4) The team proposes to switch the model to linear-bias attention because it extrapolates well. Your answer? Expected: that is a training-time choice; a checkpoint trained with rotation cannot be swapped to a score bias without retraining. (level 4) What breaks on the serving side at 128K even if quality is fine? Expected: memory for each token's keys and values, which grows with the context; the attention stack needs grouped-query or latent attention and a tiled kernel. Where it is taught. The positional encoding lesson lists the scaling tricks and the extension to 128K, and the embedding capstone explains why a learned table is bounded. Explain the mechanism Take a sentence and shuffle its words. Feed both versions through a self-attention layer that has no positional signal. How do the two outputs relate, and what are the three families of fixes you would name? Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The output rows come back shuffled in the same way and nothing else changes, because attention only computes pairwise similarities between tokens. Order carries meaning in language and code, so the model needs a second signal. The three fixes are a position vector added to the embedding, a learned table or a fixed sinusoid, a rotation of the queries and keys by an angle that grows with position, and a distance penalty added to the scores. Why the layer is blind. The score matrix is softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d)) V , built from dot products between pairs of tokens. Permute the rows of X and every dot product keeps its value; only its position in the matrix moves. The layer is permutation-equivariant by construction. Fix one: add a position vector to the input. A learned table has one row per position, so it adds max_context_length times D parameters and has no row for a position past the trained length. A fixed sinusoid uses the formula Copy with no parameters. The wavelength changes geometrically across dimensions. Low dimensions have the largest angle per position and the shortest wavelength, so they encode fine position; high dimensions have the longest wavelength and encode coarse position. The vector at position p plus k is a linear function of the vector at p, which gives attention an easy way to learn relative offsets. The position vector is summed with the token vector, not concatenated, so D stays constant and the model decides per feature how much position matters. Fix two: rotate the queries and keys. Rotary position embedding rotates each pair of coordinates in Q and K by pos * theta_i , with theta_i = base ** (-2i / d_head) and a default base of 10000. The dot product of a rotated query and a rotated key then depends only on their distance. This is the dominant choice in 2026. Fix three: bias the scores. Linear-bias attention adds -m_h * |i - j| to the score of query i and key j, with a slope per head. No table, no rotation, and strong extrapolation to longer inputs. Where each one lives. The first family changes the input to the first layer. The other two act inside attention, on the projections or the scores, so they follow the same shape contract as the embedding stage without touching the embedding. Plausible wrong answers. "The softmax makes attention order-aware." The softmax normalizes a row of similarities; it has no idea which column is first. "Add the position as one extra number on the embedding." One scalar cannot give the dot products a usable signal; the schemes spread position across many dimensions or into the scores. "Position only matters for long sequences." A two-word sentence already changes meaning when its words swap. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Why add the two vectors instead of concatenating them? Expected: the sum keeps D constant through the network and lets the model weigh token and position per feature. (level 2) What does a learned position table cost that a sinusoid does not? Expected: max_context_length times D parameters, and it cannot be indexed past the trained length. (level 2) Why do the high dimensions of the sinusoid encode coarse position? Expected: their wavelength is longest, so they change slowly across positions. (level 3) Where in the block does the rotation apply? Expected: to Q and K inside attention, after the projection and before the score matmul, never to V. Where it is taught. The positional encoding lesson compares the three families and the embedding capstone builds the learned and sinusoidal tables. Explain the mechanism The rotary scheme rotates every query and every key by an angle that is proportional to the token's absolute position. Yet everyone says it encodes relative position. Resolve the apparent contradiction, and tell me the one unit test you would write to prove the property. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The rotation acts on pairs of coordinates with the angle pos * theta_i . When a query from position m meets a key from position n, the dot product on each pair picks up cos((m - n) * theta_i) , so only the gap survives and the two absolute positions cancel. The test: rotate two random vectors at positions (a, b) and again at (a + k, b + k), then assert that the two dot products agree within floating-point error. The rotation. For each pair of dimensions (2i, 2i + 1) in a head of width d_head : Copy Each pair is a point in a plane, and the rotation turns it by pos * theta_i . Low values of i turn fast and high values turn slowly, because theta_i = base ** (-2i / d_head) . Why the dot product only sees the gap. A rotation by angle alpha followed by the dot product with a vector rotated by angle beta equals the dot product of the originals rotated by alpha - beta . Apply the same function to Q at position m and to K at position n, and every pair contributes a factor that depends on (m - n) * theta_i . The score depends on the distance even though the rotation was keyed off the absolute position. Attention gets relative position for free, with no table and no parameters. Where it applies. The rotation applies to Q and K after their projection and before the score matmul. It never touches V, because the values carry content that should not be rotated by position, and it never touches the input embedding. Why it won. It slots into attention without a change to the architecture. Its base is a clean knob: scale it and the model reaches longer contexts, which is how one model family reached a 128K context from 8K with scaling schemes such as NTK-aware interpolation and YaRN. The unit test. Copy The property is the whole point of the method. If the test fails, the rotation was applied to only one side, or the two sides use different pairs or angles. A pass does not prove the pairing or the angles match the reference: a consistent wrong pairing passes too, so also compare one rotated vector with a value computed by hand. Plausible wrong answers. "RoPE adds a position vector to the embedding." It rotates the queries and the keys inside attention; the embedding is untouched. "RoPE needs a table of size maximum length times width." The angles come from a formula; there is no table and no parameter. "Rotate the keys only and save half the work." Then the score depends on the absolute position of the key, and the relative property is gone. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why rotate Q and K but not V? Expected: position should shape the match between tokens, not the content that is returned once a token is picked. (level 3) What happens at a position the model never saw in training? Expected: the fast-turning pairs reach angles the model never learned to read; scaling the base or interpolating positions brings them back into the trained range. (level 3) How does linear-bias attention get relative position without any rotation? Expected: it adds a penalty proportional to |i - j| to the scores, one slope per head. (level 4) Why does increasing the base help a longer context? Expected: a larger base lowers every frequency except the first pair, which always turns at one radian per position, so the high-frequency pairs are not squeezed into unseen angles when the context grows; the NTK-aware rule rescales the base by the extension factor raised to d / (d - 2) . a0705: Course home / Phase 7 · Inside the Transformer The whole transformer, encoder and decoder Lesson 7.5 75 min Build Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 7 · 02 (Self-Attention), Phase 7 · 03 (Many heads looking at once), Phase 7 · 04 (Positional Encoding) Type : Build. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Attention is the star. Everything else — residuals, normalization, feed-forward, cross-attention — is the scaffolding that lets you stack it deep. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Block "One transformer layer" Stack of norm + attention + norm + FFN, wrapped in residual connections. Residual "Skip connection" x + f(x) output; enables gradient flow through deep stacks. Pre-norm "Normalize before, not after" Modern: x + sublayer(LN(x)) . Trains deeper without warmup gymnastics. RMSNorm "LayerNorm without the mean" Divide by RMS; one less op, same empirical stability. SwiGLU "The FFN everyone switched to" Swish(W1 x) ⊙ W3 x → W2 . Beats ReLU/GELU on LM ppl. Cross-attention "How the decoder sees the encoder" MHA with Q from decoder, K/V from encoder outputs. FFN expansion "How wide the middle MLP is" Ratio of hidden-size to d_model, usually 4 (LayerNorm) or 2.6 (SwiGLU). Bias-free "Drop the +b terms" Modern stacks omit biases in linear layers; slight ppl improvement, smaller model. The problem In plain words first One attention layer only lets words look at each other. A model needs much more: it has to stack dozens of layers, and each layer also needs a step that works on every word separately. The transformer block packages this: attention (words exchange information), a small feed-forward network (each word's vector is transformed on its own), a residual connection around each (the input is added back to the output, so each step only adds a correction), and a normalisation in front of each so the numbers stay in range. An encoder stacks blocks that see the whole input; a decoder stacks blocks that see only earlier words and, in translation-style models, also read the encoder's output through cross-attention . This lesson builds both from the lesson's code, counts where the parameters of real models sit, shows what happens without residuals, and rebuilds all 30 blocks of a real model, SmolLM-135M, from its weights. Nothing is trained. A single attention layer is a feature extractor, not a model. One matmul per layer is not enough capacity for language. You need depth — and depth breaks without the right plumbing. The 2017 Vaswani paper packaged six design decisions that turned one attention layer into a stackable block. Every transformer since — encoder-only (BERT), decoder-only (GPT), encoder-decoder (T5) — inherits the same skeleton. In 2026 the blocks have been refined (RMSNorm, SwiGLU, pre-norm, RoPE) but the skeleton is identical. This lesson is the skeleton. Next lessons specialize it — 06 for encoders, 07 for decoders, 08 for encoder-decoder. The idea Idea 1 · The six pieces Embedding + positional signal. Tokens → vectors. Position injected via RoPE (modern) or sinusoidal (classic). Self-attention. Every position attends to every other. Masked in decoders. Feed-forward network (FFN). Position-wise two-layer MLP: W_2 · activation(W_1 · x) . Expansion ratio 4× by default. Residual connection. x + sublayer(x) . Without this, gradients vanish past ~6 layers. Layer normalization. LayerNorm or RMSNorm (modern). Stabilizes the residual stream. Cross-attention (decoder only). Queries come from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder output. Watch a vector flow through one block: attention mixes across positions, the residual carries it forward, the FFN transforms it, and norm keeps the stream stable. Idea 2 · Encoder block (used by BERT, T5 encoder) Copy Encoder is bidirectional. No masking. All positions see all positions. Idea 3 · Decoder block (used by GPT, T5 decoder) Copy Decoder has three sublayers per block. The middle one — cross-attention — is the only place information flows from encoder to decoder. In a pure decoder-only architecture (GPT), cross-attention is omitted and you just have masked self-attention + FFN. Idea 4 · Pre-norm vs post-norm Original paper: x + sublayer(LN(x)) vs LN(x + sublayer(x)) . Post-norm lost favor around 2019 — it is harder to train deeply without careful warmup. Each block's output is an attention average of its inputs, and repeated averaging pulls every row towards the same mixture; with nothing carrying the original signal forward, the differences between tokens are erased ("rank collapse"), and a deep network would see one token repeated 64 times. With residuals, each block only adds a correction to its input, so the tokens stay distinct: similarity creeps up to 0.5 after 48 random blocks, and trained models, with smaller residual updates at initialisation, keep their tokens apart through every layer. Solutions Solution P1 · Identical without residuals With residuals, still mostly unrelated: similarity rises slowly, to about 0.2 after 24 blocks and 0.5 after 48. Without them, practically identical almost at once: 0.76 after one block and 1.000 from the second block on. Attention outputs are weighted averages of the inputs, and averaging again and again drives every row to the same vector. The residual connection adds each block's output to its input instead of replacing it, so the distinctive part of each token survives, and the gradient has the same direct path backwards. Solution B1 · No source, and a view of the future First, the decoder no longer reads the encoder at all: its "cross-attention" attends over its own states, so the output cannot depend on the source sentence, and a translation model becomes a language model that ignores its input. Second, that attention call has no causal mask, so every target position can now see the later target tokens. During training with teacher forcing, the model can copy the next token from the input, so the loss falls quickly and looks excellent, while generation, where future tokens do not exist yet, fails. The test from Step 3 catches both at once: editing the last target token would now change every decoder row, and editing the source would change none. Defend a design You inherit a decoder block written in the 2017 style: layer normalization after the residual add, a ReLU feed-forward network at four times the width, sinusoidal absolute positions summed into the input, bias terms on every linear layer, and full multi-head attention. Weigh a trade-off Three products land on your desk: a search ranking model over documents, a coding assistant that writes code, and a speech-to-text system. Which transformer shape do you pick for each, and what does the pretraining loss have to do with the choice? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Encoder-only for ranking and embeddings, decoder-only for generation, and encoder-decoder when the input is a clear source sequence such as audio to transcribe. An encoder reads both sides of every position and trains on masked prediction, which gives strong representations and no way to generate. A decoder trains on next-token prediction behind a causal mask, so it can generate, and it scales cleanest, which is why it won language. The loss decides whether the model can produce text at all. The three skeletons. Need Shape Why Classification, embeddings, question answering over text Encoder-only Bidirectional attention sees the whole input at once Text generation, chat, code, reasoning Decoder-only Causal mask plus next-token loss; one pass of attention and FFN per layer Structured input to structured output, translation, speech recognition Encoder-decoder The encoder owns the source; the decoder generates and reads it through cross-attention The one line that separates them. A decoder predicts each token's probability given the tokens before it. An encoder predicts a masked token given the unmasked ones. Same block, same attention, different mask and different target. Only the first loss produces a model that can continue a sequence. Cross-attention. A decoder block in an encoder-decoder model has three sublayers: masked self-attention, cross-attention and the FFN. In cross-attention the queries come from the decoder and the keys and values come from the encoder output. It is the only place where information flows from the source to the output. A pure decoder drops it. Why decoder-only won language. It handles comprehension and generation with one architecture, it scales cleanly, and in-context learning let one model follow examples without a new head per task. Encoder-decoder is still the best fit when the input has a strong source identity: a waveform, a sentence in another language, a table to summarize. The three answers. Ranking: an encoder, or an embedding model built on one, because you need a representation of the whole document and no generation. Coding assistant: a decoder, because the product is generation and the causal loss is what makes generation possible. Speech-to-text: an encoder-decoder, because the audio is a source sequence of its own kind and the text is a different sequence. Plausible wrong answers. "A decoder-only model cannot classify." It can, by prompting or by adding a head; the point is that an encoder is often cheaper for that job. "An encoder generates text one token at a time." It has no causal loss and predicts masked positions; it is not trained to continue a sequence. "Every transformer block has cross-attention." Only the decoder blocks of an encoder-decoder model have it. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Which sublayer exists only in the encoder-decoder shape? Expected: cross-attention, with queries from the decoder and keys and values from the encoder. (level 3) Why can a decoder-only model also do comprehension tasks? Expected: the same next-token model answers a question by continuing a prompt, and in-context learning lets it follow examples without a task head. (level 3) When would you still choose encoder-decoder for a text task? Expected: when the input is a clear source sequence that the output transforms, such as translation or summarization of a fixed document. (level 4) The ranking team wants to reuse the decoder they already serve. How? Expected: prompt it and read the logits of a label token, or attach a head and fine-tune; weigh the cost against an encoder that scores documents in one pass. Where it is taught. Weigh a trade-off The 2017 paper placed the layer normalization after the residual add. Almost every model since about 2019 places it before the sublayer. What changed, how would you demonstrate the difference in one afternoon, and what does RMSNorm change on top of that? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Post-norm sends the gradient of the skip path through a normalization at every layer, so at depth the gradient shrinks and the run needs a warmup schedule to survive. Pre-norm keeps the skip path unnormalized, so the gradient reaches the embeddings cleanly and a deep stack trains without warmup tricks. Demonstrate it by stacking twelve layers of each variant with the same initialization and printing the gradient norm at the embedding after one backward pass. RMSNorm then drops the mean subtraction, one fewer operation, with the same stability in practice. The two placements. Copy Same shapes, different training behavior. In the post-norm block the residual add is followed by the norm, so the signal that flows down the stack is normalized at each layer and the gradient that flows back must pass through every norm. At a depth of twelve and a learning rate of 3e-4 that gradient shrinks fast enough to need warmup. In the pre-norm block the norm sits inside the branch, before attention and before the MLP, and the skip path carries the raw signal. The afternoon experiment. Build a six-layer or twelve-layer stack with a pre_ln flag. Feed the same random input to both variants with identical weights. Run one backward pass and print the gradient norm at the embedding. The pre-norm stack shows an embedding gradient about an order of magnitude larger than the post-norm stack at the same learning rate. What pre-norm needs that post-norm did not. A final norm before the output head. The residual stream is unnormalized in a pre-norm model, so the head needs one normalization at the end. RMSNorm. LayerNorm subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation. RMSNorm divides by the root mean square and skips the mean subtraction. It is one operation cheaper and is empirically at least as stable, which is why the modern block uses it. Where dropout goes. After the attention softmax, on the attention output before the residual add, and after the second linear of the MLP. Never on the skip path itself, because that breaks the additive identity that lets the gradient flow at depth. Plausible wrong answers. "The two placements compute the same function in a different order." The composition differs: one normalizes the stream, the other normalizes only the branch input. "Warmup is a learning-rate detail unrelated to the norm." The lesson ties the need for warmup directly to the post-norm gradient path. "RMSNorm needs the mean to be stable." It omits the mean on purpose and matches LayerNorm in practice. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Where exactly does the norm sit in a pre-norm block? Expected: inside each residual branch, before attention and before the MLP, plus one final norm before the head. (level 3) Why does a pre-norm model need a final norm when a post-norm model does not? Expected: the pre-norm skip path is unnormalized, so the head would see an unbounded stream without it. (level 3) Your six-layer post-norm model trains fine and the twenty-four-layer version diverges. Why? Expected: the skip-path gradient attenuates at every norm, and the effect compounds with depth; add warmup or switch to pre-norm. (level 4) What would convince you to keep LayerNorm instead of RMSNorm? Expected: a measured quality or stability difference on your own run; the lesson's evidence is that RMSNorm matches it while being cheaper. Where it is taught. The full transformer lesson explains the move to pre-norm and RMSNorm, and the block capstone builds both variants and measures the gradient. Explain the mechanism A transformer block has two skip paths, one around attention and one around the feed-forward network. What do they do for training, which of the two sublayers moves information between tokens, and why does a dropout layer placed on the skip path itself break something? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The skip path makes the gradient additive across depth, so its norm stays in scale through a twelve-layer stack instead of shrinking at every layer, and it lets each block learn a small update to a running representation instead of a full replacement. Only attention mixes tokens; the MLP applies the same two layers to every position on its own. Dropout belongs after the attention softmax, on the attention output before the residual add, and after the second linear of the MLP; on the skip path it breaks the identity that carries the gradient, and early stacks that did this trained brittly. The block as a function. A decoder block takes a tensor of shape (batch, sequence, embedding) and returns the same shape. Inside, two sublayers do the work: Copy Each line is an additive update to the stream that flows top to bottom through every block. The lesson calls that tensor the residual stream. Why the additive path matters. Without the skip path, gradients vanish past about six layers. With it, the gradient of the loss with respect to an early layer has a direct term that does not pass through the sublayers, so depth adds terms instead of multiplying attenuations. The second effect is representational: a block does not have to reproduce its input; it adds what it learned. Who talks to whom. Attention is the only place tokens exchange information. The MLP is position-wise: the same weights apply to every token independently, with a hidden width of four times the embedding width and a GELU in the classic block. The modern block uses SwiGLU, three matrices at about 2.6 times the width so that the parameter count matches the old four-times MLP, and it drops the bias terms. Dropout on the branches, never on the identity. Attention dropout after the softmax, residual dropout on the attention output, and residual dropout after the second linear of the MLP. Dropout applied to the identity term randomly removes part of it, and the gradient path that made depth tractable is no longer reliable. Plausible wrong answers. "The skip path exists to keep the output shape equal to the input shape." The shape would match anyway; the skip path is about gradient flow and additive updates. "Dropout anywhere inside the block is equivalent." Dropout on the identity term damages the gradient path; dropout on the branch outputs does not. "The feed-forward network mixes information between tokens." It applies the same MLP to each position alone; mixing happens only in attention. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Which sublayer would you remove if the model only needed per-token transformations? Expected: attention; the MLP never looks across positions. (level 3) Why does the modern FFN use an expansion of about 2.6 instead of 4? Expected: SwiGLU has three weight matrices, so 2.6 times the width matches the parameter count of the two-matrix MLP at 4 times. (level 3) Why do modern stacks drop the bias terms in the linear layers? Expected: the lesson reports a slight perplexity improvement and a smaller model. (level 4) A reviewer wants to regularize a small model by dropping out the identity term. Your answer? Expected: no; keep dropout on the branch outputs, because the additive identity is what lets the gradient reach early layers. Where it is taught. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python, Rust. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line GPT predicts the next word. BERT predicts a missing word. One sentence of difference — and half a decade of everything embedding-shaped. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means MLM "Masked language modeling" Training signal: randomly replace 15% of tokens with [MASK] , predict the originals. Bidirectional "Looks both ways" Encoder attention has no causal mask — every position sees every other position. [CLS] "The pooler token" A special token prepended to every sequence; its final embedding is used as the sentence-level representation. [SEP] "Segment separator" Separates paired sequences (e.g. query/doc, sentence A/B). NSP "Next sentence prediction" BERT's second pretraining task; shown to be useless in RoBERTa, dropped after 2019. Fine-tuning "Adapt to a task" Keep the encoder mostly frozen; train a small head on top for the downstream task. Cross-encoder "A reranker" A BERT that takes both query and doc as input, outputs a relevance score. ModernBERT "2024 refresh" Encoder rebuilt with RoPE, pre-norm, GeGLU, alternating local/global attention, 8K context. The problem In plain words first BERT is a transformer encoder trained by a fill-in-the-blank game. Take a sentence, hide some of its words, and ask the model to guess them. Because an encoder has no causal mask, it can use the words on both sides of the gap, something a left-to-right model like GPT cannot do. After training on billions of sentences, the model's internal vectors capture what words mean in context, and a small "head" added on top turns it into a classifier, a search embedder or a reranker. This lesson checks the masking rules on 100,000 tokens, then works with real trained encoders: ModernBERT filling blanks with clues that come after the gap (against GPT-2, which cannot see them), ModernBERT spotting a wrong word with no mask at all, and two fine-tuned BERTs ranking documents for a search query. Nothing is trained. In 2018 every NLP task — sentiment, NER, QA, entailment — trained its own model from scratch on its own labeled data. There was no pre-trained "understand English" checkpoint you could fine-tune. ELMo (2018) showed you could pre-train contextual embeddings with a bidirectional LSTM; it helped but did not generalize. BERT (Devlin et al. 2018) asked: what if we took a transformer encoder, trained it on every sentence on the internet, and forced it to predict missing words from context on both sides? Then you fine-tune one head on your downstream task. Parameter efficiency was a revelation. The result: within 18 months BERT and its variants (RoBERTa, ALBERT, ELECTRA) dominated the NLP leaderboards of the time. By the end of 2019 Google Search was using BERT to understand queries, and BERT-style encoders became the default for classification and semantic search. In 2026 encoder-only models are still the right tool for classification, retrieval, and structured extraction: they read the whole input in one forward pass with no generation loop, small ones run comfortably on a CPU, and their embeddings are the backbone of most retrieval stacks. ModernBERT (Dec 2024) pushed the architecture to 8K context with Flash Attention + RoPE + GeGLU. The idea Idea 1 · The training signal Take a sentence: the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog . Mask 15% of tokens randomly: Copy Train the model to predict the original tokens at masked positions. Because the encoder is bidirectional, predicting [MASK] at position 1 can use brown fox jumps at positions 2+. That is the thing GPT cannot do. Idea 2 · The BERT mask rules Of the 15% of tokens selected for prediction: 80% are replaced with [MASK] . 10% are replaced with a random token. 10% are left unchanged. Why not always [MASK] ? Because [MASK] never appears at inference time. Training the model to expect [MASK] at 100% of masked positions would create a distribution shift between pretraining and fine-tuning. The 10% random + 10% unchanged keeps the model honest. Idea 3 · Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) — and why it was dropped Original BERT also trained on NSP: given two sentences A and B, predict if B follows A. RoBERTa (2019) found that removing it matched or slightly improved downstream results. Modern encoders skip it. Idea 4 · What changed in 2026: ModernBERT The 2024 ModernBERT paper rebuilt the block with 2026 primitives: Component Original BERT (2018) ModernBERT (2024) Positional Learned absolute RoPE Activation GELU GeGLU Normalization Post-norm LayerNorm Pre-norm LayerNorm, no bias terms Attention Full dense Alternating local (128) + global Context length 512 8192 Tokenizer WordPiece BPE And unlike the 2018 stack, it is Flash-Attention-native. The paper reports faster long-input inference than earlier encoders together with higher GLUE and retrieval scores. Idea 5 · Use cases that still pick an encoder in 2026 Task Why encoder beats decoder Retrieval / semantic search embeddings Bidirectional context = better embedding quality per token Classification (sentiment, intent, toxicity) One forward pass; no generation overhead NER / token labeling Per-position output, natively bidirectional Zero-shot entailment (NLI) Classifier head on top of encoder Reranker for RAG Cross-encoder scoring, 10x faster than LLM rerankers The same idea as a formula The MLM objective. Search cost. For documents, a bi-encoder embeds them once offline and answers a query with one encoder pass plus dot products; a cross-encoder needs full passes per query, so it only re-ranks a short list. The loss uses those 77 positions; a GPT-style model would get 511 next-token losses from the same sequence, about 6.6 times as many. Re-ranking for retrieval. Check your mental model ✗ "BERT only learns from the [MASK] tokens it sees." ✓ It learns from the 15% selected positions, a fifth of which are not [MASK] ; so it must also judge ordinary-looking tokens, which is what lets it notice a wrong word with no mask present (the run under "Use it"). ✗ "An encoder can generate text if you mask the next position." ✓ It predicts all masked positions independently in one pass, with no left-to-right factorisation of the probability; decoders are built for generation. ✗ "An embedding model is a different architecture from BERT." ✓ The encoder is the same; only the fine-tuning loss (contrastive) and the pooling differ. A cross-encoder reranker is the same encoder again with a one-number head. ELECTRA turned exactly this into its training task, and spelling and grammar checkers use it directly. What has the model actually learned to do, and why would it be a poor encoder? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Encoders run retrieval. Embedding models built on BERT-style encoders (for example the BGE, E5, GTE and Nomic families and all-MiniLM-L6-v2 ) serve most vector-search and RAG pipelines, through sentence-transformers , Hugging Face's Text Embeddings Inference and the vector databases' built-in embedders. Cross-encoder rerankers (BGE-reranker, the MS MARCO MiniLM cross-encoders, and hosted rerank APIs such as Cohere Rerank) re-score the top results of a first-stage search in production RAG systems. ModernBERT (December 2024) updated the encoder with RoPE, GeGLU, alternating local and global attention and an 8,192-token context, and is supported directly by transformers ; classifiers for moderation, intent and PII detection are still mostly fine-tuned encoders. From "Every morning the", hundreds of continuations are possible (GPT-2's top guess, " sun", has only 1.5%), and the decisive word comes after the gap, where a left-to-right model cannot look.
