a0707: Course home / Phase 7 · Inside the Transformer Learning by predicting the next word (GPT) Lesson 7.7 75 min Build Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 7 · 02 (Self-Attention), Phase 7 · 05 (Full Transformer), Phase 7 · 06 (BERT) Type : Build. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, Rust. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line BERT sees both sides. GPT sees only the past. The triangle mask is the most consequential single line of code in modern AI. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Causal mask "The triangle" Upper-triangular -inf matrix added to attention scores so position i only sees positions ≤ i . Next-token prediction "The loss" Cross-entropy of the model's distribution against the true next token at every position. Autoregressive "Generate one at a time" Feed output back as input; parallelism only during training, not during generation. Logits "Pre-softmax scores" Raw output of the LM head before softmax; sampling happens on these. Temperature "Creativity knob" Divide logits by $T$; $T \to 0$ = greedy, $T \to \infty$ = uniform. Top-p "Nucleus sampling" Truncate distribution to smallest set summing to $\ge p$; sample from what remains. Min-p "Better than top-p" Keep tokens where p ≥ min_p × max_p ; adapts cutoff to sharpness of distribution. Speculative decoding "Draft + verify" Cheap model proposes N tokens; big model verifies in parallel. Teacher forcing "Training trick" During training, feed the true previous token, not the model's prediction. Standard for every seq2seq LM. The problem In plain words first A GPT-style model does one thing: given the words so far, it gives a probability for every possible next word. To write text it picks one, appends it, and asks again. To train it, you show it real text and, at every position, score how much probability it gave to the word that actually came next. The trick that makes training fast is the causal mask : in attention, each position is forbidden to look at later positions, so one pass over a whole sentence produces an honest prediction at every position at once. This lesson builds the mask from a plain running average, checks with GPT-2 that one forward pass really gives a prediction per position, computes the training loss by hand and matches it to the library's, and compares greedy decoding, temperature, top-p and min-p on GPT-2's real next-word distribution. Nothing is trained. A language model answers one question: given the first t-1 tokens, what is the probability distribution over token t ? Train on that signal — next-token prediction — and you get a model that can generate arbitrary text one token at a time. To train it end-to-end on a whole sequence in parallel, you need each position's prediction to depend only on earlier positions. Otherwise the model trivially cheats by looking at the answer. The causal mask does this. It is a single upper-triangular matrix of -inf values added to attention scores before softmax. After softmax, those positions become 0. Each position can attend only to itself and earlier positions. And because you apply it once to the whole sequence, you get N parallel next-token predictions in one forward pass. GPT-1 (2018), GPT-2 (2019), GPT-3 (2020), GPT-4 (2023), GPT-5 (2025), Claude, Llama, Qwen, Mistral, DeepSeek, Kimi — they are all decoder-only causal transformers with the same core loop. What separates them is data quality, scale and architectural refinements, and post-training (SFT, RLHF, DPO, and their successors). The idea Idea 1 · The mask Given a sequence of length , build an matrix: ​ = { 0 − ∞ ​ if j ≤ i if j > i ​ Add M to the raw attention scores before softmax. , so masked positions contribute zero weight. Each row of the attention matrix is a probability distribution over previous positions only. Implementation cost: one torch.tril() call. Time to compute: nanoseconds. Impact on the field: everything. Idea 2 · Where the triangle comes from The mask is usually presented as a patch bolted onto attention. Run the derivation in the other direction and it stops being mysterious: attention is the third refinement of a prefix average, and the triangle is the loop bounds of that average, written as a matrix. Stage 1 — prefix average. The dumbest causal summary of a sequence: position becomes the mean of positions . As a loop, that is out[i] = X[:i+1].mean(0) . The same computation is one matrix multiply. Take a lower-triangular matrix of ones, divide each row by its count, multiply: Copy What you should see Copy Copy Row of is . The zeros above the diagonal are the causality. Nothing about the future was masked out; the future was never in the sum. Stage 2 — learned weights. A uniform average treats every past token as equally relevant. Replace the ones with a learned score matrix S . Now rows no longer sum to one by construction, so normalize each row with softmax instead of dividing by the count. Softmax never outputs an exact zero, which breaks causality — unless the future scores go in as -inf , because exp(-inf) = 0 : Copy What you should see Copy Copy Same triangle, same row-stochastic matrix, same one matmul. The -inf mask is not new machinery. It is stage 1's zero entries, translated into softmax's input domain. Stage 3 — content-dependent weights. In stage 2, S is fixed after training: position 7 always weighs position 3 the same, whatever the tokens say. Let the scores depend on the tokens themselves: S = Q @ K.T / sqrt(d_k) . Nothing else changes. Mask, softmax, matmul — identical. Three stages, one invariant: a lower-triangular row-stochastic matrix times the sequence. Uniform average, learned static weights, content-dependent weights. The mask was never added to attention. It survived from the average. Idea 3 · Parallel training, serial inference Training: forward-pass the whole (N, d_model) sequence once, compute N cross-entropy losses (one per position), sum, backprop. Parallel along the sequence. This is why GPT training scales — you process 1M tokens in a batch in one GPU pass. Inference: you generate token by token. Feed [t1, t2, t3] , get t4 . Feed [t1, t2, t3, t4] , get t5 . Feed [t1, t2, t3, t4, t5] , get t6 . The KV cache ( Lesson 7.12 ) saves the hidden states of t1…tn so you don't recompute them each step. But serial depth at inference = output length. That is the autoregressive tax and why decoding is the latency bottleneck of every LLM. Idea 4 · The loss — shift-by-one Given tokens [t1, t2, t3, t4] : Input: [t1, t2, t3] Targets: [t2, t3, t4] For every position i , compute -log P(target_i | inputs[:i+1]) . Sum. This is the cross-entropy for the whole sequence. Every transformer LM you've heard of trains on this loss. Pre-training, fine-tuning, SFT — same loss, different data. Idea 5 · Decoding strategies After training, sampling choices matter more than people think. Confirm outputs match greedy of the verifier. Solutions Solution P1 · It loops Something else: a loop. Greedy decoding produces " that you can live in it for a long time." and then repeats "You can live in it for a long time." until the 40 tokens run out. Once a phrase has appeared, the model's most likely continuation is to repeat it (the in-context copying the surprisal column shows), and greedy decoding always takes the most likely token, so it never escapes. Sampling with top- or min- breaks the loop because a less likely token is drawn sooner or later; serving engines also offer repetition and frequency penalties. Solution B1 · Row 0 has nothing to attend to Row 0 is now all . The lesson's apply_softmax_row returns a row of zeros, so position 0's attention output is silently the zero vector; PyTorch's softmax returns NaN for an all- row ( /0 ), and the NaN spreads through every later layer and the loss. Every other position loses its own token from its attention: it can only gather information from the past, so its prediction must come entirely through the residual stream for the current token. Strictly-earlier masks are used on purpose only with an extra "start" position to attend to; the standard causal mask includes the diagonal. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Explain the mechanism A decoder must not read tokens that come after the current position. A teammate proposes to run the softmax first and then set the weights of later positions to zero. Why is that wrong, and where does the usual triangle of negative infinity really come from? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Zeroing weights after the softmax leaves rows that no longer sum to one, and the later tokens already shaped the normalization. The mask adds minus infinity to the scores before the softmax, so the exponential gives an exact zero there and each row is a distribution over the past alone. The triangle is not a patch on attention: a causal running average is a lower-triangular row-normalized matrix, and the mask is that same zero pattern written in the input domain of the softmax. Three stages, one invariant. Start with the simplest causal summary: position i becomes the mean of positions 0 to i. As a matrix: Copy The zeros above the diagonal are the causality. Nothing was masked; the future was never in the sum. Now replace the ones with learned scores S. The rows no longer sum to one, so normalize each row with a softmax. A softmax never outputs an exact zero, so the future entries must enter as minus infinity, because exp(-inf) = 0 : Copy Finally let the scores depend on the tokens: S = Q @ K.T / sqrt(d_k) . Mask, softmax, matmul. The mask survived from the average; it was never added to attention. Why minus infinity and not zero. A score of zero still gets a weight of exp(0) = 1 before normalization. Only minus infinity gives zero weight. What it buys at training time. With the mask in place one forward pass over a sequence of N tokens gives N next-token predictions, each of which saw only its past. That is why training is parallel along the sequence. Without the mask the model reads its own target and the loss collapses while the model learns nothing useful. How a production block stores it. Register the mask as a buffer at construction, sized to the maximum context, and slice the top-left (T, T) corner at forward time. It then lives on the same device as the weights and never enters the gradient graph. Rebuilding it on each call turns the mask into an allocator hot spot at long context. Plausible wrong answers. "Set the future scores to zero." Zero is a legal score and still earns weight after the exponential; only minus infinity gives a zero weight. "The mask is a training-only trick, so serving can drop it." The prompt is processed in one pass at serving time, and without the mask the prompt tokens would read their own future. "Encoders also need the triangle." The encoder sees both sides by design; the triangle is what makes a decoder a decoder. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why not multiply the future scores by zero? Expected: a zero score still receives weight exp(0) before normalization, so the future still contributes. (level 2) Where does the mask live in a real block and why? Expected: a registered buffer at the maximum context length, sliced per forward pass, so it sits on the right device and is not allocated on every call. (level 3) Does an encoder need this triangle? Expected: no, an encoder is bidirectional; it needs a padding mask, which also uses minus infinity but follows the batch, not the diagonal. (level 3) What does the mask have to do with parallel training? Expected: it lets one pass produce every next-token prediction at once while each prediction sees only its past, so the N losses are valid together. Where it is taught. The causal language modeling lesson derives the triangle from the prefix average, and the attention capstone and the block capstone register it as a buffer. Debug a failure A new decoder-only language model on a vocabulary of 64 tokens reaches a training loss near zero after only some hundreds of steps, and the sampled text is nonsense. Name the two most likely causes and the check that tells them apart. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. On real text, a loss far below the logarithm of the vocabulary size this early, with nonsense samples, most likely means the model can see its own target. Either the causal mask is missing, so position i reads the token at i plus one through attention, or the targets were never shifted, so the input and the target are the same sequence. Check the attention weights: if any mass sits above the diagonal the mask is gone; if the weights are triangular, print one batch and compare the input and target columns. What a healthy run looks like. At the first step the loss should sit near the logarithm of the vocabulary size, about 4.16 for 64 tokens. On the lesson's repeat task it falls to well under 1.0 over three epochs because the next token equals the previous one. A loss that reaches zero on real text is not learning; it is copying. Cause one: the mask. The mask replaces every entry above the diagonal of the score matrix with minus infinity before the softmax. Forget it and every position attends to the whole sequence, including the answer. The lesson's phrase: forget the mask and you train a model that cheats. Common ways to lose it: the mask buffer is built for the maximum context and never sliced to the current length, the mask is applied after the softmax, or the attention call takes a flag that defaults to non-causal. Cause two: the shift. Given tokens [t1, t2, t3, t4] , the input is [t1, t2, t3] and the target is [t2, t3, t4] . If the data loader returns the same window twice, the model learns the identity. The loss collapses even with a perfect mask. The checks. Causality test. Perturb a token at position j and assert that the outputs at positions before j do not change. The lesson's test suite pins this property. Triangle test. Return the attention weights for one head and confirm the upper triangle is exactly zero after the softmax. Batch inspection. Print one input and target pair and confirm the target is the input shifted left by one. Held-out check. Compute the loss on held-out text with the same pipeline. A model that memorized a small corpus has a high held-out loss and samples that copy the training text; a leak gives nonsense samples. Why sampling exposes it. During training the answer leaks through the input, so the loss is low. At sampling time the model has nothing to copy from, so it emits noise. A model that learned the real task is good at both. Plausible wrong answers. "The model is just learning fast." A loss near zero on natural text is not possible without seeing the target. "Add dropout to regularize it." Dropout does not stop a leak; it only makes the copy slightly noisier. "Lower the learning rate." The optimization is fine; the objective is broken. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) What loss do you expect at step zero, and why? Expected: about the logarithm of the vocabulary size, about 4.16 for 64, because a random model spreads probability evenly. (level 2) How do you make the shift mistake impossible in the loader? Expected: slice one window of length T plus 1 and return window[:-1] and window[1:] from the same slice, with a test on one example. (level 3) Write the causality unit test in one sentence. Expected: change the token at position j, run the block again, and assert that every output before j is unchanged. (level 3) The mask and the shift are right, and the loss is still suspiciously low. What else leaks? Expected: a validation window that overlaps the training stream, or padding tokens counted as easy targets; check the split and the loss mask. Where it is taught. a0708: Course home / Phase 7 · Inside the Transformer Read-then-write models (T5, BART) Lesson 7.8 45 min Learn Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 7 · 05 (Full Transformer), Phase 7 · 06 (BERT), Phase 7 · 07 (GPT) Type : Learn. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python, Rust. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Encoders understand. Decoders generate. Put them back together and you get a model built for input → output tasks: translate, summarize, rewrite, transcribe. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Encoder-decoder "Seq2seq transformer" Two stacks: bidirectional encoder for input, causal decoder with cross-attention for output. Cross-attention "Where source talks to target" Decoder's Q × encoder's K/V. The only place encoder information enters the decoder. Span corruption "T5's pretraining trick" Replace random spans with sentinel tokens; decoder outputs the spans. Denoising objective "BART's game" Apply a noise function to the input, train the decoder to reconstruct the clean sequence. Sentinel token "The <extra_id_N> placeholder" Special tokens that tag corrupted spans in the source and re-tag them in the target. Flan "Instruction-tuned T5" T5 fine-tuned on >1,800 tasks; made encoder-decoder competitive at instruction-following. Beam search "Decoding strategy" Keep top-k partial sequences at each step; standard for translation/summarization. Teacher forcing "Training-time input" During training, feed the true previous output token to the decoder, not the sampled one. The problem In plain words first Many tasks turn one text (or recording) into another: translate this sentence, summarise this article, transcribe this audio. An encoder–decoder model splits the job in two. The encoder reads the whole input once, with no mask, and turns it into a set of vectors. The decoder then writes the output word by word like GPT, but at every step it can also look back at the encoder's vectors through cross-attention. T5 and BART pretrained such models by damaging text and asking the decoder to repair it. This lesson runs the lesson's span-corruption and noising code, then a real translation model, showing that its encoder runs once while its decoder runs once per word and which source word each German word looks at, and the original T5 filling in hidden spans the way it was trained to. Nothing is trained. Decoder-only GPT and encoder-only BERT each strip down the 2017 architecture for a different goal. But many tasks are naturally input-output: Translation: English → French. Summarization: 5,000-token article → 200-token summary. Speech recognition: audio tokens → text tokens. Structured extraction: prose → JSON. For these, encoder-decoder makes the cleanest fit. The encoder produces a dense representation of the source. The decoder generates the output, cross-attending to that representation at every step. Training is shift-by-one on the output side. Same loss as GPT, just conditioned on the encoder output. Two papers defined the modern playbook: T5 (Raffel et al. 2019). "Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer." Every NLP task reframed as text-in, text-out. Single architecture, single vocabulary, single loss. Pretrained on masked span prediction (corrupt spans in the input, decode them in the output). BART (Lewis et al. 2019). "Bidirectional and Auto-Regressive Transformer." Denoising autoencoder: corrupt input in multiple ways (shuffle, mask, delete, rotate), ask the decoder to reconstruct the original. In 2026 the encoder-decoder format lives on where input structure matters: Whisper (speech → text). Dedicated translation models (Marian/OPUS-MT, Meta's NLLB-200), which are small enough to run on a CPU. Google's T5Gemma (2025), encoder–decoder models adapted from Gemma for input-to-output tasks. Flan-T5 and variants for classification and structured extraction. Decoder-only won the spotlight, but encoder-decoder never went away. The idea Idea 1 · The forward loop Copy Crucially, the encoder runs once per input. The decoder runs autoregressively but cross-attends to the same encoder output at every step. Caching the encoder output is a free speedup for long inputs. Idea 2 · T5 pretraining — span corruption Pick random spans of the input (average length 3 tokens, 15% total). Replace each span with a unique sentinel: <extra_id_0> , <extra_id_1> , etc. The decoder outputs only the corrupted spans with their sentinel prefix: Copy Cheaper signal than predicting the whole sequence. Competitive with MLM (BERT) and prefix-LM (UniLM) in the T5 paper's ablation. Idea 3 · BART pretraining — multi-noise denoising BART tries five noising functions: Token masking. Token deletion. Text infilling (mask a span, decoder inserts the right length). Sentence permutation. Document rotation. Combining text infilling + sentence permutation produced the best downstream numbers. The decoder always reconstructs the original. BART's output is the full sequence, not just the corrupted spans — so pretraining compute is higher than T5. Idea 4 · Inference Same autoregressive generation as GPT. Greedy / beam / top-p sampling apply. Beam search (width 4–5) is standard for translation and summarization because the output distribution is narrower than chat. Idea 5 · When to pick each variant in 2026 Task Encoder-decoder? Why Translation Yes, usually Clear source sequence; fixed output distribution; beam search works Speech-to-text Yes (Whisper) Input modality differs from output; encoder shapes audio features Chat / reasoning No, decoder-only No persistent "input" — the conversation is the sequence Code completion Usually no Decoder-only with long context wins; code models like Qwen 2.5 Coder are decoder-only Summarization Either works BART, PEGASUS beat earlier decoder-only baselines; modern decoder-only LLMs match them Structured extraction Either T5 is clean because "text → text" absorbs any output format The trend since ~2022: decoder-only takes over tasks that encoder-decoder used to own because (a) instruction-tuned decoder-only LLMs generalize to anything via prompting, (b) one architecture scales easier than two, (c) most post-training tooling (SFT, RLHF, DPO) is built around decoders. Encoder-decoder holds on where input modality differs (speech, images) or where beam search quality matters. The same idea as a formula What the model computes. Cross-attention. A decoder-only model doing the same task instead carries the source tokens in its own sequence. T5 span corruption. It suits tasks with one right answer, like translation. Turning this into a model that follows instructions is what Flan's multitask tuning added. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Speech recognition is encoder–decoder. Whisper and its faster variants (distil-whisper, faster-whisper on CTranslate2) are the most widely deployed open speech-to-text models. Dedicated translation models such as Marian/OPUS-MT and Meta's NLLB-200 run in production pipelines and on-premise, because they are small and fast for one job; general LLMs handle translation in chat products. Encoder–decoders made from LLMs. Google's T5Gemma (2025) and T5Gemma 2 adapt Gemma checkpoints into encoder–decoder models aimed at summarisation and other input-to-output tasks. Sources: Whisper , faster-whisper , OPUS-MT models , NLLB-200 , T5Gemma , T5Gemma 2 . Recap What to keep from this lesson Encoder–decoder: an unmasked encoder reads the input once; a causal decoder writes the output and reads the encoder through unmasked cross-attention. T5 pretrains on span corruption (predict only the removed spans); BART on denoising (rebuild the whole text). Cross-attention learns alignments: content words point at their translations. Decoder-only models took over general tasks; encoder–decoders remain strong for speech, translation and fixed input-to-output jobs. a0709: Course home / Phase 7 · Inside the Transformer Transformers for images (ViT) Lesson 7.9 45 min Build Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 7 · 05 (Full Transformer), Phase 4 · 03 (CNNs), Phase 4 · 14 (Vision Transformers intro) Type : Build. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python, Rust. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line An image is a grid of patches. A sentence is a grid of tokens. The same transformer eats both. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Patch "The vision-transformer token" Flat vector of pixel values for a P × P × C region of the image. Patchify "Chop + flatten" Slice image into non-overlapping patches, flatten each to a vector. [CLS] token "The image summary" Prepended learnable token; its final embedding is the image representation. Inductive bias "What the model assumes" ViT has fewer priors than CNNs; needs more data to make up the gap. DINOv2 "Self-supervised ViT" Trained without labels using image augmentation + momentum teacher. Best general image features in 2026. SigLIP "CLIP's successor" ViT + text encoder trained with sigmoid contrastive loss; better than CLIP on matched compute. Swin "Windowed ViT" Hierarchical ViT with local attention + shifted windows; sub-quadratic. Register tokens "2023 trick" A few extra learnable tokens that soak up attention sinks; improves DINOv2 features. The problem In plain words first A vision transformer treats a picture like a sentence. It cuts the image into small squares (patches), flattens each square's pixels into one long list of numbers, and multiplies that list by a learned matrix to get a vector, one "word" per patch. A learned summary vector is put in front, position information is added, and an ordinary transformer encoder, the same as BERT's, processes the sequence. Nothing in it knows that patches next to each other are neighbours; it has to learn that from data, which is why ViTs need large datasets or self-supervised pretraining. This lesson runs the lesson's patchify code, checks on a real ViT that "patchify plus one matrix" is exactly the convolution libraries use, counts where its 86 million parameters sit, classifies real photos, and shows what DINOv2's patch features have learned without any labels. Nothing is trained. Before 2020, computer vision meant convolutions. Every SOTA on ImageNet, COCO, and detection benchmarks used a CNN backbone. Transformers were for language. Dosovitskiy et al. (2020) — "An Image is Worth 16x16 Words" — showed you can drop the convolutions entirely. Slice an image into fixed-size patches, linearly project each patch into an embedding, feed the sequence to a vanilla transformer encoder. At sufficient scale (ImageNet-21k pretraining or bigger), ViT matches or beats ResNet-based models. ViT was the start of a broader pattern in 2026: one architecture, many modalities. Whisper tokenizes audio. ViT tokenizes images. Action tokens for robotics. Pixel tokens for video. The transformer doesn't care — feed it a sequence and it learns. By 2026, ViT and its descendants (DeiT, Swin, DINOv2, ViT-22B, SAM 3) own most of vision. CNNs still win on edge devices and latency-sensitive tasks. Everything else has a ViT somewhere in the stack. The idea Idea 1 · Step 1 — patchify Split a H × W × C image into an N × (P·P·C) sequence of flat patches. Typical setup: 224 × 224 image, 16 × 16 patches → 196 patches of 768 values each. Copy Patch size is the lever. Smaller patches = more tokens, better resolution, quadratic attention cost. Larger patches = coarser, cheaper. Idea 2 · Step 2 — linear embedding A single learned matrix projects each flat patch to d_model . Equivalent to a convolution of kernel size P and stride P . In PyTorch this is literally nn.Conv2d(C, d_model, kernel_size=P, stride=P) — a 2-line implementation. Idea 3 · Step 3 — prepend [CLS] token, add positional embeddings Prepend a learnable [CLS] token. Its final hidden state is the image representation used for classification. Add learnable positional embeddings (ViT-original) or sinusoidal 2D (later variants). In 2024+ RoPE extended to 2D for position, sometimes without explicit embeddings. Idea 4 · Step 4 — standard transformer encoder Stack L blocks of LayerNorm → Self-Attention → + → LayerNorm → MLP → + . Identical to BERT. No vision-specific layers. This is the pedagogical punchline of the paper. Idea 5 · Step 5 — head For classification: take [CLS] hidden state → linear → softmax. For DINOv2 or SAM, discard [CLS] , use the patch embeddings directly. Idea 6 · Variants that mattered Model Year Change ViT 2020 The original. Fixed patch size, full global attention. DeiT 2021 Distillation; trainable on ImageNet-1k only. Swin 2021 Hierarchical with shifted windows. Fixed sub-quadratic cost. DINOv2 2023 Self-supervised (no labels). Best general vision features. ViT-22B 2023 22B params; scaling laws apply. SigLIP 2023 ViT + language pair, sigmoid contrastive loss. SAM 3 2025 Segment anything from text or examples; a ViT backbone plus promptable detector and mask decoder. Idea 7 · Why it took a while ViT needs a lot of data to match CNNs because it has none of the CNN inductive biases (translation invariance, locality). Without >100M labeled images or strong self-supervised pretraining, CNNs still win at matched compute. DeiT fixed this in 2021 with distillation tricks; DINOv2 fixed it permanently in 2023 with self-supervision. The same idea as a formula Patchify. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) ViT backbones under most vision products. ViT vision towers feed the vision-language models (SigLIP in Gemma 3, CLIP-style encoders in Qwen2.5-VL and Llama 4), DINOv2 and DINOv3 provide frozen features for segmentation, depth and retrieval, and SAM 2 and SAM 3 segment with ViT encoders. Registers and high resolution. Register tokens (DINOv2 with registers) remove attention artefacts in large ViTs; current models process variable resolutions and aspect ratios (NaViT-style packing, Qwen2-VL's dynamic resolution) instead of fixed 224×224 crops. CNNs where latency rules. Mobile and embedded deployments still favour CNNs or hybrids (MobileNetV4, YOLO detectors) when milliseconds and power matter. Sources: DINOv2 , DINOv3 , SigLIP 2 , SAM 3 , Vision Transformers Need Registers , Ultralytics YOLO . Feed them into a tiny PyTorch ViT and compare accuracy vs learnable positional embeddings on CIFAR-10. Hard. Build a 3-layer ViT (PyTorch), train on 1,000 MNIST images with 4×4 patches. Measure test accuracy. Now add DINOv2 pretraining on the same 1,000 images (simplified: just train the encoder to predict patch embeddings from masked patches). Does accuracy improve? Solutions Solution P1 · The parts separate They separate the scene's parts: sky, roof, wall and the grass with gravestones each come out in a distinct colour, with fairly sharp borders between them. Brightness alone would not do this (the roof and parts of the wall are similarly dark), and noise would show no regions at all. DINOv2 was trained only to give consistent features to different crops of the same image, and grouping patches by what they belong to turned out to be the best way to do that; the same PCA on the golf balls separates the balls from their labels. Solution B1 · Scrambled patches for a pretrained model The pretrained embedding matrix was learned for one pixel order. Flattening column-major transposes every patch, so each pixel is multiplied by the weight meant for a different pixel: the model sees every patch mirrored along its diagonal. A pretrained model's accuracy collapses, because none of its filters match. Training from scratch with the bug would work almost as well as without it, because would simply learn the transposed filters: the order only has to be consistent between training and inference. That is why preprocessing code (pixel order, channel order, normalisation statistics) must be copied exactly from the model's own processor. Sources and further reading Dosovitskiy et al. (2020). Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python, Rust. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Audio is an image of frequency over time. Whisper is a ViT that eats mel spectrograms and speaks back. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Mel spectrogram "Audio image" 2D representation: frequency bins on one axis, time frames on the other; log-scaled energy per cell. Log-mel "What Whisper sees" Mel spectrogram passed through log; approximates human perception of loudness. Frame "One time slice" A 25 ms window of samples; overlapping at 10 ms stride. Task token "Prompt prefix for speech" Special tokens like <\|transcribe\|> / <\|translate\|> in the decoder prompt. Voice activity detection (VAD) "Find the speech" Gate that removes silence before ASR; cuts cost massively. CTC "Connectionist Temporal Classification" Classic ASR loss for alignment-free training; Whisper does NOT use it. Whisper-turbo "Small decoder, full encoder" large-v3 encoder + 4-layer decoder; 8× faster decoding. Faster-whisper "The production wrapper" CTranslate2 reimplementation; int8 quantization; 4× faster than OpenAI's reference. The problem In plain words first Whisper turns speech into text with the same encoder–decoder transformer as a translation model. The audio is first turned into a picture: a log-mel spectrogram, which shows how much energy each band of pitches has in each 10-millisecond slice, much as the ear hears it. The encoder reads that picture (always a 30-second window), and the decoder writes text token by token, reading the audio through cross-attention. What it should do is chosen by a few special tokens at the start of the decoder's input: which language, and whether to transcribe or translate into English. This lesson runs the lesson's framing code, rebuilds Whisper's log-mel spectrogram in a dozen lines of NumPy and matches the official one, and has Whisper identify, transcribe and translate German speech, switching task by changing one token. Nothing is trained. Before Whisper (OpenAI, Radford et al. 2022), state-of-the-art automatic speech recognition (ASR) meant wav2vec 2.0 and HuBERT — self-supervised feature extractors plus a fine-tuned head. High quality, expensive data pipelines, domain-brittle. Multilingual speech recognition needed separate models per language family. Whisper made three bets: Train on everything. 680,000 hours of weakly-labeled audio scraped from the internet across 97 languages. No clean academic corpus. No phoneme labels. Multi-task single model. One decoder trained jointly on transcription, translation, voice activity detection, language ID, and timestamping via task tokens. Standard encoder-decoder transformer. Encoder consumes log-mel spectrograms. Decoder produces text tokens autoregressively. No vocoder, no CTC, no HMM. The result: Whisper large-v3 is robust across accents, noise, and languages that have zero clean labeled data. It is the default speech front-end for every open-source voice assistant and most commercial ones in 2026. The idea Idea 1 · Step 1 — resample + window Audio at 16 kHz. Clip/pad to 30 seconds. Compute log-mel spectrogram: 80 mel bins (128 in large-v3), 10 ms stride → 3,000 frames × 80 features. This is the "input image" that Whisper sees. Idea 2 · Step 2 — convolutional stem Two Conv1D layers with kernel 3 and stride 2 reduce the 3,000 frames to 1,500. Halves sequence length without adding a lot of parameters. Idea 3 · Step 3 — encoder A 32-layer (for large) transformer encoder over 1,500 timesteps. Sinusoidal positional encoding, self-attention, GELU FFN. Produces 1,500 × 1,280 hidden states. Idea 4 · Step 4 — decoder A 32-layer (for large) transformer decoder. It autoregressively produces tokens from a BPE vocabulary that is a superset of GPT-2's with a few audio-specific special tokens. Idea 5 · Step 5 — task tokens The decoder prompt starts with control tokens that tell the model what to do: Copy or Copy The model was trained on this convention. You control task by prefix. The 2026 equivalent of instruction-tuning, but applied to speech. Idea 6 · Step 6 — output Beam search (width 5) with a log-prob threshold. Timestamps are predicted every 0.02 seconds of audio when the <|notimestamps|> token is absent. Idea 7 · Whisper sizes Model Params Layers d_model Heads VRAM (fp16) Tiny 39M 4 384 6 ~1 GB Base 74M 6 512 8 ~1 GB Small 244M 12 768 12 ~2 GB Medium 769M 24 1024 16 ~5 GB Large 1550M 32 1280 20 ~10 GB Large-v3 1550M 32 1280 20 ~10 GB Large-v3-turbo 809M 32 1280 20 ~6 GB (4-layer decoder) Large-v3-turbo (2024) cut the decoder from 32 layers to 4: much faster decoding for a small loss in accuracy, mostly on translation, which turbo was not trained for. That decode speed unlock is why Whisper-turbo is the default for real-time voice agents in 2026. Idea 8 · What Whisper does not do No diarization (who is speaking). Pair with pyannote for that. No real-time streaming natively — the 30-second window is fixed. Modern wrappers ( faster-whisper , WhisperX ) bolt on streaming via VAD + overlap. No long-form context beyond 30 s without external chunking. Works well in practice because human speech rarely needs long-range context for transcription. In plain words first The idea in one line A dense 70B transformer activates every parameter for every token. A 671B MoE activates only 37B per token and matches or beats much larger dense models on most benchmarks. Sparsity is one of the most important scaling ideas of the decade. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Expert "One FFN among many" An independent feed-forward network; parameters dedicated to a sparse slice of the FFN computation. Router "The gate" A tiny linear layer that scores each token against each expert; top-k selection. Top-k routing "k active experts per token" Each token's FFN computation goes through exactly k experts, weighted by gate. Auxiliary loss "Load-balance penalty" Extra loss term that penalizes skewed expert usage. Auxiliary-loss-free "DeepSeek-V3's trick" Balance via per-expert bias on the router's selection only; no extra gradient. Shared expert "Always on" Extra expert through which every token passes; captures common knowledge. Expert parallelism "Shard by expert" Distribute different experts to different GPUs; route tokens across the network. Sparsity "Active params < total params" The ratio $k \times \text{expert size} / (E \times \text{expert size})$; 37/671 ≈ 5.5% for DeepSeek-V3. The problem In plain words first In a normal (dense) transformer every token goes through every weight of the feed-forward layers, so a bigger model costs more for every single word. A Mixture-of-Experts layer replaces that one feed-forward network with many smaller ones, the experts, plus a tiny router that picks a few of them for each token. The model can then hold far more knowledge (all experts together) while each token only pays for the few experts it uses. The catches: all experts must sit in memory, and the router must not send everything to the same few experts. This lesson runs the lesson's router, then counts the real total and active parameters of Mixtral, Qwen3, gpt-oss and DeepSeek-V3 from their configuration files, times an MoE layer against dense layers on this page's CPU, and shows the bias trick DeepSeek-V3 uses to keep experts evenly loaded. Nothing is trained. A dense transformer's FLOPs at inference equal its parameter count (times 2 for forward pass). Scale up a dense model and every token pays the full bill. By 2024 the frontier was hitting a compute wall: to be meaningfully smarter, you needed exponentially more FLOPs per token. Mixture of Experts breaks this link. Each token picks its own k experts and gets a gated mixture of their outputs. Idea 2 · The load-balancing problem If the router puts 90% of tokens through expert 3, the other experts starve. Three fixes have been tried: Auxiliary load-balancing loss (Switch Transformer, Mixtral). Add a penalty proportional to the variance in expert usage. Works, but adds a hyperparameter and a second gradient signal. Expert capacity + token dropping (early Switch). Each expert processes at most tokens; overflow tokens skip the layer. Hurts quality. Auxiliary-loss-free balancing (DeepSeek-V3). Add a learned per-expert bias that shifts the router's top-k selection. Bias is updated outside the training loss. No penalty on the main objective. 2024's big unlock. DeepSeek-V3's approach: after each training step, for every expert, check if its usage is above or below the target. Nudge the bias by ±γ . Selection uses scores + bias . Expert probabilities used for gating are the raw scores unchanged. Decouples routing from expression. Idea 3 · Shared experts DeepSeek-V2/V3 also split experts into shared and routed . Every token passes through all shared experts. Routed experts are picked via top-k. Shared experts capture common knowledge; routed experts specialize. V3 runs 1 shared expert plus top-8 of 256 routed. Solutions Solution P1 · Close to the narrow one, with overhead Close to the narrow one, but not equal: about 150 ms against 100 ms for the narrow dense layer and about 1,000 ms for the wide one (one CPU core). The MoE does the multiply-adds of a width-1,024 layer per token (4 experts of width 256) while storing as many weights as the width-8,192 layer, so most of the wide layer's cost disappears. The remaining gap to the narrow layer is the price of sparsity: the router, sorting tokens by expert, 32 small matrix products and scattering the results back. Solution B1 · The bias leaks into the output With gates from the biased scores, the balancing bias now changes how much each chosen expert contributes to the output, not only which experts are chosen. An expert that is under-used gets a positive bias, so whenever it is picked its output is weighted up, regardless of whether it fits the token. The load statistics, a bookkeeping signal, then shape the model's predictions, and the bias drifts with the batch mix, so the same token can be treated differently from batch to batch. DeepSeek-V3 keeps the bias for selection only so that balancing never alters the function the gates compute, which is why it needs no auxiliary loss on the main objective. In plain words first The idea in one line Training is parallel and FLOP-bound. Inference is serial and memory-bound. Different bottleneck, different tricks. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means KV cache "The trick that makes decoding fast" Stored K and V from every prefix token; new queries attend to them instead of recomputing. HBM "GPU main memory" High Bandwidth Memory; 80 GB on H100, 192 GB on B200. ~3 TB/s bandwidth. SRAM "On-chip memory" Per-SM fast memory, ~256 KB per SM on H100. ~30 TB/s bandwidth. Flash Attention "Tiled attention kernel" Computes attention without materializing N×N in HBM. Continuous batching "No-wait batching" Swap finished sequences out, new ones in, without draining the batch. PagedAttention "vLLM's headline" KV cache allocated in fixed blocks with a page table; eliminates fragmentation. Prefix caching "Reuse long prompts" Cache KV for a shared prefix across requests; major cost cut for agents. Speculative decoding "Draft + verify" Cheap draft model proposes tokens; big model verifies k in one pass. The problem In plain words first When a language model writes, it produces one token at a time, and each new token must attend to every earlier one. Recomputing the keys and values of all earlier tokens at every step would be wasteful, because they never change; the KV cache stores them, so each step only computes the new token's own. The cache then becomes the main user of memory during long conversations. Attention itself has a second problem: the full table of scores between all pairs of tokens is huge, and moving it in and out of a GPU's main memory is slower than the arithmetic. FlashAttention computes attention in tiles that stay in fast on-chip memory and never builds the whole table, while giving exactly the same result. This lesson runs the lesson's cache and tiled softmax, measures a real model's generation with and without the cache, checks the cache's size against the formula, and compares full, tiled and fused attention on 4,096 tokens. Nothing is trained. A naive autoregressive decoder does ) work to generate tokens: at each step it recomputes attention over the full prefix. For a 4K-token response that is 16M attention operations, most of them redundant. Every hidden state of a prefix token is deterministic once computed — you only need to run the new token's query against the cached keys and values of everything before. On top of that, attention itself moves a lot of data. Standard attention materializes an N×N score matrix, N×d softmax output, N×d final output — too many reads and writes to HBM. For N≥2K, attention becomes memory-bound before it becomes FLOP-bound. Classic attention kernels underuse modern GPUs by 4–10×. Two optimizations pushed frontier inference from "slow" to "fast": KV cache. Store the K and V vectors of every prefix token. Each new token's attention is one query against the cached keys, and each step computes keys and values for one new token instead of recomputing them for the whole prefix: over a generation of N tokens, N token states instead of about N²/2. Flash Attention (Dao et al., 2022). Tile the attention computation so the full N×N matrix never hits HBM. All of softmax + matmul happens in SRAM. FlashAttention-2 roughly doubled the first version's speed; FlashAttention-3 reaches up to about 740 TFLOP/s in FP16 on an H100, about 75% of the chip's peak. By 2026 both are universal. Every production inference stack (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang, llama.cpp) assumes them. Every frontier model ships with Flash Attention enabled. Solutions Solution P1 · About 4 times here, and growing About 4 times slower here: roughly 9 seconds with the cache and 35 without, for identical tokens. Without the cache, step reprocesses all tokens, about 21,500 token states per layer over the 200 steps instead of 207; the gap is "only" 4× because for a model this small each step's fixed overhead (Python, launching operations) is large compared with the arithmetic. The ratio grows with the length of the text: at thousands of tokens, recomputation dominates completely, which is why no serving system decodes without a cache. Solution B1 · Blocks weighted on different scales Each block's exponentials are computed relative to the maximum seen so far . Without rescaling, contributions accumulated under an old, smaller maximum are not shrunk when a larger score arrives, so earlier blocks keep weights computed on a different scale from later ones and the output becomes a wrongly weighted mixture. With one block there is only one maximum, so the bug is invisible. The error is largest when a much higher score appears late in the sequence: the early blocks' terms are then too large by a factor of ​ − m old ​ , which can be enormous, and the sum can even overflow. Testing a tiled kernel only with inputs whose maximum comes first would never catch it. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Estimate it You serve Qwen/Qwen3-8B on one GPU with a maximum model length of 8,192 tokens. At startup the server prints a maximum concurrency of 2.94, and a manager asks if the GPU can serve only three users at a time. Your users send about 512 prompt tokens and get about 128 tokens back. How do you answer? Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The startup number assumes that every user fills the full maximum model length, and real users hold much less. Count the KV bytes for one token, divide the KV pool by that number, and then divide the pool by the context that one user really holds. On the L4 in the vLLM manual, the pool of 24,096 tokens fits 37 users with 640 tokens each. Bytes for one token. Every token in a running request keeps its keys and values in GPU memory until the request ends: Copy The factor 2 counts the key and the value. Qwen/Qwen3-8B has 36 layers, 8 KV heads and a head size of 128. In BF16 a value takes 2 bytes, so one token takes 144 KiB. The KV heads decide this number, not the parameter count: Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 has more weights but takes 96 KiB for each token. From bytes to users. The server gives the KV cache the memory that is left after the weights and the startup profile. The pool line in the log gives the result in tokens: Copy The 2.94 divides the pool by the full 8,192 tokens. A user with 512 prompt tokens and 128 output tokens holds 640 tokens at the end of the answer. The same pool holds 37 such users. During the load sweep the log showed 40 running requests with the cache 99.5 percent full, because users early in their answer hold fewer tokens. What to change if it is still too small. Lower the maximum model length to the longest context that users send. This keeps one long request from taking a large share of the pool. It does not add users here, because the pool stays the same. Use an FP8 KV cache. It halves the bytes per token. Use FP8 weights to free memory for the cache. Use a GPU with more memory, or split the model across GPUs. Plausible wrong answers. "Divide the GPU memory by the model size." The weights are only one part. The users that fit depend on the KV pool and on the context per user. "The maximum concurrency in the log is the user limit." It assumes that each user fills the maximum model length, which real users do not. "More parameters always mean more KV memory per token." The bytes per token depend on the layers, the KV heads and the head size. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) What happens to a request that needs more blocks than are free? Expected: it waits in the queue. A running request that needs a block when none is free is stopped and computed again later. (level 2) Why does the mixture-of-experts model use less KV memory per token than the dense model? Expected: it has fewer KV heads, and the KV heads, not the weights, set the bytes per token. (level 3) How do you check your count after a start? Expected: read the memory line and the pool line in the startup log, and compare them with the count from the model config. (level 3) What is the cost of the FP8 KV cache? Expected: a possible loss of quality, so measure it on your own eval before you ship it. Where it is taught. The memory section of vLLM 101 counts the pool from the startup log, and the KV cache lesson builds the cache. Estimate it A decoder generates 100 tokens one at a time from an empty prompt. Count the token states each loop computes for the prefix: a naive loop, and a loop that caches the key and value vectors of earlier tokens. Then count the query-key comparisons that remain with the store, and name what the store deliberately leaves out. Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The naive loop runs every prefix token through the layer again at every step, so it computes 1 plus 2 plus 3 and so on up to 100 token states, which is 5050 and grows with the square of the length. With the stored keys and values, each step computes the state of the new token only, 100 in total. The new query still meets every stored key, so the cached loop still makes 5050 query-key comparisons: the store removes the recomputed key and value vectors, not the comparisons. The store holds no queries, because a past token never asks a question again; only the newest token does. Why the prefix can be reused. Every hidden state of a prefix token is deterministic once it is computed, and the causal mask means it never depends on a later token. So the key and the value of token t are the same at step t plus one as they were at step t. Recomputing them is pure waste. The two loops. Copy For N equal to 100 the naive count is 5050 token states and the cached count is 100. The lesson's code runs a ten-token example and counts query-key comparisons instead: it prints the same count for both loops and confirms that the outputs match. At 100 tokens those comparisons total 5050 in both loops, so the attention step itself still grows with the length at each step. For a response of a few thousand tokens the naive count of token states is in the millions, most of them redundant. What is stored. Per layer and per head, two growing lists: the keys and the values of every token so far. Copy The memory grows linearly with the generated length; that is the price for not recomputing the prefix. Why queries are not stored. The query of a token is used once, at the step where that token is the newest one. After that, the token is only ever looked up, never looking. Storing queries would cost memory and buy nothing. What does not go away. Generation is still serial: step t needs the token from step t minus one. The lesson calls this the autoregressive tax. Training avoids it by processing the whole sequence in one masked pass; inference cannot. Plausible wrong answers. "The store keeps the attention weights." It keeps keys and values; the weights are recomputed from the new query every step. "The store saves memory." It costs memory and saves compute; the trade is memory for the recomputed key and value vectors. "Queries must be stored too." A past token's query is never used again. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) What grows in memory as generation proceeds? Expected: the stored keys and values, per layer and per head, one entry per generated token. (level 2) Why is a prefix token's key still valid after new tokens arrive? Expected: the causal mask means its hidden state only ever depended on earlier tokens, so later tokens cannot change it. (level 2) You edit one word in the middle of the prompt. What happens to the store? Expected: everything from that position on is invalid and must be recomputed; the part before it stays valid. (level 3) When does attention become bound by memory traffic instead of arithmetic? Expected: when the N by N score matrix is large enough that moving it through memory dominates; the lesson puts that at about 2K tokens and beyond. Where it is taught. The KV cache lesson counts both loops and the causal language modeling lesson explains why generation is serial. Explain the mechanism A colleague refuses to enable Flash Attention on a quality-sensitive model because "approximate attention changes the outputs". Is it an approximation? Explain what the kernel changes and what it keeps, with the memory argument that motivated it. Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. It is exact. The kernel tiles the computation so the full N by N score matrix never lands in the GPU's main memory; each tile is scored, exponentiated and accumulated in on-chip memory with a running maximum and a running sum, and the final normalization matches the single-pass softmax up to floating-point reordering. What changes is the memory traffic: three round trips to main memory become one write per output tile, and the footprint drops from N squared to N. The numbers that leave the kernel are the same as standard attention. Why standard attention is slow. Copy Three round trips through high-bandwidth memory. On the reference accelerator that memory moves about 3 TB/s while the on-chip memory moves about 30 TB/s, so every round trip is a factor-of-ten slowdown against keeping the data on chip. From about 2K tokens, attention becomes memory-bound before it becomes compute-bound, and classic kernels underuse the hardware by 4 to 10 times. The tiling. Copy The score matrix exists only one tile at a time. The backward pass recomputes some values instead of storing them, which is a second memory win. Why the result is exact. The softmax needs the global maximum and the global sum over a row, and the kernel only sees one tile at a time. It keeps a running pair, maximum and sum, and whenever a new tile raises the maximum it rescales the earlier sum and the earlier partial output by the exponential of the old maximum minus the new one. At the end every term is expressed against the same global maximum and divided by the same global sum. The lesson's description is "bit-identical output to standard attention", with the caveat that 16-bit arithmetic is not associative, so reordering can move the last bits. Versions. Version Year Change Speedup on the reference hardware Flash 1 2022 tiled on-chip kernel 2 times on the earlier accelerator Flash 2 2023 better parallelism, causal-first ordering 3 times on the same Flash 3 2024 asynchrony and FP8 on the newer accelerator 1.5 to 2 times Flash 4 2026 five-stage pipeline for the latest generation inference-first, forward pass only at launch What to tell the colleague. Run the two kernels on the same inputs and compare the outputs. The difference is at the level of 16-bit rounding, the same noise you get from a different batch size, not a change to the model. Plausible wrong answers. "It drops small attention weights to save work." Nothing is dropped; every key contributes through the running sum. "It only helps at very long context." It helps whenever attention is memory-bound, and the lesson reports 2 to 4 times on the earlier accelerator for ordinary lengths. "It reduces the FLOPs of attention." The arithmetic is the same; the saving is in memory traffic. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why does the kernel keep a running maximum and not just a running sum? Expected: numerical stability; exponentials of raw scores overflow, so every exponential is taken relative to the maximum seen so far and rescaled when it changes. (level 3) Why recompute values during training instead of storing the softmax output? Expected: storing it would mean materializing the N by N matrix, which is the thing the kernel avoids. (level 4) The newest version is forward-only at launch. What does that mean for your stack? Expected: serving can use it, training keeps the previous version until the backward kernel ships. (level 4) Is the output identical across batch sizes? Expected: not bit for bit, because the reduction order changes in 16-bit arithmetic; that is a determinism question, not an approximation. It computes the attention output for one query against keys and values in blocks of four. python def tiled_softmax_dot(q, K, V, tile=4): m = float("-inf") s = 0.0 out = [0.0] * len(V[0]) for start in range(0, len(K), tile): k_block = K[start:start + tile] v_block = V[start:start + tile] scores = [sum(qi * ki for qi, ki in zip(q, k)) for k in k_block] new_m = max(m, *scores) exp_old = math.exp(m - new_m) if m != float("-inf") else 0.0 exp_new = [math.exp(sc - new_m) for sc in scores] s = s * exp_old + sum(exp_new) for j in range(len(out)): out[j] = out[j] * exp_old + sum(e * v[j] for e, v in zip(exp_new, v_block)) m = new_m return [o / s for o in out] Explain the role of exp_old , argue that the result equals the one-shot softmax(qK^T) V , and point at the input that makes this code produce a NaN. Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The loop keeps a running maximum m and a running sum s over the blocks seen so far. When a block raises the maximum, exp_old is the exponential of the old maximum minus the new one, and it rescales the sum and the partial output so that every earlier term is expressed against the new maximum; a block that does not raise the maximum gives exp_old of one. At the end each weight is the exponential of its score minus the global maximum, divided by the global sum, which is exactly the stable softmax. The fragile input is a first block whose scores are all minus infinity, as a fully masked block would be: new_m stays minus infinity, and exp_new evaluates minus infinity minus minus infinity, which is NaN. The invariant. After each block, out holds the sum over all keys seen so far of exp(score - m) * v , and s holds the sum of exp(score - m) , both relative to the current m . The identity that makes the rescale correct is Copy so multiplying the old accumulators by exp(m_old - m_new) moves them to the new reference point without touching any individual score again. The first block has no old reference, which is why exp_old is zero when m is still minus infinity: the empty accumulators contribute nothing. Why the final division is exact. Division by s happens once, at the end, with the global maximum in every exponential. That is the definition of a numerically stable softmax over the whole row, computed without ever holding the whole row. The working set is one block of keys and values and one output vector. The real kernel does this per block of queries, with blocks of keys and values streamed through on-chip memory, and writes each output tile once. The NaN. A causal kernel skips blocks that lie entirely above the diagonal; a kernel that applies the mask by setting scores to minus infinity must guard the case where every score in the block is minus infinity. Here max(-inf, -inf, ...) is minus infinity, and exp(-inf - (-inf)) is NaN, which then poisons s and out . The guard: skip a block whose maximum is minus infinity, or test new_m before computing exp_new . What a reviewer tests. Equality with the one-shot softmax on random inputs, within floating-point tolerance. A second block whose scores are all lower than the first block's maximum, so that the rescale path with exp_old equal to one is exercised. A block whose scores are all higher, so that exp_old is less than one and the earlier terms shrink. A fully masked first block, which must not produce NaN. Plausible wrong answers. " exp_old is a decay factor like a learning rate." It is an exact change of reference point; the output is identical to the one-shot formula. "You could store the scores and normalize at the end." That stores the full row, which is the memory cost the kernel exists to avoid. "Each block should be normalized by its own sum." A per-block normalization breaks the global softmax; only the final division is correct. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) What does a smaller tile cost and buy? Expected: more rescale steps and more loop overhead against a smaller working set on chip; the real kernel picks the tile to fit on-chip memory. (level 3) Why is exp_old set to zero and not one on the first block? Expected: there is no earlier term to carry; the accumulators are empty, and exp(-inf - new_m) would be zero anyway for a finite new_m . (level 4) How does the causal mask change the loop in a production kernel? Expected: blocks fully above the diagonal are skipped rather than masked, and partially masked blocks apply minus infinity per entry before the maximum is taken. (level 4) Where does the backward pass get the softmax values it needs? Expected: it recomputes them from the stored row maximum and row sum instead of storing the N by N matrix. Where it is taught. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python, Rust. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line The 2020 Kaplan paper said: bigger model, lower loss. The 2022 Hoffmann paper said: you were under-training. Compute goes into two buckets — parameters and tokens — and the split is not obvious. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Parameters (N) "Model size" Non-embedding weight count; determines capacity. Tokens (D) "Training data" Number of training tokens seen; determines how well the parameters get used. Compute (C) "FLOPs spent" Approximately 6 × N × D for a standard transformer. Chinchilla-optimal "D/N ≈ 20" Ratio that minimizes loss per FLOP of pretraining. Over-training "Past Chinchilla" Spend extra training FLOPs to save inference FLOPs; D/N >> 20. Irreducible loss "The floor" The $E$ term in the scaling law; the entropy of the data itself. Emergent capability "Sudden jumps at scale" Often a scorer artifact; continuous loss is smooth. Effective compute "Training-efficiency multiplier" Better data / optimizer / architecture multiplies how far a FLOP goes. The problem In plain words first Training a language model costs compute, and compute can be spent two ways: a bigger model, or more training text. Scaling laws are formulas, fitted to many training runs, that predict the final loss from those two numbers. The 2022 Chinchilla study found the best split for a fixed training budget is roughly 20 training tokens per parameter, far more data than earlier models used. Today's models are trained on hundreds or thousands of tokens per parameter anyway, because a smaller model is cheaper every time it answers a question. This lesson runs the lesson's Chinchilla calculator, then measures real losses of EleutherAI's Pythia models (several sizes trained on the same data, with checkpoints from during training) on the same Wikipedia text, and works out when it pays to train a smaller model for longer. Nothing is trained. When you have C FLOPs of training compute and want the best model, you face two knobs: How many parameters (N)? Bigger model, higher capacity. How many training tokens (D)? More data, better use of capacity. FLOPs scale approximately as 6 × N × D . You can push N up and D down, or D up and N down. Which is better? Before 2022, the answer was "push N hard." The team calls it an emergent ability and asks for a larger budget to find the next jump. How do you evaluate the claim before you sign? Level 4 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Ask what the scorer is. Exact match and thresholded accuracy are discontinuous: a model that gets most digits right scores zero until it gets all of them right, so a smooth gain in the underlying probabilities shows up as a cliff. Re-score the same checkpoints with a continuous metric such as the cross-entropy of the target answers; if that curve is smooth, the jump belongs to the scorer and not to the model. Plan the budget against the continuous curve, which the scaling law predicts reliably. The argument. The 2023 analysis of emergence showed that the abilities usually cited, arithmetic and multi-step reasoning among them, were measured with discontinuous scoring. Under a continuous metric the same models improve smoothly with scale. By 2026 the working consensus is: predictions from continuous loss are reliable, and benchmark jumps are often artifacts of the scorer. What to do with the checkpoints you have. Keep the prompts and the targets fixed. For each checkpoint, log the per-token probability of the correct answer and the cross-entropy over the answer tokens. Plot both against the parameter count and against the training compute. Add a partial-credit scorer, such as the share of correct digits, to see where the cliff disappears. If the probability curve is smooth, the model was getting closer all along and the benchmark hid it. What it means for the budget. Fit the loss on the checkpoints and read where the next size lands on the continuous curve. Then calibrate the discontinuous benchmark against that curve: at which loss does accuracy cross the product threshold? Sample more sizes near that point instead of betting on a surprise. A product threshold can be real for the user and still be predictable for the planner. Where real changes of regime do show up. In-context learning, following a few examples with no fine-tuning, is usually described as appearing around the 6B to 13B range. The lesson's position is still to measure it with a continuous metric before you call it a discontinuity, because the same scorer problem applies. Plausible wrong answers. "Accuracy is the ground truth and loss is a proxy." Accuracy with a hard threshold throws away the information that shows the trend; the loss is what the model optimizes and what the law predicts. "Emergence means the scaling law broke." The law describes the continuous loss, which keeps its shape while the thresholded score jumps. "Train the bigger model and see." That is the expensive experiment the analysis lets you avoid; re-score what you already have first. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Give an example of a discontinuous scorer and its continuous counterpart. Expected: exact match on a multi-digit answer against the log-probability or the digit-level accuracy of the same answer. (level 4) How does this change the way you plan a training budget? Expected: predict the loss from the law, calibrate the benchmark against the loss, and place runs near the threshold instead of hoping for a jump. (level 4) The product threshold really is binary for the user. Does the artifact argument still matter? Expected: yes; the threshold is real for the product, but its position is predictable from the smooth curve, which is what you need to budget. (level 4) What would convince you that a jump is not a scorer artifact? Expected: the continuous metric also shows a kink at the same scale, replicated across seeds and data orderings. The problem In plain words first This capstone puts every piece of the phase into one small GPT: character embeddings, positions, a stack of pre-norm blocks with causal attention and a SwiGLU feed-forward, a tied output layer and the shift-by-one loss. Trained on the complete works of Shakespeare as plain characters, such a model learns to write text that looks like Shakespeare. Training it takes many minutes even at this size, so on this page the model is built, measured and run, but not trained: the runs load the real Shakespeare file, count the model's parameters, show why its starting weights must be small, time one training step to estimate the full cost, and compare what the untrained model writes with a simple model built by counting letter pairs, which is the bar a trained model must beat. You've read every paper. You've implemented attention, multi-head splits, positional encodings, encoder and decoder blocks, BERT and GPT losses, MoE, KV cache. Now make them work together on a real task. The capstone: train a small decoder-only transformer end-to-end on a character-level language modeling task. It reads Shakespeare. It generates new Shakespeare. It is small enough to train on a laptop in under 10 minutes. It is correct enough that swapping in a bigger dataset and longer training gets you a real LM. This is the "nanoGPT" of the course. It is not original — Karpathy's 2023 nanoGPT tutorial is the reference implementation every student writes at least once. Solutions Solution P1 · Far worse Far worse: about 89 nats, against 4.17 for a uniform guess. With PyTorch's default nn.Embedding initialisation each embedding row has entries of standard deviation 1, and because the output head is tied to the embedding, each logit is a dot product of a 128-dimensional hidden state with such a row: values of to . The softmax then puts almost all probability on an essentially random character, so the true one gets a tiny probability and a huge loss. Training would spend its first steps just shrinking the weights; initialising them with standard deviation 0.02 (GPT-2's choice) starts at 4.26 instead. Solution B1 · Positions run out The position table has block_size = 256 rows. Without the crop, the 257th position asks pos_emb for row 256, which does not exist, and PyTorch raises an IndexError ; earlier, while the text is shorter than 256, nothing goes wrong, which is why the bug survives short tests. A learned position table cannot extrapolate at all. A RoPE model has no table and runs on, but its rotations reach angles never seen in training, and quality degrades past the trained length unless the frequencies are rescaled (Lesson 7.4). Cropping to the last 256 tokens keeps the model inside what it was trained on, at the cost of forgetting earlier text. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python, Rust. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Full attention is a circle. Every token sees every token, and memory pays the price. Three variants bend the shape of the circle and recover half the cost. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Sliding window attention (SWA) "Local attention" Each query attends to its last $W$ tokens; KV cache shrinks to $O(W)$. Effective receptive field "How far back the model sees" In an $L$-layer SWA stack with window $W$, up to $L \times W$ tokens. Longformer / BigBird "Local + global + random" Sparse patterns with a few always-attending global tokens; early long-context approach. Native Sparse Attention "DeepSeek's kernel trick" Learn block-level sparsity; skip zero blocks at the kernel level while keeping quality. Differential attention "Two maps, one subtracts" DIFF Transformer: subtract a learned $\lambda$ times a second attention map from the first to cancel attention sinks. Attention sink "Weight bleeds to token 0" Softmax normalization forces rows to sum to 1; uninformative queries dump weight on position 0. FlexAttention "Mask-as-Python" PyTorch 2.5+ API that compiles arbitrary mask functions into FlashAttention-shape kernels. Layer type mix "5:1 SWA-to-global" Interleave sparse and full attention layers in a stack to keep quality at lower memory. The problem In plain words first In full attention every word looks at every earlier word, so the work and the memory for the cached keys and values grow with the length of the text. Three families of variants limit who looks at whom. Sliding-window attention lets each word see only the last few hundred or thousand words; models stay able to use the whole text by keeping some layers global. Sparse attention picks a pattern of pairs (nearby words plus some far ones, or blocks chosen by a learned scorer). Differential attention computes two attention patterns and subtracts one from the other to cancel noise. This lesson draws the masks with the lesson's code, then takes a real model, Gemma 3 270M, which mixes five sliding-window layers with one global layer, and shows that it finds a pass key 1,400 tokens back, keeps less than half the cache, and fails completely once every layer is made sliding. Nothing is trained. Full attention costs ) memory and ) compute in sequence length. For a 128K-context Llama 3 70B that is 16 billion attention entries per layer, times 80 layers. Flash Attention ( Lesson 7.12 ) hides the ) activation memory but does not change the arithmetic cost — every token still attends to every other token. Three classes of variants change the topology of the attention matrix itself: Sliding window attention (SWA). Each token attends to a fixed window of neighbors, not the full prefix (Gemma 2 and 3, Mistral 7B v0.1, gpt-oss). Memory and compute drop to where is the window. Sparse / block attention. Only selected pairs (i, j) get scored; the rest are forced to zero weight. Longformer, BigBird, OpenAI sparse transformer. Differential attention. Compute two attention maps with separate Q/K projections, subtract one from the other. Kills the "attention sink" that bleeds weight into the first few tokens. Microsoft's DIFF Transformer (2024). These coexist. 2025–2026 open models mix them: Gemma 3 uses five sliding-window layers (window 1,024) for every global layer, gpt-oss alternates 128-token windows with full attention, and DeepSeek-V3.2 adds a learned sparse selection on top of full attention. Differential attention is still a research result rather than a production default. Idea 1 · Sliding Window Attention (SWA) Each query at position attends only to positions in (causal SWA) or (bidirectional). Tokens outside the window get in the score matrix. Copy For and , the score matrix has 1024 × 8192 non-zero rows in expectation — an 8× reduction. KV cache shrinks with SWA. Only the last tokens of K and V need to be kept per layer. For a Gemma-3-ish config (1024 window, 128K context), KV cache drops 128×. Quality cost. SWA-only transformers struggle with long-range retrieval. The fix: interleave SWA layers with full-attention layers. Gemma 3 uses 5:1 SWA:global. Mistral 7B used a causal-SWA stack where information "flows forward" through overlapping windows — each layer extends effective receptive field by , and after L layers the model can attend L × W tokens back. Idea 2 · Sparse / Block Attention Pick an N × N sparsity pattern ahead of time. Three canonical shapes: Local + strided (OpenAI sparse transformer). Attend to the last tokens plus every stride -th token before that. Captures both local and long-range at ​ ) compute. Longformer / BigBird. Local window + a small set of global tokens (e.g. [CLS] ) that attend to everyone and are attended by everyone + random-sparse links. Empirical 2× context at matched quality. Learned sparse attention (DeepSeek, 2025). Learn which blocks or tokens of (Q, K) matter and skip the rest at kernel level: Native Sparse Attention (research), and DeepSeek Sparse Attention in DeepSeek-V3.2, where a light "indexer" picks the tokens each query attends to. Sparse attention is a kernel-engineering story. The math is simple (mask the score matrix); the win comes from never loading the zero entries into SRAM. FlashAttention-3 and the 2026 FlexAttention API make custom sparse patterns first-class in PyTorch. Idea 3 · Differential Attention (DIFF Transformer, 2024) Regular attention has an "attention sink" problem: softmax forces every row to sum to 1, so tokens that don't want to attend to anything in particular dump weight on the first token (or the first few). This steals capacity that should have gone to real content. Differential attention fixes this by computing two attention maps and subtracting: ​ A 2 ​ DiffAttn ​ = softmax ( Q 1 ​ K 1 T ​ / d ​ ) = softmax ( Q 2 ​ K 2 T ​ / d ​ ) = ( A 1 ​ − λ ⋅ A 2 ​ ) V ​ where is a learned scalar (typically 0.5–0.8). A1 captures real content weights; A2 captures the sink. Subtraction cancels the sink, reallocates weight to relevant tokens. Reported results (Microsoft, 2024): a DIFF Transformer matched a standard Transformer's language-modelling loss with about 65% of the parameters or training tokens, and retrieved key facts from long contexts more reliably. It has not yet been adopted by the major open model families. The key sits about 1,450 tokens before the question, nearly three 512-token windows back. In theory sliding layers can relay information forward window by window ( tokens of reach), but the model was trained with global layers doing that job, and without them the information never arrives. Solution B1 · Negative starts allow the whole prefix range(lo, i + 1) with a negative lo starts at a negative index, and M[i][j] with negative j addresses columns counted from the end of the row: for row 0 with window = 4 , lo = -3 , so the loop unmasks columns and 0. The first tokens would then attend to the last tokens of the sequence, future positions the causal mask must hide, and the model could read answers during training.
