In plain words first The idea in one line Autoregressive decoding is serial. Each token waits for the previous one. Speculative decoding breaks the chain: a cheap model drafts N tokens, the expensive model verifies all N in one forward pass. When the draft is right you paid one big forward for N generations. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Draft model "The cheap one" A smaller model that proposes candidate tokens; usually 10–50× cheaper than the verifier. Verifier "The big one" The target model whose distribution we preserve; runs once per speculative step. Acceptance rate ($\alpha$) "How often the draft is right" Per-token probability that the verifier accepts the draft. 0.7–0.9 typical. Residual distribution "The rejection fallback" (q - p)_+ normalized; sampling from this on rejection preserves the verifier's distribution. Bonus token "The free one" When all N drafts accepted, sample one more from the verifier's next-step distribution. Medusa "Draft-less speculative" Multiple LM heads on the verifier predict positions t+1..t+k in parallel. EAGLE "Hidden-state draft" Tiny transformer draft conditioned on the verifier's last-layer hidden states. Lookahead decoding "Jacobi iteration" Self-speculation using a fixed-point iteration; no draft model. Tree attention "Verify many candidates at once" Branching verification that considers several draft continuations simultaneously. KV rollback "Undo rejected drafts" Scratch KV buffer; commit on acceptance, discard on reject. The problem In plain words first A large language model writes one token per full pass through its weights, and on a GPU each pass is slow mostly because all the weights must be read from memory, not because of the arithmetic. Speculative decoding lets a small, fast model guess the next few tokens, then has the large model check all the guesses in a single pass. Guesses it agrees with are kept; at the first disagreement the large model's own choice is used instead. A clever acceptance rule makes the result exactly as if the large model had generated alone, so quality is unchanged; only the number of large-model passes drops. This lesson checks that rule with the lesson's code, then runs SmolLM2-360M with SmolLM2-135M as the drafter: the output is identical and the large model runs ten times less often, yet on this page's CPU it is only slightly faster, which shows exactly when the trick pays. Nothing is trained. A 70B LLM sampling one token takes ~30 ms on an H100. A 3B draft model takes ~3 ms. If we let the 3B draft 5 tokens ahead, then run the 70B once to verify all 5, the total is ms for up to 5 accepted tokens — versus 5×30 = 150 ms for straight-line generation. That is the full speculative-decoding pitch: trade a small amount of extra GPU memory (draft model) for 2–4× lower decode latency. The trick has to preserve the distribution. Speculative sampling, introduced by Leviathan et al. (2023) and by Chen et al. concurrently, guarantees that the output sequence is identically distributed to what the big model would have produced on its own. No quality tradeoff. Just faster. Four families of draft-verifier pairs dominate 2026 inference: Vanilla speculative (Leviathan 2023). Separate draft model (e.g., Llama 3 1B) + verifier (e.g., Llama 3 70B). Medusa (Cai 2024). Multiple decoding heads on the verifier predict positions t+1..t+k in parallel. No separate draft model. EAGLE family (Li 2024, 2025). Lightweight draft that reuses the verifier's hidden states; closer acceptance rate than vanilla; 3–4× typical. Lookahead decoding (Fu 2024). Jacobi iteration; no draft model required at all. Self-speculation. Niche but dependency-free. Every major inference stack supports speculative decoding: vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM offer draft models and EAGLE drafts, and llama.cpp offers draft-model speculation. Idea 3 · Medusa — drafts without a draft model Medusa replaces the draft model with extra output heads on the verifier. At position t : Copy Each head outputs its own logits. At inference you sample from each head to get a candidate sequence, then verify with one forward pass using a tree-attention scheme that considers all candidate continuations at once. Idea 4 · EAGLE — better draft by reusing hidden states EAGLE-1/2/3 (Li et al., 2024–2025) makes the draft model a tiny transformer (typically 1 layer) that ingests the verifier's last-layer hidden states. Because the draft sees the verifier's feature representation, its predictions correlate strongly with the verifier's output distribution. Acceptance rates climb from ~0.6 (vanilla) to 0.85+. These are per-token rates on chat benchmarks, with a draft trained on matching chat data. On mixed production traffic, Phase 17 · 05 plans with 0.6 to 0.8 for EAGLE-3, and domain traffic can be lower. EAGLE-2 (2024) made the tree of candidate continuations dynamic; EAGLE-3 (2025) fuses features from several of the verifier's layers and trains the draft on its own predictions, raising acceptance further. vLLM and SGLang support EAGLE drafts for common open models. Idea 5 · The KV cache dance Verification feeds draft tokens into the verifier in one forward pass. This extends the verifier's KV cache by entries. If some drafts are rejected, you must roll the cache back to the accepted prefix length. Faster: hardly, about 7.5 seconds against 8.8, even though the target runs only 10 times instead of 96. Read the code Read this toy speculative step from the lesson. q_model is the verifier and p_model is the draft; each returns a probability vector for the next token given a prefix. python def spec_step(prefix, q_model, p_model, N, rng): drafts, p_probs = [], [] ctx = list(prefix) for _ in range(N): p_dist = p_model(ctx) d = sample(p_dist, rng) drafts.append(d) p_probs.append(p_dist[d]) ctx.append(d) q_dists = [q_model(prefix + drafts[:i]) for i in range(N + 1)] for i, d in enumerate(drafts): u = rng.random() if u < min(1.0, q_dists[i][d] / p_probs[i]): prefix = prefix + [d] else: res = residual_dist(q_dists[i], p_model(prefix)) prefix = prefix + [sample(res, rng)] return prefix return prefix + [sample(q_dists[N], rng)] Why does q_dists hold N plus 1 entries, what happens when the first draft token fails the test, and why does the residual use p_model(prefix) rather than p_probs[i] ? Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The verifier gives a distribution at every drafted position and one more, N plus 1 in total, because when every draft is accepted the extra distribution supplies a bonus token at no extra verifier cost. At the first rejection at position i the code samples from the residual, the positive part of the verifier's distribution minus the draft's, renormalized, appends that token and returns, so every later draft is discarded. The residual needs the draft's whole distribution at that position, a vector, and p_probs[i] kept only the scalar probability of the token that was drafted. Why the rule is exact. Accepting a drafted token with probability min(1, q(d) / p(d)) and otherwise sampling from (q - p) clamped at zero and renormalized gives samples distributed exactly as q. The theorem holds however poor p is: a bad draft rejects more often, and the output distribution does not move. That is the only reason the method is allowed in production. It is a latency optimization with no quality trade. Why N plus 1 verifier distributions. The verifier is queried on the prefix plus the first i drafts for i from zero to N. The first N distributions judge the drafts. The last one is the verifier's own next-token distribution after all N drafts; if everything was accepted it is free, and the step emits N plus 1 tokens from one verifier pass. In the toy the N plus 1 calls stand for a single batched forward pass over the prefix plus the drafts. The rejection branch. Return after the first rejection. Positions after it were drafted on a context that is now known to be wrong, so their verifier distributions are not for the sequence that is being generated. The step always produces at least one token, the residual sample, and at most N plus 1. The residual needs a vector. residual_dist(q, p) subtracts the two distributions element by element, clamps negatives to zero and renormalizes. p_probs[i] is one number, the draft's probability of the drafted token, enough for the acceptance test and not for the residual. The call p_model(prefix) recomputes the draft's full distribution at the position being corrected; in a real implementation the draft's distributions are kept from the drafting loop instead of being recomputed. The greedy case. At temperature zero the rule collapses to a comparison: accept if the drafted token equals the verifier's argmax, otherwise emit the argmax and stop. How you would test it. Run the step 10,000 times and compare the histogram of produced tokens with direct samples from q; a chi-square test passes within sampling error. Then perturb p away from q and watch the acceptance rate fall while the histogram stays put. Plausible wrong answers. "Accept a draft whenever the verifier gives it a probability above a threshold." A threshold changes the output distribution; the ratio test with the residual is what keeps it exact. "On a rejection, resample from the verifier's distribution at that position." That over-weights tokens the draft already favored; the residual removes exactly that mass. "Drop the bonus token to be safe." It is a sample from the verifier's own distribution and costs nothing; dropping it wastes a token per step. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) p_probs[i] is zero and the code divides by it. Can that happen? Expected: no, the token was sampled from p so its probability is positive; the production version still guards the division and accepts when p is zero. (level 3) When does residual_dist divide by zero, and what should it return? Expected: when q is nowhere larger than p, which means the two are equal; return q itself. (level 4) What does the single batched verifier pass do to the verifier's stored keys and values? Expected: it extends them by N entries, and a rejection at position j must roll the logical length back to the accepted prefix plus the correction. (level 4) How many tokens does one step emit at minimum and at maximum? Expected: one, the residual sample at an immediate rejection; N plus 1 when every draft is accepted and the bonus token is sampled. Where it is taught. Weigh a trade-off Your creative-writing product samples at a high temperature and speculative decoding gives it no speedup at all, while the same setup flies on code completion. Explain the difference, and describe what the acceptance test becomes at temperature zero. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Acceptance depends on how often the verifier agrees with what the draft sampled. At a high temperature the target distribution is flat, the draft's samples spread across many tokens, and the acceptance ratio of verifier to draft probability falls toward one over the vocabulary size, so almost every draft is rejected and the draft's cost is paid for nothing. Code and structured output are predictable, so acceptance climbs above 0.9. At temperature zero the rule becomes a comparison: accept if the drafted token equals the verifier's most likely token, otherwise emit that token and stop. Why temperature is the lever. The acceptance test is u < min(1, q(d) / p(d)) . When both distributions are peaked on the same token the ratio is near one and the draft is accepted. Raise the temperature and both distributions flatten: the draft now samples tokens that the verifier gives little probability, the ratios shrink, and the rejections pile up. The lesson's exercise runs the loop at a temperature of 1.5 to show the collapse, where the algorithm becomes slower than plain decoding because the draft overhead stays and the accepted tokens vanish. Why the task matters. Workload Measured speedup in the lesson chat 2 to 3 times code generation 3 to 5 times creative writing near zero Code and structured output have a highly predictable next token, so even an imperfect draft agrees with the verifier most of the time; the EAGLE-3 lesson puts acceptance above 0.9 on such output. Open-ended prose at a high temperature has many acceptable continuations, and the draft rarely picks the one the verifier would. The greedy case. With temperature zero both models are deterministic. The test reduces to argmax(q) == d : accept on a match, otherwise output argmax(q) and stop. The residual distribution is not needed, because the verifier's choice is a single token. What to do about it. Switch speculation off per request when the temperature is high, or route such requests to a plain decode pool; the EAGLE-3 lesson lists temperature-aware switching as a tuning knob. Do not spend the draft on very short outputs of 1 to 5 tokens either; the overhead dominates. Measure the acceptance rate per product surface and keep speculation where it pays; the production lesson's floor is about 0.55 at high concurrency. Plausible wrong answers. "Lower the temperature so speculation works." The product chose the temperature for a reason; change the decoding path for those requests, not the product. "The draft is too small; use a bigger draft." Size is not the issue when the target distribution is flat; a larger draft still cannot guess which of many acceptable tokens the verifier samples. "At high temperature speculation changes the output." The rejection rule keeps the output distribution exact at any temperature; what changes is the speed. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) What does the acceptance ratio become when the draft and the verifier agree exactly? Expected: one, so every draft is accepted and each pass yields the full draft plus the bonus token. (level 3) May the draft sample at a different temperature from the verifier? Expected: yes, as long as p is the distribution the draft actually sampled from; the output still follows the verifier's distribution, but a mismatch lowers acceptance. (level 3) How would you implement the switch in a serving layer? Expected: read the request's temperature and output length, and disable speculation above a temperature threshold or below a length threshold, with the thresholds set from measured acceptance. (level 4) Why is the loss worse at high concurrency than the formula suggests? Expected: a rejected draft costs a verify and a re-roll that serialize under a full batch, and the batch already fills the memory bandwidth that speculation was exploiting, so the tail latency suffers. Where it is taught. The Phase 7 speculative decoding lesson ties acceptance to the decoding strategy, the Phase 10 speculative decoding lesson gives the greedy case and the workload table, the EAGLE-3 lesson names the switching knob, and the production EAGLE-3 lesson sets the acceptance floor. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Transformer The neural network design behind modern language models: stacked blocks of attention and feed-forward layers Lesson 7.19 BERT The 2018 encoder-only model trained by filling in masked words Lesson 7.22 Why this came about In Lesson 5.36 the decoder used its hidden state as the query and the encoder's states as both keys and values. The 2017 transformer later · 7.19 paper made two changes that turned this into a general building block. First, self-attention : every token of a sentence attends to the tokens of the same sentence, so each token's vector can absorb information from its context. Second, separate learned projections : each token's vector is multiplied by three different matrices to produce its query, key and value, so what a token looks for, how it is found, and what it passes on can all differ. Stack this with a few other parts ( Lesson 7.19 ) and you have the architecture behind every modern language model. In plain words first A room full of people asking each other questions Picture each word of a sentence as a person in a room. Each person holds up a card saying what they offer (a key : "I'm a noun, an object, something that can be big"), keeps a note of what they would tell others (a value ), and asks a question of their own (a query : "I'm the word it ; which earlier thing am I referring to?"). Every person compares their question with everyone's cards, listens mostly to the best matches, and updates their own understanding with what those people said. After one round, "it" knows a little about "parcel". A transformer runs dozens of such rounds in parallel, with different questions each time. Step 1 · Queries, keys and values Self-attention for one token. Every token's vector is multiplied by three learned matrices to give a query (what am I looking for?), a key (what do I contain?) and a value (what will I pass on?). The query of 'it' is compared with every key, the scores become weights through softmax, and the output is the weighted sum of the values. For each token vector x (its embedding , Lesson 3.19 ), self-attention computes three new vectors with three learned matrices: query q = x · W_Q: what this token is looking for; key k = x · W_K: what this token offers to others looking; value v = x · W_V: the information this token passes on if attended to. Then each token's output is the weighted average of all the values, weighted by how well its query matches each key ( dot product , then softmax ), exactly as in Lesson 5.36 . Step 2 · By hand, for a four-token sentence Four tokens, each with a made-up embedding of 4 numbers, and three small random matrices standing in for learned weights: Copy What you should see Copy Q @ K.T computes all 16 dot products at once: entry (i, j) is how well token i's query matches token j's key. Each row is then turned into weights with softmax, and the weights mix the values: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Each row of weights is one token's attention: positive numbers adding up to 1. With random matrices the pattern means nothing; training shapes W_Q , W_K and W_V so that the patterns become useful (Step 5 shows trained ones). The output has one vector per token, the same number of tokens as the input. Each token's new vector is a blend of the value vectors of the tokens it attended to: its embedding, updated with context. dim=-1 means "along the last dimension", here along each row. Softmax along the wrong dimension is a classic bug: the columns would add to 1 instead of the rows. Step 3 · Why divide by √d The scores were divided by math.sqrt(d_k) . Here is why. A dot product of two random vectors adds up d products, so it grows with the vector size: Copy What you should see Copy The spread of raw dot products grows like √d (2, 8, about 22.6). With large scores, softmax puts essentially all the weight on one token and its gradient nearly vanishes, so training stalls ( Lesson 5.36 's debugging exercise). Dividing by √d keeps the scores at a spread of about 1 whatever the size. That is the "scaled" in scaled dot-product attention . Step 4 · The whole thing in one line Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k) V The same five operations as a pipeline, read from the bottom: multiply queries by keys, scale, mask ( Lesson 7.18 ), softmax, then multiply by the values. This is the layout used in the 2017 paper that introduced the transformer. Figure: Daniel Voigt Godoy, dl-visuals , CC BY 4.0 . That formula is the core of the transformer. PyTorch has it built in, with fast implementations for GPUs : Copy What you should see Copy unsqueeze(0) adds a batch dimension, because the built-in function expects (batch, tokens, size). On a GPU it uses FlashAttention -style kernels, which compute exactly the same result while avoiding writing the full score matrix to memory ( Lesson 7.18 ). Step 5 · Attention in a trained model Now real weights. GPT-2 small has 12 layers, each with 12 attention heads ( Lesson 7.18 ), 144 attention patterns in all. But be careful. GPT-2 reads left to right, so each token can only look at itself and earlier tokens ( Lesson 7.18 ), and the word that decides the answer, "small", comes after "it". At the position of "it", the model cannot know yet; this head links "it" to a recent noun. Change "small" to "big" and this row of weights stays exactly the same (exercise M1). The decision has to be made at later positions, such as "small", which can look back at both nouns. Solution M1 · Big instead of small The weights are exactly the same as before: " suitcase" 0.65, "The" 0.16, " trophy" 0.07. Solution D1 · Softmax along the wrong dimension dim=0 normalises each column , so the weights a token gives to all other tokens no longer add up to 1; instead, each token's received attention does. Recap Every token produces a query, a key and a value by multiplying its vector by three learned matrices. Attention scores are dot products of queries with keys, divided by √d_k, turned into weights with softmax row by row. Each token's output is the weighted average of the values: its vector updated with information from its context. The whole operation is softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V, available in PyTorch as scaled_dot_product_attention . Trained heads show patterns such as attending to the previous token, to the first token, or from pronouns to nouns; they are clues, not explanations. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Transformer The neural network design behind modern language models: stacked blocks of attention and feed-forward layers Lesson 7.19 Decoder-only A transformer that predicts the next token from left to right, such as GPT Lesson 7.22 BERT The 2018 encoder-only model trained by filling in masked words Lesson 7.22 nanoGPT Andrej Karpathy's small, readable GPT training code, the model for this lesson Lesson 7.20 Context window The most input plus output, counted in tokens, that a model can handle in one call Lesson 10.42 KV cache Stored keys and values of earlier tokens, reused so each new token is cheap to generate Lesson 7.21 State-space models (SSMs) Sequence models with a fixed-size running state, such as Mamba Lesson 7.24 Why this came about A language model generates text left to right, so during training each position must predict its next token without seeing it. RNNs got this for free by reading in order. Transformers later · 7.19 see the whole sequence at once, so the 2017 paper added a mask that hides future positions inside attention. The same paper split attention into several heads , because one weighted average can only follow one relationship at a time, while language has many at once: grammar, reference, topic. The price of letting every token look at every other token is a cost that grows with the square of the length, which is why "context length" became one of the most discussed numbers in AI, and why so much engineering since 2020 has gone into making attention cheaper. In plain words first No peeking, and several pairs of eyes Imagine a quiz in which you see a sentence one word at a time and must guess the next word. If the whole sentence were printed on the page, you could just read the answer; so the later words are covered up. That cover is the causal mask . And instead of one reader looking for one kind of clue, picture twelve readers each watching for something different: one tracks the previous word, one tracks who is doing what, one tracks what "it" refers to. Their notes are combined at the end. Those readers are the heads . Step 1 · The causal mask The causal mask. When a model is trained to predict the next token, a token must not see the tokens after it, or it could simply copy the answer. Scores above the diagonal are set to minus infinity before softmax, so their weights become exactly zero. Every row can then be trained at once, each predicting its own next token. Before softmax , the scores for future positions are replaced by minus infinity. Since e^(−∞) = 0, those positions get exactly zero weight: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output torch.triu(..., diagonal=1) ("upper triangle") marks every position to the right of the diagonal: the future. masked_fill replaces those scores with −∞; after softmax they are exactly 0. Row 1 can only attend to itself, so its weight is 1.0. Row 5 can attend to all five tokens. This is what makes training efficient: a single forward pass over a sequence of 1,000 tokens produces 1,000 next-token predictions, each made without seeing its answer. An RNN needs 1,000 sequential steps for the same work ( Lesson 5.35 ). Models that use this mask are called decoder-only later · 7.22 or causal language models: GPT, Llama, Claude, Gemini and almost every chat model. Models without it, where every token sees the whole text in both directions, are encoders , such as BERT later · 7.22 ( Lesson 7.22 ). Step 2 · Many heads Multi-head attention . The model splits each token's vector into several smaller pieces and runs attention separately on each, with its own learned queries, keys and values. Each head can follow a different relationship. The heads' outputs are joined back together and mixed by one more matrix, W_O. One attention operation produces one weighted average per token. Multi-head attention runs several in parallel. With a model width of 768 and 12 heads, each head works with queries, keys and values of 64 numbers; the 12 outputs are joined back to 768 numbers and mixed by a final matrix W_O. The total compute is about the same as one big head, but each head can learn a different pattern, as you saw in the GPT-2 viewer in Lesson 7.17 . Here is a complete causal multi-head self-attention layer, in the style of GPT-2 and Andrej Karpathy's nanoGPT later · 7.20 : Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Reading this code nn.Linear(d_model, 3 * d_model) computes queries, keys and values for all heads in one matrix multiplication , then split cuts the result into three. This is faster than three separate layers and gives the same result. view(B, T, n_heads, d_head) reinterprets each 768-number vector as 12 pieces of 64; transpose(1, 2) moves the head dimension forward so each head becomes like a separate batch. The @ then runs all 12 heads at once. contiguous().view(B, T, C) undoes that: the 12 head outputs are laid side by side into 768 numbers again. The layer has 2,362,368 parameters: 768 × 2,304 + 2,304 for qkv and 768 × 768 + 768 for proj , about 4 × d_model² . GPT-2 small has 12 of these layers. A quick check that the hand-written layer is right: PyTorch 's fused attention function with is_causal=True should give the same result from the same queries, keys and values. Copy What you should see Copy Step 3 · What a long context costs Every token attends to every earlier token, so the score matrix has about n² entries per head per layer. Double the context and that part of the work quadruples: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output At 1,000 tokens, storing every score for every head and layer would take about 2 GB, which a GPU can hold. At 128,000 tokens it would be about 34,000 GB (34 terabytes), and at a million tokens about 2 petabytes, roughly 60 times more again. No GPU could hold that: a large one has about 80 to 200 GB of memory. Models with million-token contexts exist, so they must avoid storing the matrix. FlashAttention (2022) computes exactly the same attention in small tiles, never writing the full matrix to memory; memory then grows only with n, though compute still grows with n². The compute column still grows with n². For long documents, reading the whole context costs much more than the rest of the model, which is one reason long prompts cost more and respond slower (Lessons 10.42 and 11.18 ), and one reason retrieval (the Retrieval (RAG) section) remains useful even with huge context windows later · 10.42 . Solutions Solution P1 · Masking the diagonal too With diagonal=0 the diagonal is masked as well, so the first token cannot attend to anything: its whole row is −∞, and softmax of all −∞ gives nan (0 divided by 0). The other rows can no longer attend to themselves. Every token must be allowed to see at least itself; that is why the mask starts one place above the diagonal. Solution M1 · A small layer 4 × 64² + 4 × 64 = 16,384 + 256 = 16,640. The qkv layer has 64 × 192 + 192 = 12,480 and proj 64 × 64 + 64 = 4,160, which add up to the same 16,640. The number of heads does not change the count: heads split the width, they do not add weights. Solution X1 · Four times the context Attention compute grows by (32,000 / 8,000)² = 16 times. The rest of the model ( embedding , feed-forward layers, the q, k and v projections) grows 4 times, in proportion to the number of tokens. As contexts get longer, attention becomes a larger share of the total cost. Recap The causal mask sets scores for future tokens to −∞, so each token sees only itself and earlier tokens; this lets training predict every position in one pass. Multi-head attention splits the model width into several heads, each with its own queries, keys and values, then joins and mixes their outputs with W_O. An attention layer has about 4·d_model² parameters, whatever the number of heads. Attention's compute grows with the square of the context length; storing the full score matrix becomes impossible at long contexts. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Mixture-of-experts (MoE) Only part of the model runs per token Lesson 7.24 Decoder-only A transformer that predicts the next token from left to right, such as GPT Lesson 7.22 Why this came about The 2017 transformer combined pieces that already existed: attention (2015), residual connections (2015), layer normalisation (2016) and a plain feed-forward network , plus a way to tell the model about word order. OpenAI's GPT (2018) and GPT-2 (2019) kept only the decoder half, and GPT-2 moved the normalisation to the start of each half-block ("pre-norm"), which made deeper models train reliably. That block has barely changed since. Llama, Mistral, Qwen and the other open models swap in a few improvements ( RMSNorm , rotary positions, a gated feed-forward), but if you understand GPT-2's block, you can read the code of any of them. In plain words first Two steps, repeated A transformer block does two things to the list of token vectors. First, attention : tokens exchange information, so "it" can collect something from "parcel". Second, a feed-forward network : each token's vector is processed on its own by a small two-layer network, which is where much of the model's stored knowledge seems to live. Both steps are wrapped in a normalisation (keep the numbers a sensible size) and a residual connection (add the result to what was there, rather than replacing it). A GPT is that block repeated 12, 32 or 100 times, with an embedding table at the start and a prediction layer at the end. Step 1 · Attention cannot see word order Attention compares every token with every other by dot products . Nothing in that calculation depends on where a token sits. Shuffle the tokens and the outputs are simply shuffled the same way: Sinusoidal position encodings, the first solution. Each dimension of the position vector is a wave with its own frequency (top), so every position gets a unique pattern of values (bottom, one column per position), a little like the hands of several clocks running at different speeds. Figure: Daniel Voigt Godoy, dl-visuals , CC BY 4.0 . Copy What you should see Copy Without help, "the parcel hit the courier" and "the courier hit the parcel" would look the same. So the model is given each token's position . GPT-2 uses the simplest method: a second embedding table with one learned vector per position (0 to 1,023), added to each token's vector. Copy What you should see Copy Two other methods matter: Sinusoidal positions (the 2017 paper): fixed waves of different frequencies instead of a learned table, so no training is needed and any length can, in principle, be encoded. Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) , used by Llama, Mistral, Qwen and most current models: instead of adding anything to the token vector, rotate each query and key by an angle that grows with its position. The dot product between a rotated query and key then depends only on how far apart they are, not where they are: Copy What you should see Copy The first three pairs are all two positions apart and get exactly the same score; the last pair, nine apart, gets a different one. Real RoPE does this for every pair of numbers in the query and key, each pair rotating at a different speed. Because attention then "thinks" in relative distances, RoPE models can be stretched to longer contexts than they were trained on, with some extra tricks ( Lesson 7.24 ). Step 2 · The two halves of a block One transformer block, in the pre-norm form used by GPT-2 and almost every model since. Attention lets tokens exchange information; the feed-forward network then processes each token on its own. Each half is wrapped in LayerNorm and a residual connection ( Lesson 3.18 ). For reference, the original 2017 transformer, which was built for translation and has two stacks: an encoder (left) that reads the input, and a decoder (right) that writes the output and looks at the encoder through an extra attention layer. GPT-style models keep only a decoder stack, without that extra layer, which is the block drawn above. Figure: Zhang, Lipton, Li and Smola, Dive into Deep Learning , CC BY-SA 4.0 . The feed-forward network (also called the MLP) is the two-layer network of Lesson 3.15 , applied to every token separately: widen from 768 to 3,072 numbers, apply GELU, narrow back to 768. Because it sees one token at a time, all information exchange between tokens happens in attention; the MLP then works on each token's updated vector. Research suggests that much of what a model "knows" (that Paris is in France) is stored in these MLP weights. LayerNorm ( Lesson 3.18 ) rescales each token's vector to mean 0 and spread 1 before each half. Residual connections add each half's output back to its input, so the stream of token vectors is refined, block by block, rather than replaced. People call this running sum the residual stream . Step 3 · A complete GPT in code A whole GPT. Token IDs are looked up in the token embedding table, a position embedding is added, the vectors pass through N identical blocks, a final LayerNorm, and an output layer that gives one score per vocabulary token for every position. GPT-2 small: 12 blocks of width 768, 124 million parameters. With the embedding table (a vocabulary of 32,000 to 128,000 tokens times 4,096) this gives roughly the 7 to 8 billion parameters of Llama 2 7B or Llama 3 8B, which have exactly these dimensions (their gated MLPs and grouped-query attention shift the split a little). Solution M1 · GPT-2 medium About 354.8 million (with weight tying), matching the published 355 million. The count is dominated by 24 blocks × 12 × 1,024² ≈ 302 million, plus 50,257 × 1,024 ≈ 51 million for the token embedding and about 1 million for positions. Solution D1 · Forgotten transposes attn.c_proj.weight is 768 × 768, a square matrix, so its transpose has the same shape and copy_ succeeds silently, with the matrix flipped. The others are not square (768 × 2,304 and 768 × 3,072 versus PyTorch's 2,304 × 768), so copy_ raises a shape error. A square matrix copied the wrong way round is a silent bug: always compare outputs with a reference, as Step 4 does. Recap Attention is blind to order, so positions are added: learned position embeddings (GPT-2), sinusoids, or rotary embeddings (RoPE) that make attention depend on relative distance. A block is x + Attention(LayerNorm(x)), then x + MLP(LayerNorm(x)): attention mixes information between tokens, the MLP processes each token. A GPT is token and position embeddings, a stack of identical blocks, a final LayerNorm and an output layer, often tied to the embedding table. GPT-2 small has 124,439,808 parameters; about two-thirds of the block weights are in the MLPs. Loading OpenAI's weights into the hand-written model reproduces the official predictions exactly. Training a tiny model on Tiny Shakespeare became the "hello world" of language models, because it shows every moving part of real LLM training at a size that runs on a laptop. In 2024 his llm.c project reproduced the full 124-million-parameter GPT-2 in about 90 minutes on one rented server for roughly 20 dollars, a run that had cost OpenAI far more in 2019. The code in this lesson follows the same design, scaled down further. In plain words first Same recipe, smaller pot Training a large language model and training this one use the same recipe: cut text into tokens, show the model chunks of text, ask it to predict every next token, measure the cross-entropy, and nudge all the weights downhill, millions of times. What differs is scale: their vocabulary has 100,000+ tokens (yours: 65 characters), their model has billions of parameters (yours: under a million), their data is trillions of tokens (yours: one million characters), and they use thousands of GPUs for months (you: a laptop for three minutes). Watching the small version learn makes the big one far less mysterious. Step 1 · Data and model The same data preparation as Lesson 5.35 , and the GPT code of Lesson 7.19 (copied here so this lesson runs on its own): Copy What you should see Copy How a language model's training pairs are made. Step 2 · Initialise, then check the first loss PyTorch 's default initialisation suits ordinary networks, but a transformer with a tied embedding table needs smaller starting weights. GPT-2 draws every weight matrix from a normal distribution with spread 0.02 and sets biases to 0: Copy What you should see Copy The first loss should be close to log(65) ≈ 4.17: an untrained model should be equally unsure about every character. This is a cheap, powerful check from Karpathy's "recipe for training neural networks". If the first loss were 20 or 80, the outputs would be wildly overconfident, and training would waste its first steps undoing that, or fail. With PyTorch's default initialisation this model starts at a loss of about 80; try it by skipping the nn.init lines. Step 3 · Train The loop is the one from Lesson 3.17 , with the refinements of Lesson 3.18 : AdamW with weight decay, a short warm-up then cosine decay of the learning rate, and gradient clipping. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Each step trains on 32 chunks of 64 characters: 2,048 next-character predictions at once ( Lesson 7.18 's causal mask makes each chunk 64 examples). The training loss is noisy (one random batch); the validation loss, on a fixed held-out set, is the number to watch. It is still falling at the end, so the model is not yet overfitting : it has seen each part of the training text only about 4 times on average (2,000 × 2,048 ÷ 1,003,854). On this course's test machine the run took about three minutes on two CPU cores. A laptop with more cores is usually faster; a GPU would take a few seconds. The peak learning rate, 3e-3, is higher than you would use for a big model; small models tolerate (and need) larger steps. With 1e-3 this run ends about 0.1 worse. Remember to rebuild chars , stoi and itos and set vocab_size to the new number of characters. (Solution M1.) Debugging exercise A learner changes PEAK_LR to 1e-2 and removes the warm-up. The loss drops for a few hundred steps, then jumps to about 3.3 and stays there; samples are mostly spaces and the letter "e". What happened, and what fixes it? (Solution D1.) Solutions Solution P1 · A shorter context Higher. With 16 characters of context the model can no longer use anything further back, so it loses information about the speaker, the line and the rhythm. It still beats the 8-character window network, since 16 characters is more context and attention uses it well, but it falls behind the 64-character model. Context length is one of the most valuable resources a language model has. Solution M1 · Your own text Character-level models adapt to any text: a novel gives prose and dialogue in that author's spelling; code gives code-shaped text with brackets and indentation. With a smaller text (under 500,000 characters), validation loss will stop improving sooner, so watch for overfitting and consider fewer steps or more dropout . Choose texts that are in the public domain or that you are allowed to use. Solution D1 · Learning rate too high The large learning rate pushed the model into a bad state it could not recover from: it collapsed to predicting the most common characters regardless of context (a loss around 3.3 is roughly what letter frequencies alone give). Lower the peak learning rate (1e-3 to 3e-3 for a model this size), restore the warm-up, and keep gradient clipping. When a run collapses, restart from the last good checkpoint rather than hoping it recovers. Watch validation loss, not training loss, and count how many times the model has seen the data. Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Beam search Keeping the few best partial outputs at each step instead of one Translation, older systems Top-k sampling Sampling only from the k most likely tokens Decoding Nucleus (top-p) sampling Sampling from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p Decoding KV cache Stored keys and values of earlier tokens, reused so each new token is cheap to generate Latency and memory Stop sequences Strings that end generation when the model produces them API parameters Mentioned here, taught later 2 Tool calling, vLLM This lesson mentions the ideas below before the lesson that teaches them. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Tool calling The model replies with a structured request to run a named function; your code runs it and sends the result back Lesson 14.56 vLLM An open-source server for running language models with high throughput Lesson 3.25 Why this came about A language model only gives probabilities; something else must choose the words. Early neural systems picked the most likely word each time, or used beam search (keep the few best partial sentences), which suited translation but made open-ended text dull and repetitive. In 2018 Angela Fan and colleagues proposed top-k sampling , and in 2019 Ari Holtzman and colleagues described "neural text degeneration" and proposed nucleus (top-p) sampling : sample, but only from the smallest set of words that covers most of the probability. Together with temperature , these are the dials every LLM API exposes. Meanwhile, the KV cache became the key trick that makes generation fast, and its memory use one of the main costs of serving LLMs. In plain words first Choosing the next word At each step the model hands you a ranked list: " refund" 36%, " new" 9%, " replacement" 5%, and thousands more. You could always take the top word (safe but repetitive), or roll a weighted die (varied but sometimes odd). Temperature makes the die more or less fair: low temperature favours the top words even more, high temperature evens things out. Top-k and top-p cut off the long tail of unlikely words before rolling, so you never pick something absurd. Then the chosen word is added to the text, and the model is asked again. Step 1 · Next-token probabilities from a real model Until now the models were ones you trained yourself. This lesson uses GPT-2, a real pretrained model small enough for a laptop (about 500 MB, downloaded on first run). Give it the start of a sentence and it returns a score for every one of its 50,257 tokens being next. The code loads the model, turns the scores into probabilities and prints the most likely continuations. Copy What you should see Copy From scores to a chosen token. The model gives a logit for every token in the vocabulary. Temperature rescales them, top-k or top-p throws away the unlikely tail, softmax turns what is left into probabilities, and one token is drawn at random (or the top one is taken, for greedy decoding). The chosen token is appended and the loop repeats. Step 2 · Greedy decoding The simplest strategy: always take the most likely token, append it, repeat. Generation as an animation. The decoder predicts one token, that token is appended to the input, and the whole sequence goes back in to predict the next one, until the model produces the end-of-sequence token. Figure: Hugging Face, Agents Course , Apache 2.0 . Copy What you should see Copy Greedy decoding is deterministic (same input, same output) and often fine for short, factual answers. For longer text it tends to produce the blandest possible continuation and to fall into loops: here GPT-2 small drifts into web-page boilerplate, including a repeated "Loading ...". Once a phrase is likely, repeating it keeps it likely. This is the "degeneration" that motivated sampling. Step 3 · Temperature, top-k and top-p Temperature divides the logits before softmax ( Lesson 1.25 ). Below 1 sharpens the distribution; above 1 flattens it: Copy What you should see Copy Top-k keeps only the k most likely tokens. Top-p ( nucleus sampling ) keeps the smallest set of top tokens whose probabilities add up to at least p, so it adapts: when the model is confident, few tokens survive; when it is unsure, many do. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output With no filter, all 50,257 tokens remain possible, including absurd ones; over a long text, some will eventually be drawn. Top-k 10 keeps exactly 10, however spread out the probabilities are. Top-p 0.5 needs only a few tokens here, because " refund" alone has 36%. Top-p 0.9 needs many hundreds: after "get a", the model spreads the remaining probability over a long list of plausible words. cum - softmax >= top_p marks a token for removal if the tokens before it already reached p. This keeps the token that crosses the line, so the kept set always has at least one token. Try the dials yourself on the same prompt: Turn the dials on GPT-2's next-token choice Real next-token probabilities from GPT-2 small. Lower temperature sharpens the distribution; top-k keeps only the k most likely tokens; top-p keeps the smallest set whose probabilities add up to p. Step 4 · Sampling in practice Hugging Face's generate implements all of this. Fix the random seed to get repeatable samples: Beam search with a beam of two. At each step every kept sequence is extended by every possible token, and only the two most probable sequences overall survive (circled). It finds higher-probability text than greedy decoding, and is used in translation and speech recognition; chat models sample instead, because the most probable text tends to be dull and repetitive. Figure: Zhang, Lipton, Li and Smola, Dive into Deep Learning , CC BY-SA 4.0 . Copy What you should see Copy Three continuations that share a likely opening, then go their own ways. (GPT-2 small is a base model with no instruction training, so the content wanders; the From language model to assistant section explains how assistants are trained to stay on task.) Job Typical settings Why Extraction, classification, code, tool calls later · 14.56 temperature 0 to 0.2 you want the most likely, consistent answer Chat and drafting temperature 0.7 to 1.0, top-p 0.9 to 1.0 natural variety without nonsense Brainstorming, fiction temperature 1.0 to 1.2 more surprising choices Other controls you will meet in APIs: max tokens (a hard limit on output length), stop sequences (end generation when a given string appears), frequency and presence penalties (discourage repeating tokens), and a seed . Even at temperature 0, hosted APIs are not always perfectly repeatable, because tiny numerical differences on GPUs can change which token is on top ( Lesson 11.19 ). Step 5 · The KV cache The KV cache. Without it, generating each new token reruns the whole text so far. With it, the keys and values of earlier tokens are kept in memory, and each step computes only the new token's query, key and value. Generation becomes much faster, but the cache grows with every token and every user. The greedy loop in Step 2 called the model on the whole text at every step. But in a causal model, the keys and values of earlier tokens never change when new tokens are added (they cannot see the future). So they can be computed once and kept: the KV cache . Each step then processes only the one new token. Hugging Face does this by default; turn it off to see the difference: Copy What you should see Copy The exact timings depend on your machine (which is why the code prints a yes/no), but without the cache the work grows with the square of the output length. The price of the cache is memory: for every token in the context, every layer stores a key and a value for each key/value head. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output An 8B model's weights need 16 GB in bf16 ( Lesson 3.20 ). One user with a full 128,000-token context needs another 16.8 GB of KV cache, as much as the weights. Serving 32 users at once, each with 8,000 tokens, needs about 34 GB of cache. In serving, the KV cache, not the weights, usually decides how many users fit on a GPU. Grouped-query attention (several query heads sharing one key/value head, Lesson 7.18 ) cuts the cache by four times here, which is why nearly every recent model uses it. Serving engines such as vLLM later · 3.25 manage cache memory in pages to waste less of it ( Lesson 14.137 ). The same idea as a formula greedy: x_{t+1} = argmax_v p(v | x_{≤t}) temperature: p_T(v) = softmax(z / T)_v top-k: keep the k largest z_v; top-p: keep the smallest set S of top tokens with Σ_{v∈S} p(v) ≥ p; renormalise, then sample KV cache size: 2 × layers × KV heads × head size × bytes × tokens × users work to generate n tokens: without a cache ∝ n²/2 positions processed, with a cache ∝ n Check your mental model ✗ "Temperature 0 makes the model more accurate." ✓ It makes it more consistent. If the most likely token is wrong, greedy decoding is consistently wrong. ✗ "Top-p 0.9 means the model is 90% sure." ✓ It means sampling is restricted to the top tokens that together hold 90% of the probability, however many that takes. ✗ "The KV cache stores the generated text." ✓ It stores each layer's keys and values for every token so far, numbers that are much larger than the text itself. Exercises Predict before you run For the logits in Step 1, how many tokens does top-p keep at temperature 0.5 with p = 0.9: more or fewer than at temperature 1.0? (Solution P1.) Make it your own Run the greedy decoder of Step 2 on three prompts of your own, then add repetition_penalty=1.3 to model.generate(..., do_sample=False) with the same prompts. Does the looping stop? What else changes? (Solution M1.) Practice Apply it Using kv_cache_gb , a 70B-class model has 80 layers, 8 key/value heads and a head size of 128. How much KV cache does one user with a 32,000-token conversation need in bf16? (Solution X1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Temperature and top-p together Fewer. Temperature 0.5 sharpens the distribution, so the top few tokens hold much more of the probability, and fewer are needed to reach 0.9. You can check with torch.isfinite(filter_logits(logits / 0.5, top_p=0.9)).sum() . Temperature and top-p interact; APIs usually apply temperature first, then the filters. Solution M1 · A repetition penalty A penalty of 1.3 lowers the scores of tokens that already appeared, so exact loops usually disappear. It can also push the model away from words it legitimately needs to repeat (names, "the", product terms), making text awkward. Penalties are a blunt tool; better models and sampling usually matter more. Solution X1 · A 70B-class model Per token: 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 327,680 bytes (320 KB). For 32,000 tokens: about 10.5 GB for one user, on top of about 140 GB of bf16 weights. Ten such users need another 105 GB, which is why long conversations on large models are expensive to serve. Recap A model gives probabilities; a decoding strategy chooses the token, appends it and repeats. Greedy decoding always takes the top token: consistent, but prone to repetition in long text. Temperature sharpens or flattens the distribution; top-k and top-p remove the unlikely tail before sampling. Low temperature suits extraction and tool calls; moderate temperature with top-p suits chat; higher temperature suits brainstorming. The KV cache keeps earlier tokens' keys and values so each step processes one new token; its memory grows with context length and users and often limits serving. A It compresses the weights B It skips the attention layers C Earlier tokens' keys and values are kept, so each step only processes the new token D It lowers the temperature In a causal model, earlier keys and values never change as new tokens are added. Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Encoder-only A transformer that reads the whole input in both directions and produces vectors, such as BERT Embeddings, classifiers Decoder-only A transformer that predicts the next token from left to right, such as GPT LLMs Encoder-decoder A transformer with both parts, such as T5 Translation, summarisation BERT The 2018 encoder-only model trained by filling in masked words Embeddings, rerankers Sentence-BERT BERT trained so that whole sentences get vectors comparable by cosine similarity Embedding models Cross-encoder A model that reads a query and a document together and outputs one relevance score Rerankers Semantic search Finding text by meaning, using embeddings, instead of by shared words Retrieval Mentioned here, taught later 4 Fine-tuning, Reranker, RAG, Hybrid search This lesson mentions the ideas below before the lesson that teaches them. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Fine-tuning Continuing to train a pretrained model on your own examples so that its behaviour changes. First explained in Lesson 10.36; the hands-on workshop is Lessons 7.25 to 11.8 Lesson 10.36 Reranker A second, slower and more accurate model that reorders the top search results Lesson 5.38 RAG Retrieval-augmented generation: find the relevant passages in your own documents, put them in the prompt, and have the model answer from them Lesson 10.45 Hybrid search Running keyword search and vector search together and merging the results Lesson 5.38 Why this came about The 2017 transformer had both an encoder and a decoder, for translation. In 2018 the two halves went separate ways. OpenAI's GPT kept the decoder and trained it to predict the next word. Google's BERT kept the encoder and trained it to fill in hidden words using context on both sides, which made it excellent at understanding tasks: classification, question answering, search. In 2019 Nils Reimers and Iryna Gurevych's Sentence-BERT fine-tuned later · 10.36 such encoders so that whole sentences with similar meanings get similar vectors, the basis of today's embedding models and vector search. T5 (2019) and BART kept the full encoder-decoder for text-to-text tasks, and Whisper (2022) uses the same design for speech. Decoders later grew into today's chat models, but encoders still do much of the quiet work: embeddings, reranking later · 5.38 , classification. In plain words first Readers, writers and translators An encoder is a careful reader: it sees the whole text at once, both before and after every word, and builds a rich understanding of each part. A decoder is a writer: it produces text one word at a time and can only look back at what is already written. An encoder-decoder is a translator: one part reads the whole source, the other writes the result while glancing back at the source. Which one you want depends on whether your job is to understand, to write, or to transform. Step 1 · The three families The three transformer families. Encoders let every token see the whole text in both directions and are used to understand: classify, tag, embed. Decoders see only earlier tokens and generate text one token at a time. Encoder-decoders read an input with an encoder and write a new output with a decoder that also attends to the input. A decoder-only model such as GPT. The grid on the right shows which inputs (columns) each output position (rows) may attend to: only itself and what came before, which gives the staircase. DistilBERT is a smaller, faster copy of BERT (66 million parameters): An encoder-only model such as BERT. Every position attends to every other position (the full grid), so the model reads the whole sentence at once. It is trained by hiding some tokens behind a mask token and predicting them. This two-way reading is why encoders are strong at understanding tasks; it is also why they cannot generate text naturally, one word after another. pipeline is Hugging Face's high-level helper: it downloads the model (about 270 MB the first time), tokenises the text, runs the model and decodes the result. Lesson 7.23 opens up those steps. Step 3 · Contextual embeddings, measured In Lesson 5.33 , GPT-2's embedding table gave "bank" one vector, dominated by money. Inside an encoder, each layer mixes in the surrounding words, so the same word gets different vectors in different sentences. Take the vector for "bank" from DistilBERT's last layer in three sentences: Copy What you should see Copy The two financial uses are more similar to each other than either is to the river bank. Same token, same starting embedding, different final vectors: that is a contextual embedding , built by attention ( Lesson 7.17 ). Step 4 · Sentence embeddings with mean pooling Turning a sentence into one vector. An encoder gives a contextual vector for every token; averaging them (mean pooling) gives one vector for the whole sentence. Models trained for this, such as all-MiniLM-L6-v2, place sentences with similar meanings close together, so cosine similarity measures similarity of meaning. To compare whole sentences, you need one vector per sentence. The standard recipe: run an encoder, then average its token vectors (mean pooling), ignoring padding. Models such as all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (22 million parameters, 384 numbers per sentence) were fine-tuned on hundreds of millions of sentence pairs so that this average captures meaning: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Reading this code padding=True makes all sentences in a batch the same length by adding padding tokens; attention_mask marks which tokens are real. Averaging without the mask would mix padding into the result, a common bug. "my parcel never arrived" and "the package did not get delivered" share almost no words, yet their vectors are close, because the model learned that they mean the same thing. That is exactly what TF-IDF could not do in Lesson 5.32 . sentence-transformers , a library that wraps this recipe in one call ( model.encode(texts) ), is what most code uses; here you see what it does inside. "I moved house last week" shares no word at all with "How do I change my delivery address?" and still finds it. This is semantic search , the retrieval half of RAG later · 10.45 ( Lesson 14.71 ). Keyword search still wins on exact codes and rare names, which is why production systems often combine both ( hybrid search later · 5.38 , Lesson 5.38 ). Step 6 · Embeddings as features: the ticket classifier again In Lesson 5.32 , a bag-of-words classifier scored 82% on ticket phrasings it had never seen. Replace the word counts with sentence embeddings and keep everything else the same (the same data, the same held-out templates, the same logistic regression ): Copy What you should see Copy Accuracy on unseen phrasings rises from 82% to about 97%. The embeddings already "know" that "shattered" is like "broken" and "locked" is about accounts, so the classifier needs no examples of those words. Negation and fine distinctions are still hard: "I do not want a refund" is still labelled refund, and "left it at the wrong address" lands in account because it is about an address. Embeddings capture topic better than logic; a language model reading the whole ticket (the Talking to models: APIs, messages, prompts and context section) handles such cases better, at a much higher cost per ticket. This pattern (a frozen pretrained encoder plus a tiny classifier trained on its embeddings) is one of the cheapest, most effective tools in applied NLP. Fine-tuning the whole encoder on your labels usually does better still ( Lesson 3.22 fine-tunes embedding models). Solutions Solution P1 · Fill in the verb Words like "left", "delivered" and "dropped", with "left" usually on top: verbs that fit both "the courier " and " the parcel at the door". Solution M1 · Your own queries English paraphrases usually match well. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 was trained mostly on English, so the Hindi-in-Latin-letters query may still match the damaged-item FAQ through shared or similar tokens, but less reliably. Solution D1 · Averaging the padding In a padded batch, short sentences are filled with padding tokens up to the length of the longest one. .mean(dim=1) averages those padding vectors in too, so short FAQs are pulled towards a common "padding" direction, and their similarity scores depend on the other FAQs in the batch. Use the attention mask to average only real tokens, as embed does in Step 4. Recap Encoders see the whole text in both directions and suit understanding: classification, tagging, embeddings, reranking. Decoders see only earlier tokens and generate text; scaled up, they became today's chat models. Encoder-decoders read an input and write a new output: translation, summarisation, speech recognition. Inside an encoder, the same word gets different vectors in different contexts; mean pooling with the attention mask turns token vectors into a sentence vector. Sentence embeddings power semantic search and make strong features for classifiers; on unseen phrasings they beat bag of words. Step 3 · Inside the layers: the logit lens Ask for the hidden states, and you get the residual stream ( Lesson 7.19 ) after the embeddings and after each of the 12 blocks: 13 tensors. Copy What you should see Copy The final layer's vector at the last position is turned into next-token scores by the final LayerNorm and the output layer. What if you apply that same final step to the intermediate layers? This trick, called the logit lens (nostalgebraist, 2020), shows what the model "would predict" if it stopped early: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Right after the embeddings, the "prediction" is meaningless word fragments: no block has run yet, so nothing has been worked out. Through the early and middle blocks, generic continuations of "is" (" not", " now") dominate. Around blocks 10 and 11, " France" and " Paris" rise to the top, as the model brings in what it knows about the subject. Each block adds a small update to the same residual stream, so the prediction is refined gradually rather than computed at the very end. This lesson opens the rest of the box, at the depth an AI engineer needs, and with the numbers you need to reason about context length, memory and speed. Why this came about Before 2017, language models read text one word at a time (recurrent networks), which was slow to train and forgot long-range context. The 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need" introduced the transformer , which lets every token look at every other token at once and trains in parallel on GPUs . That architecture made today's large language models possible, and its design still explains their limits: context length, memory and speed. In plain words first Every word looks at every other word A transformer turns each token into a vector, then repeatedly lets every token look at the others and decide which ones matter for it ( attention ), mixing in their information. Many such layers build up meaning: which "it" refers to which noun, what a question is asking. To write, it predicts one next token at a time, and keeps the keys and values it already computed (the KV cache ) so it does not redo work for earlier tokens. Most practical limits, such as context length, memory per request and speed, follow from this design. The whole model in one picture A decoder-only LLM turns token ids into vectors with an embedding table, passes them through a stack of identical blocks , and ends with an output head that turns the last vector into a score for every token in the vocabulary (the logits ), then a softmax into probabilities. Each block has two sublayers, attention and a feed-forward network , and each one reads from and adds back to a running vector per token called the residual stream . A decoder-only transformer block, drawn: the residual stream runs left to right; attention lets tokens share information, the feed-forward network works on each token alone, and each adds its result back to the stream. Llama 3 8B stacks 32 of these. Inside the model, in code You do not need to train models to build agents, but four mechanisms explain most of what you will see in production: why some languages cost more, why answers vary, why long prompts are slow to start, and why output tokens dominate latency. Each takes a few lines of NumPy . Attention, drawn: when the model processes 'it', every earlier token gets a weight; here most of the weight goes to 'animal', so the vector for 'it' carries the animal's meaning forward. See it drawn The Illustrated Transformer : Jay Alammar: the transformer, one picture per step The Illustrated GPT-2 and How GPT3 Works : Jay Alammar: decoder-only models and next-token generation, animated Transformers, the tech behind LLMs and Attention in transformers, step-by-step : 3Blue1Brown, Deep Learning chapters 5 and 6, 27 and 26 min How might LLMs store facts : 3Blue1Brown, the Other agent frameworks, compared section, 23 min Transformer Neural Networks, ChatGPT's foundation, Clearly Explained!!! and Decoder-Only Transformers : StatQuest with Josh Starmer, 36 and 37 min The Narrated Transformer Language Model : Jay Alammar, 30 min Attention, and why the KV cache exists A transformer's core operation is self-attention : each token builds a weighted mix of earlier tokens' information, weighted by how well its query matches their keys . A causal mask stops tokens from looking ahead. Copy What you should see Copy The zeros above the diagonal are the causal mask. The second print is the KV cache : keys and values of earlier tokens never change, so generating each new token needs only one new row instead of recomputing everything. It is why reading a long prompt ( prefill , done once, in parallel) and writing the answer ( decode , one token at a time) have very different speeds, and why prompt caching later · 11.23 across requests ( Lesson 11.23 ) can skip prefill for a repeated prefix. Attention: queries, keys and values For each token, attention computes a query ("what am I looking for?"), a key ("what do I contain?") and a value ("what do I pass on?"), each by multiplying the token's vector by a learned matrix. The score between two tokens is the dot product of one's query with the other's key; a softmax turns a row of scores into weights; the output is the weighted sum of values. Together this is scaled dot-product attention : softmax(Q Kᵀ / √d_k) V . Why divide by √d_k? Dot products of random d-dimensional vectors have a spread that grows like √d, so in large dimensions the scores become huge, the softmax puts almost all its weight on one token, and gradients through it nearly vanish. Dividing keeps scores in a range where the softmax stays soft: Copy What you should see Copy Without scaling, at d_k = 1024 attention collapses onto a single token (weight 1.00). With scaling it stays spread, so the model can learn which tokens matter. Causal masking sets the scores for future tokens to minus infinity before the softmax, so each token sees only itself and earlier tokens; this is what lets one training pass learn to predict every next token at once. Multi-head attention runs several attentions in parallel, each in a smaller slice of the vector, so one head can track syntax while another tracks which entity "it" refers to; the heads' outputs are concatenated and mixed by an output matrix. Copy What you should see Copy Four heads, each with its own 5 × 5 attention pattern, and the mask zeroes every weight on a future token. Self-attention compares a sequence with itself; cross-attention uses queries from one sequence and keys and values from another (an encoder-decoder translator, or a speech model attending to audio). Attention's cost is the catch: every token is compared with every other, so compute and memory for the scores grow with the square of the sequence length, O(n²) . Doubling the context quadruples that work, which is why long context is expensive and why the techniques below exist. Positions: telling the model about word order Attention by itself ignores order: shuffle the tokens and the weights shuffle with them. Positional encoding fixes that. Method How it works Used by Sinusoidal Add fixed sine and cosine waves of different frequencies to each embedding The original 2017 transformer Learned absolute Learn one vector per position, up to a maximum length BERT , GPT-2 RoPE (rotary) Rotate each query and key by an angle proportional to its position; the dot product then depends only on the distance between tokens Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma and most current open models ALiBi Subtract a penalty from attention scores that grows with distance BLOOM, some MPT models Copy What you should see Copy The same pair of vectors gives the same score at positions 5 and 2, 105 and 102, or 1005 and 1002: with RoPE, attention sees relative distance, not absolute position. That property is what context extension methods exploit: position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling and YaRN stretch the rotation frequencies so a model trained on 8,000 tokens can be fine-tuned to work at 128,000. The rest of the block Residual connections : each sublayer's output is added to its input ( x = x + sublayer(x) ). The stream carries information up through dozens of layers, and gradients flow straight back down it, which is what makes very deep networks trainable. Normalization : LayerNorm rescales each token's vector to zero mean and unit variance; RMSNorm skips the centering and just divides by the root mean square, which is cheaper and works as well, so Llama-family models use it. Modern models apply it before each sublayer ( pre-norm ), which trains more stably than the original transformer's post-norm. Feed-forward network (FFN) : a two- or three-matrix network applied to each token separately, usually expanding the vector about 3.5 to 4 times. It holds about two-thirds of a dense model's parameters, and interpretability work suggests much factual recall happens here. Most current models use the gated SwiGLU form. Copy What you should see Copy Each block adds a modest update to the stream rather than replacing it, which is the residual design at work. Counting parameters and the KV cache from a config Every open model ships a config with a handful of numbers. From them you can work out the model's size and, more usefully for serving, how much memory each token of context costs. Copy What you should see Copy The count lands on Llama 3 8B's published size. The KV cache line is the one to remember for serving: 128 KiB per token means one 128,000-token conversation needs 16 GiB of GPU memory on top of the weights. Grouped-query attention ( GQA ) shares each key and value head among several query heads (here 4), cutting the cache by 4 times for a small quality cost; multi-query attention (MQA) shares one across all; DeepSeek's multi-head latent attention (MLA) compresses keys and values into a small latent vector instead. Three families of transformers Family Sees Trained to Examples Use it for Encoder-only The whole input, both directions Fill in masked words (masked language modeling) BERT, RoBERTa, ModernBERT Embeddings, classifiers, rerankers later · 5.38 , named entity extraction Decoder-only Only earlier tokens (causal) Predict the next token GPT, Llama, Claude, Gemini, Qwen Generation, chat, agents: today's LLMs Encoder-decoder Encoder reads all input; decoder generates with cross-attention to it Map input to output (translation, denoising) Original transformer, T5, BART, Whisper Translation, summarization, speech recognition Decoder-only won for general models because one simple objective scales to all of the web and every task can be phrased as "continue this text". Encoders remain the right tool for fast embedding and classification, which is why most rerankers and many embedding models in Lesson 14.71 are encoders. Making attention affordable Technique What it does Effect KV cache Keep earlier tokens' keys and values instead of recomputing them ( Lesson 7.21 ) Each new token costs one row, not the whole sequence GQA / MQA / MLA Share or compress key and value heads 4 to 30 times smaller cache FlashAttention Compute attention in tiles that fit in the GPU's fast on-chip memory, never writing the full n × n score matrix to slow memory Same exact result, several times faster and far less memory; standard in every serving engine Sliding-window attention Each token attends only to the last few thousand tokens; stacked layers still pass information further Mistral 7B, Gemma's local layers PagedAttention later · 14.137 Store the KV cache in fixed-size pages, like virtual memory Far more concurrent requests per GPU ( vLLM later · 3.25 , Lesson 14.137 ) Quantization Store weights or KV cache in 8 or 4 bits Half to a quarter of the memory ( Lesson 14.137 ) Long context has a quality limit as well as a cost: models use information at the start and end of a long prompt better than the middle (" lost in the middle later · 11.27 "), so retrieval and context engineering later · 11.27 ( Lesson 11.27 ) still matter at a million tokens. Mixture of experts A mixture-of-experts (MoE) model replaces each feed-forward network with many smaller expert networks and a router that sends each token to only a few of them. The model has many parameters to store knowledge, but each token pays for only the experts it uses. Copy What you should see Copy Mixtral 8x7B stores 46.7B parameters but runs about 12.9B per token; DeepSeek-V3 stores 671B and activates 37B. The catch: every expert must still sit in GPU memory, so MoE saves compute, not memory, and training needs a load-balancing loss so the router does not overload a few experts. Beyond attention State-space models (SSMs) such as Mamba process a sequence with a fixed-size running state instead of comparing every pair of tokens, so cost grows linearly with length and there is no growing KV cache. Pure SSMs are weaker at exact recall from far back in the context, so the practical trend is hybrids that interleave a few attention layers with many SSM or linear-attention layers (Jamba, IBM Granite 4, NVIDIA Nemotron-H). Diffusion language models generate by refining a whole block of tokens in parallel over several steps rather than one token at a time; they are fast but still a minority approach. Go deeper (optional) Research directions beyond next-token prediction Everything in this course is built on transformers trained to predict the next token. Researchers are also pursuing other routes, and you will see these terms: World models : models that learn to predict how an environment changes when you act in it (the next video frames of a game, a robot's surroundings), so that an agent can plan by imagining outcomes. Video-generation models are sometimes described this way. JEPA (joint-embedding predictive architecture), championed by Yann LeCun: predict the representation of the missing part of an image or video instead of its pixels or tokens, on the argument that most detail is unpredictable and not worth modelling. Neuro-symbolic systems : a neural model paired with a symbolic engine (a solver, a proof checker, a knowledge graph later · 14.83 ) that guarantees correctness of the parts it handles. An LLM calling a calculator or a SQL engine is the everyday version (the Agents from first principles section). Continual learning : models that keep learning after deployment without forgetting. Today's models are frozen; memory systems and retrieval (Lessons 14.64 and 14.65 ) are the practical substitute. None of these has displaced the transformer language model in products. They matter as context for claims about what current models can and cannot do. Decoding: from probabilities to text Lesson 11.19 covered temperature , top-k and top-p sampling. The rest of the toolbox: Greedy decoding takes the most likely token each step. Beam search keeps the best few partial sequences and can find a more likely whole answer; it suits translation and other tasks with one right output, and is rarely used for chat because it produces bland, repetitive text. min-p keeps tokens whose probability is at least a fraction of the top token's, adapting to how confident the model is; popular with open models. Repetition, frequency and presence penalties lower the scores of tokens already used. Logprobs : most APIs can return each token's log-probability, useful for confidence scores, classification by comparing label probabilities, and spotting where an answer is shaky. Constrained decoding later · 11.21 masks every token that would break a grammar or JSON schema ; it is how structured output later · 11.21 is guaranteed ( Lesson 11.21 ). Copy What you should see Copy Greedy grabs "the" (0.5) and ends at 0.20; beam search keeps "a" alive and finds "a refund" at 0.36. Speculative decoding speeds up generation without changing the output: a small draft model guesses the next few tokens, the large model checks all of them in one forward pass, keeps the run it agrees with, and adds one token of its own. Because the big model's pass costs about the same for one token or five, every accepted guess is nearly free. Copy What you should see Copy At 80% acceptance each big-model pass yields over three tokens. Serving engines offer it as draft models, n-gram lookup from the prompt, or extra prediction heads (Medusa, EAGLE). Multimodal models A vision transformer (ViT) cuts an image into patches (16 × 16 pixels, say), embeds each patch like a token, and runs a transformer over them. CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder together so matching images and captions get similar vectors ( contrastive learning later · 14.71 , the same idea as Lesson 3.22 's embedding fine-tuning). Vision-language models such as Claude, GPT and Gemini feed image-patch embeddings into the language model alongside text tokens, which is why an image costs a predictable number of tokens. Audio works the same way with audio frames ( Lesson 6.18 ). In production Where this shows up in agent work Context budgets : KV cache per token × context length × concurrent users is the memory bill for self-hosting; GQA and quantized caches are the levers ( Lesson 14.137 ). Choosing models : an encoder for fast classification or reranking, a decoder for generation; an MoE model's speed comes from active parameters, its memory from total parameters. Debugging output : repetition loops, truncated JSON and odd tokens are decoding problems; logprobs and constrained decoding are the tools.
