Solutions Solution P1 · Quadratic attention About four times: every token attends to every other, so the score matrix grows with the square of the length. This is why long contexts are expensive. Solution B1 · The mask prevents cheating Each position can see future tokens, so predicting the next token becomes trivial and the model learns nothing useful for generation. Solution D1 · The KV cache Caching keys and values of previous tokens, so each new token computes attention only for itself against the cache. Solution M1 · Heads Multiple heads let the model attend to different relations in parallel; one head must mix them. Output shapes are the same. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism How does a transformer process text? Worked answer. Tokens become embeddings with position information; each layer applies self-attention (each token mixes information from others, weighted by query-key similarity) and a feed-forward network, with residual connections and normalization; the final layer produces probabilities for the next token. Decoding repeats this with a KV cache. A plausible wrong answer. "It reads text left to right like a person." It processes all input tokens in parallel during prefill. Follow-ups. Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Fine-tuning Continuing to train a pretrained model on your own examples so that its behaviour changes Customising models JSONL A file with one JSON object per line Datasets Chat format Training examples stored as lists of system, user and assistant messages Datasets Mentioned here, taught later 2 LoRA, Distillation This lesson mentions the ideas below before the lesson that teaches them. The one-line meaning is all you need for now; each is marked later where it first appears. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in LoRA Low-rank adaptation: freeze the model and train two small matrices added to chosen layers Lesson 3.24 Distillation Training a small student model to copy a larger teacher model Lesson 14.132 Why this came about From 2018 to 2020, fine-tuning was how everything was done: you took BERT ( Lesson 7.22 ), added a small output layer, and trained it on a few thousand labelled examples for each task. Then GPT-3 and its successors showed that one large model could do many tasks from a prompt alone, and for a few years most teams stopped training models. Fine-tuning came back from 2023 for three reasons. LoRA later · 3.24 made it cheap enough to run on one consumer GPU ( Lesson 3.24 ). Capable open-weight models (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma, Phi) gave everyone something worth tuning. And teams running millions of calls a day found that a small tuned model could match a large general one on a narrow step at a fraction of the cost and delay. Today most teams still do not fine-tune, and those that do reserve it for specific, high-volume, well-measured steps. This workshop teaches you to recognise those steps and to do the work properly. In plain words first Briefing a generalist, or training a specialist A prompt is a briefing: you explain the job to a capable generalist every single time, and they do their best from the note. Fine-tuning is training: the model practises on hundreds of worked examples until the job becomes habit, so the note can be one line. A specialist is faster and cheaper per task and very consistent, but took effort to train, knows only that job, and has to be retrained when the job changes. Most problems need a better briefing or better reference material, not a specialist. This lesson is about telling the difference, and then preparing the practice material: the dataset. Step 1 · Is fine-tuning the right tool? The customisation ladder. Each step up costs more to build and to maintain, so climb only when the step below has been tried and measured. Fine-tuning changes how a model behaves; it is not the way to give it facts that change. Fine-tuning continues a model's training on your examples, so its weights change ( Lesson 10.36 did exactly this to turn a text predictor into an assistant). That makes it good at some things and wrong for others: What you want Does fine-tuning help? What to use A fixed output format, followed every time Yes , very well A prompt with examples first; fine-tune if it still drifts, or to make a small model do it A house style or tone Yes Examples in the prompt first A narrow task done by a small, cheap, fast model Yes : this is the main production use Fine-tune, often on answers produced by a large model ( distillation later · 14.132 , Lesson 14.132 ) Reliable tool calling by a small or self-hosted model Yes Fine-tune on tool-call transcripts Knowledge of your documents, prices or policies No : facts in weights go stale and cannot be cited Retrieval (the Retrieval (RAG) section) Knowledge of today's order status No Tools (the Agents from first principles section) General intelligence, better reasoning No : a tuned model is narrower, not smarter A stronger base model Three questions decide whether a fine-tune is worth starting: Can you measure success? If you cannot write a program or a rubric that scores an answer, you cannot tell whether training helped. Have you measured the cheaper options? A good prompt with examples, on the best model you can afford. That number is your baseline. Is the volume or the constraint real? Fine-tuning pays for itself on steps that run very often, must be very fast, must run on your own hardware, or must be more consistent than a prompt achieves. Tip A useful one-line test Prompting and retrieval change what the model reads . Fine-tuning changes how the model behaves . If the problem is missing information, give it information. If the problem is behaviour that examples in the prompt cannot fix, or cannot fix cheaply enough, fine-tune. Step 2 · The project, and a task you can score A fine-tuning project is a loop, not a single training run. Most of the work is in the first three boxes and the fifth; the training itself is the short part. The workshop follows this loop over five lessons, with one running example from ShopKart, the online shop used throughout the course. Support tickets arrive as free text. Before any agent or person handles a ticket, a router must read it and produce three facts: the intent : refund , order_status , cancel , exchange or other ; the order number , if the customer gave one; whether the ticket is urgent . The router runs on every ticket, so it must be cheap and fast, and other programs read its output, so it must be exact JSON . That is a typical fine-tuning candidate: narrow, high volume, strict format. The target looks like this: Copy Because the answer is structured, a program can score it field by field. That scoring function is the metric , and writing it is the first real step of the project. Step 3 · Build the dataset Real projects get examples from logs, from people who label them, or from a large model (Step 8). To keep the workshop self-contained and repeatable, this one generates its tickets from templates: ten ways of phrasing each intent, with products, cities, order numbers and urgency filled in at random. Save this file as ft_data.py in your project folder; the next four lessons import it. Copy Reading this output Reading this code TEMPLATES holds ten phrasings per intent. build trains on the first phrasings of them (four by default) and builds the test set from the last two, which training never sees. make_example returns the ticket text and its label , the answer a perfect router would give. About one ticket in seven has no order number, so the model must learn to answer null instead of inventing one. to_messages wraps a ticket in the chat format : a list of messages with a role (system, user, assistant) and content ( Lesson 11.20 ). The assistant message holds the label as JSON text, because a language model produces text. score is the metric: it parses the model's reply as JSON and compares each field with the label. all_correct is 1 only when all three fields match. A reply that is not valid JSON scores 0 everywhere. Now build the three sets and look at them. Always read some of your data before training on it. Copy What you should see Copy Step 4 · Three sets, and checking for leaks How this workshop splits its data. Each intent has ten different ways of asking. The first attempt trains on four of them. The test set uses two phrasings that are never used for training, so it measures whether the model understood the intent or only memorised the sentences. The three sets have different jobs ( Lesson 2.26 introduced them): The training set is what the model learns from. The validation set is watched during training to decide when to stop and which settings are better. It uses the same phrasings as training but different tickets. The test set is used once, at the end, to report how good the model is. Here it uses phrasings that never appear in training, because real customers will not phrase things the way your training data did. Check the balance of the data, and check that no ticket appears in two sets: Copy What you should see Copy The classes are balanced (64 tickets each), about two thirds of tickets carry an order number, and under a third are urgent. The last line shows why build checks for duplicates. Without the check, some tickets are generated twice, and a few validation tickets are exact copies of training tickets. That is leakage : the model would be "tested" on examples it has memorised, and its score would look better than it is. With real data, leakage is usually subtler (the same customer, the same conversation split across sets, near-duplicates that differ by a space), and it is the most common reason a fine-tuned model does well in evaluation and badly in production. Step 5 · The file format every tool accepts Fine-tuning tools and services read JSONL files: one JSON object per line, each with a messages list. Write the three sets to disk: Copy What you should see Copy Each line is one complete conversation ending in the assistant's ideal reply. This is the format used by OpenAI's fine-tuning API, Amazon Bedrock, Vertex AI, Hugging Face TRL, Unsloth and Axolotl. Two older formats still appear in public datasets and tutorials: Alpaca ( instruction , input , output fields) and ShareGPT ( conversations with from and value ). Both carry the same information and convert to messages in a few lines. Watch out The format is part of the data Every example here starts with the same system message and is written in the model's chat template . The model will learn to be a router for inputs that look like this . In production you must build the prompt in exactly the same way: the same template, the same system message, the same roles. Lesson 14.130 measures what happens when the format at serving time differs from training. Step 6 · The baseline: no training, no examples Before training, measure what the untrained model does. The model is SmolLM2-135M-Instruct : 135 million parameters, small enough to train on a laptop's processor in a few minutes, and already instruction-tuned so it understands the chat format. Save this second helper file as ft_model.py ; it loads the model and holds the functions the whole workshop shares. Lesson 3.23 explains encode , make_batch and train line by line; for now you need load , reply and evaluate . Copy Copy What you should see Copy The base model understands that JSON is wanted, and sometimes starts writing some, but it invents its own keys, wraps the answer in prose, or answers the customer instead of routing the ticket. Not one reply parses as the JSON we need, so every score is 0. This is zero-shot prompting: instructions only, no examples. Step 7 · The baseline with examples in the prompt The fair comparison for fine-tuning is the best prompt you can write. Add a precise description of the fields and five solved examples, shown to the model as earlier turns of the conversation. This is few-shot prompting ( Lesson 11.25 ): Copy What you should see Copy The examples fixed the format: every reply is now valid JSON with the right keys. But the content is mostly wrong. This small model picks the right intent well under half the time, and look at the order numbers in the three replies printed: the second and third are the same number, copied from one of the examples in the prompt instead of read from the ticket (the second ticket has no order number at all). Only 15% of tickets are fully correct. The prompt also grew from 53 tokens to 349, and every one of those tokens is processed, and paid for, on every single ticket. Reading this output What the baseline tells you A much larger model would do far better with this same few-shot prompt, probably well enough to ship. That is the usual first answer, and Lesson 14.130 comes back to the comparison. The case for fine-tuning here is cost and speed at volume: a 135M model is hundreds of times cheaper to run than a frontier model , if it can be made accurate. The baseline numbers are now written down: 0% fully correct zero-shot and 15% few-shot. Whatever training achieves will be compared with these, on the same 40 test tickets. Step 8 · Where real training data comes from Templates made this workshop repeatable, but real data is harder and matters more than any training setting. Source How it works Watch out for Production logs Real inputs with the outputs your current system produced, filtered to the good ones ( Lesson 14.131 ) Personal data; training the model on your current system's mistakes Human labels People write or correct the ideal output for real inputs Cost; labellers disagreeing: write guidelines and measure agreement A large model as teacher A frontier model labels real inputs; you review a sample. This is distillation ( Lesson 14.132 ) The provider's terms of use; the teacher's errors are inherited Synthetic inputs A model writes varied inputs from a list of scenarios, personas and styles; a teacher model then labels them Low variety: generated text clusters around a few phrasings, as our templates do Public datasets From the Hugging Face Hub and similar Licence; relevance; test sets that models have already seen How many examples? Rough guides that practitioners report, to be confirmed by your own measurements: 50 to 100 carefully chosen examples can already teach a format or a tone. A few hundred to a few thousand is typical for classification, extraction and routing. Tens of thousands are used for broad behaviour changes or teaching a new domain's language. Quality and variety beat volume. A thousand near-identical examples teach less than a hundred varied ones. Lesson 14.130 measures this directly. A checklist before training on any dataset: Every example is one you would be happy for the model to copy exactly, mistakes included. The examples cover the hard and rare cases, not only the easy ones (missing order numbers, two requests in one ticket, mixed languages). Personal data is removed or masked, and you have the right to train on the data. No test example, or near-copy of one, is in the training set. The format matches production exactly: the same system message, the same fields, the same template. Check your mental model ✗ "Fine-tuning is how you teach a model your company's knowledge." ✓ It teaches behaviour and format. Knowledge that changes belongs in retrieval or tools, where it can be updated and cited. ✗ "Fine-tune first, then see if it helped." ✓ Define the metric and measure the prompt-only baseline first; otherwise you cannot know whether training was worth it. ✗ "A high validation score means the model is ready." ✓ Validation data looks like training data. Only a test set that resembles real use, with no leaked examples, tells you that. ✗ "More training data is always better." ✓ More varied , correct data is better. a0801: Course home / Phase 8 · Models That Create A map of generative models Lesson 8.1 45 min Learn Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 2 (How Machines Learn), Phase 3 (Neural Networks, Inside Out), Phase 7 · 14 (Transformers) Type : Learn. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Every image model, text model, video model, and 3D model fits in one of five buckets. Pick the wrong bucket and you will fight the math for weeks. Pick the right one and the field's last twelve years of progress stacks cleanly in your head. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Generative model "It makes new stuff" Learns a sampler for $p_{\text{data}}(x)$, optionally exposes $\log p(x)$. Explicit density "You can evaluate it" Model provides a closed-form or tractable $\log p(x)$. Implicit density "GAN-style" Only a sampler — no way to evaluate $p(x)$ of a given point. ELBO "Evidence lower bound" A tractable lower bound on $\log p(x)$; VAEs and diffusion optimize it. Score "Gradient of log-density" $\nabla_x \log p(x)$; diffusion and SDE models learn this field. Manifold hypothesis "Data lives on a surface" High-dim data concentrates on a low-dim manifold; why dimensionality reduction works. Autoregressive "Predict the next piece" Factorize joint as product of conditionals. Latent "Compressed code" Low-dim representation from which a decoder can reconstruct the input. The problem In plain words first A generative model learns from examples (photos, sentences, recordings) and then produces new ones that could have come from the same collection. There are only a handful of ways to do it. Some models can tell you how likely any given example is and build their output piece by piece (language models). Some learn a compressed code and decode from it (autoencoders). Some learn by a contest between a generator and a judge and produce an output in one shot (GANs). Some start from noise and remove it step by step (diffusion and flow models). Knowing which family a model belongs to tells you how it is trained, how it fails, and how expensive it is to run. This lesson runs the lesson's one-dimensional example of "a model that gives probabilities" against "a model that only gives samples", then times three real models from three families, GPT-2, a diffusion model and BigGAN, making text and images on this page's CPU. Nothing is trained. A generative model does one job: given training samples drawn from some unknown distribution ​ ( x ) , output new samples that look like they came from the same distribution. Faces, sentences, MIDI files, protein structures — all the same problem if you squint. The rub is that ​ lives in a space with millions of dimensions (a 512x512 RGB image is ~786k dimensions), the samples sit on a thin manifold inside that space, and you only have maybe 10M examples. Brute-forcing the density is hopeless. Every generative model is a compromise that trades one hard problem for a slightly less hard one. Five families have survived the last twelve years. Knowing which compromise each family makes tells you why it wins on some tasks and collapses on others. The idea 1. Explicit density, tractable. Write as a sum you can actually evaluate. Autoregressive models (PixelCNN, WaveNet, GPT) factorize ​ p ( x i ​ ∣ x < i ​ ) . Normalizing flows (RealNVP, Glow) build as an invertible transform of a simple base. Pro: exact likelihood, clean training loss. Con: autoregressive inference is sequential (slow for long sequences), flows need invertible architectures (architecturally restrictive). 2. Explicit density, approximate. Bound from below (ELBO) and optimize the bound. VAEs (Kingma 2013) use an encoder-decoder with a variational posterior. Diffusion models (DDPM, Ho 2020) train a denoiser that implicitly optimizes a weighted ELBO. Diffusion is the dominant image, video, and 3D backbone in 2026. 3. Implicit density. Skip density entirely; learn a generator that produces samples and a discriminator that tells real from fake. GANs (Goodfellow 2014). Fast at inference (one forward pass) but notoriously unstable during training. StyleGAN 1/2/3 remain state of the art for fixed-domain photorealism (faces, bedrooms) even in 2026. 4. Score-based / continuous-time. Learn the gradient of the log-density ​ lo g p ( x ) (the score) directly. Song & Ermon (2019) trained score networks at many noise levels, and Song et al. (2021) unified this with diffusion as a stochastic differential equation. Flow matching (Lipman 2023) is the 2024-2026 hotness: simulation-free training, straighter paths, far fewer sampling steps than DDPM. Stable Diffusion 3, FLUX.1 and F5-TTS use flow matching or rectified flow. 5. Token-based autoregressive over discrete codes. Compress high-dim data with a VQ-VAE or residual quantizer into a short sequence of discrete tokens, then use a Transformer to model the token sequence. Parti, AudioLM, VALL-E and MusicGen use this. (Sora, by contrast, is a diffusion transformer over continuous latent patches.) This is bucket 1 plus a learned tokenizer. A brief history Year Model Why it mattered 2013 VAE (Kingma) First deep generative model with a usable training loss. 2014 GAN (Goodfellow) Implicit density, no likelihood — shockingly sharp samples. 2015 DRAW, PixelCNN Sequential image generation. 2016–2018 RealNVP, Glow Invertible flows; exact likelihood with depth. 2017 Progressive GAN First megapixel faces. 2019 StyleGAN / StyleGAN2 Photorealistic faces still hard to beat for that one domain. 2020 DDPM (Ho) Diffusion becomes practical. 2021 CLIP, DALL-E 1, VQGAN Text-to-image goes mainstream. 2022 Imagen, Stable Diffusion 1, DALL-E 2 Latent diffusion + text conditioning = commodity. 2022 ControlNet, LoRA Fine control over pretrained diffusion. 2023 SDXL, Midjourney v5, Flow matching Scale + better training dynamics. 2024 Sora, Stable Diffusion 3, Flux.1 Video diffusion; flow matching wins. 2025 Veo 3, Sora 2, Kling 2, GPT-4o image generation, Gemini 2.5 Flash Image Video with sound; image editing by instruction. 2023–2025 Consistency models, adversarial distillation (SDXL-Turbo, FLUX.1-schnell) Images in 1–4 sampling steps. The five-question triage When a new generative model paper drops, answer these five questions before reading the method section. What is being modeled? Pixels, latents, discrete tokens, 3D Gaussians, meshes, waveforms? Is the density explicit or implicit? Do they write down ? Sampling: one-shot or iterative? Iterative means slower inference; one-shot usually means adversarial or distilled. Conditioning: unconditional, class, text, image, pose? This determines the loss and architecture scaffolding. Evaluation: FID, CLIP score, IS, human preference, task accuracy? Each has known failure modes (see Lesson 8.14 ). You will re-answer these five for every lesson in this phase. By the end, they will be reflex. The same idea as a formula The common goal. Fit a model ​ to data from ​ . Worked example One image, five ways, by hand A RGB image has numbers. Pixel autoregressive (PixelCNN-style): 786,432 sequential predictions, one per number; impractical at this size. Tokens: a VQ tokenizer with 16× downsampling gives tokens; an autoregressive transformer needs 1,024 sequential steps. Latent diffusion: an 8× VAE gives a latent (16,384 numbers); 30 denoising steps of a large network, all positions in parallel at each step. Distilled flow model (FLUX.1-schnell style): the same latent in 1–4 steps. GAN: one generator pass. Iteration buys flexibility and stable training, not quality by itself. Production note: five families, five inference shapes Each family maps to a different inference-server cost curve. production-inference literature frames LLM inference as prefill + decode; the same decomposition applies here: Autoregressive (bucket 1 and 5). Sequential decode dominates latency; KV-cache, continuous batching, and speculative decoding all apply directly. VAE / diffusion / flow-matching (buckets 2 and 4). There is no decode in the LLM sense. Cost = num_steps × step_cost , and the step_cost is a transformer or U-Net forward at the full latent resolution. The production knobs are step count (DDIM / DPM-Solver / distillation), batch size, and precision (bf16 / fp8 / int4). GAN (bucket 3). One forward pass. No schedule, no KV-cache. TTFT ≈ total latency. This is why StyleGAN still wins on narrow-domain UX. When you see "faster than diffusion" in a paper abstract, translate it to "fewer steps × same step cost" or "same steps × cheaper step cost". Everything else is marketing. In plain words first The idea in one line A plain autoencoder compresses then reconstructs. It memorizes. It does not generate. Add one trick — force the code to look Gaussian — and you get a sampler. That single trick, the reparameterization of , is why every latent-diffusion and flow-matching image model you use in 2026 has a VAE at the input. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Autoencoder Encode-decode network $x \to z \to \hat{x}$, learn MSE. Not generative. VAE AE with a sampler Encoder outputs a distribution, KL penalty shapes code space. ELBO Evidence lower bound $\log p(x) \ge \text{recon} - \mathrm{KL}[q(z \mid x) \Vert p(z)]$; tight when $q = p(z \mid x)$. Reparameterization $z = \mu + \sigma \cdot \epsilon$ Rewrites stochastic node as deterministic + pure noise. Enables backprop through sampling. Posterior collapse "KL term wins" Encoder ignores $x$, outputs the prior; decoder must hallucinate. β-VAE Tunable KL weight $\text{loss} = \text{recon} + \beta \cdot \mathrm{KL}$. The problem In plain words first An autoencoder squeezes an input, say a photo, into a short list of numbers (the "code" or "latent") and then rebuilds the input from that list. It is a compressor, not a generator: pick a random code and the decoder produces garbage, because nothing made the codes fill a simple, predictable region. A variational autoencoder (VAE) fixes this by making the encoder output a small cloud of possible codes instead of one point, and by charging a penalty whenever those clouds stray from a standard bell curve. Then random draws from the bell curve decode to plausible outputs. Today the VAE's main job is different again: it is the compressor in front of nearly every image and video diffusion model, which works on its compact latents instead of on pixels. This lesson checks the lesson's hand-written VAE maths without training it, then runs the real VAE from Stable Diffusion on photos: compression, reconstructions, what its latents look like, and why decoding them is the memory peak of an image server. Compress a 784-pixel MNIST digit to a 16-number code, then reconstruct. A plain autoencoder will ace reconstruction MSE but the code space is a lumpy mess. Pick a random point in the code space, decode it, and you get noise. It has no sampler. It is a compression model dressed up. What you actually want is: (a) the code space is a clean, smooth distribution you can sample from — say an isotropic Gaussian , (b) decoding any sample produces a plausible digit, and (c) the encoder and decoder still compress well. Three goals, one architecture, one loss. Kingma's 2013 VAE solves this by training the encoder to output a distribution ) , pulling that distribution toward the prior via a KL penalty, and then sampling from before decoding. At inference time, drop the encoder, sample , decode. The KL penalty is what forces the code space to be structured. In plain words first The idea in one line Goodfellow's trick in 2014 was to skip density entirely. Two networks. One makes fakes. One catches them. They fight until the fakes are indistinguishable from real. It shouldn't work. It often doesn't. When it does, the samples are still the sharpest in the literature for narrow domains. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Generator "G" Noise-to-sample network, G: z → x̂ . Discriminator "D" Classifier D: x → [0, 1] , real vs fake. Minimax "The game" $\min_G \max_D$ of a joint objective. Non-saturating loss "The fix" Use $-\log D(G(z))$ for G instead of $\log(1 - D(G(z)))$. Mode collapse "G memorized one thing" Generator produces few distinct outputs despite diverse data. WGAN "Wasserstein" Replace BCE with Earth-Mover distance + gradient penalty; smoother gradient. Spectral norm "Lipschitz trick" Constrain D's weight norms to bound its slope; stabilizes training. StyleGAN "The one that works" Mapping network + style modulation (AdaIN, then weight demodulation in StyleGAN2); strong and fast for faces and other narrow domains. The problem In plain words first A generative adversarial network (GAN) trains two networks against each other. The generator turns random numbers into a sample, say an image. The discriminator looks at a sample and guesses whether it is real or made up. Each improves by exploiting the other's mistakes, and if the contest goes well the generator ends up making samples the discriminator cannot tell from real ones, without anyone ever writing down how likely an image is. Once trained, a GAN makes an image in a single pass, which is still its great strength. Training is the hard part: the contest can stall, oscillate, or settle on a few kinds of output. This lesson checks the theory behind the contest numerically with the lesson's tiny networks (untrained, since this page trains nothing), then runs BigGAN, a large GAN trained on ImageNet, to show the quality, the diversity dial and the one-pass speed. VAEs produce blurry samples because their MSE decoder loss is Bayes-optimal for the mean image — and the mean of many plausible digits is a fuzzy digit. You want a loss that rewards plausibility , not pixel-wise proximity to any one target. There is no closed-form for plausibility. You have to learn it. Goodfellow's idea: train a classifier to distinguish real images from fakes. Train a generator to fool . The loss signal for is whatever currently thinks makes something look real. This signal updates as improves, chasing a moving target. If both networks converge, has learned the data distribution without ever writing down log p(x) . This is adversarial training. Step 1 · non-saturating loss code/main.py trains a tiny GAN on 1-D data: a mixture of two Gaussians. Generator and discriminator are single-hidden-layer MLPs. We implement forward, backward, and the minimax loop by hand. The goal is to see the two key failure modes (mode collapse + vanishing gradient) as they happen. The vanilla Goodfellow loss goes to 0 when D classifies G's fake as fake with high confidence. At that point the gradient for G is basically zero — G cannot improve. The non-saturating form has the opposite asymptote: it blows up when D is confident, giving G a strong signal. Solutions Solution P1 · A single animal, not a double exposure A single, plausible-looking animal partway between a dog and a cat (the third and fourth images of the last row), not two pictures overlaid. BigGAN's generator was trained so that every point it is given maps to an image the discriminator accepts as real; a blend of the two class vectors is just another input, and the output stays on the "realistic image" manifold. The VAE of Lesson 8.2 was trained only to reconstruct, so its latents behave like a compressed copy of the pixels, and averaging them averages the pictures. Smooth, semantic latent spaces are one of the GAN family's lasting strengths, and the reason StyleGAN latents became a tool for editing faces. Solution B1 · The generator stalls At the start the generator's samples sit in a bump near 0 where there is no real data, so the discriminator quickly learns to reject them and falls toward 0. With the original loss, the generator's gradient through the logit is , so as the discriminator gets better the generator's signal shrinks: at it is 0.01, against 0.99 with the non-saturating loss (the table in the run after Step 3). The generator barely moves while the discriminator becomes ever more confident, which makes the gradient smaller still. Both losses have the same equilibrium; only the non-saturating one gives the generator a usable signal when it is losing. Production note: one-shot inference is GAN's lasting advantage GANs no longer win on sample quality for open-domain generation, but they still win on inference cost. In production-inference literature vocabulary a GAN has: No prefill, no decode stages. A single forward pass. TTFT ≈ total latency. No KV-cache pressure. The only state is the weights. Batch size is bounded by activation memory, not cache. Trivial continuous batching. Since every request takes the same fixed FLOPs, a static batch at the server's target occupancy is usually optimal. No in-flight scheduler needed. This is why adversarial distillation (ADD in SDXL-Turbo; latent ADD in SD3.5 Large Turbo and FLUX.1-schnell) is a leading technique for fast text-to-image: it collapses a 20–50-step diffusion pipeline into 1–4 forward passes while staying close to the diffusion model's outputs. Consistency distillation (LCM) reaches the same few-step range without a discriminator. The adversarial loss survives as a training-time knob for turning slow generators into fast ones. In plain words first The idea in one line The first big unlock of 2014-2017 was controlling what a GAN makes. Attach a label, or an image, or a sentence. Pix2Pix did the image version, and its recipe is still a strong, fast baseline for narrow image-to-image tasks with paired data. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Conditional GAN "GAN with labels" G(z, c), D(x, c). Both networks see the condition. Pix2Pix "Image-to-image GAN" Paired cGAN with U-Net G and PatchGAN D + L1 loss. U-Net "Encoder-decoder with skips" Symmetric conv network; skips preserve high-freq. PatchGAN "Local-realism classifier" D outputs per-patch score instead of global score. CycleGAN "Unpaired image translation" Two G's + cycle-consistency loss; no paired data. The problem In plain words first A conditional GAN is a GAN that takes instructions: besides random noise, both networks receive a condition, such as a class label or a whole input image. The generator must produce an output that fits the condition, and the discriminator judges the pair, "is this a plausible output for this input ?". Pix2Pix applies this to image-to-image tasks with paired examples: sketch to photo, map to aerial view, black-and-white to colour. Its two tricks are an extra pixel-matching loss (L1) that keeps the output faithful to the target, and a discriminator that judges small patches rather than the whole image. This lesson shows numerically why the pixel loss alone gives blurry results, builds Pix2Pix's patch discriminator to measure exactly what it sees, and then runs Real-ESRGAN, an image-to-image GAN that upscales photos and is shipped in today's image tools. Nothing is trained. An unconditional GAN samples arbitrary faces. Useful for a demo, useless in production. You want: map a sketch to a photo , map a map to an aerial photo , map a daytime scene to nighttime , colorize a grayscale image . In all of these, you are given an input image and must output with some semantic correspondence. There are many plausible 's per . Mean-squared error flattens them into mush. An adversarial loss doesn't, because "looks real" is sharp. Conditional GAN (Mirza & Osindero, 2014) adds a condition as an input to both and . Pix2Pix (Isola et al., 2017) specialized this: condition is a full input image, generator is a U-Net, discriminator is a patch-based classifier (PatchGAN), and loss is adversarial + L1. That recipe is still hard to beat on narrow image-to-image tasks with plenty of paired examples, because it is trained on paired data : you have exactly the signal you need. The idea Conditional G. . In Pix2Pix, is dropout inside G (no input noise — Isola found explicit noise got ignored). Conditional D. . Input is the pair (condition, output). This is the key difference: D must judge whether is consistent with , not just whether looks real. U-Net generator. Encoder-decoder with skip connections across the bottleneck. Critical for tasks where input and output share low-level structure (edges, silhouette). Without the skips, high-frequency detail vanishes. PatchGAN discriminator. Instead of outputting a single real/fake score, D outputs an grid where each cell judges a receptive field of ~70×70 pixels. Averaged. This is a Markov random field assumption: realism is local. Much faster to train, fewer parameters, sharper output. Solutions Solution P1 · Bicubic wins PSNR, the GAN wins sharpness Bicubic interpolation wins on PSNR, by about 1–2 dB, and Real-ESRGAN looks much sharper. PSNR measures squared pixel error, and when the fine detail of the original is unknowable from a input, the safest guess is a smooth average, exactly what interpolation produces. Real-ESRGAN was trained with an adversarial loss to produce plausible sharp detail; where its invented detail differs from the real one, it is penalised twice by squared error (once for missing the true detail, once for adding a wrong one). That is why image-restoration papers report a perceptual metric such as LPIPS alongside PSNR. Solution B1 · Realistic but unrelated Without the input, the discriminator judges only "is this a realistic image?" and cannot notice an output that is realistic but wrong for this input: the wrong colour of a car, a building where the map shows a road. With , the L1 term is the only thing tying the output to its input, so results remain roughly faithful but the adversarial term no longer pushes consistency in detail. With as well, nothing ties output to input: the generator can learn to ignore and produce any realistic image, often the same few for every input (mode collapse), and the discriminator has no reason to object. Isola et al. compared these variants and found the conditional discriminator plus L1 best. Production note: Pix2Pix as a latency-bound baseline When you have paired data and a narrow task (sketch → render, semantic map → photo, day → night), Pix2Pix's one-shot inference beats diffusion by an order of magnitude on latency. The production comparison is usually: Path Steps Rough latency at 512² on a single L4 (order of magnitude; depends on model size) Pix2Pix (U-Net forward) 1 ~30 ms SD-Inpaint or SD-Img2Img 20 ~1.2 s SDXL-Turbo Img2Img 1-4 ~0.15-0.35 s ControlNet + SDXL base 20-30 ~3-5 s Pix2Pix wins on throughput in static batches (every request is the same FLOPs). Diffusion wins on quality and generalization. The modern play is often to ship a Pix2Pix-style distilled model for the narrow task and a diffusion fallback for tail inputs. In plain words first The idea in one line Most generators stir into every layer at the same time. That change made the latent space far more controllable and set the standard for photorealistic faces for years. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Mapping network "The MLP" $f: Z \to W$, 8 layers, decouples latent geometry from data statistics. The problem In plain words first In an ordinary GAN, the random input numbers are fed in once at the start and every property of the picture (layout, lighting, colour, texture) ends up tangled together in them. StyleGAN feeds them in differently. A small network first converts the random numbers into a "style" vector, and that style is applied at every stage of image building, from the coarse low-resolution stages that settle the layout to the fine ones that settle textures. Because each stage reads its own copy of the style, you can take the coarse stages' style from one image and the fine stages' style from another. StyleGAN2 and StyleGAN3 fixed artefacts in the original. This lesson runs the lesson's toy version, checks StyleGAN2's normalisation trick numerically, and then runs a real StyleGAN3 trained on landscape photos: the truncation trick, style mixing, and StyleGAN3's ability to move a picture smoothly. Solution B1 · Scales compound Each layer multiplies the standard deviation by the style, so 14 layers with styles of 2 give ≈ 16 , 000 times the input's scale, and styles of 0.5 give ≈ 6 × 1 0 − 5 : the signal either overflows half-precision arithmetic or drowns in rounding error and noise. Any style that is not exactly 1 on average compounds exponentially with depth. Demodulation removes the problem at its source by rescaling each output channel's weights to unit gain, so the style changes the direction of the features (which channels matter) but not their overall size; StyleGAN1's AdaIN achieved stability by renormalising the activations instead, at the cost of the droplet artefacts. Production note: why StyleGAN still ships in 2026 StyleGAN3 generates a 1024² face in one forward pass on a modern GPU, in tens of milliseconds or less: num_steps = 1 , no VAE decode, no cross-attention pass. A 30–50-step SDXL pipeline at the same resolution takes seconds, two orders of magnitude more, so for narrow-domain products (avatar services, stock face generation) StyleGAN wins on cost. Two operational consequences: No scheduler, no batcher. Static batch at the target occupancy is optimal. In plain words first The idea in one line Ho, Jain, Abbeel (2020) gave the field a recipe it could not quit. Destroy the data with noise over a thousand small steps. Train one neural net to predict the noise. Reverse the process at inference. Today every mainstream image, video, 3D, and music model runs on this loop, possibly with flow matching or consistency tricks on top. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Forward process "Adding noise" Fixed Markov chain $q(x_t \mid x_{t-1})$ that destroys the data. Reverse process "Denoising" Learned chain $p_\theta(x_{t-1} \mid x_t)$ that reconstructs the data. β schedule "The noise ladder" Per-step variance; linear, cosine, or sigmoid. α̅ "Alpha bar" Cumulative product $\prod (1 - \beta)$; gives closed-form $x_t$ from $x_0$. Simple loss "MSE on noise" $\lVert \epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t) \rVert^2$; all variational derivations collapse to this. ε-prediction "Predict noise" Output is the noise added; standard DDPM. V-prediction "Predict velocity" Output is $\alpha \cdot \epsilon - \sigma \cdot x$; better conditioning across t. DDPM "The paper" Ho et al. 2020; linear β, 1000 steps, U-Net. DDIM "Deterministic sampler" Non-Markov sampler, 20-50 steps, same training objective. Classifier-free guidance "CFG" Mix conditional and unconditional noise predictions to amplify conditioning. The problem In plain words first A diffusion model learns to generate by learning to clean. Take a training image and add a little random noise, then a little more, over many steps, until nothing but noise is left; this direction needs no learning, just a formula. Then train a network to look at a noisy image and estimate the noise in it. To generate, start from pure noise and repeatedly subtract the network's noise estimate, a small step at a time, until an image appears. The training loss is a plain squared error, which makes diffusion far more stable to train than a GAN; the price is that generating takes many network passes. This lesson checks the noising formula against step-by-step noising, runs the lesson's reverse sampler with a noise predictor worked out exactly instead of trained (and finds a bug in the lesson's settings), then runs the original 2020 DDPM model to see what it believes at each noise level and how an image emerges. Solutions Solution P1 · Something else: a cat Something else: at the guess looks like a cat's face, with only the cassette player's pale colours left (the third guess in the figure). With signal and noise at equal power, many clean images are consistent with what the network sees, and its guess is their average under its idea of what images look like, which is CIFAR-10's ten classes. A cassette player is not among them, so the most plausible explanation it finds is a cat. At and 100 the photo dominates the noise and the guess is accurate. The same mechanism explains how a diffusion model generates: from pure noise, its guesses are pulled toward the training distribution. In plain words first The idea in one line Pixel-space diffusion on 512×512 images is a computational war crime. Rombach et al. (2022) noticed that you do not need all 786k dimensions to generate an image — you need enough to capture semantic structure, and a separate decoder for the rest. Run diffusion inside a VAE's latent space. That one idea is Stable Diffusion. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means First stage "The VAE" Trained encoder/decoder pair; compresses 512² to 64². Second stage "The U-Net" Diffusion model over the latent space. CFG "Guidance scale" $(1+w) \cdot \epsilon_{\text{cond}} - w \cdot \epsilon_{\text{uncond}}$; tunes conditioning strength. Null token "Empty prompt embed" Unconditional embed used for $\epsilon_{\text{uncond}}$. Cross-attention "How text gets in" Each U-Net block attends to text tokens as K and V. DiT "Diffusion Transformer" Replace U-Net with a transformer over latent patches; scales better. MMDiT "Multi-modal DiT" SD3's architecture: text and image streams with joint attention. VAE scaling factor "Magic number" Divides latents by ~5.4 so diffusion operates in unit-variance space. The problem In plain words first Running diffusion directly on the pixels of a large image is very expensive: every one of dozens of denoising steps pushes the whole image through a big network. Latent diffusion, the idea behind Stable Diffusion, first squeezes the image with a VAE (Lesson 8.2) into a much smaller grid of numbers, runs all the denoising steps on that small grid, and decodes to pixels once at the end. Text steers the result through cross-attention: at every layer, each position of the image grid looks up the parts of the prompt that matter to it. A trick called classifier-free guidance then strengthens the prompt's pull by comparing the model's prediction with and without the prompt. This lesson computes guidance exactly on the lesson's one-dimensional example, runs a real cross-attention layer, and generates a picture on this page's CPU with a small distilled Stable Diffusion, with and without guidance. Nothing is trained. Pixel-space diffusion at 512² means the U-Net runs on tensors of shape [B, 3, 512, 512] . Each sampling step is ~100 GFLOPS for a 500M-param U-Net. Fifty steps is 5 TFLOPS per image. Train on a billion images and the compute bill is absurd. Most of those FLOPs go to pushing perceptually unimportant details through the net — the high-frequency texture that a lossy VAE could compress away. Rombach's idea: train a VAE once (the first stage ), freeze it, and run diffusion entirely in the 4-channel 64×64 latent space (the second stage ). Same kind of U-Net, on 64 times fewer spatial positions (48 times fewer numbers), so each step costs a small fraction of its pixel-space equivalent for comparable quality. This is the Stable Diffusion recipe. SD 1.x / 2.x used an 860M U-Net over 64×64×4 latents, SDXL used a 2.6B U-Net over 128×128×4 , SD3 swapped the U-Net for a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) with flow matching. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Text alone is a clumsy control signal. ControlNet lets you clone a pretrained diffusion model and steer it with a depth map, pose skeleton, scribble, or edge image. LoRA lets you fine-tune a 2B-parameter model by training 10 million parameters. Together they made Stable Diffusion a controllable production tool. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means ControlNet "Spatial control" Cloned encoder + zero-conv skips; reads a conditioning image. Zero convolution "Starts as identity" 1×1 conv initialized to zero; ControlNet starts as no-op. LoRA "Low-rank adapter" $W + BA$, $r \ll d$; 100x fewer params than a full fine-tune. rank r "The knob" LoRA compression; 4-16 typical, 64+ for heavy personalization. $\alpha$ "LoRA strength" Runtime scaling of the LoRA delta. IP-Adapter "Reference image" Small image-conditioning adapter via CLIP-image tokens. DreamBooth "Full subject fine-tune" Train the full model on ~30 images of a subject. Textual Inversion "New token" Learn a new word embedding only; legacy, mostly replaced. The problem In plain words first A text prompt cannot say exactly where things go in a picture, what pose a person is in, or what your product looks like. Three add-ons fix this without retraining the big model. ControlNet attaches a trainable copy of half of the diffusion network that reads an extra picture, such as an edge map, a depth map or a pose skeleton, and nudges the original network so the output follows its layout. LoRA teaches the model a new style or subject by learning a small "correction" to each weight matrix, stored as the product of two thin matrices, a few percent of the model's size. IP-Adapter lets a reference image act like part of the prompt. This lesson checks LoRA's arithmetic, opens a real LoRA file to see what it contains and what happens when it meets the wrong model, and builds ControlNet's zero-initialised branch on a real Stable Diffusion U-Net to show why training it starts safely. Nothing is trained. A prompt like "a woman in a red dress walking a dog on a busy street" gives the model no information about where the dog is, what pose the woman is in, or the perspective of the street. Text pins down about 10% of what you need to specify an image. The rest is visual and cannot be described efficiently in words. Training a new conditional model from scratch for every signal (pose, depth, canny, segmentation) is prohibitive. You want to keep the 2.6B-param SDXL backbone frozen, attach a small side-network that reads the conditioning, and have it nudge the backbone's intermediate features. That is ControlNet. You also want to teach the model new concepts (your face, your product, your style) without retraining the full model. You want a 100x smaller delta. That is LoRA — low-rank adapters that plug into existing attention weights. ControlNet + LoRA + text is the practitioner's toolkit: typical ComfyUI and diffusers workflows stack one or more LoRAs, a ControlNet or two, and sometimes an IP-Adapter on an SDXL, FLUX.1, FLUX.2 or Qwen-Image base. The idea Idea 1 · ControlNet (Zhang et al., 2023) Take a pretrained SD. Clone the encoder half of the U-Net. Freeze the original. Train the clone to accept an extra conditioning input (edges, depth, pose). Connect the clone back to the decoder half of the original with zero-convolution skip connections (1×1 convs initialized to zero — start as a no-op, learn a delta). Copy Zero-conv init means ControlNet starts as identity — no harm even before training. Train on 1M (prompt, condition, image) triples with the standard diffusion loss. Per-modality ControlNets ship as side models: about 360M parameters for SD 1.5 (a copy of its encoder half) and about 1.2B for SDXL, with smaller distilled variants available. In plain words first The idea in one line Text-to-image makes new things. Inpainting fixes old ones. In production, much of the paid image work is editing: swap a background, remove a logo, extend the canvas, regenerate a hand. Inpainting is where diffusion earns its keep. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Inpainting "Fill the hole" Regenerate inside a mask; keep outside pixels. Outpainting "Extend the canvas" Regenerate outside the canvas; keep inside. 9-channel U-Net "Proper inpainting model" U-Net with noisy \| encoded-source \| mask as input. SDEdit "Img2img with noise level" Noise to time t , denoise with new prompt. InstructPix2Pix "Text-only edits" Fine-tuned diffusion on (image, instruction, output) triples. RePaint "No retraining" Re-noise periodically during reverse to reduce seams. SAM "Segment Anything" Mask generator by clicks or boxes; pairs with inpaint. Flux-Kontext "Edit with context" Flux variant that accepts a reference image + instruction for edits. The problem In plain words first Inpainting regenerates only part of an image, the region inside a mask, and leaves everything else as it was: remove an object, replace a sky, fix a hand. Outpainting does the same beyond the image's edges. Image editing changes the whole picture but keeps its layout. Diffusion models handle all three because generation is gradual: at every denoising step, the known pixels can be fed back in so the generated part has to fit them. The simplest way to do this needs no retraining but can produce fills that do not match their surroundings; dedicated inpainting models see the whole known image and the mask as extra inputs. This lesson measures that mismatch exactly on the lesson's five-number example, shows how RePaint's "resampling" reduces it, and runs SDEdit, editing by partial noising, on a real photo with a small Stable Diffusion. Nothing is trained. A client sends a perfect product photo with a distracting sign in the background. You want to erase the sign and leave everything else pixel-identical. You cannot run text-to-image from scratch — the result will have a different color, different lighting, different product angle. You want to regenerate only the masked region, and you want the regeneration to respect the surrounding context. That is inpainting. Variants: Inpainting. Regenerate inside a mask, keep outside pixels. Outpainting. Regenerate outside a mask (or beyond the canvas), keep inside. Image editing. Regenerate the whole image but keep semantic or structural fidelity to the original (SDEdit, InstructPix2Pix). Most image-generation stacks ship an inpainting mode: FLUX.1 Fill, Stable Diffusion Inpaint, SDXL Inpaint, and mask-based editing in hosted APIs such as OpenAI's GPT Image models. They work on the same principle. The idea Idea 1 · The naive approach (and why it's wrong) Run standard text-to-image with a mask. At each sampling step, replace the unmasked region of the noisy latent with the forward-diffused clean image. It works... badly. Boundary artifacts bleed through because the model has no information about what is in the masked region. Idea 2 · The proper inpainting model Train a modified U-Net that takes 9 input channels instead of 4: Copy The extra channels are a copy of the VAE-encoded source image plus a single-channel mask. At training time, you randomly mask regions of the image and train the model to denoise only the masked region while the unmasked region is given as a clean conditioning signal. At inference, the model can "see" what surrounds the masked region and produces coherent completions. SD-Inpaint, SDXL-Inpaint, Flux-Fill all use this 9-channel (or analog) input. Diffusers StableDiffusionInpaintPipeline , FluxFillPipeline . Idea 3 · SDEdit (Meng et al., 2022) — free editing Add noise to the source image up to some intermediate t , then run the reverse chain from t down to 0 with a new prompt. No retraining. The choice of starting t trades fidelity for creative freedom: t/T = 0.3 → nearly identical to source, small stylistic changes t/T = 0.6 → moderate edits, preserves coarse structure t/T = 0.9 → generated from near-noise, minimal source preservation Idea 4 · InstructPix2Pix (Brooks et al., 2023) Fine-tune a diffusion model on (input_image, instruction, output_image) triples. At inference, condition on both the input image and a text instruction ("make it sunset", "add a dragon"). Two CFG scales: image scale and text scale. Idea 5 · RePaint (Lugmayr et al., 2022) Keep a standard unconditional diffusion model. At each reverse step, resample — jump back to a noisier state occasionally and regenerate. Avoids boundary artifacts. Used when you don't have a trained inpainting model. The same idea as a formula The goal. Split the image into known pixels and missing ones (mask , 1 where missing). Step 1 · 5-D DDPM data code/main.py implements a toy 1-D inpainting scheme on 5-dimensional data. We train a DDPM on 5-D mixture data where each sample is 5 floats from one of two clusters. At inference, we "mask" 2 of the 5 dimensions, inject the noisy-forward version of the unmasked three at each step, and regenerate only the masked dimensions. Copy Step 2 · train denoiser over all 5 dims Standard DDPM. Net outputs 5-D noise prediction for 5-D noisy input. Step 3 · at inference, mask-aware reverse Copy This is the naive approach and it works on toy 1-D data. Real image inpainting uses the 9-channel input because texture coherence matters more. See it drawn Replacement and resampling, with an exact denoiser main.py 's schedule at and its two-cluster, five-number data (its main() trains a network, which this page does not run). Because the data is a known Gaussian mixture, the best possible noise predictor is computed exactly, so any failure belongs to the inpainting rule, not to a model. Step 3's replacement rule fills the missing numbers for 1,000 samples, alone and with RePaint's resampling. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output With three known numbers, plain replacement works perfectly: every fill lands near with the data's spread of 0.2. With only one known number it fails badly, although the right answer is just as certain (odds of to 1): 28% of the fills land in the cluster, and the fills' spread is 0.92 instead of 0.2. The cause is the formula box's caveat. At high noise, the re-noised known number is almost pure noise, so the sampler commits the four missing numbers to a cluster almost at random; by the time the known number is clear enough to say " ", the fills have already settled and each step can move them only a little. RePaint's resampling gives them more chances to move: 5 rounds per step halve the error to 14%, 10 rounds cut it to 7%, at 5 and 10 times the cost. Image inpainting fails the same way when the context is a thin border around a large hole: colours or objects that do not match the surroundings. Step 4 · outpainting Outpainting is inpainting with the mask inverted: mask the new (previously non-existent) canvas, fill the rest with the original. Identical training objective. Pitfalls Seams. The naive approach leaves visible boundaries because gradient info doesn't flow across the mask. Fix: dilate the mask by 8-16 pixels, or use a proper inpainting model. Mask leakage. If the conditioning image's unmasked region is low-quality or noisy, it pollutes the generation inside the mask. Denoise or blur slightly. CFG interacts with mask size. High CFG on a small mask = saturated patch. Reduce CFG for small edits. SDEdit fidelity cliff. Going from t/T = 0.5 to t/T = 0.6 can lose the subject's identity. Sweep and checkpoint. Prompt mismatch. The prompt should describe the whole image, not just the new content. "A cat sitting on a chair" not "a cat". Solutions Solution P1 · More than 20% More than 20%: 28% of the fills land in the wrong cluster, even with the best possible denoiser and a known number that makes the answer certain. Replacement never conditions on the clean known value; it conditions on a noisy copy of it, and at the high-noise steps, where each sample's cluster is decided, that copy carries almost no information. Later steps, when the known value is clear, can only make small corrections. With three known numbers the combined evidence is strong enough even when noisy, so the problem disappears. Resampling (RePaint) or a model trained to see the clean context (9-channel inpainting) fixes it. Solution B1 · Noise levels that do not match The network was trained on inputs where every number has the noise level of step . With clean known numbers next to noisy unknown ones, the input is unlike anything it saw in training: at high the known numbers look like an implausibly strong signal, and the noise predictor's estimate for them, ​ − α ˉ t ​ ​ x 0 ​ ) / 1 − α ˉ t ​ ​ , is badly off because k ​ = x 0 k ​ is not t ​ ​ x 0 k ​ . Its errors feed into the estimate for the missing numbers, so fills are biased and boundaries in images show seams and colour shifts. The known values are restored at the end, so the bug hides in the output's "correct" pixels. Re-noising to the current level, as Step 3 does, keeps the input on the training distribution. Production note: edit pipelines are latency-sensitive Users editing an image expect sub-5-second round trips. A 30-step SDXL-Inpaint at 1024² is 3-4 s on an L4, plus SAM mask generation (~200 ms) and VAE encode/decode (~500 ms combined). In production framing, this is TTFT-bound rather than throughput-bound — batch 1, low concurrency, minimize every stage: SAM-H is the slow one. SAM-H at 1024² is ~200 ms; SAM-ViT-B is ~40 ms with minor quality loss. SAM 2 (video) adds temporal overhead; do not use it for single-image edits. Skip the encode when possible. Every pipeline call VAE-encodes the source image. If you have the latents from the previous generation (typical in iterative-edit UIs), pass them directly via latents=... to skip one VAE encode. Mask size does not change the cost. Both the naive and the 9-channel pipelines run the full U-Net over the whole latent at every step, so a small fix costs as much as a large one, unless you crop around the mask, inpaint the crop at full resolution and paste it back (ComfyUI's crop-and-stitch nodes do exactly this). Instruction editors collapse the stages. FLUX.2, FLUX.1 Kontext and Qwen-Image-Edit take (source_image, instruction) directly: no separate mask, no SDEdit strength sweep. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line An image is a 2-D tensor. A video is a 3-D one. The theory is the same; the compute is 10-100x harder. OpenAI's Sora (February 2024) showed it was possible. Hosted systems such as Google's Veo 3.1, Kuaishou's Kling and ByteDance's Seedance now make short clips with sound, and open-weight models (Wan, HunyuanVideo, LTX-2) run on a single GPU. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Video VAE "3-D VAE" Encoder that compresses (T, H, W, C) → spatiotemporal latent. Patches "The tokens" Fixed-size 3-D blocks of the latent; input to the DiT. Factorized attention "Spatial + temporal" Run attention over space, then over time; skip full 3-D attention. Image-to-video (I2V) "Animate this photo" Model takes an image + text, outputs a video that starts from it. Keyframe conditioning "Anchor frames" Pin specific frames to control the video's arc. Motion brush "Directional hint" UI input where the user paints motion vectors onto the image. Re-captioning "Dense captions" Using an LLM to re-label training clips with detailed prompts. Flicker "Temporal artifact" Frame-to-frame inconsistency; fixed with coupled denoising. The problem In plain words first A video is a stack of images that must agree with each other: the same objects, lighting and identities, moving smoothly. Generating each frame separately with an image model gives flicker, because nothing ties one frame's choices to the next. Video diffusion models denoise the whole clip at once: a video VAE compresses it in space and time into a small block of numbers, the block is cut into patches, and a transformer lets every patch attend to patches in other frames, so the frames are decided together. The cost is enormous, which is why video models use heavy compression, why their attention is the bottleneck, and why most of them run in data centres. This lesson measures flicker exactly on the lesson's one-dimensional clips, counts tokens and attention for a real video latent, and runs the real Wan 2.1 video VAE on a short clip. Nothing is trained. A 10-second 1080p video at 24fps is 240 frames of 1920×1080×3 pixels. That's ~1.5 GB of raw data per clip. Pixel-space diffusion is infeasible. You need: Spatiotemporal compression. A VAE that encodes videos, not frames, into a sequence of spatial-temporal patches. Temporal coherence. Frames need to share content, lighting, and object identity over seconds. The net has to model motion. Compute budget. Video training is 10-100x more expensive than image for the same model size. Conditioning. Text, image (first-frame), audio, or another video. Most production models accept all four. The architecture that solved this is the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) applied to spatiotemporal patches, trained on huge (prompt, caption, video) datasets. Same diffusion loss as Lesson 06. The idea Idea 1 · Patchify Encode the video with a 3D VAE (learned spatiotemporal compression). The latent is shape [T_latent, H_latent, W_latent, C_latent] . Split into patches of size [t_p, h_p, w_p] . For Sora-style models, t_p = 1 (per-frame patches) or t_p = 2 (every two frames). A 10-second 1080p video compresses to ~20,000-100,000 patches. Idea 2 · Spatiotemporal DiT A transformer processes the flat sequence of patches. Each patch has a 3D positional embedding (time + y + x). Attention is usually factorized: Spatial attention within each frame's patches. Temporal attention across frames at the same spatial location. Full 3D attention over all patches at once costs far more (21 times more score pairs for a 5-second clip in the run after Step 4), yet it is what current open models (CogVideoX, HunyuanVideo, Wan) use, made affordable by strong VAE compression, FlashAttention and splitting the sequence across GPUs. Factorised attention was typical of earlier models (Video LDM, AnimateDiff). Idea 3 · Text conditioning Cross-attention or joint attention with a large text encoder (T5-XXL in CogVideoX, umT5 in Wan 2.1, a multimodal LLM in HunyuanVideo). Long prompts matter: Sora's technical report describes re-captioning the training videos with a captioning model to get detailed descriptions, as DALL·E 3 did for images. Idea 4 · Training Standard diffusion loss (ε or v prediction) over spatiotemporal latents. Data: web video + ~100M curated clips + synthetic text captions. Compute: tens of thousands of GPU hours even for a modest open model; frontier-scale budgets are undisclosed and far larger. The same idea as a formula A clip is one sample. Pitfalls Independent per-frame sampling = flicker. If you run image diffusion on each frame separately, the output flickers because each frame's noise is independent. Video diffusion fixes this by coupling the frames through attention or shared noise. Naive 3D attention = OOM. Full 3D attention over a 10-second 1080p latent means half a million tokens attending to each other in every layer. Production models keep full attention but shrink the sequence (stronger VAE compression, larger patches) and split it across GPUs; factorised or windowed attention is the cheaper alternative. Solutions Solution P1 · The per-frame image latent, but it is the wrong question The per-frame image latent has fewer numbers: 29,952 against Wan's 36,864. Wan compresses time 4× but stores 16 channels per position instead of 4, which more than cancels the temporal saving. That comparison misses the point, though. What matters to the diffusion transformer is the number of tokens : Wan's latent has 4 latent frames instead of 13, so with patches it has 576 tokens against 1,872, and attention, which scales with the square of the token count, is about ten times cheaper. The extra channels let each token carry more detail, so reconstruction stays sharp. Solution B1 · Motion dictated by the noise With shared noise, every frame follows the same noise path, so the frames are almost perfectly correlated: frame 0 and frame 5 correlate at 0.94, against 0.55 in real clips, and the average frame-to-frame change is 0.15, smaller than the real 0.25. The clip no longer moves the way the data moves; its motion comes from how the frames' spreads differ, so most clips drift steadily away from zero in the direction they started (83% of them), whatever slope real clips would have. In images, shared noise gives a nearly frozen picture with textures that "swim" or stick to the screen. Consistency must come from a model that knows how frames relate, not from forcing them to share randomness. Production note: video latents are a memory-bandwidth problem A 10-second 1080p clip at 24 fps is 240 frames × 1920 × 1080 × 3 ≈ 1.5 GB of raw pixels. A Wan-style causal VAE (4× in time, 8× in each spatial direction, 16 channels) turns that into about 61 × 135 × 240 × 16 ≈ 32M numbers, ~63 MB in bf16, about 39× smaller (the run under "Use it" measures the same ratio). With 2 × 2 patches that is about 490,000 tokens. Attention over them dominates every step, so long, high-resolution video is limited by compute and by the memory needed for activations, more than by the bandwidth for reading the weights. Three production knobs, all straight from production-inference literature inference chapter: Split the sequence across GPUs. Video DiTs are parallelised over the token sequence (sequence or context parallelism, such as the xDiT/Ulysses support in Wan's and HunyuanVideo's inference code), because one clip's activations outweigh the model's weights. Latency per step drops with the number of GPUs until communication dominates. Frame batching = continuous batching. At generation time, video is conceptually a batch of frames linked by attention. Continuous batching (in-flight scheduling) applies: start rendering frame t+1 while frame t-1 is being returned, if the model architecture allows sliding-window generation. Clip-level prefill cache. For image-to-video, the first-frame conditioning is analogous to an LLM's prompt prefill: compute it once, reuse across the temporal decoder passes. This is effectively a KV-cache for video. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Audio is a 1-D signal at 16-48 kHz. A five-second clip is 80-240k samples. No transformer attends to that sequence directly. The standard solution: a neural codec (Encodec, SoundStream, DAC) compresses audio to discrete tokens at 50-75 Hz, and a transformer or diffusion model generates tokens. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Codec "Neural compression" Encoder / decoder for audio; typical output is 50-75 Hz tokens. RVQ "Residual VQ" Cascade of K quantizers; each models the residual of the previous. Token "One codec symbol" Discrete index into a codebook; 1024 or 2048 typical. Delayed parallel "Offset codebooks" Emit K token streams with staggered offsets to reduce sequence length. Flow matching "The 2024 win for audio" Straighter-path alternative to diffusion; faster sampling. Voice prompt "3-second sample" Speaker embedding or token prefix that steers the cloned voice. Mel spectrogram "The visual" Log-magnitude perceptual spectrogram; used by many TTS systems. Vocoder "Mel to wave" Neural component that converts mel spectrograms back to audio. The problem In plain words first Sound is a long list of air-pressure readings, 16,000 to 48,000 per second, far too many for a model to generate one at a time. Modern audio generators therefore work in two stages. A neural codec compresses sound into a short stream of tokens, tens of frames per second, each frame described by a few code numbers from learned codebooks, and can turn tokens back into sound. A generator then produces those tokens: a transformer writing them one step at a time, like a language model (good for speech, because it streams), or a diffusion model shaping a whole clip of continuous codes at once (common for music and effects). This lesson runs the lesson's token-counting toy, then a real codec, Meta's EnCodec, on real speech at five bit rates, and a real token generator, MusicGen, making a few seconds of music on this page's CPU. Nothing is trained. Three audio generation tasks: Text-to-speech. Given text, produce speech. Clean speech is narrow-band and has strong phonetic structure — solved well by transformer-over-tokens. VALL-E (Microsoft), NaturalSpeech 3, ElevenLabs, OpenAI TTS. Music generation. Given a prompt (text, melody, chord progression, genre), produce music. Much broader distribution. MusicGen (Meta), Stable Audio 2.5, Suno, Udio, ElevenLabs Music. Audio effects / sound design. Given a prompt, produce ambient sound or Foley. AudioGen, AudioLDM 2, Stable Audio Open. All three run on the same substrate: neural audio codec + token-AR or diffusion generator. The idea Idea 1 · Neural audio codecs Encodec (Meta, 2022), SoundStream (Google, 2021), Descript Audio Codec (DAC, 2023). A convolutional encoder compresses waveform to a per-timestep vector; residual vector quantization (RVQ) converts each vector to a cascade of K codebook indices. Decoder reverses it. EnCodec at 24 kHz produces 75 frames per second; 8 RVQ codebooks of 1,024 entries give 600 tokens per second, 6 kbps (the run under "Use it"). Copy Idea 2 · Two generative paradigms on top Token-autoregressive. Flatten RVQ tokens into a sequence, run a decoder-only transformer. MusicGen uses "delayed parallel" to emit K codebook streams in parallel with per-stream offsets. VALL-E generates speech tokens from a text prompt + 3-second voice sample. Latent diffusion. Pack codec tokens as continuous latents or model them with categorical diffusion. Stable Audio (Open and 2.x) runs a diffusion transformer on continuous VAE latents. AudioLDM 2 uses text-to-mel-to-audio diffusion. The 2024-2026 trend: flow matching is winning for music (faster inference, cleaner samples) while token-AR still dominates speech because it is naturally causal and streams well. Pitfalls Codec quality caps output quality. If the codec can't represent a sound faithfully, no amount of generator quality helps. DAC, EnCodec and Mimi are common open choices. RVQ error accumulation. Each RVQ layer models the residual of the previous. Errors on layer 1 propagate. Sampling with temperature 0 on higher layers helps. Musical structure. 30 seconds of tokens is 20k+ tokens at 75 Hz. Hard for transformers. MusicGen uses sliding window + prompt continuation; Stable Audio uses shorter clips + crossfading. Artifacts at boundaries. Crossfading between generated clips needs careful overlap-add. Clean-data appetite. Music generators need tens of thousands of hours of licensed music. Solutions Solution P1 · Far from it Far from it: even at 24 kbps, 32 codebooks, EnCodec's waveform SNR is about 7 dB, and at the usual 6 kbps about 5 dB. Yet the log-mel distance falls steadily and the spectrograms match: the reconstructions sound right. Neural codecs are trained with spectral and adversarial losses, so they reproduce what the ear is sensitive to (energy in each frequency band over time) and are free to change the waveform's fine phase, which the ear barely notices. That is why codecs, TTS and music models are evaluated with perceptual measures (mel or spectral distances, listening tests, MOS) rather than SNR. Solution B1 · Codebooks that cannot coordinate With the delay pattern, codebook 1 of a frame is chosen one step after codebook 0 of the same frame, so it is conditioned on it; codebook 2 sees codebooks 0 and 1, and so on, which matters because each codebook encodes the residual of the ones before it. In parallel decoding, all four codebooks of a frame are sampled at once, each only from earlier frames, so the fine codebooks are guessed without knowing what coarse sound they are supposed to correct. Combinations that never occur in real audio become possible, heard as noise, buzz and smeared transients. The MusicGen paper compared these patterns: flattening (exact but four times as many steps) scored best, the delay pattern was close at a quarter of the steps, and parallel decoding was clearly worse. Production note: audio is a streaming problem Audio is the one output modality users expect to arrive as it is generated , not all-at-once. In production terms this means TPOT matters (Time Per Output Token) because the user's listening speed is the target throughput — not their reading speed. For EnCodec at 75 frames per second, the server must run at least 75 decoder steps per second per listener (each step emitting one token per codebook, thanks to the delay pattern) to keep playback smooth; MusicGen's 32 kHz codec needs 50. Two architectural consequences: Flow-matching audio models cannot stream trivially. Diffusion and flow-matching models such as Stable Audio render a fixed clip length in one sampling run. To stream, you chunk the clip and overlap boundaries — think sliding-window diffusion — adding 100-300ms of latency overhead vs a codec AR model. If the product is "live voice chat" or "real-time music continuation", pick the codec AR path. If it is "render a 30-second clip on submit", flow-matching wins on quality and total latency.
