Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line 3D is the modality where 2D-to-3D leverage is strongest. The 2023 breakthrough was 3D Gaussian Splatting. The 2024-2026 generative push layers multi-view diffusion + 3D reconstruction on top to produce objects and scenes from a single prompt or photo. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means 3D Gaussian Splatting "3DGS" Scene as a cloud of 3D Gaussians; differentiable alpha-composite render. NeRF "Neural radiance field" MLP that outputs color + density at a 3D point; render by ray integration. Triplane "Three 2-D planes" Factor 3D into three 2-D axis-aligned feature grids; cheaper than volumetric. SDS "Score distillation sampling" Train 3D model by using 2D-diffusion score as pseudo-gradient. Multi-view diffusion "Many views at once" Diffusion model that outputs a batch of consistent camera views. PBR "Physically-based rendering" Material with albedo, roughness, metallic, normal channels. Densification "Grow splats" 3DGS training heuristic: split / clone splats in high-gradient regions. The problem In plain words first A 3D object or scene has to look right from every direction, and there is far less 3D training data than 2D images. Most 3D generators therefore lean on 2D: a diffusion model imagines the object from several viewpoints, and a reconstruction step turns those views into 3D, or a 3D model is compressed into a latent space and diffused there directly, as images are. A popular 3D format, Gaussian splatting, describes a scene as a cloud of soft, coloured, see-through blobs that can be drawn very fast from any camera. This lesson renders a few 3D Gaussians the way splatting does (projection, depth sorting, see-through blending) and shows why the lesson's simple "add them up" rendering gets occlusion wrong, then lifts a real photo to 3D with a depth-estimation model and turns the camera: the holes that appear are exactly what single-image 3D generators must invent. Nothing is trained. 3D content is painful: Representation. Meshes, point clouds, voxel grids, signed distance fields (SDFs), neural radiance fields (NeRFs), 3D Gaussians. Each has trade-offs. Data scarcity. ImageNet has 14M images. The largest clean 3D dataset (Objaverse-XL, 2023) has ~10M objects, most low quality. Memory. A 512³ voxel grid is 128M voxels; a useful scene NeRF needs 1M samples/ray. Generation is harder than reconstruction. Supervision. For a 2D image you have the pixels. For 3D you usually have a handful of 2D views and have to lift to 3D. Two recipes dominate. One separates the problems: first generate 2D multi-view images with a diffusion model, then fit or predict a 3D representation (often Gaussian splatting) from them. The other, used by Hunyuan3D 2 and TRELLIS, trains a 3D VAE and runs diffusion directly in its 3D latent space, then decodes a mesh or Gaussians. The idea Idea 1 · Representation: 3D Gaussian Splatting (Kerbl et al., 2023) Represent a scene as a cloud of ~1M 3D Gaussians. Each has 59 parameters: position (3), covariance (6, or quaternion 4 + scale 3), opacity (1), spherical-harmonics color (48 at degree 3, 3 at degree 0). Rendering = projection + alpha-compositing. Fast (~100 fps at 1080p on a 4090). Differentiable. Fit by gradient descent against ground-truth photos. A scene fits in 5-30 minutes on a consumer GPU. Two 2023-2024 innovations on top: - Generative Gaussian splats. Models like LGM, LRM, InstantMesh predict a Gaussian cloud directly from one or a few images. - 4D Gaussian Splatting. Gaussians with per-frame offsets for dynamic scenes. Idea 2 · Multi-view diffusion Fine-tune a pretrained image diffusion model to generate multiple consistent views of the same object from a text prompt or single image. Zero123 (Liu et al., 2023), MVDream (Shi et al., 2023), SV3D (Stability, 2024), CAT3D (Google, 2024). Usually output 4-16 views around the object, lifted to 3D via Gaussian splatting or NeRF. Idea 3 · Text-to-3D pipelines Model Input Output Time DreamFusion (2022) text NeRF via SDS ~1 hour per asset Magic3D text mesh + texture ~40 min Shap-E (OpenAI, 2023) text implicit 3D ~1 min SJC / ProlificDreamer text NeRF / mesh ~30 min LRM (Meta, 2023) image triplane ~5 s InstantMesh (2024) image mesh ~10 s SV3D (Stability, 2024) image novel views ~2 min CAT3D (Google, 2024) 1-64 images 3D NeRF ~1 min TripoSR (2024) image mesh ~1 s TRELLIS (Microsoft, Dec 2024, open) text or image Gaussians, radiance field or mesh from a structured 3D latent seconds on a GPU Hunyuan3D 2.0 / 2.1 (Tencent, 2025, open) image mesh from 3D-latent diffusion; PBR textures in 2.1 tens of seconds on a GPU Meshy, Tripo, Rodin (hosted, 2024–2025 versions) text + image PBR mesh under a minute to a few minutes 2025–2026 direction: native 3D latent diffusion (Hunyuan3D 2, TRELLIS) producing meshes with PBR materials for game engines, alongside multi-view diffusion followed by reconstruction. Objects look inside-out, and as the camera moves, the wrong things pop in front. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Diffusion models take 20-50 sampling steps because they walk a curved path from noise to data. Flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023) and rectified flow (Liu et al., 2022) trained straight paths. Straighter paths mean fewer steps mean faster inference. Stable Diffusion 3, FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, Wan and F5-TTS all train with flow matching. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Flow matching "Straight-line diffusion" Train $v_\theta(x, t)$ to match $x_1 - x_0$ along an interpolant. Rectified flow "Reflow" Iterative procedure that straightens learned flows. Velocity field "v_θ" Output of the model — the direction to move $x_t$. Straight-line interpolant "The path" $x_t = (1-t) \cdot x_0 + t \cdot x_1$; trivial target derivative. Euler sampler "1st order ODE solver" Simplest integrator; works well when paths are straight. Logit-normal t "SD3 sampling" Concentrate $t$ sampling toward mid-values where gradients are strongest. Consistency distillation "1-step sampler" Train a student to map any $x_t$ directly to $x_0$. CFG with velocity "v-CFG" $v_{\text{cfg}} = (1+w) v_{\text{cond}} - w v_{\text{uncond}}$; same trick, new variable. The problem In plain words first A diffusion sampler moves a sample from noise to data in many small steps because the route it follows bends; take big steps on a bending road and you leave it. Flow matching trains the model on the simplest possible route instead: a straight line from each noise sample to a data sample, with the model learning which direction to move (the "velocity") at every point and time. Training is a plain regression, as simple as diffusion's, and sampling is following the learned velocity with a few large steps. It is the training method behind most current image and video models. This lesson computes the best possible velocity for the lesson's two-mode data exactly, samples with 1 to 32 steps, compares with diffusion's sampler, measures how straight the paths really are, and then drives the same velocity with the real schedulers of two production flow-matching models. Nothing is trained. DDPM's reverse process is a 1000-step stochastic walk from back to the data distribution. DDIM collapsed it to 20-50 deterministic steps. You want fewer steps — ideally one. The blocker is that the ODE solving the reverse process is stiff; the path is curved. If you could train the model such that the path from noise to data was a straight line , a single Euler step from to would work. Flow matching builds this directly: define a straight-line interpolation from ​ ∼ N ( 0 , I ) to ​ ∼ data , train a vector field ​ ( x , t ) to match its time derivative, integrate at inference. Rectified flow (Liu 2022) goes further: iteratively straighten the paths with a reflow procedure that produces a progressively closer-to-linear ODE. In the rectified-flow papers, reflow followed by distillation brought sampling down to one or a few steps (InstaFlow). The idea Idea 1 · Straight-line flow Define: ​ = t ⋅ x 1 ​ + ( 1 − t ) ⋅ x 0 ​ , t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] where ​ ∼ data and ​ ∼ N ( 0 , I ) . The time derivative along this straight line is constant: d x t ​ ​ = x 1 ​ − x 0 ​ Define a neural vector field ​ ( x t ​ , t ) and train it to match this derivative: ​ , x 1 ​ , t ​ ∥ v θ ​ ( x t ​ , t ) − ( x 1 ​ − x 0 ​ ) ∥ 2 This is the conditional flow matching loss (Lipman 2023). Training is simulation-free: you never unroll the ODE. Just sample ​ , x 1 ​ , t ) and regress. Idea 2 · Sampling At inference, integrate the learned vector field backwards in time: ​ = x t ​ − Δ t ⋅ v θ ​ ( x t ​ , t ) Start at ​ ∼ N ( 0 , I ) , Euler-step down to . At the noisy point carries no information about which data point it will become, so the best velocity there points from the noise to the average data point, ( x , 1 ) = x − E [ x 0 ​ ] , and a full-length step lands exactly on that average. Solution B1 · Back to noise With the loop reversed, the sampler starts on noise at , where the field is trained to describe data, and moves against the direction it should: subtracting while increases follows the flow backwards. Even with a perfect field the result is not data. Integrating the ODE in the correct direction for the clock (from to with x += dt * v ) would turn data into noise, which is how flow models encode images into noise for editing and inversion; mixing the two directions produces neither. In plain words first The idea in one line Every generative model leaderboard cites FID, CLIP score, and a win rate from a human-preference arena. Each number has a failure mode a determined researcher can game. If you do not know the failure modes, you cannot tell a real improvement from a gaming run. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means FID "Fréchet Inception Distance" Fréchet distance of Gaussian fits to real vs gen Inception features. CLIP score "Text-image similarity" Cosine similarity between CLIP image and text embeddings. CMMD "FID's replacement" CLIP-feature MMD; less biased, no Gaussian assumption. IS "Inception score" Exp KL(p(y HPSv2 / ImageReward / PickScore "Learned preference proxies" Small models trained on human preferences; used as automatic judges. Elo "Chess rating" Bradley-Terry aggregation of pairwise wins. PartiPrompts "The benchmark prompt set" 1,600 Google-curated prompts across 12 categories. FD-DINO "Self-sup replacement" FD using DINOv2 features; better for out-of-ImageNet domains. The problem In plain words first How do you tell whether one image generator is better than another? You cannot compute the probability of an image, so evaluation compares collections : thousands of generated images against thousands of real ones, using the features of a pretrained vision network. FID measures how far apart the two clouds of feature vectors are. The CLIP score measures how well each image matches its prompt, using a model that embeds images and text in the same space. Human preference, collected as pairwise votes, is turned into a ranking. Each number is easy to fool if you do not know how it works. This lesson checks the lesson's FID code against the standard implementation and its Elo ratings against the exact formula, then computes real FID with Inception-v3 on real photos (where it shows a large bias even for identical distributions) and real CLIP scores (where it shows how easily the score is nudged). Nothing is trained. A generative model is judged on sample quality and conditioning adherence . Neither has a closed-form measure. Your model has to render 10,000 images; something has to assign them numbers; you have to trust the numbers across model families, across resolutions, across architectures. Three metrics survived the 2014-2026 gauntlet: FID (Fréchet Inception Distance). A distance between two distributions — real and generated — in an Inception network's feature space. Lower is better. CLIP score. Cosine similarity between a generated image's CLIP-image embedding and a prompt's CLIP-text embedding. Higher is better. Measures prompt adherence. Human preference. Pit two models head-to-head on the same prompt, have humans (or a GPT-4-class model) pick the better one, aggregate to an Elo score. You will also see: IS (inception score, largely retired), KID, CMMD, ImageReward, PickScore, HPSv2, MJHQ-30k. Each corrects for one failure of the previous. The idea Idea 1 · FID — sample quality Heusel et al. (2017). Steps: Extract Inception-v3 features (2048-D) for N real images and N generated. Fit a Gaussian to each pool: compute mean ​ , μ g ​ and covariance ​ , Σ g ​ . ​ − μ g ​ ∥ 2 + Tr ( Σ r ​ + Σ g ​ − 2 ⋅ ( Σ r ​ ⋅ Σ g ​ ) 0.5 ) . Interpretation: Fréchet distance between two multivariate Gaussians in feature space. Lower = more similar distributions. Failure modes: - Biased on small N. FID is mean-squared over the feature distribution — small N under-estimates covariance, gives falsely low FID. Always use . - Inception-dependent. Inception-v3 was trained on ImageNet. Domains far from ImageNet (faces, art, text images) produce meaningless FID. Use a domain-specific feature extractor. - Gaming. Overfitting to the Inception prior gives low FID without visual quality improvement. Beat it with CMMD (below). Idea 2 · CLIP score — prompt adherence Radford et al. (2021). For a generated image + prompt: Copy Average across 30k generated images → a scalar comparable between models. Failure modes: - CLIP's own blind spots. CLIP has weak compositional reasoning ("a red cube on a blue sphere" often fails). Models can rank well on CLIP score without really following complex prompts. - Short prompt bias. Short prompts have more CLIP-image matches in the wild. Longer prompts have lower CLIP scores mechanically. - Prompt gaming. Including "high quality, 4k, masterpiece" in the prompt inflates CLIP score without improving image-text binding. CMMD (Jayasumana et al., 2024) fixes some of these: uses CLIP features instead of Inception, maximum-mean discrepancy instead of Fréchet. Better at detecting subtle quality differences. Idea 3 · Human preference — the ground truth Pick a pool of prompts. Generate with model A and model B. Show pairs to humans (or a strong LLM judge). Aggregate wins into an Elo or Bradley-Terry score. Benchmarks: PartiPrompts (Google) : 1,600 diverse prompts, 12 categories. HPSv2 : a CLIP model fine-tuned on Human Preference Dataset v2 (798k pairwise choices), widely used as an automated proxy. ImageReward : a reward model trained on 137k expert comparisons of prompt-image pairs. PickScore : a CLIP model trained on Pick-a-Pic, preferences collected from real users of a generation app. Public arenas : LMArena's text-to-image and image-editing leaderboards and Artificial Analysis's image arena rank models from crowd votes. Failure modes: - Judge variance. Non-experts have different preferences than experts. Use both. - Prompt distribution. Cherry-picked prompts favor one family. Always document. - LLM-judge reward hacking. GPT-4-judge gets fooled by pretty-but-wrong outputs. Triangulate with human. Use together A production eval report should include: FID on 10-30k samples against a held-out real distribution (sample quality). CLIP score / CMMD on the same samples vs their prompts (adherence). Win rate in a blinded arena vs the previous model (overall preference). Time : about 90 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Diffusion models sample iteratively in time (denoising steps). VAR samples iteratively in scale — it predicts a 1x1 token, then 2x2, then 4x4, up to the final resolution, each scale conditioning on the previous. The 2024 paper showed VAR matches GPT-style scaling laws for image generation and beats DiT at the same compute budget. This lesson builds the core mechanism. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means VAR "Visual AutoRegressive" Image generation by next-scale prediction over a pyramid of VQ token grids Next-scale prediction "Predict coarser, then finer" The model predicts tokens at increasing resolution scales, conditioning on all previous scales Multi-scale VQ tokenizer "Residual VQ" VQ-VAE that produces K token grids of increasing resolution, with decoder summing all scales Scale k "Pyramid level k" One of K resolution levels, from 1x1 at k=1 up to (H/p)x(W/p) at k=K Parallel-within-scale "One forward per scale" All tokens at scale k are predicted in one transformer pass, not autoregressively Causal-across-scales "Scale-ordered attention" Token at scale $k$ can attend to all of scales $1 \ldots k$ but not scales $k+1 \ldots K$ Residual VQ "Additive tokenization" Each scale's tokens encode the residual left by lower scales; decoder sums all scale embeddings VAR scaling law "Image GPT scaling" FID follows a predictable power law in compute, like language models' perplexity HART "Hybrid VAR + text" Text-conditional VAR variant combining MaskGIT-style iterative decoding with VAR's scale structure Scale position embedding "(scale, row, col) triple" Positional encoding carries both the scale index and spatial coordinates within the scale The problem In plain words first Language models write text one token at a time, and that recipe scales beautifully. Applied to images, it means generating a grid of image tokens one by one in reading order, which is slow and forces the top-left corner to be decided before the model knows what the picture will be. VAR, visual autoregressive modelling, changes the order: first predict a single token summarising the whole image, then a 2 × 2 grid, then 3 × 3, and so on up to the final grid, each step adding detail to everything at once. Every token of a scale is predicted in the same pass, so a 256 × 256 image takes ten passes. This lesson runs the lesson's toy VAR, counts the passes and tokens of the real one, and then runs the authors' released VAR model on this page's CPU: a real photo decoded after more and more scales, and new images generated scale by scale. Nothing is trained. Autoregressive generation dominated language modeling because it scales predictably: more compute, more parameters, lower perplexity, better outputs. Image generation had two main AR attempts before 2024: PixelRNN/PixelCNN (pixel-by-pixel) and DALL·E 1 / Parti (token-by-token on VQ-VAE codes). Both suffered from a generation-order problem. Pixels and tokens are arranged in a 2D grid, but the AR model has to visit them in a 1D raster order. An early corner pixel has no idea what the image eventually becomes. Generation quality scaled worse than GPT-on-text and never reached diffusion-model quality at matched compute. VAR fixes the generation-order problem by changing what is being generated. Instead of predicting image tokens one by one in space, VAR predicts a whole image at increasing resolutions. Step 1: predict a 1x1 token (the overall image "summary"). Step 2: predict a 2x2 grid of tokens (coarser features). Step 3: predict a 4x4 grid. Step K: predict the final (H/8)x(W/8) grid. Each scale attends to all previous scales (causally in "scale order") and parallel within its own scale. The order problem disappears: the whole image at scale k is produced in one transformer pass. Idea 1 · VQ-VAE Multi-Scale Tokenizer VAR needs a multi-scale discrete tokenizer . For an image , it produces a sequence of progressively higher-resolution token grids: Copy Each ​ uses the same codebook (typical size 4096-16384). The tokenization at each scale is not independent — it is trained so that summing the residuals at each scale reconstructs : ( embed ( z 1 ​ ) , target_size ) + ⋯ + upsample ( embed ( z K ​ ) , target_size ) This is a residual VQ variant. Scale captures what scales missed. Decoder takes the sum of all scale embeddings and produces the image. The multi-scale VQ tokenizer is trained once (like VQGAN) and then frozen. All the generative work is done by the autoregressive model on top. Idea 2 · Next-Scale Prediction The generative model is a transformer that sees tokens from all previous scales and predicts the tokens at the next scale. Input sequence structure: Copy Position embeddings encode both scale index and spatial position within the scale. Attention is causal in scale order and block-wise inside a scale: token at scale , position can attend to all tokens at scales , including every position of scale itself. There is no intra-scale order and no intra-scale causality, so all positions within a scale are predicted in parallel. Training loss: at each scale , predict the tokens ​ given all prior-scale tokens. Cross-entropy loss on the discrete VQ codes. Same structure as GPT except the "sequence" is now scale-structured. Idea 3 · Generation At inference: Copy For scales, generation is 10 transformer forward passes. Each pass produces its entire scale in parallel — no per-token autoregression within a scale. For a 256x256 image this is 10 passes, against DiT's 25–250 sampling steps and 256 passes for a raster-order token model. After how many scales will the decoded image be recognisably the photo? (Solution P1.) Idea 4 · Why Next-Scale Wins Over Next-Token Three structural wins: 1. Coarse-to-fine aligns with natural image statistics. Human visual perception and image datasets both exhibit scale-dependent regularities: low-frequency structure is stable and predictable; high-frequency detail is conditional on low-frequency content. Next-scale prediction exploits this. 2. Parallel generation within scale. Unlike GPT-style token AR, VAR produces all tokens at a scale in one step. Effective generation length is log-scale instead of linear. 3. No generation order bias. Tokens at scale k see all of scale k-1; there is no "left-of" or "above" bias that forces early tokens to commit before late context is available. Idea 5 · Scaling Law Tian et al. demonstrated that VAR follows a power-law scaling curve for FID on ImageNet — just like GPT does for perplexity. The fitted exponents are small, as for language models: each doubling of compute lowers the loss by a modest but predictable fraction. This was the first image-generative model to exhibit this kind of scaling behavior as cleanly as language models. The result is that VAR-scale predictions become predictable from compute, not empirical guesses per architecture. Idea 6 · Relationship to Diffusion VAR and diffusion share the same data-compression story: both break the generation problem into a sequence of easier subproblems. Diffusion: gradually add noise, learn to undo one step. VAR: gradually add resolution, learn to predict the next scale. They are different axes through the problem. Both yield tractable conditional distributions. Empirically VAR is faster at inference (fewer passes, all parallel within a scale) and matches or beats DiT on class-conditional ImageNet. Text-to-image versions followed: HART (MIT and NVIDIA), Infinity (ByteDance) and Switti bring next-scale prediction to text-to-image generation at up to 1024 × 1024. After one scale the decoded image is a flat grey; after four it is a blurry pale blob; after six the dog's dark ears and white chest are in place; after eight (the grid) it is clearly the photo, and the last two scales, which hold more than half of all tokens, add only fine detail. Each scale stores the residual of the coarser ones, so composition and colour are settled early with few tokens. That is the property VAR exploits: decisions about the whole picture are made first, while a raster model must commit to its top-left corner before anything else. Solution B1 · Training and sampling disagree With a causal mask inside a scale, every training prediction of token is made knowing the true tokens before it in raster order, and the model learns to rely on them, for example copying a neighbour's colour. At generation time the whole scale is sampled in one pass, so those neighbours do not exist yet: the inputs at their positions are not the tokens the model learned to expect. Its predictions are made in a situation it never trained on, and neighbouring tokens no longer agree with each other, giving blotchy, incoherent textures. Either sample the scale token by token (losing VAR's speed) or, as VAR does, train with the same block mask used at generation, so that tokens within a scale depend only on coarser scales. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Explain the mechanism Token-by-token image generation used to mean predicting one code after another in raster order. A newer method predicts whole grids at increasing resolution instead. Explain what it predicts at each step, why that fixes the old method's main weakness, and how it compares with diffusion in the number of network passes. Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Next-scale prediction tokenizes an image into a pyramid of grids, from one code up to the full latent resolution, with a residual quantizer so that the sum of the scales reconstructs the image. The transformer is causal across scales and parallel within a scale: given all coarser grids, it predicts every code of the next grid in one pass. That removes the raster-order problem, where an early corner code had to commit before any context existed. For a 256 by 256 image the reference uses about 10 scales, so generation is about 10 passes against 28 to 50 for a diffusion transformer, and all codes of a scale come out together. The tokenizer. A multi-scale residual quantizer: encode the image to a latent, quantize it at 1 by 1, then at 2 by 2, then 4 by 4, up to the full latent grid, with one shared codebook. Each scale encodes what the coarser scales missed, and the decoder takes the sum of all upsampled scale embeddings. The codebook is typically 4096 to 16384 entries. Train it once and freeze it. The model. The input for scale 1 is a start token. The input for each later scale k is a grid built from the coarser scales only, upsampled to the size of scale k. The codes of scale k are the targets at those positions, and they enter the input only for the scales after k. Position embeddings carry the scale index and the position within the scale. The attention mask is block-causal: a code at scale k attends to every code of scales 1 to k, including all positions of its own scale, and to nothing finer. Training is cross-entropy on the codes at each scale given the coarser scales. Why it beats raster order. Coarse to fine matches image statistics: low-frequency structure is stable and predictable, and detail is conditional on it. Parallel within a scale: the generation length is logarithmic in the pixel count instead of linear. No order bias: nothing is left of or above anything inside a scale, so no early code commits before the late context exists. The scaling result. The paper reports a power law of image quality against compute, the way language models scale in perplexity, and a better quality than a diffusion transformer at matched compute on a class-conditional benchmark. Relation to diffusion. Both break generation into easier conditional steps. Diffusion adds noise and learns to remove one step of it; next-scale prediction adds resolution and learns to predict one more scale. The scale method needs fewer passes and parallelizes inside each pass; text-conditioned variants were an open research direction at the time of the lesson. Plausible wrong answers. "It is diffusion with a different name." Diffusion iterates over noise levels on continuous latents; this iterates over resolution on discrete codes and predicts a whole grid per pass. "Within a scale the codes still go one by one." The mask is bidirectional inside a scale, so one forward pass produces the whole grid. "Raster order only costs speed." It also biases generation: an early code commits before the context that should condition it exists, which capped quality below diffusion at matched compute. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does the residual structure matter for the tokenizer? Expected: each scale encodes only what the coarser scales missed, so the sum reconstructs the latent and the scales are not redundant. (level 2) What does a code at scale k see, and what may it not see? Expected: all codes at scales 1 to k, its own scale's positions included; nothing at finer scales. (level 3) What happens to quality and cost as you add scales? Expected: finer residuals and better reconstruction, at the cost of one more pass per scale; the lesson's exercise sweeps 4 to 10 scales to find the knee. (level 3) How would you add text conditioning? Expected: feed a pooled text embedding through adaptive normalization, as the hybrid variant in the lesson does, and measure the gain on text-aligned samples. Where it is taught. The visual autoregressive lesson builds the multi-scale tokenizer and the scale-ordered mask. a0901: Course home / Phase 9 · Learning from Reward States, actions and rewards Lesson 9.1 45 min Learn Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 1 · 06 (Probability & Distributions), Phase 2 · 01 (ML Taxonomy) Type : Learn. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A Markov Decision Process is five things: states, actions, transitions, rewards, a discount. Everything in RL — Q-learning, PPO, DPO, GRPO — optimizes over this shape. Learn it once, read the rest of reinforcement learning for free. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means MDP "Reinforcement learning setup" Tuple $(S, A, P, R, \gamma)$ satisfying the Markov property. State "What the agent sees" Sufficient statistic for future dynamics under the chosen policy class. Policy "Agent's behavior" Conditional distribution $\pi(a \mid s)$ or deterministic map $s \to a$. Return "Total reward" Discounted sum $\sum \gamma^t r_t$ from the current step. Value "How good a state is" Expected return under $\pi$ starting from $s$. Q-value "How good an action is" Expected return under $\pi$ starting from $s$ with first action $a$. Bellman equation "Dynamic programming recursion" Fixed-point decomposition of value / Q into one-step reward plus discounted successor value. Discount $\gamma$ "Future vs present" Geometric weight on far-future reward; effective horizon $\approx 1/(1-\gamma)$. The problem In plain words first Reinforcement learning is learning from consequences instead of from labelled answers. An agent looks at its situation (the state), picks an action, the world responds with a new situation and a number called the reward, and this repeats. The agent's goal is to choose actions that make the total reward large over time, not just right now. A Markov decision process (MDP) is the precise way to write such a problem down: the possible states, the possible actions, how actions change the state, what reward each step gives, and how much future rewards count compared with immediate ones. Every method in this phase, up to the reinforcement learning used to train chat models, works on this description. This lesson runs the lesson's grid world, solves its value equations exactly, and then reads the full rule book of a real environment from the Gymnasium library. Nothing is trained. You are writing a chess bot. Or an inventory planner. Or a trading agent. Or the PPO loop that trains a reasoning model. Four different domains, one surprising fact: all four collapse to the same mathematical object. Supervised learning gives you (x, y) pairs and asks you to fit a function. Reinforcement learning gives you no labels — only a stream of states, the actions you took, and a scalar reward. Did the move win the game? Did the restock decision save money? Did the trade make a profit? Did the token the LLM just produced lead to a higher reward from the judge? You cannot learn from this stream until you formalize it. "What I saw," "what I did," "what happened next," "how good that was" — each has to become an object you can reason about. That formalization is a Markov Decision Process. Every RL algorithm in this phase, including the RLHF and GRPO loops at the end, optimizes over this shape. The idea The five objects. States . Everything the agent needs to decide. In GridWorld, the cell. In chess, the board. In an LLM, the context window plus any memory. Actions . The choices. Move up/down/left/right. Play a move. Emit a token. Transitions ∣ s , a ) . Given state and action , the distribution over next state. Deterministic in chess, stochastic in inventory, almost-deterministic in LLM decoding. Rewards ) . The scalar signal. Win = +1, loss = -1. Revenue minus cost. A verifier's pass/fail score on a language model's answer (GRPO). Discount . How much future reward counts vs present. buys a horizon of ~100 steps; buys ~10. The Markov property ​ ∣ s t ​ , a t ​ ) = P ( s t + 1 ​ ∣ s 0 ​ , a 0 ​ , … , s t ​ , a t ​ ) . The future depends only on the present state. If it does not, the state representation is incomplete — not a failure of the method, a failure of the state. Policies and returns. A policy maps states to action distributions. The return ​ = r t ​ + γ r t + 1 ​ + γ 2 r t + 2 ​ + … is the discounted sum of future rewards. The value ( s ) = E [ G t ​ ∣ s t ​ = s ] is the expected return starting from under policy . The Q-value ( s , a ) = E [ G t ​ ∣ s t ​ = s , a t ​ = a ] is the expected return starting with a specific action. Every RL algorithm estimates one of these two, then improves accordingly. The Bellman equations. The fixed-point equations that everything in this phase uses: ( s ) Q π ( s , a ) ​ = a ∑ ​ π ( a ∣ s ) s ′ , r ∑ ​ P ( s ′ , r ∣ s , a ) [ r + γ V π ( s ′ )] = s ′ , r ∑ ​ P ( s ′ , r ∣ s , a ) [ r + γ a ′ ∑ ​ π ( a ′ ∣ s ′ ) Q π ( s ′ , a ′ )] ​ These split expected return into "this step's reward" plus "discounted value of where you land." Recursive. Every algorithm in Phase 9 either iterates this equation to convergence (dynamic programming), samples from it (Monte Carlo), or bootstraps it one step (temporal difference). The same idea as a formula An MDP is with ∣ s , a ) the transition probabilities, the reward and the discount. Iterative policy evaluation solves the same system by repeated substitution; it converges because each sweep shrinks errors by a factor (a contraction). Effective horizon. Check your mental model ✗ "The value of a state is the reward you get there." ✓ It is the expected total discounted reward from that state onward, under a given policy; change the policy and the values change. ✗ "The Markov property is a property of the world." ✓ It is a property of the state you chose ; if decisions need history, put the history into the state. ✗ "Evaluating a policy needs simulation." ✓ When the transitions are known, it is a linear system (the runs below solve it exactly); simulation is only needed when they are not. Predict before you run After Step 4, the uniform-random policy on the 4 × 4 grid is evaluated exactly with , so is the expected number of steps from the top-left corner to the bottom-right one. The shortest path takes 6 steps. How many steps does the random walk take on average: about 12, about 25, or about 60? (Solution P1.) Step 1 · a tiny deterministic MDP A 4×4 GridWorld. Agent starts top-left, terminal at bottom-right, reward of -1 per step, actions {up, down, left, right} . See code/main.py . Copy Five lines. That is the entire environment. Deterministic transitions, constant step penalty, absorbing terminal state. Step 2 · roll out a policy A policy is a function from state to action distribution. The simplest: uniform random. Copy Run the random policy 5,000 times: the average return is about −59 on this 4×4 board (exactly −59.4, as the run after Step 4 shows). The optimal return is -6 (straight-line path down-right). Closing that gap is everything in Phase 9. Step 3 · compute V^π exactly via the Bellman equation For small MDPs the Bellman equation is a linear system. Enumerate states, apply the expectation, iterate until the values stop changing. Copy This is iterative policy evaluation. It is the first algorithm in Sutton & Barto and the theoretical foundation of every RL method that follows. Step 4 · γ is a hyperparameter with physical meaning Effective horizon is roughly . → 10 steps. → 100 steps. → 1000 steps. Too low and the agent acts myopically. Too high and credit assignment becomes noisy, because many early steps share responsibility for far-future reward. LLM RLHF typically uses because episodes are short and bounded. Control tasks use 0.95–0.99 . Long-horizon strategy games use 0.999 . Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output The random policy averages over 5,000 rollouts, against the optimal ; the "greedy" policy, which picks down or right at random, averages , losing a couple of steps by bumping into walls. Policy evaluation fills each cell with its expected discounted return; with every cell is about , because the discount hides anything beyond two steps, while with the far corner is worth and values rise steadily toward the goal. The linear system reproduces the iterative values to two decimals at every , and at gives the exact expected episode length: for the random policy, which the rollouts' estimates (rollouts are also cut at 200 steps), and for the down/right policy. The horizons, 2, 10 and 100 steps, explain why sees no difference between cells. Pitfalls Non-Markovian state. If you need the last three observations to decide, the "state" is not just the current observation. Fix: stack frames (DQN on Atari stacks 4) or use a recurrent state (LSTM/GRU over observations). Sparse rewards. Win-only rewards make learning nearly impossible in large state spaces. Shape rewards (intermediate signal) or bootstrap with imitation (Phase 9 · 09). Reward hacking. Optimizing a proxy reward often produces pathological behavior. OpenAI's boat-racing agent spun in circles collecting powerups forever instead of finishing the race. Always define reward from the target outcome, not the proxy. Discount mis-spec. on an infinite-horizon task makes every value infinite. Always cap with either a finite horizon or . Reward scale. Rewards of {+100, -100} vs {+1, -1} give identical optimal policies but vastly different gradient magnitudes. Normalize to [-1, 1] -ish before plugging into PPO/DQN. Use it: the same idea with real libraries The 2026 stack reduces every RL pipeline to an MDP before touching code: Situation State Action Reward γ Control (locomotion, manipulation) Joint angles + velocities Continuous torques Task-specific shaped 0.99 Games (chess, Go, poker) Board + history Legal move Win=+1 / loss=-1 1.0 (finite) Inventory / pricing Stock + demand Order qty Revenue - cost 0.95 RLHF for LLMs Context tokens Next token Reward-model score at end 1.0 (episode ~200 tokens) GRPO for reasoning Prompt + partial response Next token Verifier 0/1 at end 1.0 Write the five tuples before writing any training loop. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Gymnasium is the standard environment API. The Farama Foundation's Gymnasium (successor to OpenAI Gym), with PettingZoo for multi-agent tasks and MuJoCo/Brax/MJX for physics, defines reset / step for most RL code; Stable-Baselines3, CleanRL and RLlib build on it. MDPs inside LLM training. RL for language models (RLHF with PPO, GRPO for reasoning, used for DeepSeek-R1 and in libraries such as TRL, verl and OpenRLHF) treats the prompt plus generated text as the state, the next token as the action and a reward model or verifier as the reward, usually with . Agentic RL environments. Training LLM agents on tool use and coding happens in sandboxed environments with programmatic rewards (tests passing, tasks completed), the same five-part MDP at a much larger scale. a0902: Course home / Phase 9 · Learning from Reward Planning when you know the rules Lesson 9.2 75 min Build Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 9 · 01 (MDPs) Type : Build. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Dynamic programming is RL with cheating. You already know the transition and reward functions; you just iterate the Bellman equation until or stops moving. It is the benchmark every sampling-based method tries to approach. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Policy iteration "DP algorithm" Alternating evaluation ($V^\pi$) and improvement (greedy $\pi$ w.r.t. $V^\pi$) until the policy stops changing. Value iteration "Faster DP" Bellman optimality backup applied in one sweep; converges to $V^{\ast}$ geometrically. Bellman operator "The recursion" $(T V)(s) = \max_a \sum P (r + \gamma V(s'))$; a $\gamma$-contraction in sup-norm. Contraction "Why DP converges" Any operator $T$ with $\lVert T x - T y \rVert \le \gamma \lVert x - y \rVert$ has a unique fixed point. GPI "Everything is DP" Generalized Policy Iteration: any method driving $V$ and $\pi$ to mutual consistency. Synchronous update "Jacobi-style" Use old $V$ throughout a sweep; cleanly analyzable but slower. In-place update "Gauss-Seidel-style" Use $V$ as it's being updated; converges faster in practice. The problem In plain words first If you know the rules of the world exactly (for every state and action, which states can follow, with what probabilities and rewards), you do not need to learn by trial and error: you can compute the best behaviour. Dynamic programming does this by repeating one simple update everywhere: a state's value is the best action's immediate reward plus the discounted value of where that action leads. Policy iteration alternates "work out how good the current plan is" with "switch to the best action everywhere"; value iteration folds both into one repeated sweep. The answers are exact, which makes them the yardstick for every learning method that follows. This lesson runs the lesson's solvers, watches the error shrink sweep by sweep, and then solves real Gymnasium environments from their own rule tables and checks the answers by playing them. Nothing is trained. You have an MDP with a known model: you can query ∣ s , a ) and ) for any state-action pair. An inventory manager knows the demand distribution. A board game has deterministic transitions. A gridworld is four lines of Python. You have a model . Model-free RL (Q-learning, PPO, REINFORCE) was invented for the case where you don't have a model — you can only sample from the environment. But when you do have one, there are faster, better methods: dynamic programming. Bellman designed them in 1957. They still define correctness: when people say "optimal policy for this MDP," they mean the policy DP would return. You need them in 2026 for three reasons. First, every tabular environment in RL research (GridWorld, FrozenLake, CliffWalking) is solved with DP to produce the gold-standard policy. Second, exact values let you debug sampling methods: if Q-learning's estimate for ( s 0 ​ ) disagrees with the DP answer by 30%, your Q-learning has a bug. Third, modern offline RL and planning methods (MCTS, AlphaZero's search, model-based RL such as MuZero, Lesson 9.12) all iterate a Bellman backup over a learned or given model. The idea Two algorithms, both fixed-point iteration on Bellman. Policy iteration. Alternates two steps until the policy stops changing. Solutions Solution P1 · About 100% About 100%: with no discount and enough time, the optimal policy on slippery FrozenLake 8 × 8 reaches the goal in every one of 10,000 games (exact value 1.0000). With there is no penalty for taking long, so the best policy uses moves whose possible slips never lead into a hole, usually pushing against walls or along safe corridors, and waits for the ice to carry it forward. With a discount below 1 the optimal policy would accept some risk to arrive sooner, and its success rate would drop. "Optimal" always means optimal for the reward and discount you specified. Solution B1 · Endless flipping With random tie-breaking, each improvement step may pick a different one of two equally good actions in some cells, so the policy changes every iteration even though nothing improves. The original test, "stop when the policy is unchanged", then never fires and the loop runs until its iteration limit. Testing the value instead fixes termination: tied policies have identical values, so the loop stops as soon as no state's value improves. The standard fixes are a fixed tie-break order (first best action, as policy_improvement does with max over a fixed action tuple) or stopping when values stop improving; never compare policies that are allowed to break ties randomly. In plain words first The idea in one line Dynamic programming needs a model. Monte Carlo needs nothing but episodes. Run the policy, watch the returns, average them. The simplest idea in RL — and the one that unlocks everything downstream. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Monte Carlo "Random sampling" Estimate expectations by averaging over iid samples from the distribution. Return $G_t$ "Future reward" Sum of discounted rewards from step $t$ to episode end: $\sum_{k\ge 0} \gamma^k r_{t+k+1}$. First-visit MC "Count each state once" Only the first visit in an episode contributes to the value estimate. Every-visit MC "Use all visits" Every visit contributes; slightly biased for finite samples, consistent in the limit, and more sample-efficient. ε-greedy "Exploration noise" Pick greedy action with prob $1-\epsilon$; random action with prob $\epsilon$. Importance sampling "Correcting for sampling from the wrong distribution" Reweight returns by $\pi(a \mid s)/\mu(a \mid s)$ products to estimate $V^\pi$ from $\mu$ data. On-policy "Learn from my own data" Target policy = behavior policy. Vanilla MC, PPO, SARSA. Off-policy "Learn from someone else's data" Target policy ≠ behavior policy. Importance-sampled MC, Q-learning, DQN. The problem In plain words first Dynamic programming needs the rule book of the world. Usually you do not have it: you can only try things and see what happens. Monte Carlo methods learn from complete experiences. Play an episode to the end, add up the rewards that followed each state, and average those totals over many episodes; the average converges to the state's true value. To improve behaviour, do the same for each action and lean toward the actions whose average is best, while still trying others now and then, because averages are only known for what you have tried. This lesson runs the lesson's Monte Carlo evaluation and control on the grid world (tabular averages that take a second), shows how badly variance behaves when you learn about one policy from another's experience, and evaluates two blackjack strategies in Gymnasium's blackjack environment by simply playing 100,000 hands each. No neural network is trained. Dynamic programming is elegant, but it assumes you can query ∣ s , a ) for every state and action. Almost nothing in the real world works that way. A robot cannot analytically compute the distribution over camera pixels after a joint torque. A pricing algorithm cannot integrate over every possible customer reaction. An LLM cannot enumerate all possible continuations after a token. You need a method that only needs the ability to sample from the environment. Run the policy. Get a trajectory s_0, a_0, r_1, s_1, a_1, r_2, …, s_T . Use it to estimate values. That is Monte Carlo. The shift from DP to MC is philosophically important: we move from known model + exact backup to sampled rollouts + averaged return . The variance jumps, but the applicability explodes. Every RL algorithm after this lesson — TD, Q-learning, REINFORCE, PPO, GRPO — is a Monte Carlo estimator at heart, sometimes with bootstrapping layered on top. a0904: Course home / Phase 9 · Learning from Reward Learning step by step (Q-learning, SARSA) Lesson 9.4 75 min Build Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 9 · 01 (MDPs), Phase 9 · 02 (Dynamic Programming), Phase 9 · 03 (Monte Carlo) Type : Build. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Monte Carlo waits until the episode ends. TD updates after every step by bootstrapping the next value estimate. Q-learning is off-policy and optimistic; SARSA is on-policy and cautious. Both are one line of code. Both underpin every deep-RL method in this phase. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means TD error "The update signal" $\delta = r + \gamma V(s') - V(s)$, the bootstrapped residual. TD(0) "One-step TD" Update after every transition using only the next state's estimate. Q-learning "Off-policy RL 101" TD update with max over next-state actions; learns $Q^{\ast}$ regardless of behavior policy. SARSA "On-policy Q-learning" TD update using the actual next action; learns $Q^\pi$ for current ε-greedy π. Expected SARSA "The low-variance SARSA" Replace sampled $a'$ with its expectation under π. GLIE "Correct exploration schedule" Greedy in the Limit with Infinite Exploration; needed for Q-learning convergence. Bootstrapping "Using current estimate in the target" What distinguishes TD from MC. Source of bias but massive variance reduction. Maximization bias "Q-learning overestimates" max over noisy estimates is upward-biased; fixed by Double Q-learning. The problem In plain words first Monte Carlo waits until an episode ends before learning anything. Temporal-difference (TD) learning updates after every single step: it compares its current guess for a state with a slightly better-informed guess, the reward just received plus its guess for the next state, and moves a little toward it. Learning from your own guesses is called bootstrapping; it introduces some bias but greatly reduces noise and works without episodes ever ending. Q-learning applies this to action values and always assumes the best action will be taken next; SARSA uses the action the agent actually takes next. That one difference decides whether the agent learns the bold path or the safe one. This lesson runs the lesson's tabular SARSA and Q-learning and checks them against exact values, then reproduces two textbook experiments in seconds: the cliff walk in Gymnasium, and the overestimation that double Q-learning fixes. The problem In plain words first A Q-table needs one entry for every situation, which is hopeless when the situation is a video-game screen. Deep Q-learning (DQN) replaces the table with a neural network that takes the screen as input and outputs one value per action, trained with the same Q-learning target as Lesson 9.4. Done naively this falls apart: consecutive screens are almost identical, and the target the network chases moves every time the network changes. DQN's fixes are a memory of past experiences sampled at random (replay), and a frozen copy of the network used to compute targets (the target network). This lesson checks numerically why each fix is needed, and why one of them is not enough on its own, then plays a full game of Pong on this page's CPU with a DQN agent trained and published by the Stable-Baselines3 team, watching its Q-values as it plays. Nothing is trained here. Tabular Q-learning needs a separate Q-value for every (state, action) pair. A chess board has ~10⁴³ states. An Atari frame is 210×160×3 = 100,800 features. Reward clipping normalizes gradient magnitudes. DQN on Atari was the first time a single architecture with a single hyperparameter set solved dozens of control problems from raw pixels. The problem In plain words first REINFORCE judges each action by the total reward that followed it, which is very noisy. Actor-critic methods add a second learner, the critic, whose only job is to predict how good a situation is. The actor (the policy) is then judged by the advantage : how much better things went than the critic expected. If the critic is good, this comparison removes most of the noise; if it is wrong, it introduces bias. Generalised advantage estimation (GAE) is a dial between trusting the critic (low noise, possible bias) and trusting the actual rewards (no bias, high noise). Pitfalls Critic bias before actor gradient. If the critic is random, its baseline is uninformative and you are training on pure noise. Warm up the critic for a few hundred steps before turning on the policy gradient, or use a slow actor learning rate. Advantage normalization. Normalize advantages to zero-mean/unit-std per batch. Solutions Solution P1 · About 95 About 95: the critic predicts 95.2 at step 490, although only 9.6 of discounted reward actually follows before the time limit cuts the episode off. Its input is the cart's position and velocity and the pole's angle and angular velocity; nothing in it says how many steps remain, so it predicts what a balanced pole is worth in general, close to . To value the remaining time correctly the time would have to be part of the state (time-aware critics add it as an input). For learning a good policy it does not matter, as long as the time limit is treated as a truncation and bootstrapped through. Solution B1 · A pessimistic critic, a misled actor With next_v = 0 at every cut, the critic is taught that each rollout's last state is followed by nothing, although the episode actually continues. States that often fall at rollout boundaries get targets far too low, and because neural critics generalise, the whole value function drifts toward "the future is short". The advantages then reward actions that collect reward quickly and punish actions whose payoff comes after the next cut, a bias toward short-sighted behaviour, and on tasks like CartPole the critic underestimates by a large, rollout-length-dependent amount. The fix is the formula box's last line: bootstrap with ​ ( s T ​ ) at truncations and use 0 only at true terminations. Sources and further reading Mnih et al. (2016). The problem In plain words first Policy-gradient methods learn from experience collected by the current policy, and after one update that experience is already slightly out of date. Reusing it for several more updates saves a lot of data, but if the policy changes too much, the old experience no longer describes what the new policy would do, and the updates can wreck a good policy. PPO (proximal policy optimisation) keeps each round of updates small in a simple way: it measures how much more or less likely each action has become, and once that ratio moves more than about 20% in the helpful direction, the action stops contributing to the update. It is the default policy-gradient method in robotics and was the original algorithm for training chat models from human feedback. This lesson runs the lesson's PPO on the grid world, computes exactly how far PPO's objective can be trusted, and reads PPO's standard diagnostics with Stable-Baselines3. No neural network is trained. A2C ( Lesson 9.7 ) is on-policy: the gradient ​ ​ [ A ⋅ ∇ lo g π θ ​ ] requires data sampled from the current ​ . Take one update, and ​ changes; the data you used is now off-policy. Re-use it and your gradient is biased. Rollouts are expensive. On Atari, one rollout across 8 envs × 128 steps = 1024 transitions and a dozen seconds of environment time. Throwing that away after one gradient step is wasteful. Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO, Schulman 2015) was the first fix: constrain each update so the KL divergence between old and new policy stays below . Theoretically clean, but requires a conjugate-gradient solve per update. TRPO is rarely used today. PPO (Schulman et al. 2017) replaces the hard trust-region constraint with a simple clipped objective. One extra line of code. Ten epochs per rollout. No conjugate gradients. Good-enough theoretical guarantees. Nine years later it is still the default policy-gradient algorithm for everything from MuJoCo to RLHF. Solutions Solution P1 · Over 100 Over 100: the unclipped surrogate claims an improvement of 160 at the largest step, nearly five times the maximum possible 33.6 and five times the true 33.4. The surrogate weights the new policy's action probabilities by the old policy's advantages and the old policy's state visits; once the policy changes a lot it goes to different states, and those weights mean nothing. This is the reason for trust regions: TRPO limits KL directly, PPO clips the ratio so that the objective it maximises stays pessimistic (about 20 here) and stops rewarding large moves. Solution B1 · Mistakes stop being corrected With the plain clipped term, every sample whose ratio has left gets zero gradient, including those that moved in the harmful direction: an action with negative advantage whose probability has risen to contributes , a constant, so nothing pushes it back down; likewise a good action whose probability has fallen below 0.8. The in PPO is asymmetric on purpose: it removes the incentive to keep improving a sample past the limit, but keeps the full gradient whenever the policy has moved the wrong way. Without it, an unlucky epoch can push some probabilities in the wrong direction and leave them there, and the policy can degrade while the loss looks stable. In plain words first The idea in one line Humans cannot write a reward function for "good assistant response," but they can compare two responses and pick the better one. Fit a reward model to those comparisons, then RL the language model against it. Christiano 2017. InstructGPT 2022. The recipe that turned GPT-3 into ChatGPT. Today, offline preference methods such as DPO and RL with automatically checked rewards do much of this work — but the mental model stays. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means RLHF "Alignment RL" Three-stage SFT + RM + PPO pipeline (Christiano 2017, Ouyang 2022). Reward Model (RM) "The scoring net" Learned scalar function fit to pairwise preferences via Bradley-Terry. Bradley-Terry "Pairwise logistic loss" $P(y_+ \succ y_-) = \sigma(R(y_+) - R(y_-))$; the standard RM objective. KL penalty "Stay near the reference" $\beta \cdot \mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta \Vert \pi_{\text{ref}})$ in the reward; the anti-reward-hacking regularizer. Reward hacking "Goodhart's law" Policy exploits RM flaws; symptoms: reward up, human eval flat. RLAIF "AI-labeled preferences" RLHF where labels come from another LM instead of humans. PRM "Process Reward Model" Scores partial reasoning steps; used in reasoning pipelines. Constitutional AI "Anthropic's method" AI-generated preferences guided by explicit rules. The problem In plain words first Nobody can write down a formula for "a good answer", but people can look at two answers and say which one is better. RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) turns many such comparisons into a reward model : a network that reads a prompt and a reply and outputs one number, trained so that the reply people preferred gets the higher number. A language model is then tuned with reinforcement learning to write replies that score well, with a penalty for drifting too far from where it started, because a reward model is only trustworthy on the kind of replies it was trained on. This lesson runs the lesson's toy pipeline, computes exactly what the penalty does and how optimising a flawed reward model goes wrong, and then scores real conversations and real model replies with a current open reward model. No model is trained or fine-tuned. You trained a language model on the next-token-prediction objective. It writes grammatical English. It also lies, rambles, and refuses to refuse. You cannot fix this with more pretraining — web text is the problem, not the cure. You want a scalar reward that says "response A is better than response B for instruction X." Writing that reward function by hand is impossible. "Helpfulness" is not a closed-form expression over tokens. But humans can compare two outputs and mark a preference. That is cheap to collect at scale. RLHF (Christiano et al. 2017; Ouyang et al. 2022) converts preferences into a reward model, then optimizes the LM via PPO against that reward. In three steps: SFT → RM → PPO. It is the recipe behind ChatGPT and the first generation of aligned chat assistants. For preference tuning, the PPO step is now often replaced by DPO (Phase 10 · 08), which is cheaper and simpler; online RL against reward models and verifiers is still used where the extra quality pays for itself. But the reward model piece still underlies every Best-of-N sampler, every RL-from-verifiable-rewards pipeline, and every reasoning model using a process reward model. Understand RLHF and you understand the entire alignment stack. The idea Stage 1: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). Start from a pretrained base model. Pitfalls Over-optimization / reward hacking. The RM is imperfect; ​ finds adversarial completions that score high but are bad. Symptoms: reward climbs indefinitely while human eval score plateaus or drops. Fix: stop early, raise , broaden RM training data. Length hacking. RMs trained on helpful responses often implicitly reward length. The policy learns to pad responses. Remediation: length-normalized reward, or RLAIF with a length-aware RM. Too-weak RM. A small or under-trained RM is easier to exploit. RMs smaller than the policy are common (InstructGPT used a 6B RM for a 175B policy), but larger RMs over-optimise more slowly (Gao et al. 2022). KL tuning. Too low β → drift and reward hacking. Too high β → policy barely changes. The standard trick is an adaptive β that targets a fixed KL per step. Preference-data noise. Labelers often disagree: in InstructGPT, trained labelers agreed with each other on about 73% of comparisons. Noise shrinks the reward gaps the RM learns (Solution B1); filter for agreement or collect several labels per pair. Off-policy problems. PPO data is slightly off-policy after the first epoch. Published pipelines combine SFT, reward-model-based rejection sampling and offline preference optimisation (Llama 3: rejection sampling plus DPO; Tülu 3: SFT, DPO, then RL with verifiable rewards).
