Take-home You get a corpus as a dictionary from words, each a tuple of byte ids, to the number of times the word occurs. Write the training loop that produces an ordered list of merges, and state the three rules that make the loop deterministic. Then tell me what the loop must not do to the caller's data. Level 2 of 4 · about 30 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Each step counts every adjacent pair inside each word, weighted by the word frequency, picks the pair with the highest count, rewrites every occurrence of that pair into one new id, and records the merge. The three rules are: pairs never cross a word boundary, ties go to the smallest pair in tuple order, and the loop stops when no pair repeats. The input dictionary and its tuples are never changed; the loop builds a new corpus each step. The loop. Copy The first ids are reserved for the raw bytes, so the first merge gets the next free id and each later merge gets the next one. The merge list in training order is the tokenizer. Encoding fresh text applies the same merges in the same order, so a change of order at inference decodes a different stream of ids. Weighted counts. A pair inside a word that occurs five times adds five to the count, not one. Counting each occurrence once makes rare long words outvote common short ones, and the merge order changes. Pairs do not cross from the end of one word to the start of the next; the word split is what keeps merges inside words and lets them generalize. Ties and the stop rule. Two pairs with the same count must resolve the same way on every run, so the smallest pair in tuple order wins. Without a fixed rule, dictionary order decides and two training runs on the same corpus produce different tokenizers. The loop stops early when the best count is below two, because a pair that occurs once does not compress anything and only spends vocabulary slots. Do not change the input. The caller's dictionary and tuples stay as they were. Clearing and refilling the dictionary in place, or rewriting tuples through a list, changes data the caller may still use. Each step builds a new dictionary from the merged words. Plausible wrong answers. "Count each pair once per word." Frequency weighting is what makes common pairs win early. "Take the first pair with the maximum count." Dictionary order is not stable across inputs, so the tokenizer becomes irreproducible. "Keep merging until the budget is spent." A pair that appears once gains nothing and wastes vocabulary. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does the symbol count fall as training proceeds, and what does that do to the cost of a step? Expected: each merge shortens words, so the pair count over the corpus shrinks and later steps are cheaper. (level 2) What does the tie rule protect? Expected: reproducibility; the same corpus must give the same merge list on every machine. (level 3) Two words merge into the same tuple after a step. What must the new dictionary do? Expected: add their frequencies together instead of keeping only the last one. (level 3) How does the vocabulary size relate to the number of merges? Expected: the base byte block plus one id per merge, plus any reserved special ids. Where it is taught. The BPE from scratch lesson gives the training loop and the merge table contract, the tokenizers lesson walks a merge sequence by hand, and the BPE practice checks the tie rule and the stop rule. Explain the mechanism Walk me through one training step of byte-pair encoding on a small corpus, and tell me what the trained artifact actually is. Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Start with every word split into base symbols, bytes or characters. Count every adjacent pair across the corpus, weighted by how often each word appears, merge the most frequent pair into one new symbol with the next free id, rewrite every occurrence, and repeat until the vocabulary reaches the target size. The artifact is the ordered list of merges; the vocabulary follows from it, and the same list applied in the same order is what encoding uses later. A worked step. Corpus: "lower" 5 times, "lowest" 2 times, "newest" 6 times. Copy Recount, and the next step sees (we,s) and (s,t) tied at 8. The lesson's implementation breaks ties by sorting on the pair itself, so two runs over the same corpus produce the same table. After enough steps "west" exists as one symbol. The three facts the loop encodes. Frequency weighting makes the pairs of common words win early. A pre-split on whitespace and punctuation keeps merges inside a word. A word-end marker also keeps "low" as a whole word distinct from "low" as the start of "lower". The merge list is ordered. Encoding applies merges in training order, so the order is part of the artifact. Byte level. With bytes as the base, the first 256 ids are the byte values and merge k gets id 256 plus k. The cost of one step is linear in the corpus as a list of symbol sequences, and the sequences shrink as merges land, so a million words to ten thousand ids runs in seconds. What you ship. The merge table and the special-token table. The vocabulary of byte strings can be rebuilt from them. Plausible wrong answers. "BPE picks the pair that makes the most meaningful piece." It picks the most frequent pair; meaning is a side effect, and the likelihood-based variant is a different algorithm. "The vocabulary is the artifact; the merge list can be discarded." Encoding needs the merges in order; the vocabulary alone does not say how to split new text. "All merges are chosen at once from the initial pair counts." Each merge changes the counts, so the loop recounts after every step. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Why weight pairs by word frequency instead of counting each distinct word once? Expected: the merges should serve the text the model will see, and common words appear many times. (level 2) Why must a tie in pair counts be broken deterministically? Expected: two training runs on the same corpus must produce the same table, or the same text would get different ids. (level 2) What happens to the encoded length of a sentence as the target vocabulary grows from 300 to 600? Expected: it falls, because more merges cover longer pieces; that curve is the compression curve. (level 3) Why split the corpus into words before you count pairs? Expected: without it, merges cross word boundaries and the vocabulary fills with whole phrases that do not generalize. Where it is taught. The tokenizers lesson works the example, the BPE capstone builds the loop with deterministic ties, and the subword lesson names the three facts. Weigh a trade-off Three subword algorithms dominate: byte-pair encoding, WordPiece and Unigram. Contrast how each builds its vocabulary, tell me which one can give two different segmentations of the same word on purpose, and name the libraries you would reach for. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Byte-pair encoding merges the most frequent adjacent pair, bottom up. WordPiece also merges bottom up but scores a pair by the count of the merged piece over the product of the counts of its parts, so it prefers pairs that co-occur more than chance, and it marks continuation pieces with a double-hash prefix. Unigram works top down: it starts from a large candidate set, assigns each piece a probability, and prunes the pieces whose removal hurts the corpus likelihood least, which is why it can also sample alternative segmentations for regularization. The criteria side by side. Copy The first asks which pair appears most. The second asks which pair appears together more often than you would expect from its parts. The third asks which pieces the corpus can best do without. Who uses what. Algorithm Direction Marker Used by Byte-pair encoding merge up leading space kept on word-initial pieces most decoder families, with vocabularies of 50,257, 128,256 and more WordPiece merge up by likelihood ratio ## for continuation pieces the classic encoder with 30,522 tokens Unigram prune down ▁ for a space when trained without pre-tokenization an encoder-decoder family with 32,000 tokens Sampling segmentations. A Unigram model is probabilistic at inference. It can return the most likely segmentation or sample another one, which gives subword regularization during training: the same word arrives in several forms and the model learns pieces more robustly. The merge-based algorithms are deterministic. Libraries. One library trains vocabularies for either the merge or the prune algorithm directly on raw text, encoding the space as a visible symbol and needing no pre-tokenization, which is why it is the default for multilingual work. A second, Rust-backed encoder is fast and matches the vocabularies of a widely used API family, but it only encodes. A third library trains and serves both algorithms in one place. Picking. Training a monolingual model: byte-pair encoding. Training multilingual: Unigram with a character coverage near 0.9995. Serving against an existing API vocabulary: the encoder-only library. Edge inference with a small model: Unigram with a smaller vocabulary. Plausible wrong answers. "WordPiece and byte-pair encoding give the same vocabulary on the same corpus." The criteria differ, so the merges differ; the likelihood ratio favors surprising pairs over merely frequent ones. "Unigram is deterministic like the merge algorithms." It is probabilistic and can sample segmentations on purpose. "The library that encodes the space as a symbol is itself an algorithm." It is a library that trains either the merge or the prune algorithm on raw text. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) What is subword regularization? Expected: training on sampled segmentations from a Unigram model so the same word appears in several forms. (level 2) What does the visible-space symbol buy? Expected: the space becomes an ordinary symbol, so the tokenizer needs no pre-tokenization and works for scripts without spaces. (level 3) Which algorithm and setting for a multilingual vocabulary? Expected: Unigram trained on raw text with character coverage near 0.9995, so rare scripts are kept rather than mapped to unknown. (level 3) Why can an encode-only library not train your tokenizer? Expected: it ships pre-built vocabularies and a fast encoder; the training step lives in the other two libraries. Where it is taught. Defend a design You are starting a 7B model that must serve many languages and also be strong at code. Design its tokenizer: the algorithm, the library, the vocabulary size, the coverage settings, and the validation plan you would gate the training run on. Level 4 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Train a byte-fallback subword vocabulary on a corpus that mirrors the target mix of languages and code, with a pre-tokenizer that keeps leading spaces and separates digits and punctuation so that code tokenizes cleanly. For a model in the 1 to 10B range the heuristic is 50 to 100k tokens, and the multilingual requirement pushes to the top of that range or beyond it; set the character coverage near 0.9995 so that rare scripts are kept rather than mapped to unknown. Gate on tokens per word per language, the unknown rate, the compression ratio against a reference encoder and a byte-exact round trip, and freeze the tokenizer file hash in CI before the first training step. Algorithm and library. The lesson's table points to the prune-based algorithm trained on raw text for multilingual work, because it needs no language-specific pre-tokenization and handles scripts without spaces, and to the merge-based algorithm for monolingual corpora. For a mixed requirement either works if the corpus is right; the corpus mix decides more than the algorithm. Use a library that trains, not one that only encodes against someone else's vocabulary. Keep byte fallback on in either case so that no input is ever unknown. Vocabulary size. Model scale Heuristic under 1B about 32k 1 to 10B 50 to 100k multilingual or frontier 200k and above A 7B model with many scripts sits at the top of the middle row. Each added row is an embedding to learn, and the embedding matrix at 128,000 rows by 4,096 dimensions is about 524M parameters, so the size is a budget decision and not a constant. The payoff is fertility: an English-heavy vocabulary gives other scripts 2 to 3 tokens per word or worse, and non-Latin text can cost 5 to 10 times more tokens; the larger multilingual vocabulary is what repairs that. Coverage and code. Character coverage near 0.9995 for a mixed corpus; refuse anything under 0.995 when rare scripts are present. Byte fallback for everything the coverage still misses. A pre-tokenizer that keeps the leading space on words, splits digit runs and punctuation, and handles whitespace runs, so that indentation and operators in code become stable pieces. Chinese characters are 3 bytes each and need merges of their own, so the corpus must contain enough of them. Reserve the special tokens and the chat markers at the start, with fixed ids that no merge can produce. The corpus. Sample the training text for the tokenizer in the proportions you want the model to be good at. A domain vocabulary can also be trained on the code corpus and merged with the base vocabulary. A tokenizer trained on an English-heavy sample will under-serve every other script for the life of the model. The validation plan. Tokens per word, per language and for code, on held-out text; this is the fertility table you publish. Unknown rate, which must be zero with byte fallback. Compression ratio against a reference encoder on the same held-out text. Round trip, encode then decode, on all of it, including emoji and literal special-token strings. Byte-exact when the tokenizer has no normalizer; with a normalizer such as NFKC, compare against the normalized text. A frozen tokenizer file hash and golden token ids in CI, so that nothing drifts between training and serving. Flag a monolingual vocabulary under 16k as under-specified, and refuse to ship a vocabulary without the hash check. Plausible wrong answers. "Pick 32k because earlier models used it." That size served monolingual models under 1B; a 7B multilingual coding model pays the tax in every language. "Set character coverage to 1.0 to be safe." Full coverage spends vocabulary on characters seen once; near 0.9995 with byte fallback keeps rare scripts without wasting rows. "Train on English now and add the other languages later." The vocabulary cannot change after training without a retrain; the languages must be in the tokenizer corpus from the start. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why does the corpus mix matter more than the algorithm choice? Expected: the merges or the pruned pieces follow the frequencies in the training text, so a script that is rare in the sample gets few pieces whatever the algorithm. (level 4) What does whitespace handling do to code? Expected: indentation is runs of spaces or tabs; a pre-tokenizer that keeps whitespace runs as their own chunks lets them become stable tokens instead of being glued to the next word. (level 4) The team wants to change the vocabulary after six months of training. What do you tell them? Expected: the embeddings and every weight were trained against the current ids; a change means a retrain, which is why the tokenizer decision is gated before the first step. (level 4) How do you report the tokenizer with the model? Expected: the fertility table per language, the size and coverage of the vocabulary, the special-token list and the file hash. Explain the mechanism At encode time a BPE tokenizer holds the complete merge table. Why does it have to replay the merges in the order they were learned, and what goes wrong when two merges could fire at the same spot? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Encoding must reproduce what training did to the same text, and training saw the merges one at a time in that order. If merge one created "th" and merge five created "the" from "th" plus "e", then "the" can only form after "th" exists. When two merges could apply at one position, the one with the lower rank, learned earlier, wins; change that rule and the same text yields different ids, so the model sees a distribution of ids it was never trained on. The naive encoder. Copy It walks the whole table for every word, so the cost is the word length times the number of merges. Correct for a merge table trained on characters, and slow. The rank-based encoder. The capstone version starts from the byte split and repeats: find the applicable merge with the lowest rank anywhere in the current sequence, apply it, and scan again, until no merge in the table applies. Production encoders keep the same semantics with a rank lookup and a priority queue of candidate pairs, which runs in close to linear time. Why the rule is the contract. The training loop and the encoder share the merge table, and that sharing is the whole contract. Training merged the most frequent pair first, so an input that contains both halves of an early merge was always merged that way in the training data. An encoder that prefers a later merge, or the longest piece, produces a segmentation the model never saw. Nothing crashes; the ids are simply different. What special tokens do here. Reserved strings such as the end-of-text marker are matched exactly before the merge loop runs and mapped to fixed ids. They never take part in a merge, so no table order can split or join them. Plausible wrong answers. "Greedily take the longest token in the vocabulary that matches." That is a different algorithm and gives a different segmentation from the training run. "Order does not matter because merges commute." A later merge depends on the symbols that earlier merges created, so they do not commute. "Sort the merges by token length." Length is not rank; a long piece may have been learned early and a short one late. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why is the naive loop slow? Expected: it scans the full merge table for every word, so the cost grows with the table size times the word length. (level 3) How do production encoders get close to linear time? Expected: a rank lookup for each adjacent pair and a priority queue that always surfaces the lowest-ranked applicable merge. (level 3) Two tokenizers were trained on different corpora to the same vocabulary size. Do they give the same ids? Expected: no; different corpora give different merge tables and different ranks. (level 3) What test pins the order? Expected: encode a held-out word and compare with recorded ids; the capstone's tests also pin the round trip and the special-token reservation. Where it is taught. The tokenizers lesson explains the ordered table, the BPE capstone implements the rank-based encoder, and the subword lesson gives the naive loop and its cost. Explain the mechanism A customer in Korea reports that the same prompt uses up far more of the context window than the English version, and the bill is higher too. Why does this happen, and what does a model builder do about it? Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The vocabulary was trained on English-heavy text, so its merges cover English and other scripts fall back to short pieces or raw bytes. Korean averages 2 to 3 tokens per word on an older vocabulary, and non-Latin text can cost 5 to 10 times more tokens than English for the same meaning; a Chinese character is 3 bytes in UTF-8, so without merges each character is several tokens. The builder's fix is a larger vocabulary trained on multilingual data, which is why one model family grew its vocabulary from 32K to 128K. Where the tokens go. A byte-level tokenizer never fails, but it only compresses what it has merges for. Each Chinese character is 3 bytes, Japanese characters are 3 to 4 bytes, an emoji is 4 bytes and can take 5 tokens. If the training corpus held little of a script, the merge table has few pieces for it, and the text stays close to one token per byte. What the customer feels. The context window is a token budget, so the same document fits less often. Pricing is per token, so the same request costs more. Latency is per generated token, so answers in that script are slower. The lesson's phrase is that a user of such a script effectively has a context window half the size of an English user's. What the builder does. Train the vocabulary on a corpus that mirrors the target language mix. Grow the vocabulary so that more merges serve non-Latin scripts; the move from 32K to 128K in one family was made mainly for this. Train with a library that works on raw text without pre-tokenization, so scripts without spaces segment well. Measure fertility per language and report it with the model. How to measure it. Take the same 10 meaning-aligned sentences in English, Spanish, Chinese, Korean and Arabic, from one parallel corpus, tokenize each with the candidate vocabulary, and compare the average tokens per character. The ratios are the tax; with sentences that do not match, report them as a spot check only. Plausible wrong answers. "Korean is harder for the model to understand." The model sees ids; the extra cost comes from the tokenizer's merges, not from the language. "Use a character-level tokenizer for Korean." Characters make every sequence longer; the fix is merges that cover the script. "The model has a smaller context window for Korean." The window is the same number of tokens; the tokenizer spends more of them per word. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Define fertility in one sentence. Expected: the average number of tokens the tokenizer produces per word, where higher means the model works harder for the same text. (level 2) How do you measure the tax for a new vocabulary? Expected: tokenize matched sentences in several languages and compare tokens per character or per word. (level 2) Why does a larger vocabulary help scripts other than English? Expected: more merges can be spent on their byte patterns, so each character or word needs fewer tokens. (level 3) What does the tax do to a product's cost model? Expected: per-token pricing and per-token latency scale with the token count, so the same feature costs more and runs slower in affected languages, and the context budget shrinks. Where it is taught. The tokenizers lesson names the multilingual tax, the subword lesson lists the pitfalls, and the tokenizer build lesson gives the byte counts per script. Read the code Two versions of a byte-level tokenizer's decode function came in for review. vocab maps each id to a bytes object. python def decode_a(self, ids): byte_sequence = b"".join(self.vocab[t] for t in ids) return byte_sequence.decode("utf-8", errors="replace") def decode_b(self, ids): return "".join(self.vocab[t].decode("utf-8") for t in ids) Both pass the English tests. Which one is correct for an emoji whose bytes were split across two tokens, why does the correct one always terminate, and what is errors="replace" for? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Join all the bytes first and decode once, which is what decode_a does. A multi-byte character such as an emoji, 4 bytes in UTF-8, can be split across two or more tokens, so decoding each token's bytes alone hits an incomplete sequence and raises or emits replacement characters. The join works because every id is either one of the 256 raw bytes or the concatenation of two earlier ids, so expanding ids to bytes always ends in raw bytes, and the full byte string is valid UTF-8 whenever the input was. The replace option keeps the decoder from raising when a model emits a partial character at the end of a stream. Why the split happens. A byte-level vocabulary starts from single bytes and learns merges from the corpus. An emoji that was rare in training may have no merge covering all 4 of its bytes, so the encoder leaves it as two tokens, perhaps 3 bytes and 1 byte. Each token on its own is not valid UTF-8. The characters of a script with 3-byte characters have the same problem whenever a merge covers part of a character. Why the join terminates and round-trips. The capstone states the guarantee: encode then decode returns the input bytes exactly. The decoder concatenates the byte expansion of every id in order. Because every id is a raw byte or the concatenation of two known ids, the recursive expansion bottoms out in raw bytes, and the concatenation of all tokens is the original byte string. UTF-8 decoding then recovers the text. The test suite pins the property on an unseen sentence, on a sentence with an emoji, and on a sentence that contains a literal special-token string. Special tokens on the way out. The capstone's decoder checks a special-token table first and appends the marker's UTF-8 bytes, then falls through to the vocabulary, and raises on an id that is in neither. That keeps a reserved id from being looked up as a merge. What errors="replace" is for. A model can stop in the middle of a character, or a stream can be cut between two tokens that share a character. Strict decoding raises; replace emits a replacement character and continues. In a streaming decoder the better pattern is to buffer the trailing bytes until they form a complete character, and to use replace only at the final flush. Plausible wrong answers. "Decode each token to a string and join the strings." A token can hold part of a character, and partial UTF-8 is not a string. "Tell the decoder to ignore errors so nothing ever raises." Ignoring drops bytes silently and the round trip is no longer exact; the replacement character at least marks the loss. "The round trip only matters for the training data." Every generated answer goes through decode, and a server that raises on an emoji drops the request. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does decode_b pass the English tests? Expected: ASCII characters are single bytes, so no token ever holds a partial character and every piece decodes on its own. (level 3) Design the streaming decoder in two sentences. Expected: accumulate bytes and emit only the longest prefix that is complete UTF-8, keeping the remainder; flush with replacement at the end of the stream. (level 3) Why can a word-level tokenizer not give the round-trip guarantee? Expected: unseen words map to an unknown id, and the unknown id cannot be mapped back to the original text. (level 3) What three inputs does the capstone's test suite use for the round trip? Expected: an unseen sentence, a sentence with an emoji, and a sentence containing the literal special-token string. Where it is taught. The BPE capstone states and tests the round-trip guarantee, the tokenizers lesson gives the join-then-decode function, and the tokenizer build lesson gives the byte counts for emoji and other scripts. Estimate it A team wants to grow the vocabulary of a new model from 32K to 128K tokens. The embeddings have 4,096 dimensions. Put numbers on what the change costs and on what it buys. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The embedding matrix goes from 32,000 by 4,096, about 131 million parameters, to 128,000 by 4,096, about 524 million, so about 400M more parameters from the tokenizer alone, and an untied output head costs the same again. In return the text compresses: an English paragraph of about 100 tokens at 32K takes about 70 tokens at 128K. Generating that same paragraph then needs about 30 percent fewer forward passes, and non-English scripts gain the most. The lesson's rule of thumb is 32k under 1B parameters, 50 to 100k from 1 to 10B, and 200k and above for multilingual or frontier models. The cost side. Copy Each row is an embedding the model has to learn, and rare rows receive few gradient updates. A small model with a huge vocabulary spends a large share of its parameters in a lookup table. The benefit side. Vocabulary Tokens per English word 30,522 about 1.4 50,257 about 1.3 100,256 about 1.2 128,256 about 1.1 200,019 about 1.0 Fewer tokens per word means shorter sequences, so each answer needs fewer forward passes and each context window holds more text. For a model that serves millions of requests, output of that kind needs about 30 percent fewer forward passes. Who gains the most. English already compresses well at 32K. Scripts that an English-heavy vocabulary splits into bytes gain far more, which is why one model family quadrupled its vocabulary from 32K to 128K. The decision. Vocabulary size scales with the model and the language mix. Under 1B parameters, the embedding would dominate the model, so stay near 32k. Between 1 and 10B, 50 to 100k. Multilingual at any scale pushes toward 200k and beyond. Validate the choice with tokens per word on a held-out set, the unknown rate, the compression ratio and a byte-exact round trip. Plausible wrong answers. "A bigger vocabulary is always better." Under 1B parameters the extra rows dominate the model and rare rows are undertrained. "The embedding is a rounding error next to the model." At 128K by 4,096 it is about 524M parameters. "Vocabulary size does not affect the cost of a request." Tokens per word set the sequence length, and the sequence length sets the forward passes and the context budget. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why do fewer tokens per word make inference faster? Expected: generation is one forward pass per token, so fewer tokens for the same text means fewer passes. (level 3) What does a 128K vocabulary do to the output side of the model? Expected: the head has one row per token, so it grows with the embedding, and an untied head doubles the extra parameters. (level 3) Why did the model family in the lesson move from 32K to 128K? Expected: fairer compression across languages; the English-heavy vocabulary gave other scripts a context window that was effectively half the size. (level 4) How do you validate a vocabulary size before training? Expected: tokens per word per language on held-out text, the unknown rate, the compression ratio against a reference encoder, and a byte-exact round trip. Where it is taught. The tokenizers lesson does the embedding arithmetic and gives the fertility table, and the subword lesson gives the size heuristic and the validation plan. Explain the mechanism Why does every current language model read subword tokens instead of whole words or single characters, and why do most of them build the vocabulary on top of raw bytes? Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A word vocabulary cannot hold every word, so each new word becomes an unknown token and the model loses the signal. Characters never fail, but they make sequences several times longer and spend attention on spelling. Subwords keep common words whole and split rare words into meaningful pieces, and starting from the 256 byte values means any input in any script encodes with zero unknown tokens. The three options. Level Vocabulary Failure Word huge, and still incomplete unknown token for anything unseen; English alone has over a million word forms Character a few hundred a 10-word sentence becomes about 50 tokens; the model relearns that t, h, e spell a word Subword 30K to 128K none of the above; rare words split into pieces A rare word such as "unhappiness" is 11 character tokens or 3 subword pieces: un, happi, ness. The pieces carry meaning the model can reuse. Why bytes at the bottom. A byte-level vocabulary treats each of the 256 byte values as a base token and learns merges on top. Any string in any encoding is a byte sequence, so nothing is ever unknown, and no language needs special handling. A well-known 50,257-token vocabulary is exactly 256 bytes plus 50,000 merges plus one special token. Why it is architecture, not preprocessing. The tokenizer fixes what the model sees for its whole life. A vocabulary that splits a common word into four pieces wastes context and compute on every request, and the choice cannot be undone after training. Pricing is per token and latency is per token, so the tokenizer sits in the cost model too. Plausible wrong answers. "Characters are the safest choice because nothing is ever unknown." Bytes give the same guarantee, and characters make every sequence several times longer. "A bigger word list solves the unknown problem." New words, misspellings, code and other languages keep appearing; no word list is complete. "A token is a word." A token can be a byte, a piece of a word, a word, or a short phrase, depending on the merges. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) What does fertility measure? Expected: the average number of tokens per word; 1.0 is one token per word and higher means the model works harder for the same text. (level 2) Why does the unknown token disappear with byte-level vocabularies? Expected: every byte is itself a token, so any input decomposes into known tokens before any merge applies. (level 2) What does a tiny vocabulary cost at inference? Expected: longer sequences, so more forward passes per answer and less text per context window. (level 3) Why can you not fix a bad tokenizer after training? Expected: the embedding rows and every weight were trained against those ids; new ids have no learned meaning and old text would map differently. Where it is taught. The subword tokenization lesson compares the algorithms and the tokenizers lesson works the three options through on examples. A To translate text between languages B To compress text for storage C To convert text into a sequence of integers that the model can process D To remove stop words from text LLMs process numbers, not text. The tokenizer converts every character, word, and symbol into integer IDs from a fixed vocabulary. This conversion is not neutral -- it determines how the model 'sees' language. Q2 What does BPE (Byte Pair Encoding) do to build its vocabulary? A Randomly assigns IDs to substrings B Uses a dictionary lookup for whole words C Splits text into individual characters only D Iteratively merges the most frequent adjacent pair of tokens until reaching the target vocabulary size BPE starts with individual bytes/characters and repeatedly merges the most common adjacent pair. 'th' + 'e' becomes 'the'. After thousands of merges, common words become single tokens while rare words are split into subword pieces. Q3 Why does vocabulary size create a tradeoff in LLM design? A Vocabulary size doesn't affect model performance B Smaller vocabularies are always more efficient C Larger vocabularies always perform better D Too small creates long sequences (more computation); too large wastes embedding parameters on rare tokens Small vocabulary (e.g., character-level) means every word is many tokens, increasing sequence length and computation. Large vocabulary wastes parameters on tokens that rarely appear in training data. Most LLMs use 32K-100K tokens. Q4 What problem does byte-level fallback solve in tokenization? A It ensures any input (emoji, rare scripts, binary data) can be encoded without 'unknown' tokens B It improves model accuracy C It reduces vocabulary size D It speeds up tokenization With byte-level fallback, the tokenizer can fall back to raw byte values (256 possible) for any character not in the vocabulary. This guarantees complete coverage -- no input is ever 'unknown.' Q5 How does the tokenizer affect non-English language performance in LLMs? A Tokenizers work equally well for all languages B Non-English text is always character-tokenized C Tokenization doesn't affect language performance D Languages underrepresented in training data get worse token merges, requiring more tokens per word and wasting context window BPE merges are learned from training data. If Japanese text is 5% of the corpus, Japanese characters get fewer merges, requiring 2-5x more tokens per word than English. This effectively shrinks the context window for non-English text. Time : about 90 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Lesson 10.1 gave you a toy. This lesson gives you a weapon. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Byte-level BPE "Tokenizer that works on bytes" BPE with a base vocabulary of 256 byte values -- handles any input without unknown tokens Pre-tokenization "Splitting before BPE" Regex or rule-based splitting that prevents BPE from merging across word boundaries NFKC normalization "Unicode cleanup" Canonical decomposition followed by compatibility composition -- "fi" ligature becomes "fi", fullwidth "A" becomes "A" Chat template "How messages become tokens" The exact format for converting a list of role/content messages into a flat token sequence -- model-specific and must match training format Special tokens "Control tokens" Reserved token IDs that bypass BPE -- [BOS], [EOS], [PAD], chat markers -- matched exactly before merge Fertility "Tokens per word" Ratio of output tokens to input words -- 1.3 for English in GPT-4, 2-3 for Korean, higher means wasted context tiktoken "OpenAI tokenizer" Rust BPE implementation with Python bindings -- 10-100x faster than pure Python Merge table "The vocabulary" Ordered list of byte-pair merges learned during training -- this IS the tokenizer's learned knowledge The problem In plain words first A working tokenizer is more than the merge algorithm. Before merging, text is cleaned up (normalised) and cut into word-sized chunks so that pieces never straddle two words. Some tokens are reserved as markers, such as "start of text" or "end of this message", and must never be produced by ordinary text. And a chat model expects a conversation laid out in one exact format, its chat template, made of those markers. This lesson builds that pipeline in Python, compares the pre-tokenisation rules of three OpenAI tokenizers, shows what normalisation does, and prints the real chat templates of three model families, including one way user text can impersonate a marker. Your BPE tokenizer from Lesson 10.1 works on English text. Now throw Japanese at it. Or emoji. Or Python code with mixed tabs and spaces. It breaks. Not because BPE is wrong -- because the implementation is incomplete. A production tokenizer handles raw bytes in any encoding, normalizes Unicode before splitting, manages special tokens that never get merged, chains pre-tokenization with subword splitting, and does all of this fast enough to not bottleneck a training pipeline processing 15 trillion tokens. GPT-2's tokenizer has 50,257 tokens. Llama 3 has 128,256. GPT-4 has roughly 100,000. These are not toy numbers. The merge tables behind those vocabularies were trained on hundreds of gigabytes of text, and the surrounding machinery -- normalization, pre-tokenization, special token injection, chat template formatting -- is what separates a tokenizer that handles "hello world" from one that handles the entire internet. You are going to build that machinery. Idea 1 · The Full Pipeline A production tokenizer is not one algorithm. It is a pipeline of five stages, each solving a different problem. Each stage has a specific job: Stage What It Does Why It Matters Normalize NFKC Unicode, lowercase optional, strip accents optional "fi" ligature (U+FB01) becomes "fi" (two chars). Without this, same word gets different tokens. Pre-Tokenize Split text into chunks before BPE Prevents BPE from merging across word boundaries. "the cat" should never produce a token "e c". BPE Merge Apply learned merge rules to byte sequences The core compression. Turns raw bytes into subword tokens. Special Tokens Inject [BOS], [EOS], [PAD], chat template markers These tokens have fixed IDs. They never participate in BPE merges. The model needs them for structure. ID Mapping Convert token strings to integer IDs The model sees integers, not strings. Idea 2 · Byte-Level BPE Lesson 10.1 's tokenizer operated on UTF-8 bytes. That was the right call. But we skipped something important: what happens when those bytes are not valid UTF-8? Byte-level BPE solves this by treating every possible byte value (0-255) as a valid token. Your base vocabulary is exactly 256 entries. Any file -- text, binary, corrupted -- can be tokenized without producing an unknown token. GPT-2 added a trick: map each byte to a printable Unicode character so the vocabulary stays human-readable. Byte 0x20 (space) becomes the character "Ġ" in their mapping, which is why GPT-2-style vocabulary files are full of "Ġ". This is purely cosmetic. The algorithm does not care. The real power: byte-level BPE handles every language on earth. Chinese characters are 3 UTF-8 bytes each. Japanese can be 3-4 bytes. Arabic, Devanagari, emoji -- all just byte sequences. The BPE algorithm finds patterns in these byte sequences exactly the same way it finds patterns in English ASCII bytes. Idea 3 · Pre-Tokenization Before BPE touches your text, you need to split it into chunks. This prevents the merge algorithm from creating tokens that span word boundaries. GPT-2 uses a regex pattern to split text: Copy This pattern splits on contractions ("don't" becomes "don" + "'t"), words with optional leading spaces, numbers, punctuation, and whitespace. The leading space is kept attached to the word -- so "the cat" becomes [" the", " cat"], not ["the", " ", "cat"]. Llama 1 and 2 used SentencePiece, which needs no regex: it treats the space as an ordinary symbol ("▁") and by default still keeps pieces from crossing word boundaries. Llama 3 switched to a tiktoken-style regex like GPT-4's. The choice matters. The regex decides, for example, whether numbers are cut into groups of three or kept whole, whether "'VE" counts as a contraction, and whether runs of spaces in code become one token (the second run under Step 6). Idea 4 · Special Tokens Every production tokenizer reserves token IDs for structural markers: Token Purpose Used By [BOS] / <s> Beginning of sequence Llama 3, GPT [EOS] / </s> End of sequence All models [PAD] Padding for batch alignment BERT, T5 [UNK] Unknown token (byte-level BPE eliminates this) BERT, WordPiece <\|im_start\|> Chat message boundary start ChatGPT, Qwen <\|im_end\|> Chat message boundary end ChatGPT, Qwen <\|start_header_id\|> , <\|end_header_id\|> Wrap the role name of each turn Llama 3 <\|eot_id\|> End of a turn Llama 3 Special tokens are never split by BPE. They are matched exactly before the merge algorithm runs, replaced with their fixed ID, and the surrounding text is tokenized normally. Idea 5 · Chat Templates This is where most people get confused and most implementations break. When you send messages to a chat model, the API accepts a list of messages: Copy The model does not see JSON. It sees a flat token sequence. The chat template converts messages into that flat sequence using special tokens. Every model does this differently: Copy Get the template wrong and the model produces garbage. It was trained on one exact format. Any deviation -- a missing newline, a swapped token, an extra space -- puts the input outside the training distribution. Idea 6 · Speed Python is too slow for production tokenization. tiktoken (OpenAI) is written in Rust with Python bindings. HuggingFace tokenizers is also Rust. SentencePiece is C++. These achieve 10-100x speedups over pure Python. For perspective: tokenizing 15 trillion tokens for Llama 3 pre-training at 1 million tokens per second (fast Python) would take 174 days. At 100 million tokens per second (Rust), it takes 1.7 days. You are building in Python to understand the algorithm. In production, you would use a compiled implementation and only touch the Python wrapper. The same idea as a formula A tokenizer is a composition of functions: with special tokens cut out of first and given fixed IDs. Decoding concatenates the byte strings of the IDs and decodes UTF-8. Decoding inverts encoding exactly only if normalisation does nothing: , which is why GPT and Llama 3 tokenizers do not normalise at all. Bytes per character in UTF-8: 1 for ASCII, 2 for most accented Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Arabic and Hebrew, 3 for most other scripts (Devanagari, Chinese, Japanese, Korean), 4 for emoji. With no merges a byte-level tokenizer therefore needs 3× as many tokens per Chinese character as per English letter. Fertility = tokens ÷ words. For languages written without spaces, "words" by whitespace are meaningless; tokens per character is the fair measure. Throughput. tokens at tokens per second take seconds: 15 trillion tokens at /s is s ≈ 174 days, at /s ≈ 1.7 days. Worked example Through the pipeline by hand Input: "Don't ﬁx it." Special tokens: a chat template would wrap the result, for example <|im_start|>user\n … <|im_end|> , each marker one fixed ID. Counting bytes. "你好" is 2 characters, 6 bytes: with no merges, 6 tokens. "🔥" is 1 character, 4 bytes. Recap What to keep from this lesson A tokenizer is a pipeline: normalise, pre-tokenise, byte-encode, merge, add special tokens. The pre-tokeniser regex decides which pieces can ever exist (numbers, contractions, spaces). Normalisation changes text; LLM tokenizers usually skip it so decoding is exact. Special tokens have fixed IDs and must not be produced by untrusted text. Always use the model's own chat template; formats differ and can drop parts silently. The GPT-2 regex has a rule \s+(?!\S) : a run of spaces that is not followed by a non-space character, which matches all but the last space of a run. So "Don't ask" becomes " Don", "'t", " ", " ask": the extra two spaces are one chunk, and " ask" still carries exactly one leading space, so it is the same token as in normal text. This keeps the vocabulary's words consistent and lets runs of spaces (indentation in code) become their own tokens. Solution B1 · Spaces get lost Spaces disappear. text.split(" ") throws the spaces away instead of keeping them in a chunk, so they are never encoded: "Hello world" decodes to "Helloworld", and "The quick brown fox." to "Thequickbrownfox.". The round-trip test that passed for every input now fails for every input with a space. And no learned token starts with a space any more ( b' model' cannot exist), so the tokenizer can no longer tell a word at the start of a text from the same word in the middle. A pre-tokeniser must split text without losing anything: every character must end up in exactly one chunk. Take-home Design and implement a tokenizer for a small language model: train it on a corpus, encode fresh text, decode ids back, and reserve two special tokens for document boundaries and padding. State the guarantees the test suite must pin, and explain how the special tokens survive both training and inference without ever being merged. Level 4 of 4 · about 45 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The base symbols are the 256 raw bytes, so every input has an encoding before any merge and decoding always terminates in bytes. Training runs on pre-tokenized chunks that never contain the special strings, so no merge can produce or consume a special id. At inference a matcher splits the text on the special strings first, maps each one to its reserved id, and runs the merge table on the text between them in training order. The suite pins the round trip on unseen text, on text with multi-byte characters, and on text that contains a literal special string with the flag off. The pipeline. Normalize the text to one Unicode form so that the same visible word gets the same bytes. Split on the special strings when the caller allows them, and map each match to its reserved id. Pre-tokenize the remaining text into chunks at whitespace and punctuation boundaries. Apply the merge table to each chunk's bytes in training order, with non-overlapping left-to-right replacement. Concatenate the ids. Decoding reverses steps two to five: expand each id to its bytes, where a merged id expands to the bytes of its two parents and a reserved special id expands to the UTF-8 bytes of its string, and decode the byte string. Normalization is not reversible. A decomposed accent comes back as the composed character, so the round trip is exact only for text that is already in the normalized form. Why pre-tokenization. Without the split, merges cross word boundaries and the vocabulary fills with common phrases that do not generalize. The split keeps merges inside a word. The chunk boundaries also stop a merge from spanning the end of one word and the start of the next at inference, which is how training and inference stay consistent. Special tokens. The ids after the byte block are reserved by hand. The training loop never sees the special strings, because the corpus is split and the strings are removed before pair counting, so no merge target can be a special id and no merge can include one. At inference the encoder takes a flag. With the flag off, the characters of a special string are ordinary bytes and tokenize as such. With the flag on, the exact string maps to its reserved id and is not subject to any merge. The matcher tries longer special strings first so that one string that contains another is matched whole. The guarantees to pin. Guarantee Test Round trip on unseen text encode then decode returns the exact bytes of the normalized input Multi-byte characters a sentence with a four-byte emoji round-trips Literal special string, flag off the string decodes back as text, not as a boundary Special string, flag on exactly one id, the reserved one, appears Merge order the same merge list gives the same ids on repeated encodes Reserved range no merge in the table has a special id as a parent or a child The compression curve. The number of ids for a held-out sentence falls as the merge budget grows. Training with a target vocabulary of 300 and then of 600 ids on the lesson corpus shows the drop directly; that curve is the measurement that justifies the vocabulary size. Plausible wrong answers. "Add the special tokens to the corpus so the model learns them." Then they can be merged with neighbors and stop being single ids. "Match special strings after the merges." The merges have already split the string into byte pieces, so the matcher never sees it. "Decode by looking up a string per id in a dictionary." Ids are bytes, and a multi-byte character can be split across ids; concatenate bytes first, then decode. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why are the first 256 ids reserved for bytes rather than for the characters of the corpus? Expected: any input, including text in scripts the corpus never had, can then be encoded without an unknown token. (level 4) Where do chat template markers fit in this design? Expected: they are special tokens like the boundary token, matched exactly before the merges, with fixed ids that the model was trained on; a wrong template puts the input outside the training distribution. (level 4) How do you protect a deployed model from a tokenizer that drifts? Expected: hash the merge table and the special-token map, and check the hash in the pipeline before training and before serving; a different table decodes different ids. Where it is taught. The BPE from scratch lesson gives the byte floor, the reserved specials and the round-trip tests, the production tokenizer lesson adds normalization, pre-tokenization and exact matching of special strings, and the BPE practice is the merge step inside it. Debug a failure A fine-tuned chat model answers well in the training notebook. The deployed service, with identical weights, returns rambling text that runs until the token limit. Where do you look first, and what do you expect to find? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. At the flat token sequence the model actually receives, not at the list of messages. A chat model was trained on one exact layout of role markers, special tokens and newlines; a missing newline, a swapped marker or an extra space puts the input outside the training distribution, and the end-of-turn token stops being predicted. Print the token ids of the same request from both paths and diff them, and check that the special tokens arrived as their reserved ids and not as the bytes that spell them. The model never sees the JSON. The service holds a list of role and content pairs. The model sees one flat sequence built by the chat template, which inserts markers such as a begin-of-text token, a header for each role and an end-of-turn token after each message, with specific newlines between them. Every model family lays this out differently. The template is part of the model, in the same way the vocabulary is. The three ways it breaks. A different template. The service used a generic layout or an older version. Each message now sits in a frame the model never saw, and the end-of-turn marker it learned is absent or misplaced, so it never predicts the stop token. Special tokens spelled out. Special tokens must be matched exactly before the merge loop and mapped to fixed ids. If the service built the prompt as plain text and encoded it with the allow flag off, the marker string became ordinary bytes and pieces. The model sees text that looks like a marker and is not one. Stop token mismatch. The service stops on the generic end-of-sequence id while the model emits its end-of-turn id. Generation continues past the real end. The check that settles it. Copy Then decode each id back to its string and look for a marker that decoded as several pieces instead of one reserved id. If the two lists match, the input is fine and the stop token is next: compare the stop ids in the service config with the end-of-turn id that the template puts after each message. The fix. Use the model's own template function, pass special tokens through the reserved-id path, and configure the stop token to the id the template ends a turn with. Freeze the tokenizer file and the template together with the weights. Plausible wrong answers. "The sampling temperature is too high in the service." Temperature changes which token is picked, not whether the stop token is ever predicted; the ids differ before sampling. "The fine-tune overfit." The same weights behave in the notebook; the difference is in the input layout. "Trim the output on the client." That hides the symptom and the model still wastes compute on text it should not generate. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) What does the end-of-turn token do at inference? Expected: it is the model's signal that the answer is complete; the server must stop on that id, or generation runs to the limit. (level 3) A user types the literal string of a special token into the chat box. What should happen? Expected: with the allow flag off it becomes ordinary bytes, which is the safe default for user text; with it on, the user could inject a control marker. (level 3) How do you test a template implementation? Expected: build the sequence for a fixed message list and compare it id by id with the output of the model's own template code. (level 4) The template is correct and the ids still differ between notebook and service. What else? Expected: a different tokenizer file version, a different normalization step, or a different setting for adding special tokens at the start; hash the tokenizer file and compare the flags. Where it is taught. The tokenizer build lesson shows the templates and the special-token path, the BPE capstone explains the allow flag, and the subword lesson lists the drift and whitespace pitfalls. Explain the mechanism Before any merge runs, a production tokenizer cuts the text into chunks with a regular expression. Show me what the classic pattern does to Hello, world! Don't stop. and explain why the cut exists at all, given that the merges could run on the raw stream. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The pattern cuts the sentence into eight chunks, Hello , , , world , ! , Don , 't , stop and . : each word after the first keeps the space in front of it, contractions split at the apostrophe, and punctuation stands alone. The merges then run inside each chunk and can never join symbols across a chunk boundary. Without the cut, training learns merges that span words, the vocabulary fills with whole phrases, and the pieces generalize worse to new text. The pattern. Copy In order: common contraction endings, a word with an optional leading space, a run of digits with an optional leading space, a run of punctuation, and whitespace. The \p{L} and \p{N} classes need the third-party regex module; the standard library falls back to ASCII classes, which is wrong for multilingual text. Why the leading space travels with the word. hello and hello are different tokens. Keeping the space on the word means a word-initial piece and a word-internal piece stay distinct, and the decoder can rebuild the spacing from the tokens alone. The same reason forces every caller to be explicit about whether a prefix space is added at the start of a prompt. Why cut at all. The merge loop is greedy on frequency. In a raw stream the pair "e" followed by a space followed by "t" is frequent, so the loop would happily learn a piece that ends one word and starts the next. Such pieces do not transfer: the next text has different word pairs. Cutting first keeps every merge inside a word, which is where the regularities that generalize live. The other design. A tokenizer that works on raw text treats the space as an ordinary symbol and lets the merge or prune algorithm find the boundaries. It needs no language rules and handles scripts without spaces, and it allows cross-word pieces, which can compress a little better and read a little worse. The capstone's version. A small split on whitespace and punctuation. It is enough to keep merges inside words for a small training set, and the rest of the pipeline stays the same. Plausible wrong answers. "Pre-tokenization is just splitting on spaces." The pattern also handles contractions, digits, punctuation and runs of whitespace, and it keeps the space attached to the word. "The cut is cosmetic; the merges would find the same pieces." Without the cut the merges cross word boundaries and the vocabulary fills with phrases. "Attach punctuation to the word it follows." Then world! and world are different pieces, and the vocabulary pays for every punctuation variant. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does a prompt that starts without a space tokenize differently from one that starts with a space? Expected: the space is part of the word-initial token, so the first word maps to a different id; set the prefix-space behavior explicitly. (level 3) Why does the regex module matter for this pattern? Expected: the Unicode letter and number classes cover scripts beyond ASCII, which the standard library's engine lacks. (level 3) What is the trade in skipping the cut and running on raw text? Expected: no language rules and good behavior for scripts without spaces, against cross-word pieces that compress slightly better and are less interpretable. (level 3) A tokenizer file is unchanged but ids differ between two machines. What in this stage can cause it? Expected: one machine fell back to the ASCII pattern because the regex module was missing, so the chunks differ. Where it is taught. The tokenizer build lesson gives the pattern and its output, the BPE capstone explains why merges stay inside words, and the subword lesson lists the whitespace pitfall. Take-home This is a take-home we send: implement a byte-level byte-pair tokenizer with training, encoding and decoding, two reserved special tokens, and a test suite. Describe the design you would submit, the tests you would ship, and the one figure you would include in the write-up. Level 3 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Reserve ids 0 to 255 for the raw bytes and a small block above them for the end-of-text and pad markers, split the corpus on whitespace and punctuation, train by counting frequency-weighted adjacent pairs and merging the top pair with a deterministic tie-break, encode by applying the lowest-ranked merge that fits until none fits, and decode by joining the byte expansions and decoding UTF-8 once. The tests pin the byte-exact round trip on an unseen sentence, on an emoji and on a literal special-token string with the allow flag on and off, plus the merge-order property and the reserved ids. The figure is the compression curve: the encoded length of a held-out sentence as the target vocabulary grows from 300 to 600. The design. Copy Keep the input bytes as they are, so that the round trip is byte-exact. Compatibility normalization maps a ligature or a fullwidth letter to its plain form and is lossy, so add it only if the write-up limits the round-trip promise to normalized text. Pre-split into words and punctuation so that merges stay inside a word; the regex pattern of the large production tokenizers is an optional extension. Train : count adjacent pairs across the split corpus weighted by word frequency, merge the top pair into the next free id, record the merge, repeat to the target size. Break ties on the pair itself so two runs give the same table. Encode : match special tokens exactly first when the allow flag is on; for ordinary text start from the bytes and repeatedly apply the lowest-ranked applicable merge. Decode : special ids map to their marker strings, every other id to its bytes; join all bytes, then decode once with replacement for a partial trailing character. The tests. Round trip on a sentence the tokenizer never saw. Round trip on a sentence with an emoji, where the character's 4 bytes may span tokens. Round trip on a sentence containing the literal end-of-text string, with the flag off it becomes bytes and with the flag on it becomes the reserved id. Merge order: a held-out word encodes to the recorded ids, and a shuffled table does not. Reserved ids never appear as merge targets and never collide with byte ids. Determinism: training twice on the same corpus gives the same table. The figure. Train to several target sizes, encode the same held-out sentence each time, and plot the token count against the vocabulary size. The count falls as merges cover longer pieces. A second line with the compression ratio, tokens over input bytes where 0.50 means half as many tokens as bytes, shows the same thing in a unit that transfers between corpora. What a reviewer grades. Correctness of the round trip, determinism, clean separation of the special-token path from the merge path, the quality of the tests, and a write-up that names the bug the candidate hit. Speed is not graded: Python at this scale finishes in well under a second, and production libraries in compiled languages are 10 to 100 times faster for the same algorithm. Plausible wrong answers. "Use Unicode code points as the base symbols." Code points number in the hundreds of thousands and leave gaps for unseen characters; bytes are 256 and complete. "Decode each token to a string and join the strings." A token can hold part of a multi-byte character; join the bytes first and decode once. "Skip the pre-split to get better compression." Merges then cross word boundaries and the vocabulary fills with phrases that do not transfer. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why do the raw bytes take ids 0 to 255 before anything else? Expected: every input can then be expressed in the vocabulary before any merge exists, so nothing is ever unknown. (level 3) The input spells out the end-of-text marker as plain text. What does the allow flag change? Expected: off, the string is ordinary bytes and pieces; on, it maps to the reserved id and is skipped by the merge loop. (level 3) Why must a tie in pair counts be broken deterministically? Expected: two runs on the same corpus must give the same table, or the same text gets different ids across machines. (level 4) Replace the simple split with the production regex pattern. What do you compare? Expected: the vocabularies and the encoded lengths on the same corpus, looking at how contractions, digits and leading spaces are handled. Where it is taught. The BPE capstone defines the design, the special tokens and the tests, the tokenizer build lesson adds normalization and the regex extension, and the tokenizers lesson defines the compression ratio. Debug a failure After a routine dependency upgrade, an evaluation score for a deployed model fell sharply. No model weights changed. Give me a diagnosis plan that starts at the tokenizer, and the control you add so it cannot happen again. Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A model trained with one vocabulary and served with another gets different ids for the same text and produces garbage, so first hash the tokenizer file in both environments and compare. If the hashes match, check the settings that change ids without changing the vocabulary: whether special tokens are added, whether a prefix space is added, and the normalization step, because a leading space or a ligature that normalizes differently moves whole tokens. Then freeze the tokenizer hash in CI and keep golden token ids for a fixed corpus so any change fails a test before it ships. Step one: the file. The merge table and the vocabulary are the tokenizer. A library upgrade can pull a different file, or resolve a model name to a newer revision. Compare the hash of the tokenizer file in the evaluation environment with the one the model was trained with. Step two: the settings around the file. Setting What changes Symptom Add special tokens a begin-of-text id appears or disappears at the start every position shifts by one Add prefix space the first word gets a word-initial id or a word-internal id the first token of every prompt differs Normalization a ligature such as the two-letter "fi" becomes two characters, or a fullwidth letter becomes ASCII the same word gets different pieces in the two environments Pre-tokenizer engine the Unicode-aware pattern falls back to ASCII classes non-Latin text splits differently Each of these is a default that a library version can change. None of them touches the vocabulary file, so the hash alone does not catch them. Step three: prove it. Take a fixed sample of prompts from the evaluation. Encode them in both environments and diff the id lists. The first position that differs tells you which setting moved. Decode the differing ids to see the pieces. The controls. Pin the tokenizer file by hash in the deployment and fail the build when it changes. Store golden token ids for a fixed corpus that covers English, non-Latin scripts, code, emoji and a prompt with a leading space; the test encodes the corpus and compares. Assert a round trip, encode then decode, on the same corpus. Compare against the text that the configured normalizer produces, and require byte-exact equality for text that the normalizer leaves unchanged. Record the tokenizer settings next to the weights, so the serving config cannot drift from the training config. The validation plan from the lesson. Average tokens per word on a held-out set, the unknown rate, the compression ratio and the round-trip equality. Those four numbers, tracked over time, show drift before an evaluation does. Plausible wrong answers. "The weights did not change, so the model is the same." The model is the weights and the mapping from text to ids; change the mapping and the model sees different inputs. "Retrain the model on the new tokenizer." A multi-week fix for a configuration bug; restore the training-time tokenizer and settings. "Lowercase everything so the normalization does not matter." That changes the ids again and throws away information the model was trained with. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) How does a prefix space change the ids? Expected: the space is part of the word-initial token, so with it the first word gets one id and without it another, and the shift can continue through the merges. (level 3) What does the compatibility normalization do, and when is it harmful? Expected: it maps compatibility characters to their plain forms, such as a ligature to two letters or a fullwidth letter to ASCII; it is lossy, so code or text that depends on the exact form changes meaning. (level 4) The hashes match and the ids still differ on non-Latin text only. What moved? Expected: the pre-tokenizer engine; the environment without the Unicode-aware module fell back to the ASCII pattern. (level 4) Design the CI gate in two sentences. Expected: a test that encodes a fixed multilingual corpus and compares against stored golden ids and a stored tokenizer hash; any difference fails the build and prints the first differing position. Where it is taught. The subword tokenization lesson lists the drift and whitespace pitfalls and the validation plan, and the tokenizer build lesson covers normalization and the regex engines. Sources and further reading OpenAI tiktoken source -- Rust BPE implementation used by GPT-3.5/4 HuggingFace tokenizers -- Rust tokenizer library supporting BPE, WordPiece, Unigram Llama 3 paper (Meta, 2024) -- details on 128K vocabulary and tokenizer training SentencePiece (Kudo & Richardson, 2018) -- language-agnostic tokenization GPT-2 tokenizer source -- the original byte-to-Unicode mapping Check your understanding Q1 Why does a basic BPE tokenizer break on multilingual or code input? A BPE only works on ASCII B BPE is inherently monolingual C Multilingual text can't be tokenized D Without proper Unicode handling, byte fallback, and pre-tokenization regex, it produces incorrect or inefficient token sequences A naive BPE implementation may not handle multi-byte Unicode characters, may merge across word boundaries incorrectly, and may not have byte-level fallback for characters outside the trained vocabulary. Q2 What is the role of pre-tokenization regex in a production tokenizer? A It splits text at word boundaries before BPE merges, preventing merges across spaces and word boundaries B It compresses whitespace C It converts text to lowercase D It removes punctuation Pre-tokenization regex splits text into chunks (typically at word boundaries, numbers, and punctuation) so BPE merges only happen within chunks. Without this, BPE could merge 'end' with the space before the next word. Q3 What is a special token and why are tokenizers designed to handle them? A Reserved tokens like <|endoftext|> or [PAD] that control model behavior and must be encoded as single, specific IDs B Tokens with the highest embedding values C Tokens used only during evaluation D Tokens that appear frequently Special tokens serve structural purposes: marking document boundaries, padding sequences, indicating start/end of generation. They must be recognized and encoded as their exact IDs, not broken into subwords. Q4 How do you evaluate whether a custom tokenizer is good? A By measuring compression ratio (tokens per character) across diverse text and comparing to established tokenizers like tiktoken B By checking if it can tokenize your name C By measuring encoding speed only D By counting the vocabulary size Compression ratio (bytes per token or tokens per word) measures efficiency. A good tokenizer produces fewer tokens for the same text, which means more content fits in the context window. Compare across languages and domains. Q5 Why is byte-level BPE preferred over word-level tokenization for modern LLMs? A Word-level tokenization is more accurate B It can represent any input without unknown tokens while still learning efficient subword merges for common patterns C It produces smaller vocabularies D It's faster Word-level tokenizers can't handle unseen words (producing [UNK] tokens). Byte-level BPE starts from raw bytes (guaranteeing coverage of any input) and learns merges for common sequences, balancing coverage with efficiency.
