a1007: Course home / Phase 10 · Build Your Own Language Model Rewarding good answers (RLHF with PPO) Lesson 10.7 90 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Build a reward model that scores response quality from human preference pairs (chosen vs rejected) Implement the PPO training loop that optimizes a language model policy against the reward model with a KL penalty Explain why RLHF requires three models (SFT, reward, policy) and how the KL constraint prevents reward hacking Evaluate the effect of RLHF by comparing response quality before and after preference optimization Before you start Needs : Phase 10, Lesson 06 (Instruction Tuning / SFT) Type : Build. Time : about 90 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line SFT teaches the model to follow instructions. But it doesn't teach the model which response is BETTER. Two grammatically correct, factually accurate answers can differ enormously in helpfulness. RLHF is how you encode human judgment into the model's behavior. It's what makes Claude helpful and GPT polite. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means RLHF "Training with human feedback" Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: a three-stage pipeline (SFT, reward model, PPO) that optimizes language model outputs using human preference signals Reward model "A model that scores responses" A transformer with a scalar output head, trained on pairwise human preferences using the Bradley-Terry loss Bradley-Terry "The comparison model" A probabilistic model where $P(A > B) = \mathop{\mathrm{sigmoid}}(\text{score}(A) - \text{score}(B))$, converting pairwise preferences into a consistent scoring function PPO "The RL algorithm" Proximal Policy Optimization: updates the policy to maximize reward while clipping the update magnitude to prevent instability KL divergence "How different two distributions are" A measure of the difference between the policy model's token distribution and the reference model's -- used as a penalty to prevent reward hacking KL penalty "The leash on the model" $\beta \cdot \mathrm{KL}(\text{policy} \Vert \text{reference})$ subtracted from the reward signal -- prevents the policy from diverging too far from the SFT checkpoint Reward hacking "Gaming the reward" When the policy finds degenerate high-reward outputs by exploiting weaknesses in the reward model instead of genuinely improving Preference pair "Which is better, A or B?" A training example consisting of (prompt, preferred_response, rejected_response) -- the fundamental unit of RLHF training data Reference model "The frozen SFT checkpoint" A copy of the SFT model whose weights never change -- used as the anchor for KL divergence computation The problem In plain words first SFT teaches a model to answer, but it treats every training answer as equally good. RLHF adds a sense of "better": people compare pairs of answers, a reward model learns to predict their choices, and the language model is then trained with reinforcement learning (PPO) to write answers the reward model scores highly. A penalty for drifting too far from the SFT model, measured by KL divergence, keeps it from exploiting the reward model's blind spots. Lesson 9.9 covered reward models and the KL-regularised objective in depth; this lesson runs the lesson's end-to-end pipeline and measures, with two real models, how large the KL between a tuned model and its base actually is, and how the estimators that training libraries log behave. No model is trained. Ask a model "Explain quantum computing" and it might produce: Response A: "Quantum computing uses qubits that can exist in superposition, meaning they can be 0, 1, or both simultaneously. This allows quantum computers to process certain calculations exponentially faster than classical computers. Key algorithms include Shor's algorithm for factoring large numbers and Grover's algorithm for searching unsorted databases." Response B: "Quantum computing is a type of computing that uses quantum mechanical phenomena. It was first proposed in the 1980s. Richard Feynman suggested that quantum systems could be simulated by quantum computers. The field has grown significantly since then. Many companies are now working on quantum computers. IBM, Google, and others have made progress. Quantum supremacy was claimed by Google in 2019." Both responses are factually correct. Both are grammatically sound. Both follow the instruction. But Response A is clearly better. It's more concise, more informative, and better structured. A human would pick A every time. SFT can't capture this distinction. It trains the model on "correct" responses, but it has no mechanism for saying "this response is better than that one." It treats every training example as equally good. If both A and B appeared in the SFT dataset, the model would learn from both equally. RLHF solves this. It trains a reward model to predict which response a human would prefer, then uses that reward signal to push the language model toward higher-quality outputs. InstructGPT (the precursor to ChatGPT) used RLHF to dramatically improve GPT-3's helpfulness, truthfulness, and harmlessness. OpenAI's labelers preferred the outputs of the 1.3B InstructGPT to those of the 175B GPT-3, despite it being over 100× smaller, and preferred the 175B InstructGPT to GPT-3 85% of the time. Idea 1 · The Three Stages RLHF is not a single training run. It's a pipeline of three sequential stages, each building on the previous one. Stage 1: SFT. Train a base model on instruction-response pairs ( Lesson 10.6 ). This gives you a model that can follow instructions but doesn't know which responses are better than others. Stage 2: Reward Model. Collect human preference data: show annotators two responses to the same prompt and ask "which is better?" Train a model to predict these preferences. The reward model takes (prompt, response) as input and outputs a scalar score. Stage 3: PPO. Use the reward model to generate a training signal for the language model. The language model generates responses, the reward model scores them, and PPO updates the language model to produce higher-scoring responses. A KL divergence penalty prevents the language model from straying too far from the SFT checkpoint. Idea 2 · The Reward Model The reward model is a language model repurposed as a scorer. Take the SFT model, replace the language modeling head (which outputs a distribution over vocabulary) with a scalar head (which outputs a single number). The architecture is identical up to the final layer. Input: a prompt concatenated with a response. Output: a single scalar reward score. Training data is human preference pairs. For each prompt, annotators see two responses and pick the better one. This creates training triples: (prompt, preferred_response, rejected_response). The loss function uses the Bradley-Terry model of pairwise preferences: ( reward ( preferred ) − reward ( rejected )) ) This is the key equation. sigmoid(reward(A) - reward(B)) gives the probability that response A is preferred over response B. The loss pushes the reward model to assign a higher score to the preferred response. Why pairwise comparisons instead of absolute scores? Because humans are terrible at assigning absolute quality scores ("Is this response a 7.3 or a 7.5 out of 10?") but very good at relative comparisons ("Is A better than B?"). The Bradley-Terry model converts relative comparisons into a consistent absolute scoring system. InstructGPT numbers: the reward-model training set had about 33,000 prompts, each with 4 to 9 responses ranked by about 40 contractors; every ranking of K responses yields K(K − 1)/2 comparison pairs. Idea 3 · PPO: Proximal Policy Optimization PPO is a reinforcement learning algorithm. In RLHF, the "environment" is the reward model, the "agent" is the language model, and the "action" is generating a token. The objective: The first term pushes the model to generate high-reward responses. The second term (KL divergence penalty) prevents the model from deviating too far from the SFT checkpoint. Why the KL penalty? Without it, the model finds degenerate solutions. The reward model is trained on a finite dataset of human preferences. It has blind spots. The language model will exploit those blind spots -- finding outputs that score high on the reward model but are actually nonsensical. Classic examples: Repeating "I'm so helpful and harmless!" scores high on helpfulness/harmlessness reward models Producing verbose, formal-sounding but empty responses that pattern-match to "high quality" Exploiting specific phrases that happened to correlate with high reward in the training data The KL penalty says: you can improve, but you can't become a completely different model. Stay close to the SFT version, which was already reasonable. Wander too far and the KL cost dominates the reward. InstructGPT numbers: PPO used a KL coefficient β = 0.02 and 256K episodes (prompt-response pairs), and mixed in pre-training gradients ("PPO-ptx") to limit regressions on public benchmarks. Idea 4 · The PPO Objective in Detail PPO uses a "clipped surrogate objective" to prevent excessively large updates. The ratio between the new policy and old policy probabilities is clipped to the range , where is typically 0.2. clipped_ratio loss ​ = π new ​ ( action ∣ state ) / π old ​ ( action ∣ state ) = clip ( ratio , 1 − ϵ , 1 + ϵ ) = − min ( ratio ⋅ advantage , clipped_ratio ⋅ advantage ) ​ The advantage function estimates how much better the current response is compared to the expected quality. In RLHF: Copy The baseline is often the average reward over recent responses. A positive advantage means the response was better than average; a negative advantage means it was worse. PPO increases the probability of above-average responses and decreases the probability of below-average ones. The clipping prevents catastrophic updates. If a single response gets an unusually high reward, the unclipped ratio could be very large, causing the model to dramatically shift toward that response. Clipping caps the update, maintaining training stability. Idea 5 · Reward Hacking The dark side of RLHF. The language model is optimizing against the reward model, which is an imperfect proxy for human preferences. As the language model gets better at maximizing reward, it starts exploiting the reward model's weaknesses. Common failure modes: Failure What happens Why Verbosity Model produces longer and longer responses Human annotators often preferred longer, more detailed responses, so the reward model assigns higher scores to length Sycophancy Model agrees with everything the user says Annotators preferred responses that agreed with the premise of the question Hedging Model refuses to commit to an answer Hedged responses ("This is a complex topic with many perspectives...") rarely get marked as wrong Format gaming Model uses bullet points and headers excessively Formatted responses looked more "polished" to annotators Mitigation strategies: stronger KL penalty (prevents the model from straying far enough to exploit weaknesses), training the reward model on adversarial examples (patch known failure modes), and using multiple reward models with different architectures (harder to hack all simultaneously). Solutions Solution P1 · About 0 About 0: the demo prints a KL of 0.0000 in every episode. Its "PPO update" adds random noise of order to the MLP weights, unrelated to the generated tokens, so the policy stays essentially identical to the reference. A real PPO step moves the policy in the direction that makes high-advantage tokens more likely; after a few dozen steps the KL to the reference is clearly non-zero, and the KL penalty and clipping exist precisely to stop it from growing too fast. Solution B1 · The penalty stops being a KL It no longer penalises the KL divergence. The KL is the expectation of the log ratio under the policy, and its token-level estimate is negative whenever the sampled token became less likely than under the reference; those negative values are what make the average equal the true divergence. Taking the absolute value counts every move in either direction as a cost, so the penalty grows with the noise of sampling, not with how far the distributions differ: it is biased upward (like ​ , more so the noisier the tokens are) and adds a pull towards making the policy deterministic in a way the reward model never asked for. If a non-negative per-token penalty is wanted, use ​ , which is non-negative and unbiased. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Explain the mechanism You need a reward model for a helpfulness objective. A product manager suggests asking raters to score each answer from one to ten and regressing on the scores. Why do most pipelines collect pairwise comparisons instead, and what loss do you train with? Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. People are poor at absolute scores and good at relative judgments, so pipelines show two answers to one prompt and ask which is better. The reward model is the SFT model with its vocabulary head replaced by a scalar head. It trains with the Bradley-Terry loss, the negative log of the sigmoid of the reward difference between the preferred and the rejected answer. The difference in reward becomes a log-odds of preference, which turns many relative judgments into one consistent scale. The loss. Copy The sigmoid of the difference is the probability that the preferred answer wins. Training pushes the preferred reward up and the rejected reward down. The model reads the hidden state at the last position, because causal attention has seen the whole prompt and answer there, and projects it to one number. What accuracy to expect. A random reward model ranks half of the pairs right. The reference pipeline in the RLHF lesson trained its reward model on 33,000 comparisons from 40 raters, about 5 minutes each, and reached about 72 percent accuracy on held-out pairs. That sounds low, but the raters agreed with each other about 73 percent of the time. That agreement estimates the noise in the labels. It is not a hard bound, but a score far above it is a reason to look for a leak. Noise in the labels. Roughly 30 percent of human labels are noisy or ambiguous. Filter pairs by rater agreement, or add a temperature to the sigmoid. Pairs where both answers are bad still teach the model which one is less bad. Size. A reward model that is too small cannot score the policy's outputs faithfully. The lesson's table lists a 6B reward model for a 175B policy in one pipeline, and a 52B reward model trained on 22,000 comparisons in another. Larger reward models gave more stable signals to the RL stage. Where the reward model lives later. The same scalar head powers best-of-N sampling at decode time and the reward side of reasoning pipelines. It is the entry to the whole alignment stack. Plausible wrong answers. "Regress on a one-to-ten score; it is more information per label." Absolute scores drift between raters and sessions; a pairwise judgment is cheap and consistent, and the Bradley-Terry fit recovers a scale from it. "72 percent accuracy means the reward model is broken." The raters agreed only about 73 percent of the time; the model is near the agreement of its labels. "Use a small reward model to save compute." A reward model that cannot represent the policy's outputs gives a noisy signal, and the policy exploits its blind spots. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why read the last token's hidden state and not a mean over positions? Expected: with a causal mask the last position has attended to the whole sequence, so it holds the most complete summary; mean pooling is an alternative worth a test. (level 2) Your reward model ranks 90 percent of the test pairs right. Good news? Expected: suspicious; with rater agreement near 73 percent, that score suggests a leak or a shortcut such as length, so check what the model keys on. (level 3) How do you turn comparisons into a reward for several criteria at once? Expected: one reward model per criterion, such as helpfulness and safety, combined with weights; a single model learns a blur of the criteria. (level 4) Why does the reward model need protection from the policy later? Expected: it saw only in-distribution answers; a policy under optimization moves off that distribution and finds answers that score high for the wrong reasons, which is why the RL stage carries a KL penalty. Where it is taught. The RLHF lesson builds the reward model and its pairwise loss, and the reward modeling lesson places it in the full pipeline. A The SFT model rating its own answers, so no human labels are needed B Human preference pairs: given two responses, which one humans preferred C Raw web text: answers that read like high-quality web pages score higher D Benchmark scores: answers that would score higher on MMLU count as better The reward model is trained on preference data: pairs of responses to the same prompt where a human labeled which is better. A To speed up training by stopping PPO early once the policy has moved far enough from the SFT model B To reduce memory usage by letting the policy and the SFT model share most of their weights in training C To encourage the policy to explore answers the SFT model would never give, so it finds better ones D To prevent the policy from diverging too far from the SFT model, which would lead to reward hacking Without the KL penalty, the model finds degenerate ways to maximize the reward score (e.g., producing repetitive text that exploits reward model weaknesses). A When adversaries attack the reward model so that it gives high scores to harmful or unsafe responses B When the reward model is trained on corrupted or mislabelled preference pairs from human raters C When the learning rate is too high, so the policy's reward score swings wildly between PPO steps D When the policy finds ways to maximize the reward score without actually improving response quality The reward model is an imperfect proxy for human judgment. The policy can discover patterns that score high rewards (e.g., verbose responses, excessive hedging) without actually being more helpful. The KL penalty limits this. Q5 What does PPO's clipping mechanism prevent? A The KL penalty growing until it outweighs the reward entirely B Excessively large policy updates that could destabilize training C The reward model scoring answers unlike anything it was trained on D Gradients growing so large they overflow, capped at a fixed maximum PPO clips the probability ratio between the new and old policy to a range like [0.8, 1.2]. Time : about 90 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line RLHF works. It also requires training three models (SFT, reward model, policy), managing PPO's instability, and tuning a KL penalty. DPO asks: what if you could skip all of that? DPO directly optimizes the language model on preference pairs. No reward model. No PPO. One training loop. Same results. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means DPO "RLHF without RL" Direct Preference Optimization: a supervised learning algorithm that optimizes the language model directly on preference pairs, bypassing the reward model and PPO Implicit reward "The reward is in the model" The reward function is determined by the log-probability ratio between the policy and reference models -- no separate reward model needed Beta (DPO) "The temperature" Controls how far the policy can deviate from the reference model -- small beta allows large deviations, large beta keeps the model close Log-probability ratio "How much the model changed" $\log \pi(y \mid x) - \log \pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)$ -- positive means the current model assigns higher probability than the reference Reference model "The frozen checkpoint" A copy of the SFT model whose weights never change -- serves as the anchor for computing probability ratios KTO "DPO without pairs" Kahneman-Tversky Optimization: works with unpaired "good" or "bad" labels instead of requiring preference pairs ORPO "One-step alignment" Odds Ratio Preference Optimization: combines SFT and alignment into a single training loop by adding a preference term to the SFT loss SimPO "No reference needed" Simple Preference Optimization: eliminates the reference model by using length-normalized average log-probability as the implicit reward Alignment tax "The cost of making models safe" The additional compute, data, and complexity required to go from a base model to an aligned model -- DPO reduces this significantly The problem In plain words first RLHF needs a separate reward model and a fragile reinforcement-learning loop. DPO (direct preference optimisation) gets to the same goal with an ordinary training loss: for each pair of answers where people preferred one, nudge the model so that, compared with the frozen starting model, the preferred answer becomes relatively more likely than the rejected one. The maths behind it shows that the model's own probabilities, divided by the starting model's, act as a hidden reward model, so no separate one is needed. This lesson runs the lesson's DPO code, computes exactly how the DPO loss weights each pair and why both answers can become less likely while the loss improves, and measures a real DPO-trained model's implicit reward on human preference data. No model is trained. You built an RLHF pipeline in Lesson 07. Three stages. Three models. The SFT model, the reward model, and the policy model optimized with PPO. The reward model alone required thousands of human preference pairs and a separate training loop. PPO required careful tuning of the KL coefficient, learning rate, clip ratio, and number of epochs. In practice, PPO training is notoriously unstable. Small hyperparameter changes cause the training to diverge. The reward model is an imperfect proxy for human preferences, and the policy finds ways to exploit its weaknesses. The KL penalty helps but requires its own tuning -- too low and you get reward hacking, too high and the model barely learns. This complexity is why most open-source models struggled with RLHF for years after InstructGPT was published. The three-stage pipeline is fragile. Each stage has its own failure modes, and errors compound. In May 2023, Rafael Rafailov, Archit Sharma, and colleagues at Stanford published "Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model." The key insight: you don't need a separate reward model. The optimal reward function is mathematically determined by the language model's own token probabilities. You can skip the reward model entirely and optimize the language model directly on preference pairs. DPO reduces RLHF to a single supervised learning step. One model. One loss function. One training loop. No reinforcement learning. Zephyr-7B, one of the first models to use DPO at scale, matched or beat models trained with full RLHF on several benchmarks. Meta used DPO, rather than PPO, for Llama 3's preference stage. Idea 2 · The DPO Loss ​ = − lo g sigmoid ( β ( lo g π ref ​ ( y w ​ ∣ x ) π ( y w ​ ∣ x ) ​ − lo g π ref ​ ( y l ​ ∣ x ) π ( y l ​ ∣ x ) ​ ) ) Let's unpack each piece: ​ = preferred (winning) response ​ = rejected (losing) response = prompt = current model (being trained) ​ = reference model (frozen SFT checkpoint) = temperature parameter controlling deviation from reference (typically 0.1 to 0.5) The ratio log pi(y|x) / pi_ref(y|x) is the log-probability ratio. Idea 3 · Why DPO is Simpler Aspect RLHF (PPO) DPO Models to train 3 (SFT + reward + policy) 1 (policy only) Training loops 3 (SFT, RM training, PPO) 2 (SFT, DPO) Hyperparameters lr, KL coeff, clip ratio, RM lr, epochs x3 lr, beta, epochs Reward model Required (separate training) Implicit in model probabilities RL algorithm PPO (complex, unstable) Supervised learning (stable) GPU memory 3-4 models in memory during PPO 2 models (current + reference) Training stability Sensitive to hyperparameters Robust, similar to SFT DPO needs two models in memory during training -- the current model and the frozen reference. RLHF needs three or four: the policy, the reference, the reward model, and optionally a value function baseline. For a 70B model, each copy takes 140GB in FP16. The memory savings from eliminating the reward model are substantial. Idea 4 · When DPO Beats RLHF Small datasets. With 5,000-20,000 preference pairs, DPO often matches or exceeds RLHF. The reward model in RLHF needs enough data to generalize -- with limited data, it overfits and produces unreliable reward signals. DPO bypasses this problem by not needing a reward model at all. Limited compute. DPO requires roughly one-third the compute of full RLHF (one training loop instead of three). For teams without large GPU clusters, this is the practical choice. Rapid iteration. Want to try 10 different preference datasets to see which produces the best model? DPO lets you run each experiment in hours. RLHF requires retraining the reward model for each dataset. Idea 5 · When RLHF Beats DPO Large-scale training. At the scale of GPT-4 or Claude, RLHF's separate reward model can capture more nuanced preference signals. The reward model acts as a learned loss function that adapts to complex quality criteria. Complex reward signals. When "better" involves multiple dimensions (helpfulness, harmlessness, honesty), a reward model can learn this multi-objective tradeoff. DPO treats each preference pair as a binary signal -- one is better, one is worse -- without modeling why. Iterative alignment. RLHF pipelines can generate new responses with the current policy, have humans rate them, and retrain the reward model in an online loop. DPO works on a fixed dataset of preference pairs. Constitutional AI (Anthropic's approach) uses this iterative property of RLHF extensively. Idea 6 · Beyond DPO: KTO, ORPO, SimPO DPO inspired a family of simplified alignment methods. KTO (Kahneman-Tversky Optimization, 2024): You don't even need pairs. KTO works with unpaired feedback -- just label each response as "good" or "bad" without comparing it to an alternative. This dramatically simplifies data collection. Instead of showing annotators two responses and asking "which is better?", you show one response and ask "is this good?" The loss function applies loss aversion from prospect theory: bad responses are penalized more than good responses are rewarded. ORPO (Odds Ratio Preference Optimization, 2024): Combines SFT and alignment in a single training step. Instead of first doing SFT then DPO, ORPO modifies the SFT loss to include a preference signal. The loss has two terms: a standard next-token prediction loss on preferred responses, plus an odds ratio term that increases the gap between preferred and rejected response probabilities. One training loop instead of two. SimPO (Simple Preference Optimization, 2024): Eliminates the reference model entirely. Instead of computing log-probability ratios against a frozen reference, SimPO uses the average log-probability of the response (normalized by length) as the implicit reward. This saves memory (no reference model needed) and simplifies training. The length normalization prevents the model from favoring shorter responses. Method Year Models in Memory Needs Pairs? Copy Step 2 · Sequence Log-Probability The DPO loss requires computing the total log-probability of a response given a prompt. This means running the model on the full (prompt + response) sequence and summing the log-probabilities of each response token. Copy This function is the workhorse of DPO. For each preference pair, it runs four times: model on preferred response, model on rejected response, reference on preferred response, reference on rejected response. Step 3 · The DPO Loss The core of the paper in code. One function. One loss. No reward model. Copy The preferred_ratio and rejected_ratio are the log-probability ratios from the DPO derivation. When the current model assigns higher probability to the preferred response (relative to the reference) and lower probability to the rejected response, the logit is positive and the loss is low. The training signal pushes the model in exactly this direction. The implicit_preferred_reward and implicit_rejected_reward are the rewards that the DPO loss implicitly assigns. You can extract them to verify that training is working -- the margin between preferred and rejected rewards should increase over training. Step 4 · DPO Training Loop A standard supervised training loop. No PPO. No reward model. Just forward passes and gradient updates. Copy The training loop is refreshingly simple compared to RLHF. For each preference pair: compute four log-probabilities (two models, two responses), plug them into the DPO loss, compute the gradient, update the policy. No generation step. No reward model inference. No advantage estimation. No clipping. Reference solution and notes Copy Why the policy is a reward model The objective of RLHF has a closed form optimum: ( y ∣ x ) ∝ π re f ​ ( y ∣ x ) exp ( r ( x , y ) / β ) . Solve it for and you get / π re f ​ ) plus a term that depends only on the prompt. The preference model of Bradley and Terry uses only the difference of two rewards for the same prompt, so that term cancels. The result is a loss on the policy alone. What the gradient does The gradient pushes up the preferred log probability and pushes down the rejected one. The weight is ​ − r w ​ ) . A pair that the model already ranks well gets a small weight. A pair that the model ranks wrong gets a weight near 1. The paper shows that this weight is what keeps DPO stable. Without it, the model loses quality. The numerical trap The lesson adds 1e-8 inside the log. That caps the loss of a very wrong pair at about 18.4 and makes the loss of a very good pair about 1e-8 , not 0. np.logaddexp gives the exact value in both directions. The role of beta A small lets the policy move far from the reference before the loss saturates. A large makes the loss sensitive to small changes in the log ratio. Solutions Solution P1 · About 0.693 About 0.693, unchanged: the loss prints 0.6931 in all three epochs, exactly . At initialisation the policy is a copy of the reference, so every log-ratio is 0 and . A working loop would move the loss below 0.693 within the first epoch, since it is trained on these six pairs. Solution B1 · It favours short answers Without the reference, is just the difference in the policy's own log-probabilities, so the model is rewarded for making the chosen reply more likely than the rejected one in absolute terms . Summed log-probabilities are lower for longer replies (every token adds a negative number), so a long chosen reply starts with a large handicap against a short rejected one, and the easiest way to reduce the loss on many pairs is to make long replies, of either kind, unlikely: the model drifts toward short answers. There is also nothing left to anchor it to the SFT model, which was the job of the KL term. SimPO removes the reference deliberately but fixes both problems: it uses length- averaged log-probabilities and a target margin, and still starts from an SFT model. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Debug a failure During a DPO run the loss falls and the reward margin that the trainer logs grows every epoch. Yet the model's samples get shorter and less fluent, and the policy now gives the chosen training answers a lower probability than they had under the reference. Explain the mechanism and what you change. Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The DPO loss cares only about the difference of two log ratios. It can lower the probability of the chosen answer as long as the rejected answer falls faster, and the margin still grows. This is the degraded chosen response failure: the policy moves probability mass away from both training answers, often toward short degenerate outputs. Log the absolute chosen log-probability, add a penalty on downward moves of the chosen term as the behavior-preserving variant does or switch to a loss with a bounded margin, and keep a generation eval next to the margin. Why the margin can lie. The DPO gradient pushes the chosen log ratio up and the rejected log ratio down, but only their difference enters the loss. If the rejected answers are easy to suppress, the cheapest way to grow the margin is to suppress them hard while the chosen answers drift down too. The implicit reward gap is also unbounded: a weak preference can produce an arbitrarily large gap. Nothing in the loss asks the policy to keep generating the chosen answers. What you log. The absolute chosen log-probability under the policy, per epoch, next to the margin. The capstone's margin function reports the difference; add the chosen term alone. Sample lengths and a small generation eval. A margin that grows while samples degrade is the signature. The KL to the reference. The move away from both answers shows up as a growing distance. The fixes. A penalty on downward moves of the chosen log-probability. The behavior-preserving variant of the family adds that one correction and reports a gain over plain DPO on reasoning tasks. A bounded margin. The identity-mapping variant replaces the log sigmoid with a squared error on a target of one over two beta, so the gap and the preference strength stay proportional. A conservative beta and early stopping, chosen against a generation eval, not against the training margin. Better pairs. Pairs where both answers are rare under the reference produce arbitrary implicit rewards; filter them. Why this is still over-optimization. Direct alignment methods remove the explicit reward model, not the proxy. The quantity they optimize is a ratio against the reference, and that ratio can be pushed to places the preference data never covered. The same peak-and-collapse curve that reward models show appears here across KL budgets. Plausible wrong answers. "The margin grows, so training works; the samples are a decoding problem." The margin can grow while both answers lose probability; the generation eval is the objective, not the margin. "Raise beta until the samples recover." A higher beta slows the drift but does not change the direction of the gradient on the chosen term; the penalty on that term does. "Train more epochs; the chosen probability will come back." The loss has no term that rewards a higher chosen probability on its own, so more epochs push further the same way. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why does length matter in this failure? Expected: a long rejected answer has a more negative total log-probability by construction, so suppressing it is cheap and the gap grows for the wrong reason; length normalization removes that incentive. (level 3) How does a reference-free, length-normalized loss change the picture? Expected: it scores the average log-probability per token with a margin, which removes the length bias and the reference, but it also removes the anchor, so drift needs its own guard. (level 4) Which variant do you pick when preference strengths vary widely across pairs? Expected: the bounded one; it keeps the gap proportional to the preference, so strong pairs do not saturate the loss and weak pairs do not blow up. (level 4) Does a lower beta help here? Expected: no; a lower beta lets the policy move further from the reference for the same margin, which makes the degradation worse. Where it is taught. The DPO family lesson names this chosen-answer failure and the variants that fix it, and the DPO capstone derives the gradient that pushes the chosen up and the rejected down. Explain the mechanism DPO is often described as RLHF without a reward model. Walk me through where the reward went. Start from the RLHF objective with its KL term and end at the loss you would implement. Level 2 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The penalized objective has a closed-form optimum: the optimal policy equals the reference policy times the exponential of reward over beta, normalized per prompt. Invert it and the reward equals beta times the log ratio of policy to reference, plus a term that depends on the prompt alone. Put that reward into the Bradley-Terry preference probability and the prompt-only term cancels, because both answers share the prompt. What is left is a loss in the policy's own log-probabilities: minus the log sigmoid of beta times the difference of the two log ratios. The derivation in four lines. Copy The log Z term depends on the prompt alone, so it is the same for the chosen and the rejected answer and drops out of the difference. What you compute per pair. Four sequence log-probabilities: the policy and the reference on the chosen answer, and both on the rejected answer. Each is the sum of next-token log-probabilities over the answer tokens only, with the prompt positions masked. The reference runs under no gradient. The implicit reward. beta * (log pi(y|x) - log pi_ref(y|x)) is the reward that DPO assigns to an answer. Log the margin between the chosen and the rejected implicit rewards; it should grow during training. The gradient on the chosen log-probability is -beta * (1 - sigmoid(z)) , negative for every z, so training pushes the chosen answer up and the rejected answer down. Where the KL went. No KL term appears in the loss. The constraint is structural: a large move from the reference makes the log ratio large, the sigmoid saturates, and the gradient fades. Beta sets how far the policy may move. The DPO lesson gives 0.1 to 0.5 as the range and 0.1 to 0.3 as the usual sweet spot. A small beta allows large moves and risks degenerate answers; a value near 1.0 pins the policy to the reference. What it saves. Two models in memory instead of three or four, and one supervised loop instead of PPO. For a 70B model each copy takes 140GB in FP16, so the reward model you never load is a large saving. Plausible wrong answers. "DPO has no reference model, that is the point." It removes the reward model and PPO; the frozen reference stays in the loss, and the methods that drop it are a later variant. "DPO maximizes the probability of the chosen answer." It maximizes the margin of two log ratios; the chosen absolute probability can fall as long as the rejected falls faster. "Beta is a learning rate." Beta scales the implicit reward and sets how far the policy may move from the reference; the optimizer step size is a separate setting. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why must the policy start as a copy of the reference? Expected: the derivation treats the optimum as the reference plus a learned shift, and a copy makes every implicit reward start at zero. (level 2) What does a positive log ratio mean? Expected: the policy now gives that answer a higher probability than the reference does. (level 3) Why does the derivation need both answers to share one prompt? Expected: the partition term depends on the prompt only; with different prompts it would not cancel, and the implicit rewards would not be comparable. (level 4) Which assumptions of the derivation fail in practice? Expected: that the optimum is reachable, that the pairs are in-distribution for the reference, and that the reference is the true anchor; each later method in the family repairs one of them. Weigh a trade-off A team of four engineers with eight GPUs has about 20,000 preference pairs for a customer support assistant and wants it aligned in three weeks. One engineer wants the full RLHF stack with a reward model and PPO. Another wants DPO. Which do you pick, and under what conditions would you reverse the choice? Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Pick DPO. With tens of thousands of pairs it matches or beats the full stack, it trains one model against a frozen reference in a supervised loop, it needs about a third of the compute, and each experiment takes hours instead of days. Reverse the choice when the signal has several dimensions and needs a learned reward you can inspect and reuse, when you want an online loop that rates fresh samples, or when DPO plateaus on your eval. What DPO buys. Aspect RLHF with PPO DPO Models trained three: SFT, reward, policy one: the policy Models in memory three or four during PPO two: policy and reference Hyperparameters learning rate, KL coefficient, clip ratio, reward model rate, epochs for each stage learning rate, beta, epochs Stability sensitive to the settings close to SFT For a 70B model each copy takes 140GB in FP16, so one model fewer in memory is a different hardware tier. When DPO wins. Small datasets, 5,000 to 20,000 pairs. A reward model needs enough data to generalize and overfits below that; DPO never fits one. Limited compute. One training loop instead of three, roughly one third of the full stack. Fast iteration. Trying 10 preference sets takes ten runs of hours each, with no reward model to retrain for each one. The lesson's reference result: a 7B model aligned with DPO on 60K pairs scored 6.47 on a chat benchmark against 6.86 for a 70B chat model trained with the full stack, within six percent of a model ten times its size. When the full stack wins. Several quality dimensions at once, such as helpfulness, harmlessness and honesty. A reward model learns the trade-off; DPO sees each pair as one binary signal. An online loop: sample from the current policy, rate, retrain the reward model, continue. DPO works on a fixed set. A reward model you can reuse for best-of-N sampling or as a judge at decode time. The largest scales, where a separate reward model has captured more nuance in published pipelines. The practical path. Start with DPO. Switch to the full stack when the eval plateaus. Several production pipelines run both: the full stack first for broad alignment, DPO after it for targeted refinement. Plausible wrong answers. "RLHF is the proven path, so start there." The full stack is fragile to tune and needs three training loops; the lesson's practical guidance starts with DPO and switches only on a plateau. "DPO needs no SFT stage." It needs a reference policy, and that reference is the SFT checkpoint; the single-stage methods are different losses. "DPO has no hyperparameters to worry about." Beta decides how far the policy moves from the reference, and the lesson's sweep shows degenerate answers at a small value and no learning at a large one. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) What does the DPO run still need from the RLHF recipe? Expected: an SFT checkpoint as the frozen reference, a held-out eval, and a beta choice that plays the role of the KL coefficient. (level 3) The pairs come from an older model's outputs. Does that matter for DPO? Expected: yes; pairs that are rare under the reference produce arbitrary implicit rewards, so sample the pairs from the SFT model or filter them by reference likelihood. (level 4) How would you turn the three weeks into an iterative loop without PPO? Expected: run DPO, generate from the new policy, collect preferences on those samples, run DPO again; the lesson's exercise calls this iterative DPO. (level 4) Which failure mode do both methods share? Expected: over-optimization of a proxy, the reward model in one case and the ratio to the reference in the other; both need a blind eval and early stopping. Where it is taught. The DPO lesson compares both methods on data, compute and memory, and the reward modeling lesson places each in the layered alignment stack. Read the code A teammate wrote the core of a DPO trainer. The loss stays at its starting value for the whole run, and the logged margin never moves. Read the code and find what is wrong. python policy = TinyGPT(config) reference = policy def sequence_log_prob(model, prompt_ids, completion_ids): ids = torch.cat([prompt_ids, completion_ids]) logits = model(ids[:-1].unsqueeze(0))[0] log_probs = logits.log_softmax(-1) targets = ids[1:] return log_probs[torch.arange(len(targets)), targets].sum() def dpo_loss(prompt, chosen, rejected, beta=0.1): pi_w = sequence_log_prob(policy, prompt, chosen) pi_l = sequence_log_prob(policy, prompt, rejected) ref_w = sequence_log_prob(reference, prompt, chosen) ref_l = sequence_log_prob(reference, prompt, rejected) z = beta * ((pi_l - ref_l) - (pi_w - ref_w)) return -torch.nn.functional.logsigmoid(z) Level 2 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Three things. The reference is the same object as the policy, so both log ratios are zero by construction and the loss is a constant with no gradient; build the reference as a separate copy, freeze it, and run it under no gradient. The margin has the wrong sign, so once the aliasing is fixed the trainer promotes the rejected answer. The log-probability also sums over the prompt positions, which the capstone masks out. Bug 1: the reference is the policy. reference = policy binds a second name to one module. Every forward pass through reference uses the current policy weights, so pi_w - ref_w and pi_l - ref_l are exactly zero, and the loss is a constant. The optimizer sees a zero gradient. A deep copy alone is not enough either: the reference needs requires_grad=False on every parameter, its forward passes belong under torch.no_grad() , and the policy must start from the same weights, for example with policy.load_state_dict(reference.state_dict()) . Bug 2: the margin has the wrong sign. The loss is minus the log sigmoid of beta times the chosen log ratio minus the rejected log ratio. The code subtracts in the other order. The gradient with respect to the chosen log-probability must be negative, so that raising it lowers the loss. With the reversed sign, the trainer lowers the chosen answer and raises the rejected one. A unit test that checks the gradient sign on one pair catches this. Observation 3: the prompt is in the sum. sequence_log_prob sums over every position, the prompt included. With one shared prompt, the prompt terms cancel in the margin, so the value is right. But the trainer computes and backpropagates through positions that carry no preference signal, and the cancellation breaks when a long sequence is cut at a maximum length. Start the sum at the first answer position, as the capstone does. How to test the fix. The loss on one pair falls when you raise the chosen log-probability by hand. The reference log-probabilities are identical between epochs. The mean chosen minus rejected margin under the policy grows over training. Plausible wrong answers. "Lower the learning rate; the loss is flat because the steps are too small." The gradient is exactly zero while the reference aliases the policy; no step size fixes that. "The sign does not matter, the optimizer finds the direction." The sign decides which answer the trainer promotes; reversed, it trains the model to prefer the rejected answers. "Replace the sum with a mean to stabilize the loss." That turns the objective into a length-normalized variant; it is a design choice, not the fix for a constant loss. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) After the fix, how do you confirm that the reference never moves? Expected: assert that no reference parameter requires a gradient, and compare its log-probabilities on a fixed pair before and after an epoch. (level 3) Why does every pair start at the same loss before training? Expected: the policy equals the reference, so both log ratios are zero and the sigmoid sits at one half; the margin grows from there. (level 3) The margin grows, but the generated answers get worse. What do you log next? Expected: the absolute chosen log-probability; DPO can push it down as long as the rejected falls faster. (level 4) Would you keep the prompt positions if the two answers had different prompts? Expected: no, and the loss would be wrong anyway; the derivation needs one prompt per pair, because the partition term cancels only then. Where it is taught. The DPO capstone pins the reference invariance and the gradient sign with tests, and the DPO lesson computes the four log-probabilities for each pair. Defend a design Four teams bring you four datasets. One has thumbs-up and thumbs-down clicks on single answers. One has paired comparisons whose preferred answers are mostly twice the length of the rejected ones. One has no SFT checkpoint and wants a single training stage from the base model. One has pairs where some preferences are near coin flips and others are unanimous. Which preference loss do you recommend to each team, and why? Level 3 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The clicks team gets the prospect-theory loss that works on single labels. The length-skewed team gets the reference-free loss that normalizes by length and adds a margin, so a longer winner does not win by its token count. The team without an SFT stage gets the odds-ratio loss, which adds a preference term to the SFT likelihood and trains from the base in one pass; the team with mixed preference strengths gets the identity-mapping loss, whose margin is bounded. Each one repairs one assumption that plain DPO makes. Start from what DPO assumes. The DPO derivation assumes paired data, an SFT reference that is the true anchor, in-distribution pairs, and a preference that maps to an unbounded log-odds. Each member of the family drops or repairs one of these. Data or constraint Loss What it changes Single answers with good or bad labels KTO prospect-theory utility on one label; losses weigh more than gains; no pairs needed Winners much longer than losers SimPO average log-probability per token plus a margin; no reference model No SFT checkpoint, one stage ORPO SFT negative log-likelihood plus an odds-ratio preference term; the SFT term is the regularizer Preference strength varies widely IPO squared error on a target of one over two beta; the gap is bounded Chosen log-probability falls in the DPO logs BPO DPO plus a penalty on downward moves of the chosen answer A large clean paired set DPO a conservative beta The reasoning for each team. Clicks are plentiful and unpaired. Forcing them into pairs throws away most of the data; the unpaired loss uses every label. In plain DPO a long winner has a more negative log-probability by construction, so the gap grows for the wrong reason and the policy learns length. Normalizing by length removes the incentive. Without a reference, drift needs a guard of its own. The single-stage loss trains the base model to follow instructions and to prefer the chosen answer at once; the likelihood term keeps it anchored where DPO used the reference. In DPO a near coin-flip pair and a unanimous pair both push toward an unbounded gap. The bounded loss keeps the gap proportional to the preference strength. What every team keeps. A held-out eval with generation, early stopping, and a check on the absolute chosen log-probability. None of these losses escapes over-optimization; they move where it bites. How to decide in practice. Run the candidates on one battery and pick per task. The lesson's point is that the best loss for math reasoning has no reason to be the best loss for safety. Plausible wrong answers. "Convert the clicks into pairs by matching a good and a bad answer for the same prompt." It keeps only prompts with both labels and invents comparisons the raters never made; the unpaired loss uses the labels as they are. "Truncate the long winners so that the pairs are balanced." That destroys the answers people preferred; the fix is in the loss normalization, not in the data. "Use DPO everywhere and tune beta per team." Beta cannot create pairs, remove a reference, bound a gap or supply an SFT stage; each of those is a different loss. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) The clicks team also has a small paired set. Combine them? Expected: yes; train with the unpaired loss on the clicks and validate on the pairs, or weight the two losses; the pairs are the cleaner signal for the eval. (level 3) Why does removing the reference save memory, and what does it cost? Expected: one model in memory instead of two; the cost is no anchor, so the policy can drift, and the margin term and early stopping carry that job. (level 4) A team runs DPO and watches the probability of its chosen answers drop while the margin grows. Which row applies, and why is it not a tuning problem? Expected: the chosen-preserving variant; the gradient of plain DPO cares only about the difference, so no beta fixes the direction. (level 4) How do you argue to a skeptic that these losses still over-optimize? Expected: the published curves of gold reward against KL for direct methods show the same peak and collapse as reward-model pipelines; the implicit reward queries out-of-distribution samples, and KL regularization does not stabilize it. Where it is taught. The DPO family lesson gives each loss and the failure mode it fixes, and the DPO lesson tabulates the models, pairs and reference that each method needs. A DPO produces better models B DPO uses less training data C DPO eliminates the need for a separate reward model and PPO, training directly on preference pairs in a single loop D DPO works without any preference data RLHF requires training a reward model separately, then running PPO optimization. DPO folds both steps into a single training objective that directly optimizes the language model on preference pairs. Q2 What role does the reference model play in DPO? A It serves as the anchor that prevents the trained model from diverging too far, similar to the KL penalty in RLHF B It generates training data C It handles tokenization D It evaluates model quality The DPO loss compares log probabilities under the trained policy and the reference (usually SFT) model. The reference model constrains how far the policy can drift, preventing reward hacking without explicit KL tuning. Q3 What does the beta parameter in DPO control? A The batch size B The learning rate C The number of training epochs D How strongly the policy is constrained to stay close to the reference model -- higher beta means more conservative updates Beta scales the implicit KL divergence penalty. Beta=0.1 allows the model to diverge significantly from the reference (potentially better but riskier). Beta=0.5 keeps it close (safer but less learning). Q4 How does DPO implicitly represent a reward model? A It doesn't -- DPO has no concept of reward B The DPO loss function can be derived by showing that the optimal policy under a reward function is directly expressible through policy log probabilities C It trains a hidden reward model inside the language model D DPO uses the loss function as the reward Rafailov et al. showed that the closed-form solution of the RLHF objective expresses the reward as a function of the policy's log-probabilities relative to the reference. DPO optimizes this directly, implicitly learning the reward. Q5 When might RLHF still be preferred over DPO? A When training smaller models B When you have less preference data C Always -- RLHF is strictly better D When you need a reusable reward model for evaluating multiple policies or when online data collection is beneficial DPO is offline (fixed preference data). RLHF allows online data collection where the reward model scores new generations, discovering reward-hacking patterns. A standalone reward model is also useful for evaluation and other policies. Time : about 45 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line RLHF needs humans in the loop. Constitutional AI replaces most of them with the model itself. Write a list of principles, have the model critique its own outputs against those principles, and train on the critiques. DeepSeek-R1 pushed this further in 2025: let the model generate millions of reasoning traces, grade them with a rule, and run GRPO on the outcome. Most of the "alignment work" in a 2026 frontier model is the model alignment itself. This lesson builds both loops. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Constitutional AI "The model aligns itself" A two-stage pipeline (self-critique + RLAIF) that replaces most human preference labels with model self-judgments against a written constitution RLAIF "RLHF without humans" Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback -- PPO or DPO on preferences generated by the model itself GRPO "PPO without a value function" Group-Relative Policy Optimization -- sample G responses per prompt, use z-scored group rewards as advantages ORM "Reward the answer" Outcome Reward Model -- a single scalar reward on the final answer only PRM "Reward each step" Process Reward Model -- reward on every intermediate reasoning step, often trained from step-labeled data Rule-based reward "Deterministic grader" A verifier (regex, sympy, test suite) that returns a binary or numeric score without a learned model Rejection sampling FT "Keep the winners, retrain" Sample many responses, filter to the highest-reward ones, add to SFT data, retrain Mode collapse "The model stopped being diverse" Post-training policy concentrates on a narrow region of the response space; measured as falling reward std across a group KL budget "How far you can drift" The total KL divergence from the reference model that the optimizer is allowed to accumulate before training stops R1 moment "The model learned to backtrack" DeepSeek's reported behavior where a policy trained only on outcome rewards spontaneously developed self-checking and backtracking in its chain-of-thought The problem In plain words first Human preference labels are slow and expensive, so two cheaper sources of feedback took over much of the work. Constitutional AI writes the rules down, such as "do not refuse reasonable requests", and lets a model critique and rewrite its own answers, or judge pairs of answers, against them. For tasks with checkable answers, like maths or code, a program checks the answer and reinforcement learning (GRPO) rewards the attempts that beat their group's average. Both loops can be repeated, each round training on the model's own best outputs. This lesson runs the lesson's version of both loops, uses a small real model as a constitutional judge to show how unreliable judging can be, and computes exactly what self-improvement can and cannot create. No model is trained. You built RLHF in Lesson 10.7 and DPO in Lesson 08. Both depend on the same expensive input: human preference pairs. OpenAI's InstructGPT reward model was trained on rankings for about 33,000 prompts. Llama 2 Chat used over 1.4 million comparisons collected by Meta. This data is slow, expensive, and biased toward whatever the annotators happened to believe on the day they were rating. The 2022 Constitutional AI paper asked a simple question. What if the model generates the preference labels itself? Give it a list of written principles -- the "constitution" -- and have it critique its own responses. The critiques become the training signal. In 2024, DeepSeek took the idea further. They showed that for any task with a verifiable outcome (math with a known answer, code that either passes tests or fails, a game that either wins or loses), you can skip the critic entirely. Generate many candidate solutions. Grade each one with a deterministic rule. Run a policy-gradient algorithm on the rewards. DeepSeek-R1-Zero was trained this way with no human preference data at all, and DeepSeek-R1 (which added a small supervised "cold start" and later preference rewards) matched o1-class reasoning performance. These two loops -- Constitutional AI for subjective behavior and rule-based RL for verifiable behavior -- are now widely used post-training recipes. The human preference budget that used to go into RLHF now pays for a much smaller step: picking the constitution and picking the reward rules. Idea 1 · The Constitutional AI Loop Bai et al. (2022) structured the pipeline in two stages. Stage 1: Supervised Learning from AI Feedback (SL-CAI). Start with an SFT model that is helpful but possibly harmful. Prompt it with potentially harmful requests. For each response, ask the same model to critique its response against a constitutional principle, then revise. Fine-tune on the revised responses. The dataset is (prompt, revised_response) pairs. Stage 2: Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF). Sample pairs of responses. Ask the model which one better follows the constitution. The pairwise preferences train a reward model. Then run PPO or DPO on the model using that reward. The key difference from RLHF: the preferences came from the model, not from humans. The constitution is the lever. Anthropic's original had 16 principles (later expanded). A principle reads like "Please choose the response that is least likely to be objectionable to anyone from a wide variety of cultural backgrounds." You pick the principle for each step, sometimes at random, sometimes based on the prompt category. Idea 2 · What the Constitution Actually Does The constitution moves the alignment contract from data to text . Changing behavior under RLHF means re-labeling thousands of pairs. Changing behavior under CAI means editing a paragraph. This is the main practical win. It has a cost. The model's self-judgments are only as good as its starting calibration. If the SFT model has blind spots -- for instance, it cannot recognize manipulative phrasing -- the critique step inherits those blind spots. CAI compresses the alignment loop but cannot amplify signal past the base model's ceiling. This is why the original CAI pipeline still used human preference labels for helpfulness; only the harmlessness labels came from the model. Idea 3 · GRPO: Group-Relative Policy Optimization DeepSeek introduced GRPO in the DeepSeekMath paper (2024) and used it as the backbone of DeepSeek-R1 (2025). GRPO is a variant of PPO that removes the value function. Recall PPO's objective (from Lesson 10.7 ): ​ = E [ min ( r ( θ ) ⋅ A , clip ( r ( θ ) , 1 − ϵ , 1 + ϵ ) ⋅ A ) ] where A is the advantage, typically estimated with GAE using a learned value network V(s) . The value network is a second model the same size as the policy. It doubles memory and introduces its own training loop. GRPO throws out the value function. For each prompt, it samples a group of responses (typically or 64). The reward for each response is computed, then normalized within the group: ​ = std ( r 1 ​ , … , r G ​ ) r i ​ − mean ( r 1 ​ , … , r G ​ ) ​ The advantage is the z-score of the response's reward relative to its siblings. No value function. The group acts as its own baseline. ​ = E [ min ( r ( θ ) ⋅ A group ​ , clip ( r ( θ ) , 1 − ϵ , 1 + ϵ ) ⋅ A group ​ ) ] − β ⋅ KL ( π ∥ π ref ​ ) The KL penalty against the reference model is still there, same as PPO. The clip ratio is still there. What's gone is the separate critic. Idea 4 · Why GRPO Matters for Reasoning For reasoning tasks the reward is often sparse and binary: the final answer is right or wrong. A value function trained on sparse binary rewards is a waste -- it cannot learn useful intermediate estimates because nearly every state has the same expected return until the final step. GRPO's group normalization gives you an immediate relative signal: among 16 attempts on the same math problem, which attempts were above average for this problem? This is the exact shape of signal you get from rule-based rewards: Math : sympy or a symbolic checker decides if the final answer matches. Code : a test suite decides pass/fail. Formatting : a regex decides whether the answer is in the required XML tag. Multi-step proofs : a proof assistant (Lean, Coq) decides validity. DeepSeek-R1-Zero was trained with only two rule-based rewards: accuracy (a checker for maths answers, test results for code) and format (reasoning inside <think> tags, the answer after them). No human preferences. No critic model. The "aha moment" the DeepSeek paper described -- the model spontaneously learning to self-check and backtrack -- emerged from GRPO on sparse rule rewards alone. Idea 5 · Process Reward Models vs Outcome Reward Models You still have a design choice: reward the final answer (Outcome Reward Model, ORM) or reward each intermediate step (Process Reward Model, PRM). Axis ORM PRM Signal per trace 1 number N numbers (one per step) Supervision source Final answer check Step-level labels or self-judging Training cost Cheap Expensive Credit assignment Sparse, noisy Dense, targeted Reward hacking risk Lower Higher (model optimizes PRM artifacts) Used by DeepSeek-R1, R1-Zero OpenAI's "Let's Verify Step by Step" (PRM800K), Math-Shepherd The 2024-2025 consensus was that ORMs plus GRPO scale better than PRMs. PRMs are more sample-efficient per token but require expensive step-labeled data and tend to collapse into shortcut behaviors (writing steps that look good to the PRM but don't advance the proof). For most teams, ORM + GRPO is the first thing to try. Idea 6 · Self-Improvement: The Feedback Multiplier Once you have the two-loop pattern (critique/revise and group-relative RL with rule rewards), you can chain them. Start with an SFT model. Generate many candidate responses per prompt. Score them with a rule-based reward (for verifiable tasks) or a constitutional critic (for subjective tasks). Keep the top candidates as new SFT data or as preference pairs. Fine-tune. Go to step 2 with the improved model. DeepSeek called this "rejection sampling fine-tuning" when applied after R1-Zero. The pattern is: each iteration amplifies the signal already in the model. It does not add new signal. If the model cannot solve problem class X at all, no amount of self-improvement will create that capability. The danger is mode collapse. Self-generated data is always a narrower distribution than the training corpus. Repeated rounds of training on self-generated data narrow the distribution ("model collapse"): models lose diversity on creative tasks, become overconfident, and develop a characteristic "AI voice" (repeated phrasings, formulaic structure). Production pipelines mix self-generated data with a small fraction of fresh human data to keep the distribution honest. Idea 7 · When To Use What Pure CAI : Subjective behavior (tone, safety, refusal style). You have a well-defined constitution. You don't have clean verifiable outcomes. GRPO + ORM : Verifiable tasks (math, code, structured extraction). You can cheaply check correctness. Reward is sparse and binary. DPO on self-generated pairs : Hybrid. Use the constitution to produce preference pairs, then train with DPO ( Lesson 10.8 ) instead of PPO/GRPO. Full RLHF : Still appropriate when you need multi-objective tradeoffs that neither a rule nor a short constitution can express. Published pipelines combine several of them. CAI for safety layers. GRPO for the reasoning post-training pass. DPO for the preference polish. Small RLHF passes for residual behaviors that resist the other methods. Each generation is a perfectly reasonable maximum-likelihood fit to 50 samples from the previous one, yet the spread decays steadily: median σ 0.92 after 5 generations, 0.67 after 20, 0.12 after 100, and 92% of the chains end below half the original spread. Each fit slightly underestimates the variance and loses whatever was rare in its sample; errors compound because nothing pulls the distribution back. This is model collapse in its simplest form, and the reason self-training pipelines keep a share of real data in every round. Use it: the same idea with real libraries Running code/main.py runs both loops end to end. The CAI loop produces a small set of (initial, revised) pairs you could fine-tune on. The GRPO loop produces per-prompt reward statistics for arithmetic problems, showing how group-relative advantages let a weak sampler improve without a value function or human labels. The numbers are not the point. In a real run with a trained model the reward mean should climb across rounds, the reward std should stay positive (if it collapses to zero, the policy has mode-collapsed and you should stop), and the KL to the reference should grow slowly. Those three curves -- mean reward up, std stable, KL bounded -- are the production health check for a GRPO or CAI pipeline. Inference only, about 15 seconds. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output The judge is certain and useless: it says "A" with probability 1.00 for every pair, whichever reply is in position A. When the better reply comes first it is "right" six times; when the same pairs are swapped it is wrong six times, so it gets 6 of 12, exactly chance, and its verdict never survives swapping the order. These are not subtle cases: a refusal to explain how to boil an egg, a fabricated stock prediction, instructions for breaking into a neighbour's home. A 0.5B model has not learned to compare two texts against a principle; it has learned that "A" is a likely answer to "A or B?". Larger judges are far better but share the same biases in milder form: position, length (longer looks better) and self-preference. Every RLAIF pipeline therefore uses strong judges, asks each question in both orders, and checks a sample of verdicts against human labels before training on them. Break it on purpose In the arithmetic reward, give full credit (1.0) to any answer that is a well-formed number, right or wrong, instead of 1.0 only for the correct one. What happens to the group advantages, and what would GRPO learn? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Written principles at scale. RL with verifiable rewards. Maths checkers (math-verify), unit-test harnesses and proof assistants supply rewards for GRPO-family training of reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3, Tülu 3's RLVR). LLM judges. Strong models as judges and generative reward models produce preference labels; swapping answer order, using several judges, and calibrating against human labels are standard checks for their biases. The 0.5B judge answers "A" for every pair regardless of content, so it is right on all six pairs when the better reply is shown first and wrong on all six when it is shown second. Asking twice with the order swapped is what exposes this: a judge whose verdict flips with the order carries no information about the replies. Solution B1 · The reward stops separating right from wrong Every sampled reply contains a number, so every reply now earns 1.0, plus 0.1 if it is wrapped in <answer> tags. Within a group the only differences left are the format bonus: tagged replies get positive advantages, untagged ones negative, regardless of whether the arithmetic is right. GRPO would learn to put answers in tags and nothing about arithmetic; and if all replies in a group happen to share the same format, every advantage is zero and the group teaches nothing at all. A reward has to separate what you want from what you do not; checking that the reward's spread within groups stays above zero, and that it correlates with real correctness on a held-out set, catches this before a long run.
