Time : about 90 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Goodhart's Law: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Every frontier lab games benchmarks. MMLU scores go up while models still can't reliably count the number of R's in "strawberry." The only eval that matters is YOUR eval -- on YOUR task, with YOUR data. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means MMLU "The benchmark" Massive Multitask Language Understanding -- 15,908 multiple choice questions across 57 subjects, saturated above 88% by 2025 HumanEval "Code eval" 164 Python function-completion problems from OpenAI, tests only isolated function generation SWE-bench "Real coding eval" 2,294 GitHub issues from 12 Python repos, measures end-to-end bug fixing including test generation Perplexity "How confused the model is" $\exp(-\mathop{\mathrm{avg}}(\log P(\text{token}_i \text{ given context})))$ -- lower means the model assigns higher probability to the actual tokens ELO rating "Chess ranking for models" A relative skill rating computed from pairwise win/loss records, used by Chatbot Arena to rank 100+ models LLM-as-judge "Using AI to grade AI" A strong model scores a weaker model's outputs against a rubric, ~80% agreement with human judges at ~$0.01/judgment Data contamination "The model saw the test" Training data includes benchmark questions, inflating scores without improving real capability Eval suite "A bunch of tests" A versioned collection of (input, expected_output, scorer) triples that measure a specific capability Pass rate "What percentage it gets right" Fraction of eval cases scoring above a threshold -- more actionable than mean score because it measures reliability Chatbot Arena "Model ranking website" LMSYS platform with 2M+ human preference votes, producing the most trusted LLM leaderboard via ELO ratings The problem In plain words first Evaluation decides which model you ship, so it has to measure what you care about. Public benchmarks (multiple-choice exams, coding puzzles) are cheap and comparable but leak into training data and saturate. Perplexity measures how well a model predicts ordinary text, a quick health check. Pairwise judgements by people or by a strong model, turned into Elo-style ratings, capture open-ended quality. And custom evals built from your own task are the only ones that predict production behaviour. This lesson runs the lesson's mock eval pipeline, then measures real perplexity for three small models with different tokenizers, and scores a real benchmark the way lm-evaluation-harness does, with confidence intervals. No model is trained. MMLU was published in 2020 with 15,908 questions across 57 subjects. Within three years, frontier models saturated it. GPT-4 scored 86.4%. Claude 3 Opus scored 86.8%. Llama 3 405B scored 88.6%. The leaderboard compressed into a 3-point range where differences are statistical noise, not real capability gaps. Meanwhile, those same models fail at tasks that a 10-year-old handles without thinking. Claude 3.5 Sonnet, scoring 88.7% on MMLU, initially could not count the letters in "strawberry" -- a task that requires zero world knowledge and zero reasoning, just character-level iteration. HumanEval tests code generation with 164 problems. Models score 90%+ on it while still producing code that crashes on edge cases any junior developer would catch. The gap between benchmark performance and real-world reliability is the central problem of LLM evaluation. Benchmarks tell you how a model performs on the benchmark. They tell you almost nothing about how that model will perform on your specific task, with your specific data, under your specific failure modes. If you are building a customer support bot, MMLU is irrelevant. If you are building a code assistant, HumanEval only covers function-level generation -- it says nothing about debugging, refactoring, or explaining code across files. You need custom evals. Not because benchmarks are useless -- they are useful for rough model selection -- but because the final evaluation must match your deployment conditions exactly. Idea 1 · The Eval Landscape There are three categories of evaluation, each with different cost and signal quality. Benchmarks are standardized test suites. MMLU, HumanEval, SWE-bench, MATH, ARC, HellaSwag. You run a model against the benchmark and get a score. The advantage: everyone uses the same test, so you can compare models. The disadvantage: models and training data increasingly contaminate these benchmarks. Labs train on data that includes benchmark questions. Scores go up. Capability may not. Custom evals are test suites you build for your specific use case. You define the inputs, the expected outputs, and the scoring function. A legal document summarizer gets evaluated on legal documents. A SQL generator gets evaluated on your database schema. These are expensive to create but they are the only evaluation that predicts production performance. Human evals use paid annotators to judge model outputs on criteria like helpfulness, correctness, fluency, and safety. The gold standard for open-ended tasks where automated scoring fails. Chatbot Arena has collected over 2 million human preference votes across 100+ models. The downside: cost ($0.10-$2.00 per judgment) and speed (hours to days). Idea 2 · Why Benchmarks Break Three mechanisms cause benchmark scores to stop reflecting real capability. Data contamination. Training corpora scrape the internet. Benchmark questions live on the internet. Models see the answers during training. This is not cheating in the traditional sense -- labs do not intentionally include benchmark data. But web-scale scraping makes it nearly impossible to exclude. Teaching to the test. Labs optimize training mixtures for benchmark performance. If 5% of the training mix is MMLU-style multiple choice, the model learns the format and the answer distribution. MMLU is 4-way multiple choice. Models learn that the answer distribution is approximately uniform across A/B/C/D, which helps even when the model does not know the answer. Saturation. When every frontier model scores 85-90% on a benchmark, the benchmark stops discriminating. The remaining 10-15% of questions may be ambiguous, mislabeled, or require obscure domain knowledge. Improving from 87% to 89% on MMLU may mean the model memorized two more obscure questions, not that it got smarter. Idea 3 · Perplexity: A Quick Health Check Perplexity measures how surprised a model is by a sequence of tokens. Formally, it is the exponentiated average negative log-likelihood: 1 ​ i ∑ ​ lo g P ( token i ​ ∣ context ) ) A perplexity of 10 means the model is, on average, as uncertain as choosing uniformly among 10 options at each token position. Lower is better. In the GPT-2 paper, the smallest GPT-2 scored 37.5 on WikiText-103 and the 1.5B model 17.5 (zero-shot). Perplexities computed with different tokenizers are not directly comparable, because the "options" are different-sized pieces; bits per byte is the fair cross-model unit (the run under Use it). Perplexity is useful for comparing models on the same test set, but it has blind spots. A model can have low perplexity by being good at predicting common patterns while being terrible at rare but important patterns. It also says nothing about instruction following, reasoning, or factual accuracy. Use it as a sanity check, not a final verdict. Idea 4 · LLM-as-Judge Use a strong model to evaluate a weaker model's output. The idea is simple: ask GPT-4o or Claude Sonnet to rate a response on a 1-5 scale for correctness, helpfulness, and safety. This costs a fraction of a cent to a few cents per judgment, and in the MT-Bench study GPT-4 as judge agreed with human experts about as often as the experts agreed with each other (over 80% when ties are excluded). The scoring prompt matters more than the model. A vague prompt ("Rate this response") produces noisy scores. A structured prompt with a rubric ("Score 5 if the answer is factually correct and cites a source, 4 if correct but unsourced, 3 if partially correct...") produces consistent, reproducible scores. Failure modes: judge models exhibit position bias (prefer the first response in pairwise comparisons), verbosity bias (prefer longer responses), and self-preference (GPT-4 rates GPT-4 outputs higher than equivalent Claude outputs). Mitigations: randomize order, normalize for length, use a different judge than the model being evaluated. Idea 5 · ELO Ratings from Pairwise Comparisons Chatbot Arena's approach. Show two responses to the same prompt from different models. A human (or LLM judge) picks the better one. From thousands of these comparisons, compute an ELO rating for each model -- the same system used in chess. ELO advantages: relative ranking is more reliable than absolute scoring, handles ties gracefully, and converges with fewer comparisons than scoring every output independently. Chatbot Arena (now LMArena) fits a Bradley–Terry model to all votes at once rather than updating Elo one game at a time, and reports confidence intervals; the top models change every few months and often overlap within those intervals. Idea 6 · Eval Frameworks lm-evaluation-harness (EleutherAI): the standard open-source eval framework. Supports 200+ benchmarks. Run any Hugging Face model against MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC, etc. with one command. Used by the Open LLM Leaderboard. RAGAS : evaluation framework specifically for RAG pipelines. Measures faithfulness (does the answer match the retrieved context?), relevance (is the retrieved context relevant to the question?), and answer correctness. promptfoo : config-driven eval for prompt engineering. Define test cases in YAML, run against multiple models, get a pass/fail report. Useful for regression testing prompts -- make sure a prompt change does not break existing test cases. Idea 7 · Building Custom Evals The only eval that matters for production. The process: Define the task. What exactly should the model do? Be precise. "Answer questions" is too vague. "Given a customer complaint email, extract the product name, issue category, and sentiment" is a task you can evaluate. Create test cases. Minimum 50 for a prototype eval, 200+ for production. Each test case is an (input, expected_output) pair. Include edge cases: empty inputs, adversarial inputs, ambiguous inputs, inputs in other languages. Define scoring. Exact match for structured outputs. BLEU/ROUGE for text similarity. LLM-as-judge for open-ended quality. F1 for extraction tasks. Combine multiple metrics with weights. Automate. Every eval runs with one command. No manual steps. Store results in a format that enables comparison over time. Track over time. An eval score is meaningless in isolation. You need the trendline. Did the score improve after the last prompt change? Did it regress after switching models? Version your eval alongside your prompts. Solutions Solution P1 · Higher Higher: 25.7 for the instruct model against 22.6 for the base on the same WikiText text (1.10 against 1.05 bits per byte). Post-training moves probability mass toward the assistant's way of writing (answers, lists, chat markers) and away from continuing encyclopaedia prose. That is the intended trade: a lower raw-text perplexity is not the goal of an assistant model, and a small rise is normal. A large rise would be a warning sign of forgetting. Solution B1 · Different tokens, different units Perplexity is "average uncertainty per token", and the two models use different tokens: SmolLM2 splits the text into 4,690 pieces and GPT-2 into 4,503 of different sizes, so a perplexity of 22.6 and one of 39.5 are not measured in the same unit, and "twice as good" has no meaning. Compare total information instead: bits per byte (or per character, or per word) divides the total negative log-likelihood by a quantity that does not depend on the tokenizer. Here that gives 1.05 against 1.19, a 12% advantage for SmolLM2. Ratios of perplexities across tokenizers can exaggerate or hide differences in either direction. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Defend a design A model you fine tuned jumped eight points on a public benchmark after you added a new web scraped corpus to the training mix. Leadership wants to announce it. Design the audit that tells you whether the jump is capability or leakage, and say what you would publish instead if it is leakage. Level 4 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Audit for contamination before anyone announces anything. Search the new corpus for the benchmark questions and their close paraphrases and report the share found, then rerun the model on a versioned custom eval that the corpus cannot contain and diff the individual test cases against the previous model. If the overlap is material and the custom eval did not move, the jump is memorization, and you publish the custom eval result with the contamination share. Why the jump is suspect. Training corpora scrape the web and the benchmark questions live on the web. Nobody has to intend it. A new scraped corpus is the most likely path for the test to enter training, and a saturated benchmark rewards memorization with large jumps. The same lesson lists teaching to the test and saturation as the other two mechanisms that move a score without moving capability. The audit. Contamination search. Check what share of the eval questions, or close paraphrases of them, appear in the new corpus. Report exact matches and near matches separately with the method. Model diff. Compare the two model versions case by case: which items improved, which regressed, which stayed. If the improvements cluster on the items the search found, the diff names the leak. Custom eval. Run both models on your own versioned suite of at least 200 cases with edge cases, kept separate from every training and prompt example. A real gain shows there with an interval; a leak does not. Separation check. Confirm that no eval case overlaps with the prompt examples or the fine tuning data, because a test case that was also a training example measures memorization. What to publish. The custom eval numbers with intervals, the contamination share and the method, and the benchmark score with that caveat attached. Never a bare benchmark number. And add the dedup step to the training pipeline so the next corpus is checked against every eval set before training starts. Plausible wrong answers. "We did not include the benchmark on purpose, so it is clean." Web scale scraping includes it without intent; the lesson calls this the normal path to contamination. "Eight points is too large to be noise." Noise is not the alternative; memorization is, and it produces large jumps. "Announce the benchmark and add the caveat later." Publish the custom eval with intervals and the contamination share; a bare benchmark number is the claim you cannot defend. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) The search finds exact matches for a small share and paraphrases for more. Which count? Expected: both; paraphrases leak the answer as well, so report exact and near matches separately with the method. (level 3) The custom eval also rose. Is the jump real? Expected: more likely, if the suite is versioned, separate from training data and large enough that the rise exceeds its interval. (level 4) How do you prevent the question next time? Expected: deduplicate training corpora against every eval set before training, keep eval data out of prompts and fine tuning data, and record the check in the training report. Where it is taught. The evaluation lesson explains contamination and sets the contamination detection and model diff exercises, and the evaluation and testing lesson warns against testing on training examples. Explain the mechanism A vendor shows you that their new model scores 89 percent on a public multiple choice benchmark and the model you run today scores 87. They say the gap proves the new model is smarter. Why are you not convinced, and what do you ask for instead? Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Public benchmarks stop telling models apart once every frontier model sits in a narrow band near the top. Three mechanisms cause this: training data that contains the test, training mixes tuned to the test format, and saturation, where the questions that remain are ambiguous or mislabeled. A gap of two points in that band is noise or memorization. Ask for a run on your task with your data. The compression. The benchmark in the lesson has 15,908 questions across 57 subjects. Within three years the frontier models compressed into a 3-point range at the top. A model that scored 88.7 percent on it could not count the letters in a short word, a task that needs no world knowledge. The score measures the benchmark, not the job. Three mechanisms. Data contamination. Training corpora scrape the web, and the questions live on the web. Nobody has to cheat for the answers to end up in training. Teaching to the test. Labs tune the training mix toward the format. On a 4-way multiple choice test, a model that learns the answer distribution gains points without knowing the answers. Saturation. When every model scores 85 to 90 percent, the remaining 10 to 15 percent of questions are often ambiguous, mislabeled or obscure. Moving from 87 to 89 can mean two more memorized questions. What to ask for. A custom eval on your task: at least 50 cases for a prototype and 200 or more for a production decision, with edge cases and adversarial inputs. Per-category results, not one aggregate. A contamination check: search the training corpus for the eval questions and close paraphrases. Benchmarks still help with rough model selection. The final decision needs your eval. Plausible wrong answers. "Two points on a standard benchmark is a real gap." At the top of a saturated benchmark the remaining questions are often ambiguous or obscure, so two points can be two memorized questions. "Labs cheat by training on the test." Web scale scraping pulls the questions in without intent; the effect is the same, and the fix is a contamination audit, not an accusation. "Use the coding benchmark instead." A function completion benchmark with 164 problems covers isolated function generation and says nothing about debugging or refactoring across files. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Name the three categories of evaluation. Expected: public benchmarks, custom evals on your own data, and human evals. (level 2) A model does not know an answer. How does the test format still help it? Expected: the test has four options with a near uniform answer distribution, so format knowledge alone raises the score. (level 2) What are benchmarks still good for? Expected: rough model selection before you build a custom eval. (level 3) How would you test whether a benchmark leaked into training? Expected: search the training corpus for the eval questions and close paraphrases, and report the share that appears. Where it is taught. The evaluation lesson in the LLMs from scratch phase explains contamination, teaching to the test and saturation. Debug a failure A faithfulness dashboard reports a mean of 0.85 over a thousand cases, above the 0.8 release threshold. Support tickets say the assistant invents policy details in some answers. The eval owner says the metric is green. Where do you look, and what do you change in the report? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A mean hides the tail. A mean of 0.85 is consistent with a 5 percent slice of catastrophic failures, and that slice is what becomes tickets. Sort the cases by score and read the lowest 10 percent. Then add a pass rate at a threshold and a bottom quantile alert to the report, next to the mean. Why the dashboard is green. Most cases score high while a small slice scores near zero. The average barely moves, because the slice is small. The users in that slice get an invented policy, and no average tells them it was rare. What to report. Pass rate. The fraction of cases above a threshold. It measures reliability, which is what users feel, so it is more actionable than the mean. Bottom quantile. The lesson refuses aggregate only reporting without the lowest 10 percent surfaced. Read those cases by hand every run. Per-category scores. If the tail comes from one category, the fix is local and the gate should watch that category. How to debug it. Pull the lowest scoring cases and read them. Confirm they match the tickets. Check how missing scores were counted. A judge that returned bad JSON produces a missing score, and dropping missing scores raises the mean. Check that the judge was calibrated at the low end. A hand labeled set made of easy cases says nothing about the tail. Plausible wrong answers. "The mean passed, so the release passed." A mean of 0.85 often hides a 5 percent catastrophic slice; the gate needs the tail. "Raise the mean threshold to 0.9." A higher mean threshold still hides a small slice of zeros; add a distribution measure. "The judge is noisy at the bottom, so ignore those cases." That is where the failures live; calibrate the judge on low scoring cases too. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does the lesson prefer the share of cases above a cutoff to the mean? Expected: it counts how many cases are good enough, so it measures reliability. (level 2) The lowest cases all come from one category. What changes? Expected: the fix is local; report per-category scores and gate on the weakest category, not the aggregate. (level 3) Missing scores from parse failures were dropped before averaging. What did that do? Expected: it raised the mean, because the worst outputs often fail to parse; count them as failures or report them separately. (level 3) Which alert do you add to the release gate? Expected: a floor on the lowest 10 percent and a pass rate threshold, both next to the mean. Where it is taught. The LLM evaluation frameworks lesson lists the raw aggregate pitfall and the bottom quantile rule, and the evaluation lesson defines pass rate as the more actionable summary. Explain the mechanism A colleague reports that the new checkpoint reaches a perplexity of 10 on the held out text, better than last week, and wants to ship it as the stronger model. What does the number mean, and what does it not tell you? Level 1 of 4 · about 5 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Perplexity is the exponential of the mean negative log likelihood per token. A value of 10 means that at each position the model is as uncertain as a uniform choice among 10 options. Lower is better only while the test set and the tokenizer stay fixed. It says nothing about instruction following, reasoning or factual accuracy, so treat it as a sanity check and run the task evals before you ship. The definition. Copy A perplexity of one means the model assigns probability one to every real token. A perplexity equal to the vocabulary size means the model is uniform and learnt nothing. A strong base model on a standard corpus sits around eight to twelve; a bad one on the same text sits at fifty plus. What it misses. A model can reach low perplexity by predicting common patterns well while it is bad at rare but important ones. The number also ignores everything a chat model is for: following instructions, reasoning and being right. Use it to catch a broken checkpoint or a tokenizer mismatch, not to pick a winner. Two checks before you trust it. Same text, same tokenizer. The number depends on both. Two models measured on different held out sets cannot be compared. Honest counting. Sum the loss over real token positions and divide once at the end. Pad positions must not be in the denominator, and the logits at one position predict the next token. A value below one is impossible. It means the summed negative log likelihood came out negative, and the usual cause is an adapter that returned log p instead of negative log p. Plausible wrong answers. "Lower perplexity means a better assistant." It measures fit to the text distribution, not instruction following or correctness. "Perplexities from two papers are comparable." They depend on the test set and the tokenizer, so only same set comparisons hold. "Aim for a perplexity near one." The held out text is not the model's own output; a value near one would suggest the test text was in the training data. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Which perplexity value means the model is never surprised? Expected: one, because every real token then has probability one. (level 2) Two models were measured on different test sets. Can you compare their perplexities? Expected: no; the number depends on the text and the tokenizer, so measure both on the same set. (level 2) The adapter reports a perplexity of 0.8. What happened? Expected: the summed loss is negative, most likely because the adapter returned log p instead of negative log p; a perplexity below one is impossible, so the contract was violated. (level 3) Why does the eval sum the loss over non pad positions and divide at the end instead of averaging per batch perplexities? Expected: averaging per batch gives each token of a short batch more weight than each token of a long batch, and pad positions shrink the loss; the sum over real tokens matches the definition. Where it is taught. The evaluation lesson presents perplexity as a quick health check, and the perplexity and calibration capstone gives the corpus level computation and its contract. Weigh a trade-off Your product generates answers with one model, and your eval pipeline grades them using that same model plus a rubric. Scores rose after the last release and the team is pleased. A reviewer asks why the gain might not be real. What is the risk, and what do you change? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A model that grades its own family prefers its own style, so self evaluation inflates scores by about 10 to 20 percent. The rise can mean the judge likes the new outputs more, not that users do. Move the judge to a different model family, calibrate it against human labels, and score the baseline and the new version again under that judge. Where the bias comes from. A judge is a model with preferences. It favors longer answers, answers from its own model family and answers that match the prompt style. When the judge comes from the generator's own family, every release that moves the output toward the judge's taste looks like an improvement. The lesson calls this self preference and measures the inflation at about 10 to 20 percent. Why the release looked better. A release changes tone, length and structure as well as content. The judge rewards the first three. Without a separate signal you cannot tell which part of the gain is content. What to change. Pick a judge from a different model family. Use the cheapest model that still meets the calibration threshold. Calibrate it: hand label at least 50 cases, the lesson uses 100, and require a Spearman correlation of 0.7 or more with the human ranking. Score the old and the new release under the same judge and report the difference, not the absolute score. Normalize for length, or state in the rubric that length does not count. Plausible wrong answers. "The judge has a rubric, so its family does not matter." The rubric does not remove the preference for its own style; the lesson measures a 10 to 20 percent inflation. "Use the strongest model we have as the judge, which is the one we ship." Strength does not remove self preference; a different family at similar strength is the fix. "Scores went up, so quality went up." The score is a proxy; the output may have moved toward what the judge rewards, such as length and tone. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Which two other judge biases does the lesson name next to self preference? Expected: position bias in pairwise comparison and verbosity bias toward longer answers. (level 2) The judge from another family is cheaper but correlates less with people. Which one do you take? Expected: the cheapest judge that still meets the calibration threshold; below the threshold the number is noise whatever the family. (level 3) You cannot change the judge family this quarter. What limits the damage? Expected: calibrate against human labels and publish the correlation, normalize for length, and read only relative changes under the frozen judge. (level 3) After the switch, how do you tell a real gain from a judge preference? Expected: both versions scored by the new judge, the difference with a confidence interval, and a human labeled slice of the cases that moved most. Where it is taught. The LLM evaluation frameworks lesson lists self evaluation as a pitfall, and the evaluation lesson names self preference among the judge failure modes. Sources and further reading Hendrycks et al., 2021 -- "Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding" -- the MMLU paper, still the most cited LLM benchmark despite its saturation Chen et al., 2021 -- "Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code" -- the HumanEval paper from OpenAI, established code generation evaluation methodology Zheng et al., 2023 -- "Judging LLM-as-a-Judge" -- systematic analysis of using LLMs to evaluate LLMs, including position bias and verbosity bias findings Arena (formerly LMSYS Chatbot Arena) -- crowdsourced model comparison platform with 2M+ votes, the most trusted real-world LLM ranking Check your understanding Q1 Why have benchmarks like MMLU become less useful for comparing frontier models? A They test the wrong subjects B MMLU was designed for smaller models C Frontier models have saturated MMLU (scoring 86-89%), compressing the leaderboard to a range where differences are statistical noise D The questions are too easy When GPT-4, Claude 3, and Llama 3 all score 86-89% on MMLU, a 1-point difference is not meaningful. The benchmark no longer discriminates between models, yet it still dominates leaderboard culture. Q2 What is Goodhart's Law in the context of LLM evaluation? A When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure -- models and teams optimize for benchmarks instead of real capabilities B A law about model scaling C A theorem about attention mechanisms D A rule about learning rate schedules Labs optimize for benchmark scores (data contamination, benchmark-specific prompting). The score goes up, but real-world capability doesn't necessarily improve. Your own task-specific eval is the only reliable measure. Q3 What is the LLM-as-judge evaluation approach? A Having a human judge evaluate every response B Using a strong LLM (e.g., GPT-4) to score responses against rubrics, replacing expensive human evaluation at scale C Training a separate classifier for evaluation D Using the model to evaluate itself LLM-as-judge uses a capable model to score responses against defined criteria. It's cheaper and faster than human evaluation, though it has biases (e.g., preferring verbose responses) that must be calibrated. Q4 Why is building a custom evaluation suite important rather than relying on public benchmarks? A Public benchmarks are always wrong B Custom evals are easier to build C Public benchmarks are too expensive D Public benchmarks test general capabilities; your application has specific requirements that only a custom eval can measure A model scoring 90% on MMLU might fail on your specific task (e.g., extracting dates from legal documents in your format). Only a custom eval with your data, your edge cases, and your success criteria measures what matters. Q5 What is data contamination in the context of LLM benchmarks? A When training data is corrupted B When benchmark questions appear in the model's pre-training data, inflating scores without reflecting true capability C When evaluation data is mislabeled D When the model generates incorrect data If MMLU questions appeared in the training corpus, the model memorized the answers rather than reasoning about them. This inflates scores and makes benchmark comparisons unreliable. It's a growing problem as training corpora expand. Time : about 120 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line A 70B model in FP16 needs 140GB. Two A100s just for weights. Quantize to FP8: one 80GB GPU. INT4: a MacBook. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means FP16 "Half precision" 16-bit float with 5 exponent bits and 10 mantissa bits, max value 65,504, standard inference format BF16 "Brain float" 16-bit float with 8 exponent bits (same range as FP32) and 7 mantissa bits, designed by Google for training FP8 "Eight-bit float" Two variants: E4M3 (inference, more precision) and E5M2 (training, more range), native on H100 INT8 "Eight-bit integer" 256 uniformly spaced values from -128 to 127, needs a scale factor to map from floats INT4 "Four-bit integer" 16 levels total, requires sophisticated methods (GPTQ, AWQ) to maintain quality Per-channel quantization "One scale per row" Uses a separate scale factor for each output channel instead of one for the whole tensor, dramatically reduces error GPTQ "The Hessian method" Post-training quantization using second-order information to minimize output error, one layer at a time AWQ "Activation-aware" Scales salient weights (those multiplied by large activations) before quantization to protect them GGUF "The llama.cpp format" Self-contained model file with mixed-precision layers, optimized for CPU and Apple Silicon inference PTQ "Quantize after training" Convert a trained model's weights to lower precision without retraining, fast but limited at extreme compression QAT "Quantize during training" Insert fake quantization into the forward pass so the model learns to tolerate rounding, better at INT4/INT2 Calibration data "The 128 examples" A small dataset run through the model to compute activation statistics for setting scale factors Scale factor "The multiplier" Converts between floating-point range and integer range: float_val = int_val * scale Perplexity delta "How much worse" Difference in perplexity between original and quantized model, < 0.5 is excellent, > 2.0 is a problem The problem In plain words first A model's weights are stored as 16-bit numbers, so a 70-billion-parameter model needs 140 GB just to load. Quantization stores them with fewer bits, 8 or 4 instead of 16, by sharing one scale factor among a group of weights and keeping only a small integer per weight. That cuts memory two to four times and speeds up generation, which is limited by how fast weights can be read. The price is rounding error, and how much it hurts depends on the number of bits, on how finely the scales are shared, and on a few unusually large values that every model has. This lesson runs the lesson's simulations, looks at exactly what each number format can represent, and quantizes a real 135M-parameter model to 8, 4 and 3 bits, measuring the damage by perplexity. No model is trained. Llama 3 70B has 70 billion parameters. Each parameter is a 16-bit floating point number. That is 140 billion bytes. 140GB. A single A100 has 80GB of VRAM. You cannot even load the weights, let alone run inference, on a single GPU. You need two A100s at $2/hour each just to serve one model. But 16 bits per parameter is wasteful. Most weights in a neural network cluster near zero. The full dynamic range of FP16 (from 0.000000059 to 65,504) is almost entirely unused. Weights are concentrated near zero with a few much larger outliers (in SmolLM2-135M, the run under Use it, the largest weight is about 9 while half are below 0.1 in magnitude), and a well-chosen 4- or 8-bit code with a shared scale captures most of that information. Quantization replaces high-precision numbers with lower-precision ones. FP16 to FP8 cuts memory in half. FP16 to INT4 cuts it to a quarter. That 140GB model becomes 35GB. It fits on a single consumer GPU. Push to 2-bit quantization (aggressive, lossy, but usable for some tasks) and the same model runs on a 16GB laptop. The cost is accuracy. Every bit you remove destroys information. The question is how much accuracy you lose and where. A well-quantized INT4 model retains 95-99% of the original's quality on most benchmarks. A naive quantization to INT4 can destroy the model entirely. The difference is technique. Llama 3 turned out to be more sensitive to low-bit quantization than Llama 2 (Huang et al., 2024), a sign that models trained on more tokens pack more information into each weight. FP8 inference is routine on H100-class GPUs, and the GGUF format powers llama.cpp, running 70B models on MacBooks with M-series chips. Quantization is not a hack. It is a standard deployment path. Idea 1 · Number Formats: What Each Bit Does Every floating-point number has three parts: sign, exponent, and mantissa (also called significand). The sign is one bit. The exponent determines the range (how large or small the number can be). The mantissa determines the precision (how many decimal places you get). Copy FP32 is full precision. 23 mantissa bits give you about 7 decimal digits of precision. Range: roughly to . Training used to happen exclusively in FP32. It still does for accumulation (running sums during matrix multiplication). FP16 halves the bits. 10 mantissa bits give about 3.3 decimal digits. The exponent shrinks to 5 bits, reducing the range dramatically (max value ~65,504). This is fine for weights (which cluster near zero) but dangerous for activations and gradients that can spike during training. FP16 training requires loss scaling to prevent underflow. BF16 (Brain Float 16) keeps the 8-bit exponent from FP32 but shrinks the mantissa to 7 bits. Same range as FP32, less precision than FP16. Google designed it specifically for deep learning. The intuition: range matters more than precision for neural networks. A gradient of that underflows to zero in FP16 survives in BF16. A weight of 0.07342 that rounds to 0.0732 in BF16 is close enough. Every modern training run uses BF16 or a BF16/FP32 mix. FP8 comes in two flavors. E4M3 (4 exponent, 3 mantissa) is used for weights and activations during inference. E5M2 (5 exponent, 2 mantissa) is used for gradients during training where range matters more than precision. FP8 inference on H100 GPUs achieves 30-50% speedup over FP16 with negligible quality loss. INT8 is an integer format. No exponent, no mantissa. Just 256 evenly spaced values from -128 to 127. You need a scale factor to map floating-point weights into this range. The advantage: integer arithmetic is faster and more power-efficient than floating-point. INT8 matrix multiplication on an A100 runs at 624 TOPS versus 312 TFLOPS for FP16. INT4 pushes further. Only 16 possible values. The scale factor does heavy lifting. Quality depends entirely on how you choose the scale and which weights you quantize. State-of-the-art INT4 methods (GPTQ, AWQ) retain 95%+ of original model quality. Idea 2 · How Quantization Works The core operation is simple. Take a tensor of floating-point values, find a scale factor, multiply, round to the nearest integer, and store the integers plus the scale factor. Quantize: Copy Dequantize: Copy For INT8 with a symmetric range (-127 to 127): Copy The error is the rounding error. Each value can be off by at most scale / 2 . The total error across a layer depends on how many weights you have and how sensitive the model is to perturbations in those weights. Per-tensor vs per-channel quantization. Per-tensor uses one scale factor for the entire weight matrix. Simple but lossy: if one column has large values and another has small values, the small values lose most of their precision. Per-channel uses one scale factor per output channel (per row or column of the weight matrix). More overhead (you store N scale factors instead of 1) but dramatically better quality. Every production quantization method uses per-channel or finer granularity. Asymmetric quantization adds a zero-point offset: quantized = round(tensor / scale) + zero_point . This handles distributions that are not centered at zero. ReLU activations, for example, are always non-negative. Symmetric quantization wastes half the integer range on negative values that never appear. Asymmetric quantization maps the actual range [min, max] to the full integer range. Idea 3 · Sensitivity Hierarchy Not everything in a model tolerates quantization equally. There is a clear hierarchy. Weights (most robust). Model weights change slowly during training and follow a roughly Gaussian distribution centered near zero. They quantize well. INT8 weights with per-channel scales produce nearly lossless results. INT4 requires more sophisticated methods but works. Activations (moderate sensitivity). Activations are the intermediate values flowing through the network during inference. They have wider dynamic range than weights and contain outliers. A single attention head might produce activation values 100x larger than the mean. These outliers are critical for model quality. Quantizing them naively destroys information. Solutions: keep outlier channels in higher precision (LLM.int8()), use per-token or per-channel activation scales. KV cache (high sensitivity). The key-value cache stores attention states for all previous tokens. At long context lengths, the KV cache dominates memory. For Llama 3 70B at 32K context, the KV cache is about 10 GB in FP16 even with grouped-query attention, and would be about 86 GB without it. Quantizing the KV cache to FP8 or INT8 saves massive memory but any error compounds across all future attention computations. The quality impact scales with sequence length. Attention logits (most sensitive). The softmax in attention is highly sensitive to small changes in its inputs. A quantization error of 0.01 in a pre-softmax logit can shift the attention distribution meaningfully. Most quantization schemes keep attention computation in higher precision (FP16 or BF16) even when everything else is quantized. Idea 4 · PTQ vs QAT Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) quantizes an already-trained model. No retraining. You take the FP16 weights, compute scale factors, round, and deploy. Fast (minutes to hours) and cheap. Works well for INT8 and FP8. For INT4, naive PTQ often fails badly because rounding errors accumulate. Advanced PTQ methods (GPTQ, AWQ) use calibration data to minimize the quantization error. Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) inserts fake quantization operations into the forward pass during training. The model learns to place its weights where rounding errors are small. Gradients flow through the fake quantization using the straight-through estimator (STE): pretend the rounding operation has gradient 1. QAT produces better INT4 and INT2 models than PTQ but requires a full training run. Google released QAT versions of Gemma 3 for 4-bit deployment, and Meta used QAT with LoRA for its quantized Llama 3.2 1B and 3B models. Aspect PTQ QAT Cost Minutes to hours Full training run Quality at INT8 Excellent (< 0.1% loss) Excellent Quality at INT4 Good with GPTQ/AWQ (1-3% loss) Better (< 1% loss) Quality at INT2 Poor Usable for some tasks Calibration data 128-1024 examples Full training dataset When to use Deployment, iteration Maximum quality at low bit-width Idea 5 · GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF GPTQ (GPT Quantization) is a one-shot PTQ method. It quantizes weights one layer at a time, using a small calibration dataset (128 examples is typical) to measure the Hessian (second-order information about how sensitive the output is to each weight). Weights that the Hessian says are important get quantized more carefully. GPTQ was the first method to make INT4 quantization practical for LLMs. The TheBloke on Hugging Face popularized GPTQ by releasing quantized versions of hundreds of models. AWQ (Activation-Aware Weight Quantization) observes that a small fraction of weights (about 1%) are disproportionately important because they multiply with large activation values. AWQ identifies these salient weights using calibration data and scales them up before quantization (then scales the corresponding activations down). This keeps the important weights in a range where INT4 quantization is accurate. AWQ typically matches or slightly beats GPTQ quality and needs no weight reconstruction, only a per-channel rescaling. GGUF (GPT-Generated Unified Format) is the file format used by llama.cpp and its ecosystem. It supports mixed quantization: different layers get different bit widths. The first and last layers (embedding and output head) are typically kept at higher precision. Middle layers get INT4 or INT3. GGUF files are self-contained: weights, tokenizer, metadata all in one file. The format is designed for CPU inference and Apple Silicon, where loading the entire model into memory and running matrix multiplications on the CPU or Metal GPU is the standard path. Q4_K_M is the most popular GGUF quantization variant, balancing quality and size. Idea 6 · Quality Measurement How do you know if your quantized model is still good? Perplexity. The most common metric. Lower is better. Compute perplexity on a held-out dataset (WikiText-2 is standard) for both the original and quantized model. The delta tells you how much information the quantization destroyed. Rules of thumb: delta < 0.5 is excellent, 0.5-1.0 is good, 1.0-2.0 is acceptable for most tasks, > 2.0 means something went wrong. Task-specific benchmarks. Run the quantized model on MMLU, HumanEval, GSM8K, or your custom eval suite. Compare against the original. Quantization affects different capabilities unevenly. Math and code tasks are more sensitive to precision loss than general knowledge. Output comparison. Generate responses from both models on the same prompts and compare. LLM-as-judge ( Lesson 10.10 ) works well here. Compute a win rate: what fraction of prompts does the quantized model match or beat the original on? Latency and throughput. Quantization exists to make models faster and cheaper. Measure tokens per second, time to first token, and memory usage. A quantized model that is slower than the original is worse than useless. INT4 costs 1-2 MMLU points but doubles throughput and quarters memory. The tradeoff is worth it for almost every deployment. Idea 7 · Real Numbers FP16 to FP8 on H100: 30-50% inference speedup, < 0.1% quality loss. This is the no-brainer quantization. Every H100 deployment should use it. FP16 to INT8 (LLM.int8()): 2x memory reduction, < 0.5% quality loss. The mixed-precision approach keeps outlier features in FP16 while quantizing everything else to INT8. FP16 to INT4 (GPTQ/AWQ): 4x memory reduction, 1-3% quality loss depending on the model and method. Enables 70B models on a single 48GB GPU. FP16 to INT4 (GGUF Q4_K_M): 3.5x memory reduction, 1-2% quality loss. Optimized for CPU inference. A 70B model at Q4_K_M is about 40GB; on an M3 Max with 64GB it generates under 10 tokens/second, because reading 40 GB per token at 400 GB/s caps it near 10. FP16 to INT2: 8x memory reduction, 5-15% quality loss. Only viable for specific narrow tasks where you can tolerate degradation. Research frontier, not production-ready for general use. With 4 bits there are only 16 levels, and the per-row scale is set by the largest weight in the row. SmolLM2's weights have heavy tails (the largest is about 9 while half are below 0.1), so in a row with one large weight most of the others fall into the zero code or the levels next to it. Smaller groups (64 or 32 weights, each with its own scale) bring the perplexity down to about 27–28, and calibration methods like GPTQ and AWQ go further. Solution B1 · The outliers are clipped With the mean instead of the maximum, the largest representable value becomes the row's mean magnitude, so every weight larger than the mean is clipped to ±7 steps: in SmolLM2's first layer that is 36% of all weights, including every outlier. Typical weights do get finer steps, but the clipped ones lose most of their value. Applied to all linear layers of SmolLM2-135M this sends the WikiText-2 perplexity from 20.6 to about 33 million: the model is destroyed. Outliers carry a disproportionate share of a model's function, which is why practical methods keep the maximum (or a carefully searched clipping value, as GPTQ and AWQ do) and handle outliers explicitly rather than cutting them off. Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Pick a published 4-bit checkpoint over quantization at load time, and pick the format from the engine and the workload. For a GPU server AWQ with the Marlin kernels is the default, GPTQ when you also serve LoRA adapters on the base, and GGUF only for CPU or edge serving, because its kernels are not built for GPUs. The manual started an AWQ Qwen3-14B on an L4 with 9.44 GiB of weights and a pool of 36,272 tokens, loaded Qwen3-1.7B with bitsandbytes in 1.33 GiB against 3.22 GiB in BF16, which is 41 percent, and loaded a GGUF file of 0.55 GiB through a plugin that the documentation calls experimental. The weights took 9.44 GiB and the pool held 36,272 tokens. Speed and accuracy were not measured. bitsandbytes. Without the plugin, the server stopped with Unknown quantization method: bitsandbytes . With it, Qwen3-1.7B loaded in 1.33 GiB against 3.22 GiB in BF16, which is 41 percent, and the pool grew from 92,960 to 108,512 tokens. The 41 percent includes the embeddings and the output layer, which stay in 16-bit, so the share differs on a larger model. GGUF. With the plugin, a 4-bit file of Qwen3-0.6B loaded 0.55 GiB of weights and a chat request returned HTTP 200. The second GPU of the node was throttled during these starts, so the manual gives no speeds, and it measured no accuracy for either small format. The lesson's picking guide. CPU or edge serving: GGUF, with the medium 4-bit variant as the production default. GGUF is a file format that bundles several quantization variants, keeps the first and last layers at higher precision, and runs best in llama.cpp, the fastest CPU engine. In vLLM it is slow, about 93 tokens per second on a 7B model in the lesson's numbers, because the format is not built for GPU kernels. GPU serving with routine chat and no adapters: AWQ. It protects the most salient weights during quantization; with the Marlin kernels it gave about 741 tokens per second on a 7B model, the best code accuracy among the 4-bit formats, and a 10.9 times speedup over a naive kernel. GPU serving with many LoRA adapters on one base: GPTQ with Marlin, about 712 tokens per second on a 7B model and 2.6 times faster than without Marlin, because it supports LoRA in vLLM and the microscaling 4-bit formats did not at the start of 2026. Reasoning-heavy work: FP8, and accept the memory cost; the lesson puts the AWQ loss on math at several points. Two traps. The calibration set must match the domain: AWQ and GPTQ pick the weights to protect from a calibration pass, and generic web text makes them protect the wrong weights for code, medical or legal traffic. Calibrate on hundreds of in-domain samples and test on the eval set. And the KV cache is separate from the weights: a 70B model at 4-bit is about 35 GB of weights, and at 128 concurrent requests with a 2k context its cache is near 20 GB on top. The accuracy caveat. A 4-bit model can lose more accuracy than an FP8 model, and the loss depends on the model and the method. The manual ran its GSM8K check on FP8 and not on the 4-bit formats. Test the candidate formats on your own prompts, and when it is ambiguous run a 1,000-sample eval on each. Plausible wrong answers. "GGUF is the most popular format, so use it on the GPU server." It is the CPU and edge default; in vLLM it needs an experimental plugin, and its kernels are not built for GPUs, about 93 tokens per second on a 7B model in the lesson's numbers. "Quantize at load time with bitsandbytes, it is one flag." Without the plugin the server stops with an unknown method error, and the result is a checkpoint that nobody evaluated; use a published AWQ or GPTQ checkpoint and test it. "4-bit loses as little as FP8." A 4-bit model can lose more, and the loss depends on the model and the method; AWQ loses several points on math in the lesson, so run your own check. "The memory saving is 41 percent for any model." The measured 41 percent is one small model with its embeddings and output layer in 16-bit; the share differs on a larger model, and the KV cache is separate from the weights. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why pick a published checkpoint over bitsandbytes at load time? Expected: load-time quantization adds load time and gives a checkpoint that nobody evaluated; a published checkpoint has a known method and often a published accuracy, and vLLM reads the method from its config with no flag. (level 3) The bitsandbytes load saved 41 percent on a 1.7B model. Will a 14B model save the same share? Expected: not the same; the 41 percent includes the embeddings and the output layer, which stay in 16-bit, and they are a smaller share of a larger model, so the saving changes. (level 3) You need LoRA adapters on the 4-bit base. Which format? Expected: GPTQ with the Marlin kernels, because it supports LoRA adapters in vLLM; the microscaling 4-bit formats did not support LoRA at the start of 2026. (level 4) A domain model quantized with AWQ on generic web text loses several points on its own eval. Why, and what do you do? Expected: AWQ picks the weights to protect from a calibration set, and generic text makes it protect the wrong ones for the domain; calibrate on hundreds of in-domain samples and test on the eval set before you ship. Where it is taught. Fit a bigger model with FP8 weights lists the formats and the three starts, and the production quantization lesson and the quantization lesson give the picking guide. A 70 GB B 140 GB C 35 GB D 280 GB 70 billion parameters * 2 bytes per FP16 parameter = 140 billion bytes = 140 GB. This exceeds a single A100 (80GB), requiring at least two GPUs just to load the weights. Q2 What is quantization in the context of LLMs? A Reducing the numerical precision of weights (e.g., FP16 to INT4) to decrease memory usage and increase inference speed B Compressing the training data C Removing unused model layers D Reducing the vocabulary size Quantization maps high-precision floating point weights to lower-precision integers. INT4 quantization stores each weight in 4 bits instead of 16, reducing memory by 4x with minimal accuracy loss. Q3 What is the key difference between post-training quantization (PTQ) and quantization-aware training (QAT)? A QAT doesn't use gradients B PTQ requires more data C PTQ quantizes after training with no retraining; QAT simulates quantization during training so the model learns to tolerate reduced precision D PTQ is more accurate PTQ is fast (just calibrate and quantize) but can lose accuracy. QAT includes fake quantization during training, allowing the model to adjust its weights to be more robust to precision loss. QAT usually gives better accuracy. Q4 What does 'per-channel' quantization mean and why is it better than 'per-tensor'? A It quantizes each output channel separately, using different scale/zero-point for each, reducing quantization error B It processes one color channel at a time C It's a type of data parallelism D It uses separate GPUs per channel Per-tensor uses one scale factor for the entire weight matrix. Per-channel uses a separate scale for each output channel (row). Since different channels have different value ranges, per-channel captures them more accurately. Q5 Why do 95% of weights in Llama 3 70B fall between -0.1 and +0.1? A The weights haven't converged yet B Weight decay and normalization during training push weights toward small values, making the full FP16 range wasteful C This is specific to the Llama architecture D The model is poorly trained Weight decay regularization shrinks weights toward zero. Layer normalization keeps activations centered. Combined, they produce weight distributions concentrated near zero, making low-precision quantization effective. Time : about 120 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Two phases define LLM inference. Prefill processes your prompt in parallel -- compute-bound. Decode generates tokens one at a time -- memory-bound. Every optimization targets one or both. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Prefill "Processing the prompt" Computing attention over all input tokens in parallel -- compute-bound because the full matrix multiplication keeps GPU cores busy Decode "Generating tokens" Producing one token per forward pass, reading the full model weights each time -- memory-bound because compute finishes before the next weights arrive KV cache "Caching attention states" Storing the key and value projections for all previous tokens so they are not recomputed at each decode step -- trades memory for compute Continuous batching "Dynamic batching" Inserting new requests into the running batch as soon as any request finishes, evaluated at every decode iteration rather than waiting for the whole batch PagedAttention "Virtual memory for KV cache" Allocating KV cache in fixed-size pages instead of contiguous blocks, eliminating memory fragmentation and enabling copy-on-write for shared prefixes Speculative decoding "Draft and verify" Using a fast draft model to propose multiple tokens, then verifying them all in one target model forward pass -- mathematically exact, 2-3x speedup EAGLE "Self-speculative decoding" A speculative decoding variant that trains a lightweight head on the target model's own hidden states, achieving higher acceptance rates than a separate draft model Prefix caching "Reusing system prompt KV" Storing computed KV cache entries for common prefixes (system prompts, few-shot examples) and reusing them across requests to skip redundant prefill Ops:byte ratio "Arithmetic intensity" The ratio of compute operations to memory bytes read -- determines whether a workload is compute-bound (high ratio) or memory-bound (low ratio) Time to first token "TTFT" Latency from receiving a request to producing the first output token -- dominated by prefill time for long prompts The problem In plain words first Serving a language model is mostly a scheduling problem. Generating each new token means reading all the model's weights from memory, so one user at a time leaves the GPU's arithmetic units almost idle; serving many users in the same step shares that read. Inference engines therefore cache each conversation's past (the KV cache), store that cache in small pages so memory is not wasted, slot new requests into the running batch the moment others finish, reuse the cache for shared prompt beginnings, and let a small model guess several tokens that the big model then checks in one pass. This lesson runs the lesson's simulators, computes the limits exactly from GPU specifications, and runs real speculative decoding with two small models, checking that it changes nothing but the speed. No model is trained. You deploy Llama 3 70B on 4xA100 GPUs. A single user gets ~50 tokens per second. Feels fast. Then 100 users hit the endpoint simultaneously. Throughput drops to 3 tokens/second/user. Your $25,000/month GPU bill is serving responses slower than a human types. The model itself does not change between 1 user and 100 users. Same weights, same architecture, same math. What changes is how you schedule the work. Naive inference wastes 90%+ of available GPU compute. A user waiting for token 47 holds an entire batch slot open while the GPU memory bus sits idle between matmuls. Meanwhile, a new user's 2,000-token prompt could fill that dead time with useful compute. This is not a scaling problem. It is a scheduling problem. The techniques in this lesson -- KV caching, continuous batching, PagedAttention, speculative decoding, prefix caching -- can cut the hardware needed for the same traffic several times over. As an illustration, vLLM serving Llama 3 70B on 4xA100-80GB reaches roughly 50 tokens/second/user at low concurrency (close to the bandwidth limit computed after Step 6), and sustains 15-25 TPS/user at 100 concurrent requests through continuous batching and PagedAttention. Without these optimizations, the same hardware serves 5 TPS/user at that concurrency. Same GPUs, same model, 4x the throughput. Idea 1 · Prefill vs Decode Every LLM inference request has two distinct phases. Prefill processes the entire input prompt. All tokens are known, so attention can be computed in parallel across the full sequence. This is a large matrix multiplication -- GPU cores stay busy. The bottleneck is compute: how many FLOPS your hardware can deliver per second. An A100 does 312 TFLOPS (BF16). Prefill for a 4,096-token prompt on a 70B model needs about 5.7 × 10^14 FLOPs: roughly 0.5 s at peak on the four A100s the model needs (the second run after Step 6). Decode generates output tokens one at a time. Each new token attends to all previous tokens, but only one token is produced per forward pass. The weight matrices are the same size as during prefill, but you are multiplying them by a single vector instead of a matrix. The GPU cores finish in microseconds, then wait for the next batch of weights to arrive from memory. The bottleneck is memory bandwidth: how fast you can stream model weights from HBM to the compute units. An A100 has 2 TB/s bandwidth. A 70B model in FP16 is 140 GB. Reading the full model once takes 70ms -- that is your floor for a single decode step. The ops:byte ratio (also called arithmetic intensity) captures this tradeoff. It measures how many operations you perform per byte loaded from memory. Copy During prefill with a batch of 4,096 tokens, you perform ~4,096 multiply-accumulate operations per weight loaded. The ratio is high -- you are compute-bound. During decode with batch size 1, you perform ~1 operation per weight loaded. The ratio is low -- you are memory-bound. The fundamental insight: decode is memory-bound because you read the entire model to produce a single token . Every optimization below either reduces what you read, increases the batch of tokens processed per read, or avoids reads entirely. Idea 2 · KV Cache During attention, each token's query attends to every previous token's key and value vectors. Without caching, generating token N requires recomputing the key and value projections for all N-1 preceding tokens. Token 1 gets projected when generating token 2, then again for token 3, then again for token 4. By token 1,000, you have projected token 1 a total of 999 times. The KV cache stores the key and value projections from all previous tokens. When generating token N, you only compute the key and value for token N, then concatenate them with the cached K/V from tokens 1 through N-1. Memory formula for KV cache: Copy For Llama 3 70B (80 layers, 8 KV heads with GQA, head_dim=128, BF16): Copy A single 128K-context conversation for Llama 3 70B consumes 40 GB of KV cache -- half an A100's memory. With 100 concurrent users at 4K tokens each, KV cache alone requires 128 GB. This is why KV cache management is the central challenge of inference optimization. Idea 3 · Continuous Batching Static batching waits until a batch of N requests arrives, processes them together, and waits until all finish before accepting new requests. If one request needs 500 tokens and another needs 10, the short request sits idle for 490 decode steps after it finishes. Continuous batching (also called iteration-level batching) inserts new requests into the batch as soon as any request completes. The batch is reevaluated at every decode step. A request that finishes after 10 tokens is immediately replaced by a waiting request. The throughput improvement depends on how much output lengths vary. With uniform lengths, continuous batching matches static batching. With variable lengths (the common case), continuous batching can deliver 2-5x higher throughput because GPU slots never sit empty. Idea 4 · PagedAttention The KV cache for each request is a contiguous block of memory. As requests arrive and depart, memory fragments -- exactly like RAM fragmentation in operating systems. A 4K-token request needs 1.28 GB contiguous. Even if you have 2 GB free total, you might not have 1.28 GB contiguous . You either waste memory or reject the request. PagedAttention (from vLLM) applies OS-style virtual memory to KV cache. Instead of allocating one contiguous block per request, it allocates fixed-size "pages" (typically 16 tokens each). Pages can be anywhere in physical GPU memory. A page table maps each request's logical sequence positions to physical page locations. PagedAttention also enables copy-on-write for shared prefixes. If 50 requests share the same system prompt, the KV cache pages for that system prompt are stored once and referenced by all 50 requests. Only when a request diverges (different user messages) does it get its own pages. This cuts memory usage dramatically for applications with shared system prompts. vLLM reports near-zero memory waste (~4% vs ~60-80% in naive allocation) through PagedAttention. Idea 5 · Speculative Decoding Decode is slow because it is sequential -- you generate one token, feed it back, generate the next. But what if you could guess the next 5 tokens cheaply, then verify them all at once? Speculative decoding uses a small, fast draft model to generate K candidate tokens. The large target model then processes all K candidates in a single forward pass (which looks like a prefill -- parallel, compute-bound, efficient). If the target model agrees with the draft model's predictions, you accept all K tokens in the time of one target forward pass. If it disagrees at position j, you accept tokens 1 through j-1 and discard the rest. The speedup depends on the acceptance rate -- how often the draft model's predictions match the target. For a Llama 3 8B drafting for Llama 3 70B, acceptance rates of 70-85% are typical on natural language. This translates to 2-3x decode speedup. Three approaches to speculative decoding: Method Draft source Acceptance rate Overhead Draft-target (Leviathan et al.) Separate small model 70-85% Draft model memory EAGLE (Li et al.) Lightweight head on target 75-90% ~1% extra parameters N-gram lookup Token n-gram table 40-60% Negligible EAGLE trains a small autoregressive head on top of the target model's hidden states. It predicts the next token's embedding using the target model's second-to-last layer features. Because it operates on the target model's own representations (not a separate model's), it achieves higher acceptance rates with minimal extra memory. EAGLE-2 adds a dynamic draft tree that adjusts candidate count based on context. N-gram speculative decoding maintains a table of n-gram continuations from the current context or a prebuilt corpus. If the draft matches what appeared before in the same conversation (repetitive patterns, code, structured output), it fires with zero neural network overhead. Acceptance rates are lower on average but the cost per speculation is essentially free. Speculative decoding is mathematically exact -- the output distribution is identical to the target model's distribution. It is not an approximation. The verification step ensures that every accepted token has exactly the probability the target model would have assigned. Idea 6 · Prefix Caching Many requests share the same prefix. A chatbot system prompt. A RAG context block. A few-shot example set. Without prefix caching, every request recomputes the KV cache for these shared tokens from scratch. Prefix caching stores the KV cache for common prefixes and reuses it across requests. When a new request arrives with a known prefix, the system copies (or references) the cached KV entries and only computes the KV for the unique suffix. For a 2,000-token system prompt shared across all requests, prefix caching eliminates ~400ms of prefill per request. At 100 requests/second, that saves 40 seconds of GPU compute per second -- more than one GPU's worth of work. SGLang's RadixAttention implements prefix caching with a radix tree (trie) that indexes prefixes by their token content. Any request matching a stored prefix gets its KV cache for free. The tree enables partial prefix matches -- if you share 1,500 of 2,000 prefix tokens with a cached entry, you reuse those 1,500 and recompute only 500. Idea 7 · Inference Engines Three engines dominate production LLM serving: Engine Key innovation Best for vLLM PagedAttention, continuous batching General-purpose serving, highest compatibility SGLang RadixAttention (prefix caching), structured generation Multi-turn chatbots, constrained decoding TensorRT-LLM NVIDIA kernel fusion, FP8 quantization Maximum single-GPU throughput on NVIDIA hardware vLLM is the default starting point. It supports the widest range of models, runs on any GPU vendor (NVIDIA, AMD, Intel), and achieves strong throughput through PagedAttention + continuous batching. The OpenAI-compatible API means you can drop it in as a replacement for any OpenAI API call. SGLang builds on the same foundations as vLLM but adds RadixAttention for prefix caching and a domain-specific language for structured LLM programs. If your workload involves multi-turn conversations, tool use, or constrained decoding (JSON output, regex-guided generation), On workloads with heavy prefix reuse SGLang has reported several-fold higher throughput; on others the two are close, and both now implement most of each other's techniques. TensorRT-LLM compiles models into optimized NVIDIA GPU kernels. It fuses operations (attention + linear + activation in one kernel), uses FP8 on H100 GPUs, and integrates with NVIDIA Triton Inference Server for production deployment. It achieves the highest single-GPU throughput on NVIDIA hardware but requires more setup and only works on NVIDIA GPUs. The ops:byte ratio tells you whether you are compute-bound or memory-bound, which determines which optimizations matter. Copy When ops:byte is low (decode, small batches), you hit the memory bandwidth roof. Adding more compute (higher clock, more cores) does not help. You need to reduce memory reads (quantization, KV cache compression) or increase the batch size to amortize reads across more useful work. When ops:byte is high (prefill, large batches), you hit the compute roof. Memory bandwidth optimization does not help. You need faster GPUs, kernel fusion, or reduced precision to squeeze more FLOPS. With greedy decoding the target keeps a drafted token only if it is the token the target itself would choose, so the text cannot change (in float32 all three outputs match exactly). The speed depends on how cheap the draft is relative to the target and how often its guesses are accepted. Here the draft costs over a third of the target per token and runs on a CPU, so speculation ranges from somewhat faster to slower depending on the prompt. The 2–3× speedups reported for speculative decoding come from GPUs, where checking several tokens costs about the same as generating one, and from much smaller drafts. Solution B1 · Not always Not always. In bfloat16 the first prompt's output already differs at the first token: the target's top two candidates ("Here" and "```") are 0.125 apart in logit, exactly one bfloat16 rounding step at that magnitude, and the verifying pass over several tokens rounds slightly differently from a one-token pass, enough to flip the choice. The algorithm is exact in exact arithmetic; floating-point results depend on the shape of the computation, so near-ties can break differently. Production engines accept this, as they do for batching, which changes shapes in the same way. When bit-identical outputs matter (tests, reproducibility), use float32 or deterministic kernels, and compare outputs as distributions rather than strings. Decode generates tokens autoregressively one at a time (limited by memory bandwidth for loading model weights). Different optimizations target each phase. Q2 What does KV-cache eliminate during autoregressive generation? A The embedding lookup B The need for attention masks C The softmax computation D Redundant recomputation of key and value vectors for all previous tokens at each generation step Without KV-cache, generating token N requires recomputing attention keys and values for all N-1 previous tokens. KV-cache stores these vectors, so each new token only computes its own K and V, saving O(N) computation per step. Q3 What is continuous batching and why does it improve throughput? A Batching across multiple models B Using larger batch sizes C Processing all requests in one large batch D Dynamically adding and removing requests from the running batch as they start and finish, instead of waiting for the entire batch to complete In static batching, a short request holds its batch slot until the longest request finishes. Continuous batching immediately fills completed slots with new requests, keeping the GPU busy and improving overall throughput. Q4 What problem does PagedAttention (used in vLLM) solve? A It improves tokenization speed B It reduces model size C It manages KV-cache memory in fixed-size blocks like virtual memory, eliminating fragmentation from variable-length sequences D It speeds up the attention computation KV-cache for variable-length sequences causes memory fragmentation (wasted gaps between allocations). PagedAttention allocates KV-cache in fixed blocks and maps them with a page table, like OS virtual memory. Q5 What is speculative decoding? A Using a small draft model to propose multiple tokens that the large model verifies in parallel, speeding up generation B Predicting which tokens the user wants C Generating multiple responses and picking the best D Caching frequently generated sequences A small fast model generates N candidate tokens. The large model verifies all N in a single forward pass (parallel). If K tokens are accepted, you've generated K tokens in the time of roughly 1 large-model step.
