In plain words first The idea in one line Everything from Lessons 01 to 12 is one stage of one pipeline. This lesson is the scaffold that turns those stages into a single end-to-end run: tokenize, pre-train, scale, SFT, align, evaluate, quantize, serve. You will not train a 70B model on a laptop. You will produce the orchestration layer, the manifest, the eval gate, and the rollback plan that a 2026 frontier team uses to decide what gets shipped. This is the capstone. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Manifest "The recipe file" YAML or JSON describing pipeline version, seed, per-stage config, and gate thresholds — sufficient to replay a run Content-addressed "By hash not name" Artifacts stored by SHA-256 of their contents, so you can never confuse version A with version B Eval gate "The ship criteria" Numeric thresholds on benchmark metrics and safety scores that must pass before an artifact is marked shippable KL budget "How far alignment drifted" A cap on cumulative $\mathrm{KL}(\text{policy} \Vert \text{reference})$ across alignment stages, enforced as a gate MFU "How much of the GPU you used" Model FLOPs Utilization — achieved FLOPs divided by theoretical peak. 40% is typical at 70B scale, 55% at 7B Rollback plan "What we do when it breaks" Pre-written set of actions per stage on failure: re-run, fall back, retrain with revised inputs Orchestrator "The conductor" The process that reads the manifest, dispatches stages, verifies hashes, halts on any contract violation Artifact store "Versioned S3 for weights" Immutable content-addressed object store — single source of truth for checkpoints, datasets, eval reports Reproducible "Same metrics on replay" Different bit-level weights but equivalent downstream metrics — the realistic target for distributed LLM training Cost gate "You cannot exceed X" Pre-run cost estimate plus in-run tracker — the pipeline refuses to start if the estimate exceeds budget The problem In plain words first Each lesson so far is one stage of a single pipeline: tokenizer, data, pre-training, scaling, fine-tuning, alignment, evaluation, quantization, serving. Running them as a pipeline means every stage writes a typed output, every output is identified by a hash of its contents so the next stage can check it received exactly what was produced, a manifest file records everything needed to replay the run, and numeric gates decide automatically whether the result may ship. This lesson runs the lesson's orchestrator, estimates training costs from first principles and checks them against published numbers, and verifies a real model's files against the content hashes the Hugging Face Hub stores. No model is trained. The previous lessons each work. Tokenizer trained. Tiny GPT pre-trained. SFT dataset assembled. Reward model trained. DPO run. Evals measured. Quantized weights exported. Inference server spun up. Each one is a notebook. Each one has its own conventions, its own output paths, its own seed. A frontier training run is not a notebook. Llama 3 405B took about 30.8 million H100 GPU-hours. DeepSeek-V3 used around 2.8 million H800 hours. During that time, one corrupted checkpoint, one data contamination, one eval regression can cost a team a week of wall-clock and a month of GPU budget. The way teams survive this is through pipeline hygiene: every stage has a deterministic input, a deterministic output, a manifest, a hash, and a gate. This is the capstone. You will not run the pipeline end-to-end on a laptop. You will write the orchestrator that coordinates the stages, the manifest that describes the run, the verifier that gates ship decisions, and the replay plan that lets a third party re-run your work from a single file. The code is small; the discipline is large. The pattern scales from 100M to 1T parameters unchanged. The same four components -- manifest, orchestrator, eval gate, artifact store -- run Llama 3 and also run your hobby GPT. The difference is the size of the numbers inside each stage's config, not the shape of the pipeline. Idea 1 · The Twelve Stages Every Phase 10 lesson is a stage. Here is the full dependency graph. Stages 07 and 08 can run in parallel. Everything else is a hard dependency. A change in stage 02 (tokenizer) invalidates every downstream artifact. A change in stage 10 (eval) invalidates only the ship decision. Idea 2 · The Manifest A manifest is a single file that describes a run completely enough to replay it. Nothing the pipeline produces should depend on state that is not in the manifest. The fields are boring and mandatory. Copy The output hash of stage N is the input hash of stage N+1. Any deviation and the pipeline halts. This is how you catch data corruption early. It is also how a teammate on a different continent verifies that their replay of a deterministic stage produced the same artifact as yours. In practice teams use a small YAML schema plus a manifest checker that diffs against the previous successful run. Any delta outside the expected fields (cost, wall clock) is a red flag. Idea 3 · Artifact Typing Each stage's output is a typed artifact. Not a directory blob, not a pickle, but a named type with a known schema. Stage Artifact Type Key Fields 01-02 Tokenizer vocab.json, merges.txt, config.json, hash 03 Dataset shards[], row count, token count, dedup stats 04-05 Checkpoint weights.safetensors, config.json, optimizer state, step count 06 SFT Model checkpoint + SFT recipe + data mix 07 Reward Model RM checkpoint + preference data hash 08-09 Policy checkpoint + reference hash + beta + KL budget consumed 10 Eval Report benchmark scores + regression diffs + eval data hash 11 Quantized Model quantized weights + calibration data + accuracy delta vs FP16 12 Server Spec endpoint + model hash + config + observability hooks The typing prevents the most common failure mode: using a stage 08 output as a stage 06 input, shipping a DPO-trained model through the SFT path. Typed artifacts and typed stage signatures make these errors compile-time failures, not day-five failures. Idea 4 · The Eval Gate Shipping is not "training finished." Shipping is "training finished and the eval gate passed." The gate is defined before the run starts. Copy Every gate is a numeric threshold. No "looks good" gates. No subjective sign-offs. If every gate passes, the artifact is marked shippable. If any gate fails, the run is held pending explicit override by a named reviewer, which itself is logged in the manifest. Two gates catch most disasters. A regression gate (the new model must be at least as good as the previous on core benchmarks) catches training bugs. A KL budget gate (the aligned policy must not have drifted further than X from its reference) catches alignment overcooking. Every production pipeline has both. Idea 5 · The Orchestrator A small piece of code that reads the manifest, dispatches stages, tracks artifacts, and halts on any contract violation. This is not Airflow. This is not Kubeflow. For pipeline hygiene you want something boring that you wrote. The orchestrator's job is narrow: Resolve the DAG from the manifest. For each stage, check if the expected output already exists at the correct hash (skip if so). Run the stage, capture stdout/stderr, measure wall clock and cost. Verify the output hash against the downstream stage's expected input hash. On failure, write a partial manifest with the exact failing stage and exit nonzero. That is 200 lines of Python. It will look like the file code/main.py in this lesson. Under the hood, the real pipeline uses torchrun or ray to execute individual stages on clusters, but the orchestrator itself runs on a single box. Idea 6 · Experiment Tracking and Artifact Storage Two external systems anchor the pipeline. Experiment tracker (wandb, neptune, mlflow). Logs loss curves, eval metrics, system telemetry per stage. The tracker is where you go when you need to compare run A against run B three weeks later. Teams almost always use a hosted tracker for this -- writing your own loses time that should go into training. Artifact store (S3, R2, GCS). Immutable object store for checkpoints, datasets, tokenizers, eval reports. Artifacts are addressed by hash, not by filename. A filename like latest.pt is a foot-gun; ckpt-7b-step-20000-sha256:abc123.safetensors is a contract. The orchestrator writes to both. The tracker is for humans looking at charts. The artifact store is for the next stage looking up inputs. Idea 7 · Costing A frontier run has a dollar number attached. Budget discipline happens in two places. Pre-run estimate. From the manifest, compute expected FLOPs (for pre-training: 6 x params x tokens), expected GPU hours (FLOPs / peak throughput / utilization), and dollar cost at the current rental rate. If the estimate exceeds the budget gate, the pipeline refuses to start. In-run tracking. Stage-by-stage wall clock and cost are logged to the manifest. After every stage, the remaining budget is checked. If a stage overran, the next stage's gate is evaluated with the new remaining budget. You do not find out you are out of money when the VC calls. Meta did not publish a dollar cost for Llama 3; at rental prices of about $2 per GPU-hour its 30.8 million H100-hours come to roughly $61M. DeepSeek-V3 reported $5.6M for the main pre-training run. The ratio is mostly hardware efficiency plus mixture-of-experts -- but the specific cost is visible because both teams tracked it per stage, not per run. Idea 8 · Reproducibility vs Determinism These are not the same. Reproducible means the same manifest plus the same code plus the same infrastructure produces a checkpoint with equivalent downstream metrics. Deterministic means bit-identical output. Modern LLM training is reproducible but not deterministic. Distributed training's reduce-order, GPU kernel non-determinism (cuBLAS, flash-attn), and mixed precision rounding combine to produce floats that differ at the 1e-5 level between runs. This is fine for the final metrics, which do not move. It is fatal if you are trying to debug with bit-level diffs. The cure is to log every stage's input hash, output hash, and headline metrics. On a replay, the hashes match only for deterministic stages, such as data processing and tokenization. A training stage writes new weights, so its output hash changes. For those stages, the run is "reproduced" when the headline metrics match, even though the weights are not bit-identical. Idea 9 · Rollback Plan Before the run starts, write down what happens on failure of each stage. Three categories. Cheap to re-run (hours): tokenizer, eval, quantization, inference server. Just re-run. Medium (days): SFT, DPO, CAI. Keep the base model; re-run only the alignment stages. Expensive (weeks and millions of dollars): pre-training. The rollback plan here is not "re-run." It is "use the last good checkpoint and re-run the cheaper downstream stages with revised data." Because stage dependencies are typed and hashed, the orchestrator can compute the rollback set automatically: invalidate the failed stage plus every descendant. A failure at stage 06 (SFT) invalidates 06, 07, 08, 09, 10, 11, 12. A failure at stage 11 (quantization) invalidates only 11 and 12. Naming this up front avoids improvising while the team is exhausted at 4am. Idea 10 · Production Recipes Observed in 2026 Published recipes (Llama 3, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3, Tülu 3, Kimi K2) share a similar skeleton. Tokenizer: 128k BPE with byte fallback. Trained on a small, balanced multilingual slice. Pre-training: 10-20T tokens, mostly web plus code plus synthetic. Muon or AdamW optimizer. FSDP2 or DeepSpeed ZeRO-3. Gradient checkpointing. BF16 weights, FP32 master. SFT: 500k-2M instruction pairs, mixed human and synthetic, with strict dedup against the eval set. Alignment: DPO or CAI + GRPO. RLHF only where the preference signal is too multidimensional for DPO. Eval: MMLU-Pro, MATH, HumanEval+, GPQA, SWE-Bench Verified, LiveBench, plus a private held-out set the public never sees. Quantization: 4-bit GPTQ or AWQ for serving, 8-bit for safety evals where accuracy deltas matter. Serving: vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, or in-house. Continuous batching. Speculative decoding. Solutions Solution P1 · Within 10% Within 10%: × 2 × 1 0 12 = 8.4 × 1 0 22 FLOPs; at 40% of an A100's 312 TFLOP/s that is /1.248 × 1 0 14 = 6.7 × 1 0 8 seconds, 186,966 GPU-hours, 1.4% above the 184,320 Meta reported. Solution B1 · A silent change of inputs The repository can change under the same name: its owner may push new weights, a fixed tokenizer or a different chat template, and from_pretrained("HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M") silently downloads the latest version. Your replay then starts from a different base model, every downstream hash differs, and if you do not record hashes you will not even notice: evaluation numbers shift and nobody can say why. Pin revision=<commit hash> when loading, record the commit and the SHA-256 of each file in the manifest, and let the orchestrator refuse to run if a downloaded file's hash does not match. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Defend a design Design the service behind a chat product with 10,000 daily active users who send about 5 queries each, with roughly 1,500 input tokens and 400 output tokens per query. Users must see a response start quickly, the tail must stay bounded, and the product has a unit cost target. Lay out the request path, the components, the budgets you hold each one to, and how you would scale it. Level 3 of 4 · about 25 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The request enters through a gateway that authenticates and rate limits per user, passes input guardrails, is matched against a semantic cache, and on a miss goes to the model with streaming, then through output guardrails, an eval logger and a cost tracker. The budgets are a median under 2s, a p99 under 10s, a cache hit rate above 30%, a guardrail block rate under 5%, and a cost per request under $0.01. At 50,000 queries a day this runs on a few async servers behind a load balancer; the servers are I/O bound, so a single async process holds a hundred or more concurrent requests and scaling means more servers, not more cores. The path. Gateway for authentication, rate limits of 10-50 requests a minute per user and CORS; input guardrails for injection patterns and personal data; a prompt router that picks the template and version; a semantic cache keyed by query embedding with a similarity threshold and a time to live; the model call with streaming and a fallback chain; output guardrails; an eval logger; a cost tracker; a server-sent events response. Seven components, each one a known piece; the engineering is the wiring and the budgets. Budgets. Metric Target Why Median latency Under 2s The typical experience p99 latency Under 10s The tail drives churn Cache hit rate Above 30% Direct cost savings Guardrail block rate Under 5% Higher means false positives Cost per request Under $0.01 Unit economics Streaming puts the first token inside the median budget even when the full answer takes seconds. Maximum token limits on input and output bound both the cost and the tail. Every external call has a timeout. Load and capacity. Traffic is 50,000 queries a day, and with the measured cache hit rate about 32,500 reach the model. Peak matters more than the average; size for the busiest minute. The servers wait on network I/O, so one async process serves 100+ concurrent requests and a box with four workers serves 400+. The lesson's scaling table puts this tier at a few async servers with a cache and a queue, for about $500 a month of infrastructure, with the model bill on top. Connection pooling to the provider avoids a new TLS handshake per request, which costs 100-200ms. Work that is not interactive, such as summarization, goes to a queue with workers and a job id the client polls. Observability. Every request writes one structured log line with the request id, the user, the template and version, the model, the input and output token counts, the latency, the cache result, the guardrail results and the cost. Traces across the components show where the time went. The five numbers in the table sit on one dashboard. If the model is self-hosted. The pipeline lesson's serving stage adds continuous batching, speculative decoding, and KV cache eviction, with quantized weights for serving and the eval gate rerun on the quantized model. The same gateway, cache and guardrails sit in front of it. Before launch. The deployment checklist has fifteen items; the ones people skip are per-user rate limits, maximum token limits, a health endpoint that reports dependency status, timeouts on every external call, and a load test with 100 concurrent users. Plausible wrong answers. "Scale the model servers first." The service is I/O bound at this traffic; the gateway, cache and async servers are the design, and the model is a dependency. "Skip the cache; the model is the product." A third of the traffic repeats, and the cache is the largest single saving in the bill. "The p99 is a vendor problem." Timeouts, maximum tokens, streaming and the fallback chain are what bound the tail on your side. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) A user pastes a document far longer than the context window. Where is that caught? Expected: at the maximum input token limit before the model call, with a clear error, not at the provider. (level 3) Why does cost per user matter when cost per request is already under target? Expected: a few heavy users dominate the bill; per-user tracking and a daily cap move them to a cheaper model or stop them. (level 4) The provider has a regional outage during the daily peak. Walk the request path. Expected: backoff and retries on the primary, fall through the chain to a second model, then cached answers for repeated queries, then an unavailable message; the cost tracker shows the fallback's price and the dashboard shows the step that answered. (level 4) How do you prove the service meets its budgets before the first user? Expected: a load test at 100 concurrent users against the staging stack with the dashboard metrics as pass criteria, plus a shadow run of the prompts on logged traffic. Where it is taught. Defend a design A team trains and aligns models in a multi-stage pipeline and ships the result to serving. Design the evaluation platform that decides whether an artifact is shippable: what it reads, what a gate is, which two gates catch most disasters, how it handles a failed gate, and how a third party replays a decision. Level 3 of 4 · about 20 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The platform reads a manifest that describes the run completely, with a seed, a code revision, and an input and output hash for every stage, and it evaluates numeric gates that were written before the run started. A regression gate holds the new model to the previous one on core benchmarks and catches training bugs; a KL budget gate caps how far the aligned policy drifted from its reference and catches alignment overcooking. A failed gate holds the run for a named reviewer whose override is logged in the manifest, and anyone can replay the decision because the eval report is content-addressed and the eval data hash is part of it. What the platform reads. The manifest is the single file that describes the run well enough to replay it: pipeline version, seed, code revision, and per stage a recipe, an input hash, an output hash, wall clock and cost. The output hash of one stage is the input hash of the next, so a corrupted or swapped artifact stops the pipeline before any evaluation. Artifacts are typed: an eval report carries benchmark scores, regression diffs and the hash of the eval data, so a report cannot be confused with a checkpoint or attached to the wrong model. Gates. Every gate is a numeric threshold written before training starts, for example a core benchmark at least the baseline plus 0.5, a coding benchmark at least the baseline plus 1.0, a truthfulness benchmark with no drop, a safety refusal rate at most 0.05, a KL from the reference at most 25.0, and a total cost at most 50000. No "looks good" gates and no subjective sign-offs. If every gate passes the artifact is marked shippable; if any fails the run is held. The two gates that matter most. Regression: the new model must be at least as good as the previous one on the core set. This catches training bugs, bad data mixes and broken tokenizers. KL budget: the aligned policy must not drift further than a set amount from its reference. This catches alignment that overcooked the model into a narrow behavior. Every production pipeline has both. Contamination. A gate that compares the eval data hash against the training shards by exact match or long n-gram overlap, and fails when the overlap passes a small fraction, keeps a benchmark gain honest. The pipeline lesson's exercise sets that fraction at 0.1% with 13-gram matching. Holds, overrides and replay. A held run is a decision point, not a failure. A named reviewer either approves the rollback or overrides, and the override is written into the manifest with the name. Replay works because the manifest, the content-addressed eval report and the eval data hash identify the exact inputs; a teammate on another continent runs the gate against the same hashes and must get the same verdict. Reproducible is not deterministic: weights can differ at the level of small rounding between runs, so replay checks hashes and headline metrics, not bit-identical tensors. Where the platform plugs in. The gate runs after evaluation and after quantization, because quantized weights must pass the same thresholds as the full model. The three commands are plan, run and gate; plan is free and catches missing thresholds and stale hashes before any compute is spent. Plausible wrong answers. "Have a reviewer look at samples and sign off." Subjective sign-offs are not gates; a gate is a number that can fail, and the reviewer's role is the logged override. "Rerun training to confirm a result." Pre-training costs weeks; replay checks hashes and metrics against the manifest instead. "One benchmark is enough if it is the right one." The regression set and the KL budget catch different failures, and a safety gate catches a third. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why must the thresholds be written before the run? Expected: a threshold chosen after seeing the scores is moved to pass the model; a gate is only a gate if it can fail. (level 3) A change to the eval set invalidates what? Expected: only the ship decision; the eval data hash changes, the report is recomputed, and the training artifacts stay valid. (level 4) The quantized model passes every gate except the safety refusal rate, which rose slightly. What do you ship? Expected: nothing without a logged override; the gate exists for the serving artifact, and the lesson's recipe keeps safety evals on a higher-precision quantization where deltas matter. (level 4) How does the platform stop a model trained through the wrong stage from reaching the gate? Expected: typed artifacts and typed stage signatures, so a preference-tuned checkpoint cannot be fed into the supervised path and the mismatch fails at plan time. Where it is taught. The complete LLM pipeline lesson defines the manifest, the typed artifacts, the eval gate and the override and replay rules. Defend a design A team wants to adapt an open model in the 8B class to its own domain and serve it at a measurable cost per million tokens. Design the pipeline so that one command runs it end to end: the stages, the hardware per stage, the data hygiene, the ablations you require, the serving measurements, and what the release must include. Level 3 of 4 · about 25 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Five stages, each with a config file in version control: data preparation with deduplication, a quality filter, personal data scrubbing and a contamination check against the eval sets; supervised fine-tuning for 2-3 epochs on 8xH100 with a cosine schedule and packed sequences; one epoch of preference tuning on 4xH100 with a swept beta; quantization into three formats; and serving with speculative draft heads and autoscaling on queue wait. The deliverable is an ablation table of base, SFT only, SFT plus DPO and SFT plus GRPO on the task benchmarks, serving numbers at batch 1, 8 and 32 with the draft acceptance rate and cost per million tokens, a safety pass rate, and a model card with seeds, configs and commit hashes. Stages and hardware. Stage What Hardware in the capstone Data Deduplicate, filter quality, scrub personal data, split with a seed CPU Contamination check Near-duplicate hashing of every validation split against the public test sets; reject overlap CPU SFT Sharded optimizer, fast attention kernels, packed sequences, 2-3 epochs 8xH100 Preference tuning One epoch of DPO on pairs, or GRPO with a verifiable reward; sweep beta 4xH100 Quantize Three formats for deployment flexibility; record size and throughput One GPU Serve Draft heads for speculation, autoscaling on queue wait Serving GPUs Eval and card Benchmark matrix, safety eval, model card CPU plus eval GPU In the capstone's example run the data stage keeps 280k of 300k examples, SFT takes 6h12m and moves validation loss from 1.42 to 1.03, DPO runs 1h40m at a beta of 0.08, the quantized weights are 4.6 GB, and serving shows a draft acceptance rate of 0.74 with a p99 of 126ms at a batch of 8. Hygiene is a gate, not a step. The contamination check runs before training and fails the pipeline on overlap. The capstone's exercise leaks a small share of test answers into training and watches a benchmark jump unrealistically; the check is what makes the eval delta believable. The pipeline lesson adds the mechanism: a manifest with an input and output hash per stage, so the SFT stage refuses data that does not match the hash the contamination check approved. Ablations are the deliverable. The question the pipeline answers is not whether the model got better but which stage paid for it. Run the eval matrix on the base, on SFT only, on SFT plus DPO and on SFT plus GRPO. The example reports gains of +3.2 on one benchmark and +0.41 on another after the full run. Without the ablation, a regression from preference tuning hides behind the SFT gain. Serving measurements. Tokens per second at batch sizes 1, 8 and 32, the acceptance rate of the draft heads, and the cost for each million tokens against a hosted alternative at matched quality. Acceptance measured on the domain data, not generic chat, because the draft heads were trained for the domain and the latency budget depends on it. The release. A model card with the data sources and licenses, the training configs, the eval matrix, the safety pass rate, a reproducibility section with seeds and commit hashes, and the quantization deltas. One command reruns the pipeline with identical seeds; the rubric weights reproducibility and data hygiene as heavily as the eval gain. Plausible wrong answers. "Skip the contamination check; the data is internal." Internal data copies public text all the time, and one leaked test set makes the whole eval table meaningless. "Report the final model against the base and stop." Without the per-stage ablation nobody knows whether preference tuning helped or hurt. "Measure serving at batch one only." Throughput and cost per million tokens come from batched decoding; batch one measures latency, not economics. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why does preference tuning need fewer GPUs than SFT? Expected: it runs one epoch on a much smaller set of pairs, and the capstone sizes it at half the SFT hardware. (level 3) Which stage gets rerun when the safety eval fails on the quantized model? Expected: quantization and serving only; the pipeline lesson's rollback invalidates the failed stage and its descendants. (level 4) The acceptance rate on domain traffic is far below the number from generic chat data. What does that do to the design? Expected: the latency budget was set on the wrong number; retrain the draft heads on domain data or size serving without the speculation gain. (level 4) A smaller model with a low-rank adapter matches quality at a tenth of the memory. How does the pipeline change? Expected: the SFT stage swaps to adapter training with the same data and eval gates, and the quantization and serving stages consume the merged weights unchanged. Where it is taught. The end-to-end fine-tuning capstone gives the five stages, the hardware, the example run and the rubric, and the complete LLM pipeline lesson gives the manifest, the hash chain and the rollback set. Weigh a trade-off A twelve-stage training pipeline runs from tokenizer to inference server, and the pre-training stage costs weeks and millions of dollars. Before the run starts you must write what happens when each stage fails. Lay out the plan, explain how the orchestrator computes what to rerun, and say what "reproduce the run" can and cannot promise. Level 4 of 4 · about 20 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Sort the stages by the cost to rerun them: tokenizer, evaluation, quantization and the server are cheap and rerun in hours, supervised tuning and alignment take days, so the base checkpoint is kept and only those stages rerun, and pre-training takes weeks and a budget in the millions, so the plan is the last good checkpoint plus revised downstream stages. The rerun set falls out of the typed, hashed dependency graph: invalidate the failed stage and every descendant. A replay promises the same code, recipe and source data hashes and the same headline metrics, not bit-identical weights or the same output hashes. Three cost classes. Class Stages Plan on failure Cheap, hours Tokenizer, eval, quantization, inference server Rerun Medium, days SFT, DPO, constitutional refinement Keep the base model, rerun alignment Expensive, weeks and millions Pre-training Last good checkpoint plus revised downstream stages Writing this before the run means nobody improvises at four in the morning with an exhausted team. How the rerun set is computed. Every stage has typed inputs and outputs, and the output hash of a stage is the input hash of the next. A failure at the SFT stage invalidates it and every descendant: the reward model, the DPO policy, the refined policy, the eval report, the quantized weights and the server, which is stages six through twelve. A failure at quantization invalidates only quantization and the server. The orchestrator reads the graph from the manifest, so the rollback set is computed, not remembered. A change to the tokenizer invalidates everything downstream; a change to the eval set invalidates only the ship decision. Why hashes make it safe. Artifacts live in an immutable store addressed by content hash, never by a name such as latest. A partial rerun checks whether each expected output already exists at the right hash and skips the stage if it does. That is also how a partial rollback saves most of the wall clock: stages one through eight stay cached while nine through twelve rerun. The pipeline lesson's exercise measures exactly that saving. What reproduce means. Reproducible: the same manifest, code and infrastructure give a checkpoint with equivalent downstream metrics. Deterministic: bit-identical output. Distributed reduce order, kernel nondeterminism and mixed precision rounding make modern training reproducible but not deterministic; weights differ at a level around 1e-5 between runs while the metrics do not move. The cure is to log the input hash, the output hash and the headline metrics per stage. If the code, recipe and source data hashes and the headline metrics match, the run is reproduced even when a weight artifact and the input hashes after it get new values, and a bit-level diff is the wrong debugging tool. The lesson's rule that the input hash, the output hash and the metrics all match holds in full for the stages with deterministic output, such as the tokenizer and the eval data; for a weight artifact, which cannot be bit-identical, the metrics carry the check. Budget as part of the plan. The pre-run cost estimate uses six times parameters times tokens for the training compute, divided by peak throughput and utilization, at the rental rate. If the estimate exceeds the cost gate the pipeline refuses to start. After each stage the remaining budget is rechecked, so an overrun in one stage changes the gate for the next instead of being discovered when the money is gone. Plausible wrong answers. "Rerun from the start to be safe." The expensive stage costs weeks; the typed graph tells you exactly which stages are invalid. "Keep the latest checkpoint file and overwrite it each step." A mutable name cannot be verified or replayed; content addressing is what makes the rollback set trustworthy. "If the weights are not bit-identical, the pipeline is not reproducible." Distributed training is not deterministic; reproducibility is defined on the code, recipe and source data hashes and the metrics. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why not name artifacts by version string? Expected: two artifacts can share a name and differ in content; the hash is the identity, and a name like latest is a trap. (level 4) The reward model and the DPO policy both depend on the SFT checkpoint. What can run in parallel and what must wait? Expected: the two can run together after SFT; the refined policy waits for both, and its input hash must be a deterministic combination of both outputs. (level 4) A corrupted checkpoint is discovered after alignment finished. Which plan applies? Expected: the expensive class; take the last good pre-training checkpoint and rerun the medium and cheap stages, never the full pre-training. (level 4) A teammate reports that their replay has different weights. Is the run broken? Expected: not by itself; compare the code, recipe and source data hashes and the headline metrics, and only a mismatch there means the run is not reproduced. Where it is taught. The complete LLM pipeline lesson gives the three cost classes, the descendant rule, the content-addressed store and the distinction between reproducible and deterministic. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib), Rust. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line You built a GPT-2 Small from scratch in Lesson 04. Frontier open models in 2026 are the same family with five or six concrete changes. RMSNorm instead of LayerNorm. SwiGLU instead of GELU. RoPE instead of learned positions. GQA or MLA instead of full MHA. Mixture-of-Experts at scale. The math you already know covers 95% of them. This lesson reads Llama 3, DeepSeek-V3, Mixtral, Qwen, and Gemma side by side and names the exact line where each architecture diverges. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means RMSNorm "LayerNorm without the mean" Normalize by root mean square only, with a learned scale — cheaper and comparable to LayerNorm RoPE "Rotary positions" Rotate each Q and K vector in 2D pairs by an angle that depends on position — extrapolates beyond training length with scaling tricks SwiGLU "The new MLP activation" Gated linear unit with Swish: (xW1) * sigmoid(xW1) * xV — standard in every 2024+ open model GQA "Middle ground attention" Grouped-Query Attention: G groups of Q heads share one K and one V head — shrinks KV cache without MQA's accuracy hit MLA "DeepSeek's attention" Multi-Head Latent Attention: compress K/V into a shared low-rank latent, decompress per head — smallest KV cache for large models MoE "Sparse experts" Mixture of Experts: N MLPs per block, router picks top-k per token — huge total params, small active params Top-k routing "Pick k experts per token" The router computes a score per expert and activates the k highest — typical k is 2 (Mixtral) to 8 (DeepSeek) YaRN "Stretch RoPE" Yet another RoPE extension — interpolates rotary angles to extend context from 8k to 128k+ at inference time Sliding-window attention "Don't attend to everything" Each token attends only to the last $W$ tokens — caps attention cost at $O(W)$ per token, used in Gemma 2 and early Mistral Active params "What runs per token" For MoE models, the parameter count that sees a forward pass per token (much smaller than total params) — governs per-token FLOPs The problem In plain words first Today's open models (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma, DeepSeek) are still GPT-2's design: token embeddings, a stack of attention-plus-MLP blocks, and an output layer. What changed is a handful of well-understood parts: a cheaper normalisation (RMSNorm), positions encoded by rotating vectors (RoPE), a gated MLP (SwiGLU), attention heads that share keys and values to shrink the memory cache (GQA, MLA), and mixture-of-experts layers that switch on only a few sub-networks per token. Everything you need to know about a model's size and memory follows from its config.json . This lesson runs the lesson's calculator, builds six real models from their published configs without downloading any weights to count their parameters exactly, and checks three of the six "knobs" numerically. No model is trained. In Lesson 10.4 you wrote 350 lines of numpy and had a GPT-2-shaped model. Llama 3 405B has a 200-page technical report. Your instinct is that these are different beasts. They are not. The 200 pages describe the same object with five or six well-motivated modifications, plus a thousand implementation details about scaling. The skeleton -- embedding, transformer blocks, attention, MLP, norm, head -- is unchanged. This lesson is a diff. For each major open model family, we list exactly what changed from GPT-2, why, and what it cost. When you are done you can read a fresh model card and mentally translate it back to the GPT-2 baseline. The practical payoff is that when Meta releases Llama 5 or DeepSeek releases V4, you will not need a new mental model. You will look at the config, see which of the well-known knobs moved, and know what the downstream implications are. The 2026 architectures are a finite toolbox. Each new model picks a different subset. Idea 1 · The Invariant Core All autoregressive open models share: Token embedding matrix (vocab_size x hidden_dim). Stack of N decoder blocks: norm, self-attention, residual, norm, MLP, residual. Final norm and linear head projecting to vocab_size (often weight-tied with embeddings). Causal mask, next-token cross-entropy loss. That is the shape. The rest is knobs. Idea 2 · The Six Knobs That Actually Move Across every 2024-2026 frontier open model, the same six design choices get picked over and over: Normalization. LayerNorm -> RMSNorm. Positional encoding. Learned absolute -> RoPE (plus variants: YaRN, NTK). Activation. GELU -> SwiGLU (or GeGLU). Attention head sharing. MHA -> GQA -> MQA -> MLA. Dense vs sparse MLP. Dense -> Mixture-of-Experts. Pre-norm placement. Pre-norm stays. Post-norm is gone. Everything else (learning rate schedule, data mix, batch size, context length) lives in the training config, not the architecture. Six knobs. Idea 3 · Knob 1: RMSNorm LayerNorm subtracts mean, divides by std, scales, and shifts. RMSNorm keeps only the scale: ( x ) = mean ( x 2 ) + ϵ ​ x ​ ⋅ γ No mean subtraction. No bias. No mean to compute and no bias to add. Zhang and Sennrich (2019) argued it matched LayerNorm on machine translation while being 10% faster. Every modern open model runs it. Cost: none. Benefit: small throughput win, simpler code. Idea 4 · Knob 2: RoPE Learned position embeddings were a 1024-slot lookup table in GPT-2. Context 1025 is off the end of the table. Models cannot extrapolate beyond their training length. Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE, Su et al. 2021) injects position by rotating each Q and K vector in pairs before the attention dot product. The angle of rotation is a deterministic function of position, so there is nothing learned and nothing to run out of. With scaling tricks (NTK-aware interpolation, YaRN), a model trained on 8k context can stretch to 128k at inference with modest accuracy loss. Copy Every Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, and Gemma uses RoPE. Gemma 2 uses a hybrid (RoPE on most layers, local sliding-window attention on others). Idea 5 · Knob 3: SwiGLU GPT-2's MLP is x -> gelu(xW1 + b1) -> (...)W2 + b2 . SwiGLU (Shazeer 2020) replaces the activation with a gated product: ( x ) = ( x W 1 ​ ) ⋅ sigmoid ( x W 1 ​ ) ⋅ x V Two projections in parallel instead of one, gated by the Swish activation. Empirically stronger on perplexity per parameter. PaLM and the first LLaMA (2023) adopted it, and everyone followed. The MLP's hidden size is usually set so that total parameter count matches the original dense MLP: if GPT-2 used ff_dim = 4 * hidden , SwiGLU uses ff_dim = (2/3) * 4 * hidden = 8/3 * hidden . Idea 6 · Knob 4: Attention Head Sharing GPT-2 used Multi-Head Attention (MHA) : every head has its own Q, K, V projection. Multi-Query Attention (MQA, Shazeer 2019) shares one K and one V across all heads. Cuts the KV cache by num_heads, which is a 12x to 32x reduction on a typical model. Accuracy drops slightly on hard benchmarks. Grouped-Query Attention (GQA, Ainslie et al. 2023) is the middle ground: groups of Q heads share one K and one V. Llama 3 8B uses GQA with 32 Q heads and 8 KV heads ( ), so the KV cache shrinks 4x versus full MHA. Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA, DeepSeek 2024) compresses K and V into a shared low-rank latent, projecting them back up per head. Further reduces KV cache while preserving per-head expressiveness. DeepSeek-V2 and V3 rely on this for their long-context performance. Scheme KV Heads KV Cache Accuracy MHA num_heads full best GQA num_groups (G < num_heads) num_heads / G reduction near-MHA MQA 1 num_heads reduction small hit MLA latent, per-head decompression smaller than MQA near-MHA For any model above ~13B parameters, GQA or MLA is effectively mandatory. Full MHA at scale is a KV cache disaster. Idea 7 · Knob 5: Mixture of Experts A dense MLP activates all its parameters for every token. An MoE MLP has K experts per block and a router that picks the top-k experts per token (typically top-2). Only those experts' weights see a forward pass for that token. Copy The appeal: you can have 64 experts of size 7B each (so total param count is huge) while only running 2 of them per token (so per-token compute matches a dense 7B model). Mixtral 8x7B has 47B total parameters but activates only 13B per token. DeepSeek-V3 has 671B total parameters but activates only 37B per token. Pros: same compute, more parameters, better capacity. Cons: the expert memory still has to live somewhere (so serving needs more VRAM than a dense equivalent), load-balancing the router is hard, and fine-tuning the router during alignment is its own research area. Idea 8 · Knob 6: Pre-norm stays The original transformer applied layer norm after each sublayer. Every open model since GPT-2 puts it before each sublayer. Pre-norm is strictly easier to train at depth. Nothing to argue about. Idea 9 · Model-by-Model Diff Here is the table that makes all of this concrete. RMSNorm is universal. SwiGLU or its GeGLU cousin is universal. RoPE is universal. GQA is universal above 7B except when replaced by MLA. MoE is the differentiator at the top end. Idea 10 · Reading a config.json Llama 3 8B config: Copy Every field corresponds to something you have already implemented. Newer configs add a few fields that change the arithmetic, so the calculator reads them when they are present: head_dim : set explicitly when it is not hidden_size / num_attention_heads . Gemma 2 9B has hidden 3584 and 16 heads but head_dim 256, so its Q projection is 3584 x 4096, not square. tie_word_embeddings : whether the LM head reuses the embedding matrix. Llama 3 8B does not tie, which is 525M parameters you miss if you only count the embedding once. layer_types and sliding_window : which layers attend to the full context and which only to the last W tokens. hidden_size : embedding dimension. intermediate_size : MLP hidden size (3.5x hidden -- SwiGLU math). num_hidden_layers : stack depth. num_attention_heads : Q heads. num_key_value_heads : KV heads (GQA). max_position_embeddings : training context length. rope_theta : RoPE base frequency. Meta scaled it from the default 10k to 500k for long-context extrapolation. rms_norm_eps : numerical stability. vocab_size : tokens. From these alone you compute total parameters, KV cache, and peak activation memory. See code/main.py for the exact formulas. Idea 11 · Activation memory budget Activations dominate training memory above a few billion parameters. The rule of thumb for pre-training (with gradient checkpointing): Copy For Llama 3 8B at batch 1, seq 8192, BF16, 32 layers, hidden 4096: about 2 GB of activations with full checkpointing (one BF16 copy of each layer's input), and tens of GB without checkpointing even with FlashAttention. This is why flash-attention and ring-attention matter -- they rewrite the attention computation so activations fit. Idea 12 · KV Cache budget For inference at max context: Copy Llama 3 8B at 128k context, BF16, head_dim = hidden / num_heads = 128: 2 * 32 * 8 * 128 * 131072 * 2 = 17.2 GB per sequence. The 8B weights are 16 GB in BF16. The KV cache for a single 128k sequence is larger than the weights. This is the memory pressure driving GQA, MLA, and KV cache quantization research. The formula assumes every layer caches the whole sequence. A sliding-window layer only ever needs the last W tokens, so for hybrid models the sum runs per layer: Copy Spark-X2.5 4B runs three sliding-window layers ( ) for every full-attention layer: 9 full and 27 sliding out of 36. At its 1M-token context that is about 38.7 GB (36 GiB) per sequence in BF16. If all 36 layers cached the full context it would be 154.6 GB (144 GiB). The full layers carry nearly the whole cost, which is why the ratio of full to sliding layers is the number to read first on a long-context model. Idea 13 · When Each Model Wins Single 80GB GPU, no MoE : Llama 3 8B, Mistral 7B, Gemma 2 9B. Easy to serve, wide tooling. Single node (8x80GB), big capacity : Llama 3 70B, Qwen 2.5 72B. Highest dense open capability. Biggest open capability, accept MoE complexity : DeepSeek V3, Mixtral 8x22B. Best capability per active FLOP. Long-context needs : Llama 3 (128k with RoPE scaling), DeepSeek (MLA advantage). Low-latency serving : Gemma 2 9B (sliding window cuts long-context compute). Long context on a small memory budget : hybrid sliding-window models such as Spark-X2.5 4B, where only a quarter of the layers pay for the full context. In plain words first The idea in one line Lesson 7.16 proved the math: the Leviathan rejection rule preserves the verifier's distribution exactly. This lesson is the training-stack view of 2026 production speculative decoding. EAGLE-3 turned the draft model from a cheap approximation into a purpose-built tiny network trained on the verifier's own hidden states, then added a training-time test loop that aligns its train and inference distributions. Result: 3× to 6.5× end-to-end speedup, accepted per-token rates above 0.9 on chat, no distributional tradeoff. Every production inference stack Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Leviathan rule "min(1, q over p)" Bernoulli accept/reject with probability min(1, q(d)/p(d)) , preserves the verifier distribution exactly when you sample from the residual on rejection Residual distribution "(q minus p) plus, normalized" (q - p)_+ clamped at zero and renormalized — the correct distribution to sample from on rejection Acceptance rate α "how often the draft is right" Expected per-token Bernoulli-success probability under the rejection rule; governs all speedup math EAGLE-1 "hidden-state draft" Tiny transformer draft conditioned on the verifier's last-layer hidden state (Li et al., 2024) EAGLE-2 "dynamic draft tree" EAGLE-1 plus a tree of candidate continuations scored with tree attention in one verifier pass EAGLE-3 "training-time test" Drops the feature-prediction loss, trains on direct token prediction with the draft fed its own outputs during training Training-time test (TTT) "exposure bias fix" Run the draft autoregressively during training so train and test input distributions match — the direct analog of scheduled sampling KV rollback "undo rejected drafts" Bookkeeping that resets the verifier's KV cache to the accepted-prefix length after a rejection Bonus token "the free one" When all N drafts accept, sample one extra from q_{N+1} at no additional verifier cost Tree attention "verify many candidates at once" Attention with a non-causal mask that respects the topology of a draft tree; computes q_i for every node in the tree in one forward pass The problem In plain words first A big language model writes one token per forward pass, and each pass is slow mainly because all its weights must be read from memory. Speculative decoding lets a small, fast draft guess the next few tokens; the big model then checks all the guesses in one pass. A clever accept/reject rule keeps exactly the guesses the big model would have produced at the same rate, and replaces the first wrong one with a correct sample, so the output is identical in distribution to running the big model alone, only faster. How much faster depends almost entirely on one number: the acceptance rate α, how often the big model agrees with the draft. EAGLE-3, the 2025 state of the art, is a tiny draft network that reads the big model's own hidden states so that α is high. This lesson runs the lesson's simulator, computes the theory exactly, and measures α between two real models (SmolLM2 135M drafting for SmolLM2 360M) on chat, code and list prompts. No model is trained. Autoregressive decoding on a 70B model runs at maybe 35 tokens per second on one H100 (in FP8, so that the 70 GB of weights fit). The GPU is nowhere near saturated. Memory bandwidth is the ceiling: every token loads 70B of weights from HBM, does one step of arithmetic, and produces one float. The compute units sit mostly idle. Speculative decoding turns that into a throughput problem you can actually solve. A cheap draft proposes N tokens in N small forward passes. The verifier runs once on the prefix plus all N drafts. If the verifier's distribution at position i agrees with the draft (in a statistical sense we will make precise), we accept; if not, we reject and sample a correction from the residual distribution. A single big-model forward produces up to N+1 accepted tokens instead of one. The theorem that matters is Leviathan, Kalman, Matias (ICML 2023): the output distribution is identical to what sampling from the verifier directly would have produced. Not approximately. Identically. This is the entire reason speculative decoding is acceptable in production — it is a pure latency optimization with no quality tradeoff. What Lesson 7.16 gave you was the math. What this lesson gives you is the training stack. A good draft is worth 2× more speedup than a cheap draft. EAGLE, EAGLE-2, and EAGLE-3 (Li et al., 2024–2025) turned "draft = smaller version of the same model" into a precise engineering discipline. In 2026, production inference servers support EAGLE-3 drafts for most popular open models. Idea 1 · The invariant: Leviathan rejection sampling Let p(t) be the draft's distribution for the next token given some prefix, and q(t) be the verifier's. Sample a draft token d ~ p . Accept with probability min(1, q(d) / p(d)) . On reject, sample from the residual distribution (q - p)_+ / ||(q - p)_+||_1 . The resulting samples are distributed according to q . This is true regardless of how bad p is — the worse it is, the more often you reject, but the output remains exact. Stack N of these calls back to back using one verifier forward pass on prefix + d_1 + ... + d_N . The verifier returns q_1, q_2, ..., q_{N+1} simultaneously. Walk left to right. On the first rejection at position j , sample from residual(q_j, p_j) and stop. On full acceptance, sample one bonus token from q_{N+1} . Idea 2 · What determines speedup Let α be the expected acceptance rate per drafted token. Let c = cost(draft) / cost(verifier) be the cost ratio. The expected number of accepted tokens per verifier forward is: 1 − α N + 1 ​ The expected total wall time per accepted token is (N * c + 1) / E[accepted] . Minimize that with respect to N and you get the sweet spot. For α = 0.8, c = 0.05 the formula gives a speedup of about 3× from N ≈ 5 upward (best at 8, 3.1×). For α = 0.95, c = 0.02 it keeps improving to very long drafts (5.3 tokens per call at N = 5, about 10× at N ≈ 30). Real systems use far shorter drafts, because the formula assumes independent acceptances and a verifier whose cost does not grow with N (see the exact computation after Build it). The single biggest lever is α . Going from α = 0.6 (vanilla draft) to α = 0.9 (EAGLE-3) at fixed N = 5 takes you from 2.4 expected tokens per verifier forward to 4.7. Nearly 2× more throughput from the same verifier. Idea 3 · The two-year progression Vanilla speculative (Leviathan, 2023). Draft model is an independently trained smaller LLM from the same family. Easy to wire up, α ≈ 0.6 , speedup around 2× at best. EAGLE-1 (Li et al., 2024). Draft is a tiny transformer — typically one or two layers — that takes the verifier's last-layer hidden state as input and predicts the next token directly. Because the draft sees the verifier's feature representation, its distribution is much closer to the verifier's. α climbs to 0.7–0.8. EAGLE-2 (Li et al., 2024). Adds a dynamic draft tree: instead of proposing a single sequence of N tokens, propose a small tree of candidates, score each with the verifier in one forward pass (tree attention), and walk the highest-probability path. Draft length becomes adaptive per step. α per accepted-path token climbs above 0.85. EAGLE-3 (Li et al., 2025, NeurIPS). Two more changes. First, drop the feature-prediction loss entirely — EAGLE-1/2 trained the draft to match the verifier's hidden states, which caps how much data helps. EAGLE-3 trains directly on token prediction. Second, training-time test (TTT): during draft training, feed the draft's own previous predictions back as inputs over multiple steps, the same way it operates at inference. This aligns the train and test distributions and stops error accumulation. Measured speedup: up to 6.5× on chat, 38% throughput improvement at batch 64 in SGLang on H100. Idea 4 · KV cache rollback Verification extends the verifier's KV cache by N entries in one pass. If rejection happens at position j , the cache contents past position j-1 are now wrong. Two common implementations: write to a scratch buffer and commit on acceptance (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM), or keep a physical KV cache plus a logical length and truncate on reject. Either way, the rollback cost is bytes per layer per head, which is negligible next to the forward-pass cost. For EAGLE-2 tree search, the verifier runs attention with a non-causal mask that respects tree topology. The engineering is fiddly but the computation is a standard flash-attention call with a custom mask. Debug a failure Two changes shipped in one week: the target model moved to its next version, and a new customer whose traffic is mostly code was routed onto the same cluster. Speculative decoding has been on for months. Since then the mean inter-token latency fell 25 percent, the P99 rose 15 percent, and throughput at the usual concurrency is down. Diagnose it. Level 4 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Both changes attack acceptance. The draft head was trained against the previous target version, so its distribution drifted and more drafts reject; the code traffic shifts the input distribution away from the general chat data the head was trained on, where acceptance falls into the 0.4 to 0.6 band. A rejected draft costs a verify and a re-roll, two passes that serialize under a full batch, which is exactly a tail that worsens while the mean still improves. Read acceptance per traffic slice and per target version from the engine's speculative metrics, retrain or roll back to a head aligned with the new target, and gate speculation per request class. Why mean and tail move in opposite directions. Most requests still accept most drafts, so their inter-token latency falls and the mean improves. The requests that reject early pay the draft steps, the verify and a second target pass for the correction, and under a full batch those passes queue behind each other. The tail is where the rejected requests live. Watch P99, not P50. Cause one: a draft one version behind. A hidden-state draft is trained to predict a specific target's next token from that target's features. A new target version changes the features and the distribution, and the draft's agreement with it drops. The capstone's first exercise is to measure this degradation and to build the alert for it. Cause two: a domain the head never saw. A head trained on general chat sits at 0.6 to 0.8 acceptance there and at 0.4 to 0.6 on code, medical or legal traffic. Code tokens are predictable for a draft trained on code, and poorly predicted by one that was not. Below an acceptance of about 0.55 at high concurrency speculation is net negative, so the new customer may have pushed the cluster under the floor. The diagnosis. Pull accepted draft tokens and proposed draft tokens per request from the engine, divide the first by the second, and split by target version and by customer or request class. One number for the whole cluster hides both causes. Compare the chat slice before and after the upgrade: if it fell, the version drift is real. Compare the code slice against the chat slice at the same version: if it sits far lower, the domain shift is real. Confirm the tail story by bucketing P99 by acceptance; the slow tail should be the low-acceptance slice. The fix. Retrain the head against the new target version, or roll the target back until the aligned head is ready. Route the code customer to a plain decode pool, or train a code-specific head; the training job is light next to fine-tuning the target. Gate speculation per request class on measured acceptance, with an n-gram or draft-free fallback below the floor. Alert on acceptance per slice so the next version bump cannot ship without the draft. Plausible wrong answers. "Increase the draft length to win back throughput." More drafts at low acceptance are mostly rejected and their cost is still paid; the tail gets worse. "Turn speculation off everywhere." The chat slice may still pay; gate by slice and fix the head. "The new target is just slower; speculation has nothing to do with it." A plain-decode benchmark of the new target settles that in minutes, and the mean improving while the tail worsens points at rejections. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why can the mean improve while throughput falls? Expected: the accepted requests get faster, but the rejected ones consume two target passes each, and at a full batch that extra work displaces other requests. (level 4) Design the alert in two sentences. Expected: compute acceptance per slice and per target version over a short window and compare against the baseline recorded at rollout; page when a slice crosses the floor or drops a fixed share from its baseline. (level 4) What is the fallback when acceptance drops on one slice only? Expected: switch that slice to an n-gram draft or to plain decoding while the head is retrained, and keep speculation where it still pays. (level 4) How does this change your release process? Expected: a target upgrade ships together with a draft trained against it, and the benchmark that gates the release reports acceptance and P99 per slice. Where it is taught. The speculative decoding server capstone sets the drift measurement and the fallback exercises, the production EAGLE-3 lesson explains the tail and the acceptance floor, and the EAGLE-3 lesson explains why the draft is tied to one target version. Explain the mechanism Walk the line from a separate small draft model to the current generation of hidden-state drafts. What limitation did each step remove, and why does feeding the draft the verifier's internal features help so much? Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A separate small model from the same family accepts around 0.6 of its tokens, because its distribution drifts from the verifier's. The first hidden-state draft replaces it with a one or two layer network that reads the verifier's last-layer features, so the draft starts from the verifier's own representation and acceptance rises to 0.7 to 0.8. The second generation proposes a tree of candidates and verifies every branch in one pass with a tree-shaped attention mask, lifting acceptance per accepted-path token above 0.85. The third drops the feature-matching loss, trains on direct token prediction, and feeds the draft its own previous outputs during training, which removes exposure bias and reaches 0.88 to 0.92. The progression. Generation Draft Acceptance Training cost Separate small model an independently trained smaller model 0.55 to 0.70 none Extra heads on the verifier several output heads predicting positions ahead 0.65 to 0.75 about 1B supervised tokens First hidden-state draft one transformer layer on the verifier's last hidden state 0.70 to 0.80 about 60B tokens Dynamic draft tree the same plus a tree of candidates 0.80 to 0.88 about 60B tokens Multi-layer features plus training-time test fuses several verifier layers; trained on its own outputs 0.88 to 0.92 about 60 to 200B tokens Why the hidden state helps. A separate draft re-derives from raw tokens what the verifier has already computed. The verifier's last hidden state at position t is a rich summary of the prefix, and a tiny network that reads it predicts the verifier's next token far better than a small model that reads only the token ids. The draft becomes a reader of the verifier instead of an imitation of it. What the tree adds. A linear chain of drafts dies at the first miss. A tree proposes several candidates at each depth, grows wider where the draft is uncertain and stays narrow where it is confident, and the verifier scores every node in one forward pass with a mask that lets each node attend only to its ancestors. The longest accepted path wins. Verification cost barely moves, because it is still one forward pass. What the third generation fixes. The earlier hidden-state drafts were trained to match the verifier's features, which capped how much extra data could help. The third generation trains on token prediction directly, and during training it feeds the draft its own previous predictions over several steps, the way it runs at inference. That aligns the training inputs with the inference inputs and stops error accumulation, the same fix that scheduled sampling gave sequence models. The paper reports up to 6.5 times end-to-end on chat and a 38 percent throughput gain at a batch of 64 on a production engine. The draft is only as good as its traffic. A general-purpose draft head trained on chat data drops to 0.4 to 0.6 acceptance on code, medical or legal traffic. A domain-specific head recovers it, and training one is a light job next to fine-tuning the verifier. Plausible wrong answers. "A larger separate draft model is the main lever." Alignment with the verifier matters more than size; a one-layer draft on hidden states beats a far larger independent model. "The hidden-state draft changes the verifier's output distribution to gain acceptance." The rejection rule keeps the output exact; the draft only changes how often it is right. "A tree needs one verifier pass per branch." All branches are verified in one pass under the tree mask. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why did matching the verifier's features cap the first generations? Expected: the feature loss asks the draft to reproduce hidden states rather than predict tokens, so more training data stopped helping; the third generation trains on tokens. (level 3) What is exposure bias in this setting? Expected: the draft was trained on teacher-forced verifier inputs and run on its own outputs; the mismatch compounds over the draft steps. (level 4) What does the tree cost? Expected: a non-causal attention mask that follows the tree topology, extra stored keys and values for the tree nodes, and scheduler complexity; the verifier still runs once. (level 4) How do you compare the extra-heads design with the hidden-state draft? Expected: no second model to deploy and simpler serving, against a somewhat lower acceptance and a supervised fine-tuning stage on the verifier. Where it is taught. In plain words first The idea in one line Softmax attention spreads a small amount of probability over every non-matching token. Over 100k tokens that noise adds up and drowns the signal. Differential Transformer (Ye et al., ICLR 2025) fixes it by computing attention as the difference of two softmaxes, subtracting the shared noise floor. DIFF V2 (Microsoft, January 2026) is the production-stack rewrite: matching decode latency to baseline Transformer, no custom kernels, FlashAttention-compatible. This lesson is V1 to V2 end-to-end, with a working toy implementation of the difference operation you can r Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Differential attention "Two softmaxes minus each other" Split Q, K into two halves, compute two softmax maps, subtract the second (scaled by $\lambda$) from the first, then multiply by V Noise floor "The non-zero tail of softmax" The $O(1/N)$ weight softmax puts on every unrelated token, which sums to $O(1)$ across long contexts lambda "The subtraction scale" Per-head learnable scalar parameterized as exp(lq1.lk1) - exp(lq2.lk2) + lambda_init ; can be negative DIFF V1 "The ICLR 2025 version" Original Differential Transformer; halves head dim to preserve parameter count, needs custom kernel, slower decode DIFF V2 "The January 2026 fix" Doubles Q heads keeping KV heads; matches baseline decode speed and works with FlashAttention Per-head RMSNorm "The V1 stabilizer" Extra norm V1 applied after the difference; V2 removed it to prevent late-training instability Signal-to-noise ratio "How much attention is wasted" Ratio of weight on the true signal position to average weight on unrelated positions Lost in the middle "Long-context failure mode" Empirical phenomenon where retrieval accuracy dips for documents in the middle of a long context — DIFF attention reduces this Arithmetic intensity "FLOPs per byte loaded" Ratio V2 increased at decode by doubling queries per KV load; important for memory-bound decode The problem In plain words first Softmax attention can never give a token exactly zero weight, so every irrelevant token in a long context gets a little attention, and over a hundred thousand tokens those little amounts add up. Differential attention computes two attention maps and subtracts one from the other, like noise-cancelling headphones: whatever both maps agree on (the background) cancels, while what only the first map sees (the signal) survives. Version 2 (January 2026) makes the idea cheap: the same speed and memory at decode as a normal Transformer and no special kernels. It is still a research architecture; no widely used open model ships it yet. This lesson runs the lesson's toy, computes exactly when subtraction helps and when it hurts, and measures how a real model's attention heads actually behave on a long context with one fact hidden in it. No model is trained. Standard softmax attention has a mathematical property that turns into an operational headache at scale. For a query q , the attention weights are softmax(qK^T / sqrt(d)) . Softmax can never produce exact zeros: every non-matching token gets some positive mass. That residual mass is noise, and it scales with context length. At 128k tokens, even if each non-matching token gets only 0.0001% of the probability, 127,999 of them combined contribute about 13% of the total. The model has to learn to route around a noise floor that grows with context. Empirically this shows up as attention-head interference: hallucinated citations in long-context RAG, lost-in-the-middle failures on 100k-token retrieval tasks, and subtle accuracy degradation on needle-in-haystack benchmarks past 32k. The Differential Transformer paper (arXiv:2410.05258, ICLR 2025) measured the gap: DIFF Transformers hit lower perplexity, higher long-context accuracy, and fewer hallucinations than same-size baselines. DIFF V1 had three problems that kept it out of frontier pre-training pipelines. Its value cache had to be loaded twice per decode step, it required custom CUDA kernels that broke FlashAttention compatibility, and its per-head RMSNorm had to scale outputs up by about √n (about 90× at 8K tokens), which made training unstable at high learning rates. DIFF V2 (Microsoft unilm blog, January 20, 2026) fixed all three. This lesson walks both versions, builds the difference operator, and benchmarks noise cancellation on a toy query. Idea 1 · The noise floor of softmax For a query q and keys K = [k_1, ..., k_N] , attention weights are: ​ = ∑ j ​ exp ( q ⋅ k j ​ / d ​ ) exp ( q ⋅ k i ​ / d ​ ) ​ No w_i is ever zero. If k_i is completely unrelated to q , the score q . k_i is not 0 — it fluctuates around zero with variance ||q||^2 / d . After softmax normalization, each unrelated token still contributes O(1/N) to the weighted sum. The total contribution of unrelated tokens is O((N-1)/N) = O(1) — not a small quantity. What the model wants is something like a hard top-k: high weight on matching tokens, near-zero weight everywhere else. Softmax is too smooth to do that directly. Idea 2 · The differential idea Split each head's Q and K projections into two: ​ , Q 2 ​ ) and ​ , K 2 ​ ) . Compute two attention maps: ​ A 2 ​ ​ = softmax ( Q 1 ​ K 1 T ​ / d ​ ) = softmax ( Q 2 ​ K 2 T ​ / d ​ ) ​ Output: = ( A 1 ​ − λ ⋅ A 2 ​ ) V The subtraction cancels whatever noise distribution the two maps share. If both maps have roughly uniform weight on the 127k unrelated tokens (which they will, at random initialization), those cancel. The signal — peaked weight on the few actually relevant tokens — only cancels if it appears in both maps at the same magnitude, which it will not once the model trains. lambda is a learnable scalar per head, parameterized as lambda = exp(lambda_q1 dot lambda_k1) - exp(lambda_q2 dot lambda_k2) + lambda_init . It can be negative. In V1, lambda_init depends on the layer l : 0.8 - 0.6 * exp(-0.3 * (l - 1)) , which rises from 0.2 in the first layer toward 0.8. V2 replaces all of this with a per-token, per-head λ: a small projection of the token's hidden state passed through a sigmoid, so λ lies between 0 and 1. Idea 3 · Why this matches headed noise-canceling Think of two noisy microphones recording the same voice. Both pick up the speaker plus correlated background noise. Subtract one from the other and the shared noise drops out. The voice survives because the two signals differ in phase or amplitude by enough to prevent full cancellation. The per-head lambda learns exactly this balance. Idea 4 · V1 vs V2: the diff V1 kept the parameter count equal to the baseline Transformer. To get two queries per head it halved the head dimension. That cost head expressiveness and — more painfully — halved the value cache per head. Decode had to load the value cache twice per step (once per softmax branch). Result: decode slower than baseline despite matching parameter count. V2 doubles the number of query heads and keeps the KV heads the same. Adjacent query heads form a pair that shares the same keys and values (the same GQA group), so one standard FlashAttention call computes both maps of every pair. The head dimension stays the same as baseline. After the subtraction, the extra dimension is projected back down to match baseline Transformer's ​ projection. Three things happen at once: Decode speed matches baseline (KV cache is loaded once). FlashAttention runs unchanged (no custom kernel). Arithmetic intensity at decode goes up (more compute per byte loaded from HBM). V2 also removes the per-head RMSNorm that V1 applied after the subtraction. When attention is spread out, the subtracted output is small (about 1/√n of the values' size), so the norm must multiply it by about √n, roughly 90× at 8,192 tokens, and the resulting large gradients made training unstable at high learning rates. With the per-token sigmoid λ and shared values, the authors found the norm unnecessary, and V2's gradient norms match a standard Transformer's. Many heads use the first token as a parking place: at up to 2,047 tokens the median head puts 35 to 44% of its weight on token 0, and at 4,095 tokens 30% of the 480 heads still put more than half there. This attention sink is how a softmax head says "nothing here is relevant", since it cannot give everything zero. It is exactly the problem that learned sinks (gpt-oss) and output gates (Qwen3-Next) address in production, and that differential attention addresses by subtraction. Two limits of this test. A single exact-match fact is the easiest long-context task; failures appear with several similar facts, paraphrased questions or much longer contexts, which is where the differential-attention papers report gains. And 4K is half of this model's trained context; real lost-in-the-middle tests go to 32K and beyond. Break it on purpose Set λ = 1 and give both branches identical query and key projections. Production models handle the same softmax problems in other ways: Attention sinks : softmax needs somewhere to put weight when nothing is relevant. gpt-oss adds a learned sink logit to each head; StreamingLLM-style serving keeps the first tokens in the cache for the same reason. Gated attention : Qwen3-Next multiplies each head's output by a sigmoid gate computed from the token, which removes the sink and reduces activation outliers. QK-norm : OLMo 2, Qwen3 and Gemma 3 normalise queries and keys before the dot product to keep attention logits from growing and destabilising training.
