Short answer. The expected tokens per verifier pass are (1 - alpha^(K + 1)) / (1 - alpha) ; at an acceptance of 0.8 and K of 4 that is 3.36, so about 3.36 times fewer big-model calls. The wall time per token is (K c + 1) over that expectation, where c is the draft's cost relative to the verifier, so a longer draft adds cost linearly while the geometric series saturates; at 0.8 acceptance and c of 0.05 the optimum sits around 5 to 7 drafts for about 3.2 times. The lever that matters is the acceptance rate: at a fixed K, a rise from 0.6 to 0.9 about doubles the expected tokens per pass. The formula. Each drafted token is accepted independently with probability alpha, and the step ends on the first rejected token, so the number of accepted drafts is a truncated geometric variable. Add the bonus token on full acceptance and the expectation is Copy alpha K tokens per pass 0.8 4 3.36 At a fixed K, a higher alpha raises every term of the series, so the expectation climbs steeply as alpha nears one. Where the draft's cost enters. One step costs K draft forwards plus one verifier forward, K c + 1 in verifier units. Divide by the expected tokens and you have the time per token. For a verifier at about 30 ms and a draft at about 3 ms, five drafts plus one verify is about 45 ms per step. The step emits between one and six tokens, so divide the 45 ms by the expected tokens per pass and compare the result with 30 ms for one plain token. As K grows the numerator grows linearly and the expectation flattens toward 1 / (1 - alpha) , so there is an optimum. alpha c best K speedup 0.8 0.05 about 5 to 7 about 3.2 times 0.95 0.02 about 8 to 10 toward 5 times What moves alpha. How close the draft's distribution is to the verifier's, which is a function of how the draft was built; the sampling temperature, where greedy against greedy accepts most; and the task, where code and structured output accept more than free-form prose. Where the formula stops being the whole story. At high concurrency the verify pass is no longer free: the decode batch already fills the memory bandwidth, and a rejected draft costs a verify and a re-roll. The production lesson's rule is that below an acceptance of about 0.55 speculation is net negative at high concurrency, so measure alpha on real traffic before you set K. Plausible wrong answers. "The speedup equals the draft length." Only if every draft is accepted; the geometric series and the draft cost cut it well below K. "Doubling K doubles throughput." Beyond the optimum the extra drafts are mostly rejected and their cost is paid anyway. "A draft ten times cheaper gives ten times the speedup." The draft cost sets c; the acceptance rate sets the expectation, and a cheap draft that is often wrong gains little. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) At an acceptance of 0.95 and a draft cost of 0.02, where is the optimum? Expected: around 8 to 10 drafts, with the speedup pushing toward 5 times. (level 3) Why does the expectation saturate as K grows? Expected: it is a geometric series; the probability that all drafts up to position K are accepted falls as alpha to the K, so late positions add almost nothing. (level 4) How does batch size change the arithmetic? Expected: the verifier's extra work per draft is no longer hidden behind idle bandwidth, so the effective cost of verification and of a rejection rises, and the break-even acceptance climbs toward 0.45 to 0.55. (level 4) What single measurement do you add to the dashboard? Expected: accepted draft tokens divided by proposed draft tokens, per traffic slice, so alpha is visible where the formula needs it. Where it is taught. The Phase 10 speculative decoding lesson derives the expectation, the EAGLE-3 lesson adds the draft cost and the optimum, the Phase 7 speculative decoding lesson gives the millisecond example, and the production EAGLE-3 lesson sets the break-even. a1034: Course home / Phase 10 · Build Your Own Language Model Trading compute for memory (gradient checkpointing) Lesson 10.34 70 min Build Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 10 Lesson 04 (Pre-Training Mini-GPT), Phase 10 Lesson 05 (Scaling & Distributed) Type : Build. Time : about 70 minutes. Code in : Python (with numpy, optional torch). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Backprop keeps every intermediate activation. At 70B parameters and 128K context that is 3 TB of activations per rank. Checkpointing trades FLOPs for memory: recompute instead of save. The question is which segments to drop, and the answer is not "all of them." Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Gradient checkpointing "Save memory by redoing forward" Store segment inputs only; recompute intermediates during backward to get gradient-support tensors Activation recomputation "Same as checkpointing" The HPC-flavored name for the same technique Segment size (k) "How many layers per checkpoint" Number of layers whose intermediates are dropped and rematerialized together Selective checkpointing "Korthikanti's trick" Recompute only expensive-to-store activations (attention softmax); keep cheap ones Full checkpointing "The naive version" Recompute every layer's intermediates in every segment Block checkpointing "Coarse-grained" Checkpoint whole transformer blocks; largest granularity FLOP overhead "The compute tax" Extra FLOPs per step = (recompute FLOPs) / (fwd + bwd FLOPs); 33% naive, 5% selective Activation offload "Ship to CPU" Move activations to CPU RAM across forward->backward; alternative to recompute sqrt-L rule "The classical optimum" For uniform-cost layers, optimal checkpoint spacing is $\sqrt{L}$ layers Attention-softmax volume "The O(L^2) problem" $L^2 \cdot \text{heads} \cdot \text{batch}$ floats; dominates activation memory at long contexts The problem In plain words first To compute gradients, backpropagation needs the intermediate results of the forward pass, so training normally keeps all of them in memory, and for long sequences that is far more than the model's own weights. Gradient checkpointing keeps only a few of them (say, each layer's input) and recomputes the rest during the backward pass when they are needed: more computation, much less memory, and exactly the same gradients. Selective checkpointing goes further by recomputing only what is cheap to recompute but expensive to store. This lesson runs the lesson's numpy version, computes the published memory formulas, and measures real checkpointing in PyTorch and Hugging Face on a real model. No model is trained. Training a transformer stores, for each layer, the inputs to every op that is differentiated in backward: the attention inputs, the Q/K/V projections, the softmax output, the FFN inputs, the norm outputs, and the residual stream. For a layer with hidden size d , sequence length L , batch B , this is on the order of 12 * B * L * d floats per layer. For d=8192, L=8192, B=1 , that's about 805M values, or 1.6 GB/layer in BF16 by this rough count. Korthikanti et al.'s exact count is 34 bytes per element of B·L·d without the attention scores, 2.1 GiB per layer and about 136 GiB for 64 layers when FlashAttention avoids storing scores, plus 5·heads·L/d bytes per element (another 20 GiB per layer at this length) if the scores are kept. That is before you multiply by microbatch size or factor in tensor-parallel copies. The two-sided bill: BF16 weights plus optimizer state might fit in 80GB, but activations push you past. Gradient checkpointing (aka activation recomputation) is the standard fix. Drop most activations; redo the forward during backward to get them back. Cost: extra FLOPs. Benefit: memory drops by the ratio of checkpoint segments to total layers. Done naively, checkpointing costs roughly 33% more FLOPs per step: one extra forward pass. Done well — selective checkpointing per the "smart selection" of Korthikanti et al. — you save 5x memory for under 5% FLOP overhead. And with FP8 matmuls, FSDP offload, and expert-parallel MoE this really matters: you can't afford either the memory or the wasted compute. Idea 1 · What Backward Actually Needs output = layer(input) . Backward wants grad_input and grad_params . To compute them it needs: input (to compute grad_params = input.T @ grad_output for linear layers) some activation derivative intermediates (the derivative of ReLU/GELU/softmax depends on the activation value) The forward pass stores these automatically in the autograd graph. Every tensor.retain_grad() and every op that needs its input retains a reference. Idea 2 · Naive Full Checkpointing Split the network into N segments. During forward, store only the input to each segment. When backward needs intermediates, rerun the segment's forward pass to materialize them, then differentiate. Example: 32-layer transformer split into 32 segments of 1 layer each. Memory: 32 layer-inputs (small) vs 32 * (activation volume per layer) (huge). Extra compute: 1 extra forward per segment, i.e., ~33% more forward FLOPs total (since backward is 2x forward, full step becomes 1 + 1 + 2 = 4 units instead of 1 + 2 = 3). This is the original Chen et al. 2016 recipe: one checkpoint every sqrt(L) layers to balance memory and compute. For , that's 8 checkpoints. Idea 3 · Selective Checkpointing (Korthikanti 2022) Not all activations cost the same. The attention softmax output is B*L*L*heads and grows quadratically with sequence length. The FFN hidden activation is B*L*4d and grows linearly. For long sequences the softmax dominates. Selective checkpointing keeps the cheap-to-store activations (linear projections, residuals) and recomputes only the expensive ones (attention). You pay minimal FLOPs to recompute but save the ) memory. Megatron-Core implements this as "selective" activation recomputation. Used in most 2024+ frontier training runs. Idea 4 · Offload Alternative to recompute: ship activations to CPU RAM between forward and backward. Requires PCIe bandwidth; beneficial when idle bandwidth exceeds the cost of rematerialization. Mixed strategies are common: checkpoint some layers, offload others. PyTorch offers activation offload as the context manager torch.autograd.graph.save_on_cpu() ; FSDP2's CPUOffloadPolicy offloads parameters, gradients and optimizer state instead. Offload shines when GPU is bottlenecked on memory but CPU-GPU transfer has headroom. Idea 5 · Recompute Cost Model Per-step FLOPs with naive checkpointing every k layers out of L : Copy With selective checkpointing you recompute only the attention kernel, not the whole layer: Copy Idea 6 · Memory Savings Model Activation volume per layer: A . For L layers, total activation memory: L * A . Full checkpoint (segment size 1): store only L * input_volume (~ L * 1/10 A for a standard transformer). Saves ~ 9 * L * A * 1/10 . Checkpoint every k layers: store L/k * A plus k-1 layers' worth within the active segment. At k = sqrt(L) , memory and recompute cost both scale with sqrt(L) — the optimal tradeoff for uniform-cost layers. Idea 7 · When Not to Checkpoint The innermost layers of a pipeline stage already in-flight. They have to finish anyway. The first and last layers if they dominate the stage's compute (rare in transformers). Attention kernels already using FlashAttention — Flash already recomputes the softmax fast, so additional layer-level checkpointing adds little on top. Idea 8 · Implementation Patterns Function wrapper: wrap a segment in torch.utils.checkpoint.checkpoint(fn, input) . PyTorch stores only input , recomputes everything else on backward. Decorator-based: label layers as checkpointable; the trainer decides at config time which segments get wrapped. Manual explicit recompute: write the backward pass yourself, calling a custom recompute_forward that duplicates the forward with the stored input. All three give the same functional result. Wrappers are the standard idiom. Idea 9 · Interaction with TP / PP / FP8 Tensor parallel: checkpoint inputs must be gathered or rescattered on recompute; handle the communication cost. Pipeline parallel: typical pattern is to checkpoint each pipeline-stage's forward so reverse-order microbatches can reuse activation memory. FP8 recompute: amax histories updated during recompute must match the original forward's, or the FP8 scale drifts. Most frameworks snapshot the scale. The same idea as a formula Activation memory per layer (Korthikanti et al., 16-bit, sequence , batch , hidden , heads, no tensor parallelism): ​ = s b h ( 34 + h 5 a s ​ ) bytes . The first term (projections, MLP, norms, dropout masks) grows linearly in ; the second (attention scores and softmax) quadratically. FlashAttention and selective recomputation both remove the second term. Use it: the same idea with real libraries torch.utils.checkpoint : from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint — the canonical wrapper in PyTorch. Wraps a function; stores only inputs, recomputes on backward. Megatron-Core activation recomputation : supports selective , full , and block modes. Standard in 2024+ frontier training. Activation offload in PyTorch : with torch.autograd.graph.save_on_cpu(pin_memory=True): around the forward pass moves saved activations to CPU memory and back during backward. (FSDP2's CPUOffloadPolicy offloads parameters, gradients and optimizer state, not activations.) DeepSpeed : ZeRO-Offload moves optimizer states and gradients to the CPU; its activation-checkpointing settings can also keep checkpoints in CPU memory ( cpu_checkpointing ). Selective checkpointing in PyTorch : torch.utils.checkpoint.checkpoint(..., context_fn=partial(create_selective_checkpoint_contexts, policy)) with a policy that marks ops as must-save or recompute (run after Use it). Hugging Face : model.gradient_checkpointing_enable() checkpoints every decoder layer. Part 2: twelve MLP blocks run without checkpointing, with PyTorch's selective checkpointing (a policy that saves matrix-multiply outputs and recomputes the rest) and with full checkpointing. No training; about 70 seconds on CPU. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Part 1. Without checkpointing, autograd keeps 2,633 MiB for one step of SmolLM2-135M on 2 × 512 tokens, about five times the model's weights in fp32 (540 MB). With Hugging Face's gradient_checkpointing_enable() it keeps 569 MiB: the 30 layer inputs (68 MiB), plus what sits outside the checkpointed layers, mostly the logits (192 MiB) and the loss computation over a 49,152-token vocabulary. Loss and gradients are identical (difference 0.0). The step took about 5% longer here; on GPUs the cost of one more forward pass is closer to the theoretical third, because there the backward pass is not as dominant. Part 2. For twelve MLP blocks, no checkpointing keeps 2,304 MiB, full checkpointing 192 MiB (just the block inputs) and selective checkpointing, which saves the outputs of the matrix multiplies and recomputes LayerNorm and GELU, 1,152 MiB. Selective cost no extra time (recomputing elementwise ops is cheap), full cost about 6% here. All three give identical gradients. Choosing what to save is a policy: save what is expensive to recompute (matrix multiplies), recompute what is cheap but large (elementwise results, attention scores). Break it on purpose Checkpoint a block that contains dropout, and recompute it during backward without restoring the random number generator's state. What happens to the gradients? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Selective activation recomputation (Megatron-Core's selective mode, PyTorch's selective activation checkpointing with policies) is the default in large-model training; full recompute is kept for the tightest memory budgets. FlashAttention in every training stack removes the quadratic attention-score memory, the biggest single activation cost at long context. Activation offload to CPU (PyTorch save_on_cpu , Megatron-Core fine-grained offloading) for long-context training where recompute is too slow. Sources: Korthikanti et al. , Chen et al. , PyTorch checkpoint docs , Megatron Bridge activation recomputation , FlashAttention-2 , PyTorch autograd saved tensors hooks . Recap What to keep from this lesson Backward needs forward intermediates; storing all of them can dwarf the weights. Checkpointing stores segment inputs and recomputes the rest: one more forward, identical gradients. Per layer: 34·sbh bytes plus 5·a·s²·b for attention scores; FlashAttention removes the second. Selective checkpointing keeps expensive-to-recompute tensors and recomputes cheap ones. Offload trades memory for PCIe traffic instead of FLOPs. Sweep segment size k from 1 to L . Plot FLOP overhead and memory. Find the knee of the curve. Implement selective checkpointing: store the attention-module input but not its intermediates. Measure memory (via torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated ) and step time. Solutions Solution P1 · Not quite to 68 MiB, and only slightly slower Not quite to 68 MiB: memory falls from 2,633 MiB to 569 MiB. The 30 layer inputs are indeed only 68 MiB, but the logits (2 × 512 × 49,152 numbers, 192 MiB) and the loss computation sit outside the checkpointed decoder layers and are still stored. With large vocabularies the output layer is a big part of what remains; chunked or fused cross-entropy losses exist for this reason. And the step was only about 5% slower on this CPU, with exactly the same gradients. Solution B1 · Different dropout masks, wrong gradients The recomputed forward uses different dropout masks, so the activations rebuilt in backward differ from the ones that produced the loss, and the gradients are computed for a network that never ran: wrong, and differently wrong at every step. Training may still appear to work, just worse and less reproducibly. This is why torch.utils.checkpoint saves and restores the random number generator state by default ( preserve_rng_state=True ), and why Megatron tracks separate RNG states for tensor-parallel ranks. The same applies to any non-deterministic op, and FP8 scaling factors must be replayed for the same reason. Covers 10.9 Models that critique themselves (Constitutional AI) Core ideas STaR : fine-tune on own rationales that reach correct answers. Repeat. Rationalization : give the correct answer as a hint on failed problems. Constitutional AI : the model critiques and revises against written principles. GRPO : PPO with no value function. The group is the baseline. AlphaEvolve : LLM edits programs. A machine-checkable evaluator scores them. DGM : the agent edits its own scaffolding. A benchmark scores it. RSI : system S_n proposes the edit that makes S_{n+1} . Answer-conditioned gradient : the loop rewards final answers, not steps. One recipe: generator plus evaluator STaR loop Model : samples a reasoning trace plus answer for each problem. Filter : keeps the trace only if the final answer is correct. Rationalize : on failed problems, hints the correct answer and samples again. Fine-tune : trains on the kept and rationalized traces. Repeat : the next round uses the new model. V-STaR : trains a DPO verifier on correct and incorrect traces. Picks best-of-N. First explained in Lesson 10.36; the hands-on workshop is Lessons 7.25 to 11.8 Lesson 10.36 Hallucination A fluent statement that is not supported by the model's input or by fact Lesson 10.38 Why this came about GPT-2 (2019) was trained on 40 GB of web pages linked from Reddit, and OpenAI noticed that bigger models trained on more text kept getting better in a surprisingly regular way. In 2020 Jared Kaplan and colleagues measured this: loss falls as a smooth power law in model size, data and compute. In 2022 DeepMind's Chinchilla paper (Hoffmann and colleagues) corrected the recipe: for a fixed budget, models of the day were too big and trained on too little data; about 20 tokens per parameter was the sweet spot. Since then, the work of building a base model has become mostly a data problem: collecting, cleaning, deduplicating and mixing trillions of tokens, then spending months of GPU time on next-token prediction. In plain words first Read the library, then predict the next word Pretraining is the next-token game of Lessons 5.34 and 7.20 , played on a large fraction of everything ever written online, plus books, code and scientific papers. The model sees each piece of text roughly once and gets slightly better at predicting the next token each time. Because predicting text well requires knowing grammar, facts, styles, reasoning patterns and code, the model picks all of those up along the way. The result, a base model , is a superb text continuer but not yet an assistant: ask it a question and it may answer, or continue with five more questions. How a modern assistant is made. Pretraining on trillions of tokens produces a base model that continues text. Supervised fine-tuning on example conversations teaches it to answer. Preference tuning (RLHF or DPO) makes its answers more helpful and safe. Reinforcement learning on checkable problems teaches step-by-step reasoning. Most of the compute goes into pretraining; most of the behaviour people notice comes from the later stages. Step 1 · Where the data comes from Source What it contributes Typical issues Web crawl (for example Common Crawl, billions of pages a month) breadth: every topic, style and language spam, boilerplate, duplicates, toxic or private content Code (public repositories) programming ability, structured reasoning licences, secrets accidentally committed Books, papers, encyclopedias long coherent text, specialised knowledge copyright and licensing Curated and synthetic data later · 10.41 maths, reasoning, instruction-like text quality control, bias from the model that generated it Scale has grown fast: GPT-2 used about 9 billion tokens, GPT-3 (2020) about 300 billion, Llama 2 (2023) 2 trillion, and Llama 3 (2024) over 15 trillion. Open datasets such as FineWeb (2024, about 15 trillion tokens of filtered Common Crawl) document their processing in detail. The steps below are simplified versions of what such pipelines do. Step 2 · Cleaning: heuristic quality filters Most raw web text is not worth training on: menus, cookie banners, keyword spam, and pages that repeat the same line. Simple rules remove much of it: Copy What you should see Copy Real pipelines use dozens of such rules (the Gopher and C4 rules are well-known sets), plus classifiers trained to recognise "educational" or "high-quality" text; FineWeb-Edu, for example, used an LLM to label samples and trained a small classifier on those labels to score every page. Step 3 · Deduplication The web is full of copies: mirrored pages, quoted articles, templates. Duplicates waste compute and make models memorise and repeat text. Exact duplicates are found by hashing; near duplicates by comparing overlapping word sequences (shingles): Copy What you should see Copy a and b differ only in case and spacing, so after normalising they hash the same. c changes two words and still shares half its three-word shingles (0.50), enough to count as a near-duplicate under typical thresholds of around 0.5; d is unrelated. Comparing every pair is impossible for billions of documents, so real systems use MinHash and locality-sensitive hashing to find similar pairs quickly. The same tool decides whether test questions leaked into training data ( Lesson 2.26 's leakage, Lesson 10.47 's contamination). Step 4 · Filtering with a language model's perplexity A small language model later · 10.43 trained on clean text finds clean text unsurprising. Its perplexity ( Lesson 7.23 ) can rank documents: Copy What you should see Copy Natural prose scores low (about 25), and the keyword spam high (about 210): it is not how people write. But the menu scores as low as real prose, because once "Home | About | Contact" has appeared, the model easily predicts it repeating. Perplexity filters catch unnatural text well but miss repetitive boilerplate, which the rules of Step 2 caught; that is why pipelines combine several filters. Filters also have a cost: text that is unusual for the scoring model (dialects, rare languages, technical notation) can be removed unfairly, so filtering choices shape what the final model is good and bad at. Step 5 · Scaling laws The central empirical finding of modern AI: a model's loss falls smoothly and predictably as you add parameters (N), training tokens (D) and compute (C ≈ 6ND, Lesson 3.20 ). The Chinchilla paper fitted a formula of the form L(N, D) = E + A / N^α + B / D^β where E is the loss no model can beat (the text's own randomness), the second term shrinks as the model grows, and the third as the data grows. With a fixed compute budget you must trade size against data: Predicted loss for four fixed compute budgets, using the Chinchilla scaling law (as re-fitted in 2024). For each budget, a model that is too small cannot use the compute well, and one that is too big sees too little data. The best size (dots) grows with the budget, and sits at roughly 20 training tokens per parameter. Using the constants from a 2024 re-estimate of the Chinchilla fit (Besiroglu and colleagues at Epoch AI), find the best model size for several budgets: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The best number of tokens per parameter stays close to 20 across budgets: Chinchilla's rule of thumb. Each tenfold increase in compute buys roughly a threefold bigger model trained on roughly three times more data, and lowers the loss by a smaller amount each time: steady but diminishing returns. These are predictions for one model family and dataset. The exact constants change with architecture and data quality; the shape of the curves has held up remarkably well. Step 6 · Why real models break the rule "Compute-optimal" means the best model for a fixed training budget. But a model is trained once and used millions of times, and a smaller model is cheaper every time it runs. So labs often train smaller models on far more data than the rule suggests: Copy What you should see Copy Llama 3 8B saw almost 100 times more tokens than "optimal" and keeps improving: the extra training lowers its loss well below the Chinchilla-optimal 8B, making a small model that is cheap to run much more capable. The cost is a bigger training bill, and eventually a shortage of good data, which is one reason for the growing use of synthetic data and of the later training stages (Lessons 10.36 and 10.37 ). Tip What scale buys, and what it does not Lower loss has come with abilities that small models lack: following examples given in the prompt ( in-context learning later · 10.47 , first shown clearly with GPT-3 in 2020), writing working code, solving multi-step problems. Whether some abilities appear suddenly at a certain size ("emergence") or only look sudden because of how they are measured is still debated. What scale alone does not fix: models still state falsehoods confidently, know nothing after their training data ends, and cannot act in the world. Lesson 10.38 covers these limits, and the sections from Talking to models: APIs, messages, prompts and context to Retrieval (RAG) the techniques that work around them. Make it your own Add a rule to quality_checks that drops documents where more than 30% of lines are identical to another line in the same document (a common boilerplate signal), and test it on a short multi-line string you write. (Solution M1.) Practice Apply it Using predicted_loss , compare a 1-billion-parameter model trained on 1 trillion tokens with a 10-billion-parameter model trained on 100 billion tokens. It has 10 words (enough to pass the length check), no repeated words, no symbols, and ends with "!". Solution M1 · Repeated lines Copy Add if repeated_lines(text): problems.append("repeated lines") to quality_checks . Navigation menus and footers that repeat on every line of a scraped page are caught by this kind of rule. Solution X1 · Size against data Both runs use about the same compute (6 × 10⁹ × 10¹² = 6 × 10²¹ and 6 × 10¹⁰ × 10¹¹ = 6 × 10²¹ FLOPs). The 1B model on 1T tokens (1,000 tokens per parameter) has a predicted loss of about 2.26; the 10B model on 100B tokens (10 tokens per parameter) about 2.18. With equal compute, the formula slightly prefers the bigger model here, as 10 tokens per parameter is closer to the optimum of about 20 than 1,000 is. But the 1B model is ten times cheaper to run afterwards. Recap Pretraining is next-token prediction on trillions of tokens of web text, code, books and papers; it produces a base model that continues text. Data pipelines extract text, filter quality with rules and classifiers, remove duplicates, and mix sources; data choices shape what the model is good at. Scaling laws describe loss falling smoothly with parameters, data and compute; Chinchilla found about 20 tokens per parameter optimal for a fixed training budget. Deployed models are often smaller and trained far longer, trading training cost for cheaper use. Scale brings new abilities but does not remove hallucination later · 10.38 , knowledge cutoffs or the inability to act. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in LoRA Low-rank adaptation: freeze the model and train two small matrices added to chosen layers Lesson 3.24 PPO The RL algorithm classically used for RLHF Lesson 9.13 Reasoning model A model that works through a problem in hidden thinking tokens before it answers Lesson 10.37 LLM-as-a-judge Using a model with a rubric to grade another model's output Lesson 14.77 System prompt The instructions given to the model before the conversation, which set its role and rules Lesson 11.20 Why this came about GPT-3 (2020) could do remarkable things if you phrased the prompt cleverly, but asked a question directly it might ignore it or ramble. In 2022 OpenAI's InstructGPT paper showed a fix in three steps: fine-tune on examples of good responses written by people; collect people's comparisons of pairs of responses and train a reward model on them; then use reinforcement learning to make the model produce responses the reward model scores highly ( RLHF ). A 1.3-billion-parameter InstructGPT was preferred by people over the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3. ChatGPT, released in November 2022, used the same recipe. In 2023 DPO showed the preference step could be done without a separate reward model or reinforcement learning, and it became widely used for open models. In plain words first A well-read intern, then on-the-job training A base model is like a brilliant new hire who has read the whole library but never worked a help desk: ask them something and they might reply, or might continue your sentence. Instruction tuning is a few weeks of shadowing: they study thousands of examples of good answers in the house format. Preference tuning is feedback from a manager: shown two of their drafts, the manager says which is better, and they learn to do more of what gets chosen. After that, the same knowledge comes out as helpful answers. Step 1 · Same size, same knowledge, different behaviour SmolLM2 is a family of small open models from Hugging Face, released both as a base model and as an instruct version fine-tuned from it. Give both the same request: Copy What you should see Copy The base model treats the request as the title of some web page and continues it: a heading, then the start of an article. That can look helpful, but it is continuing a document, not answering you; with other prompts, base models often add more questions or drift off topic. Now the instruct model, given the request as a chat message: Copy What you should see Copy The instruct model answers the question, in steps. It has the same architecture and the same pretraining as the base model; the difference comes from a much smaller amount of further training on conversations. (A 360-million-parameter model is tiny by today's standards, so its advice is generic; the behaviour change is the point.) Step 2 · Chat templates A chat is turned into one long text before the model sees it. Special tokens mark where each message starts and ends and who is speaking. The model was fine-tuned on text in exactly this format, and generates the assistant's reply token by token until it produces the end-of-turn token. A chat model still reads one sequence of tokens. A chat template turns the list of messages into that sequence, using special tokens to mark each turn: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Each message is wrapped in <|im_start|>role ... <|im_end|> (the "ChatML" style; Llama, Gemma and others use their own markers). These are single special tokens that never appear in normal text. add_generation_prompt=True ends the text with <|im_start|>assistant , the cue for the model to write the assistant's turn. It stops when it generates <|im_end|> . The system message holds standing instructions (role, rules, tone). Lesson 11.20 covers how to use the message roles through an API. Using the wrong template, or none, makes a chat model behave much worse, because it was trained only on text in its own format. apply_chat_template reads the correct one from the model's files. Step 3 · Supervised fine-tuning, and what is trained on Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) continues training with the same next-token loss, on conversations that show the desired behaviour: questions with good answers, instructions with good completions, multi-turn dialogues. Typical datasets range from tens of thousands to a few million examples, tiny compared with pretraining. One detail matters: the model should learn to write the assistant's replies, not to imitate users. So the loss is computed only on the assistant's tokens; the rest are masked out with the label −100, which PyTorch 's cross-entropy ignores. Copy What you should see Copy Only the reply (and its end-of-turn token) contributes to the loss. Fine-tuning a whole model this way needs the memory of Lesson 3.20 (about 16 bytes per parameter); in practice most teams use LoRA later · 3.24 , which trains small added matrices instead ( Lesson 14.132 ). Step 4 · Learning from preferences Learning from preferences. People (or a model following written principles) compare two answers to the same prompt. A reward model learns to score answers the way they would. The assistant is then tuned to produce answers that score well (RLHF), or tuned directly on the preferred-versus-rejected pairs (DPO). Writing perfect answers is slow; judging which of two answers is better is fast and captures things that are hard to write down, such as tone and helpfulness. Preference tuning uses many such comparisons. RLHF, step 1: a reward model. A reward model (usually a copy of the language model with a single-number output) is trained so that the preferred answer gets a higher score. The standard Bradley–Terry model says the probability that A is preferred over B is the sigmoid of the score difference ( Lesson 2.24 ), and the loss is the binary cross-entropy of that: Copy What you should see Copy When the reward model already ranks the pair correctly by a wide margin, the loss is small; when it ranks them the wrong way round, the loss is large and training pushes the scores apart in the right direction. RLHF, step 2: reinforcement learning. The assistant generates answers, the reward model scores them, and an algorithm such as PPO later · 9.13 nudges the assistant towards higher-scoring answers ( Lesson 2.27 's reward loop). A penalty keeps it close to the SFT model, so it cannot drift into strange text that happens to fool the reward model, a failure called reward hacking . DPO (Direct Preference Optimisation, 2023) skips the reward model and the reinforcement learning. It trains directly on (prompt, chosen, rejected) triples, raising the probability of the chosen answer and lowering that of the rejected one, measured relative to a frozen copy of the starting model: Copy What you should see Copy At the start, the model equals the reference and the loss is log 2 ≈ 0.693. Making the chosen answer more likely and the rejected one less likely (relative to the reference) lowers the loss. beta controls how far the model may move from the reference. Many open models use DPO or variants of it; frontier labs use mixtures of methods. Step 5 · Who provides the feedback, and what it aims at Approach Feedback from Notes RLHF human raters comparing answers expensive; raters' preferences and blind spots are learned too RLAIF / Constitutional AI (Anthropic, 2022) an AI model judging answers against a written set of principles scales cheaply; the principles are explicit and can be inspected Verifiable rewards automatic checks: is the maths answer right, do the tests pass? the basis of reasoning models later · 10.37 ( Lesson 10.37 ) The usual goals are summed up as helpful, honest and harmless . Preference tuning also has side effects: models can become sycophantic (agreeing with the user, flattering), because raters often prefer agreeable answers, and verbose, because longer answers can look more thorough. Recognising these tendencies is part of using models well ( Lesson 10.38 ). The same idea as a formula SFT loss: −Σ_t m_t log p_θ(x_{t+1} | x_{≤t}) / Σ_t m_t, with m_t = 1 only on assistant tokens Bradley–Terry: P(A ≻ B) = σ(r(A) − r(B)); reward-model loss = −log σ(r(chosen) − r(rejected)) RLHF objective: maximise E[r(y)] − β · KL(π_θ ‖ π_ref) DPO loss: −log σ(β[(log π_θ(y_w) − log π_ref(y_w)) − (log π_θ(y_l) − log π_ref(y_l))]) Check your mental model ✗ "An instruct model knows more than its base model." ✓ Nearly all knowledge comes from pretraining. Instruction and preference tuning change how that knowledge is expressed. ✗ "RLHF teaches the model what is true." ✓ It teaches what people (or a judge model later · 14.77 ) prefer. Preferred and true usually agree, but not always; sycophancy is the visible gap. ✗ "The chat template is just formatting and can be skipped." ✓ The model was trained on exactly that format; skipping it degrades behaviour badly. (Solution P1.) Make it your own Give the instruct model of Step 1 a system message such as "You answer in at most two sentences and always ask for the order number." and the same user request. How does the answer change? (Solution M1.) Practice Apply it With dpo_loss , keep the rejected answer fixed at the reference ( logp_rejected = ref_rejected = -38 ) and raise logp_chosen from −40 to −30 in steps of 2 (reference −40). How does the loss change, and what does beta = 1.0 instead of 0.1 do? (Solution X1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Masking a longer conversation Both assistant replies are trained on, while the system message, both user messages and all the template tokens around them are masked. For short replies, that is usually well under half of the tokens. To mask correctly in multi-turn data, compute the boundaries of each assistant turn; libraries such as TRL do this for you. Solution M1 · A system message The reply typically becomes shorter and asks for the order number, because instruct models are trained to follow system instructions. Small models follow them less reliably than large ones; test any system prompt later · 11.20 on many inputs before relying on it ( Lesson 11.28 ). Solution X1 · Exploring DPO As the chosen answer's log-probability rises from −40 to −30 (relative to the reference), the margin grows from 0 to 1.0 and the loss falls from 0.693 towards about 0.31. With beta = 1.0 the same changes give margins ten times larger, so the loss falls much faster (to about 0.00005): a larger beta trusts the preference data more and lets the model move further from the reference. Recap A base model continues text; an instruct model, fine-tuned from it, answers requests. Knowledge comes mostly from pretraining. Chat templates turn messages into one token sequence with special tokens marking roles and turns; models must be used with their own template. Supervised fine-tuning trains on good example conversations, computing the loss only on the assistant's tokens. RLHF trains a reward model on human comparisons (Bradley–Terry) and then optimises the assistant against it with a penalty for drifting; DPO optimises directly on preference pairs. Feedback can come from people, from AI judges following principles, or from automatic checks; preference tuning can also introduce sycophancy and verbosity. Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Self-consistency Sampling several answers and taking the most common one Reasoning Thinking budget A limit on how many tokens a reasoning model may spend thinking before it answers Reasoning models RLVR Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards: reward answers that a program can check Training reasoning models GRPO A reinforcement learning method that compares a group of sampled answers with each other Training reasoning models Mentioned here, taught later 2 Chain-of-thought (CoT), PPO This lesson mentions the ideas below before the lesson that teaches them. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Chain-of-thought (CoT) Prompting a model to show reasoning steps Lesson 11.26 PPO The RL algorithm classically used for RLHF Lesson 9.13 Why this came about In 2022 Jason Wei and colleagues at Google showed that simply including worked examples with step-by-step reasoning in a prompt (" chain-of-thought later · 11.26 prompting") greatly improved large models on maths and logic problems; the same year, "Let's think step by step" was found to work even without examples. Xuezhi Wang and colleagues then showed that sampling several reasoning paths and taking the majority answer ( self-consistency ) improved results further. In September 2024 OpenAI released o1, a model trained with reinforcement learning to produce long internal reasoning before answering, and in January 2025 DeepSeek published R1 , describing how reinforcement learning on problems with checkable answers ( RLVR ), using an algorithm called GRPO , taught a model to reason. Since then, most frontier labs offer "reasoning" or "thinking" modes. In plain words first Scratch paper and second opinions Ask someone to multiply 48 by 17 in their head and blurt the answer: they may slip. Give them scratch paper and they write 48 × 10 = 480, 48 × 7 = 336, total 816, and get it right. A language model is similar: each token gets a fixed amount of computation, so a hard answer produced in one token is a guess, while an answer reached after writing out steps has had much more computation, and its intermediate results sit in the context where later steps can use them. Asking several times and taking the most common answer, or checking answers before accepting one, are the "second opinion" versions of the same idea. Step 1 · Why thinking out loud helps A model's computation per generated token is fixed: about 2 × parameters FLOPs ( Lesson 3.20 ). The only way to spend more computation on a question is to generate more tokens. Compare the work done: Copy What you should see Copy Hundreds of times more computation for the reasoning version, plus a written record of intermediate results that later tokens can attend to ( Lesson 7.17 ). That is why "think step by step" helps on multi-step problems, and why it helps little on questions that need recall rather than steps ("What is the capital of Peru?"). Three ways to spend more computation on one question at test time. Thinking: write out intermediate steps before answering, so the model has more tokens to work with. Voting: sample several independent answers and take the most common. Verifying: sample several and keep one that passes a check, such as unit tests. Reasoning models are trained to do the first well, and systems combine all three. Step 2 · Voting: when it helps and when it hurts Self-consistency : sample several answers at a moderate temperature ( Lesson 7.21 ) and take the most common one. Simulate a solver that is right 40% of the time: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output When mistakes are scattered (each wrong path ends somewhere different), the right answer is the most common single answer even at 40% accuracy, and voting climbs from 40% to nearly 100%. When the model makes the same mistake most of the time (here "w1" gets 45% of all answers), voting makes things worse : it confidently picks the popular wrong answer. Real models show both patterns. Voting helps most on problems with one exact answer (numbers, multiple choice) and random slips; it cannot fix a systematic misunderstanding. Step 3 · Verifying: the power of a checker If you can check an answer automatically (run the unit tests, substitute the solution back into the equation, validate the JSON ), you only need one good attempt among many: Copy What you should see Copy Even a model that solves a coding task only 10% of the time solves it 88% of the time with 20 attempts and a reliable test suite. This is why coding agents run tests and retry (the Agents from first principles section), and why "can we check the output?" is one of the most useful questions when designing an AI system. Without a reliable checker, sampling more just produces more unverified answers. Step 4 · Training to reason: reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards Reasoning models turn these ideas into training. For problems with checkable answers (maths with a known result, code with tests), the model generates several complete attempts, including its reasoning; each attempt gets a reward of 1 if the final answer is right and 0 if not; and the model is updated to make the successful attempts more likely. No human needs to write the reasoning; the model discovers which ways of thinking lead to correct answers. GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimisation, used for DeepSeek-R1) scores each attempt against the others in its group: the advantage of an attempt is its reward minus the group's average, divided by the group's spread. Attempts better than their siblings are reinforced, worse ones discouraged: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output On the hard problem , the single successful attempt gets a large positive advantage (2.65): the rare correct line of reasoning is strongly reinforced. The seven failures are mildly discouraged. On the easy problem , the one failure is strongly discouraged and the successes only gently reinforced: there is little left to learn. On a problem that is too hard (every attempt fails), all advantages are zero and nothing is learned. Training data for reasoning RL is therefore chosen to be hard but not impossible for the current model. Using the group as its own baseline means no separate value model is needed, which made GRPO simpler and cheaper than PPO later · 9.13 ( Lesson 10.36 ). During such training, DeepSeek reported that responses grew longer and that behaviours like re-checking work ("wait, let me verify") appeared on their own, because they led to more correct answers. Step 5 · Using reasoning models well Use a reasoning (thinking) model or mode for Prefer a standard model for multi-step maths, logic, planning short factual answers, extraction, classification hard coding tasks, debugging simple rewriting, summaries, chat problems where a wrong answer is costly and checking is hard high-volume, low-latency work agent tasks that need planning over many steps anything where speed and cost dominate Practical points: Cost and latency : thinking tokens are generated (and usually billed) like any output tokens; thousands of them add seconds and cost to every answer. Many APIs let you set a thinking budget or effort level ( Lesson 11.25 ). Visible reasoning is not a full explanation : research has found that models' written reasoning does not always reflect the factors that actually drove the answer. Treat it as useful evidence, not a guarantee. More thinking is not always better : on easy questions, long reasoning can add errors ("overthinking"). Match the effort to the task. Checks still matter : a reasoning model is still a language model; for important outputs, use verifiers, tests and tools (the Agents from first principles section). The same idea as a formula compute for an answer of T tokens from an N-parameter model: about 2NT FLOPs (plus attention over the growing context) majority voting with n samples: correct if the right answer is the single most frequent one best-of-n with a perfect verifier: P(success) = 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ GRPO advantage for attempt i in a group: Aᵢ = (rᵢ − mean(r)) / std(r); the update raises the log-probability of attempts with Aᵢ > 0 Check your mental model ✗ "A reasoning model knows more facts." ✓ It spends more computation per answer and has been trained to use it on multi-step problems. Recall of facts improves little. ✗ "Sampling many answers always helps." ✓ Voting helps when errors are scattered and hurts when the model repeats one mistake; sampling with a verifier helps only if the verifier is reliable. ✗ "The model's written reasoning shows exactly why it answered." ✓ It is often informative but can omit or misstate what actually drove the answer. Exercises Predict before you run In Step 2, what happens to majority-vote accuracy with scattered wrong answers if the solver is right only 20% of the time and there are six different wrong answers? (Solution P1.) Make it your own Change same_mistake to ["w1", "w2", "w3", "w4"] (still four options, but all different) and rerun. Why does the result change so much? (Solution M1.) Practice Apply it A team's coding agent passes the test suite on 25% of first attempts. How many attempts does it need to reach a 90% chance of at least one passing, assuming attempts are independent? What could make the independence assumption wrong? (Solution X1.) Solutions Solution P1 · A weaker solver Each wrong answer gets about 80% ÷ 6 ≈ 13% of samples, while the right answer gets 20%. The right answer is still the single most common one, so voting still helps as samples grow, but slowly: about 23% with 5 samples, 31% with 15 and 46% with 45, compared with nearly 100% for the 40% solver. Voting depends on the right answer being more common than any single wrong one. Solution M1 · Spreading the mistakes With four distinct wrong answers, each gets 60% ÷ 4 = 15% of samples, below the right answer's 40%, so voting climbs towards 100% again (about 55% with 5 samples, 78% with 15 and 97% with 45). In the original list, "w1" appeared three times out of four, getting 45% of all samples, more than the right answer. What matters is not the total error rate but whether any single wrong answer is more popular than the right one. Solution X1 · Attempts needed Solve 1 − 0.75ⁿ ≥ 0.9: 0.75ⁿ ≤ 0.1, so n ≥ log(0.1)/log(0.75) ≈ 8.0, about 8 attempts. Attempts are not really independent: a model that misunderstands the task tends to fail the same way every time, and identical prompts at low temperature give near-identical attempts. Raising temperature, varying the prompt, or feeding back the test errors (as agents do) makes attempts more diverse and the estimate more realistic. Recap Each generated token gets a fixed amount of computation; writing out steps spends more computation on an answer and keeps intermediate results in context. Majority voting improves accuracy when errors are scattered and hurts when one mistake dominates. With a reliable verifier, success with n attempts is 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ: checking is one of the most powerful tools in AI systems. Reasoning models are trained with reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards; GRPO reinforces attempts that beat their group's average. Use reasoning modes for hard multi-step work, not for simple or high-volume tasks, and keep external checks for important outputs. Q3 In GRPO, what happens on a problem where all eight attempts fail? A The failures are strongly discouraged B The model gets a large reward C All advantages are zero, so the model learns nothing from that problem D The problem is solved by voting Advantages compare attempts within the group. l2704: Course home / Phase 10 · Build Your Own Language Model What language models get wrong, and why retrieval, tools and agents exist From Zero to Agents Lesson 10.38 55 min Core Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Explain why language models produce fluent falsehoods ("hallucinations"), from how they are trained Recognise the main limits: knowledge cutoff, arithmetic and exact lookup, context limits, prompt injection, sycophancy and run-to-run variation Demonstrate several of these limits with a real model Map each limit to the technique that addresses it: retrieval, tools, agents, evaluation and human review Before you start Needs : Lessons 10.35 to 10.37 , Lesson 7.23 (scoring text with a model). Depth : Core, for everyone; this lesson motivates the rest of the course. Lesson 10.47 covers measuring hallucination . Time : about 55 minutes. Next : Lesson 10.39 covers choosing and running models. Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Hallucination A fluent statement that is not supported by the model's input or by fact Reliability Grounded Based on supplied sources that can be checked, instead of on the model's memory Retrieval Mentioned here, taught later 5 RAG, Context window, Lost in the middle, Prompt injection, System prompt This lesson mentions the ideas below before the lesson that teaches them. The one-line meaning is all you need for now; each is marked later where it first appears. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in RAG Retrieval-augmented generation: find the relevant passages in your own documents, put them in the prompt, and have the model answer from them Lesson 10.45 Context window The most input plus output, counted in tokens, that a model can handle in one call Lesson 10.42 Lost in the middle Models use the start and end of long contexts better than the middle Lesson 11.27 Prompt injection Text that tricks a model into following an attacker's instructions instead of yours Lesson 15.24 System prompt The instructions given to the model before the conversation, which set its role and rules Lesson 11.20 Why this came about When ChatGPT reached a hundred million users in early 2023, so did its mistakes: invented court cases cited in real legal filings, fake references in student essays, confident wrong answers about recent events. Researchers had studied "hallucination" in neural translation and summarisation since about 2018; now it was everyone's problem. The responses that shaped today's AI engineering came quickly: give the model documents to read ( retrieval-augmented generation later · 10.45 ), let it call tools (search, calculators, databases), wrap it in loops that act and check (agents), and measure it rigorously (evaluations). A 2025 OpenAI paper argued that hallucination is partly built in by how models are trained and scored: like students on a multiple-choice exam, models are rewarded for guessing rather than for saying "I don't know". In plain words first A brilliant improviser Imagine an actor who has read an enormous library and is superb at improvising. Ask about anything and they will give a fluent, plausible answer in the right tone. Most of the time it is right, because the library was full of right answers. But if they do not know, nothing stops them improvising anyway, and it sounds just as confident. They also have not read anything published since they left the library, cannot use a calculator, and will follow instructions slipped into any document you hand them. Building with language models is mostly about giving this improviser reference books, tools and supervision. Step 1 · Fluent, confident and wrong A language model is trained to continue text plausibly ( Lesson 10.35 ), not to check facts. Ask GPT-2 small about a capital city: Copy What you should see Copy This small model puts " Marse" (the start of Marseille) slightly above " Paris". Larger models get this right, but the mechanism is the same: the answer is whatever continuation seems most plausible. Now ask about a country that does not exist: Copy What you should see Copy There is no Zentoria, but the model writes about its capital's location and its space agency's founder in the same confident register as real facts. Nothing in next-token prediction says "stop if unsure". Instruction tuning ( Lesson 10.36 ) teaches modern assistants to say "I'm not sure" more often, and larger models know more, but the tendency never disappears completely. Step 2 · Plausible is not the same as true Does the model at least prefer true statements to false ones? Compare the loss ( Lesson 7.23 ) of matched pairs: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output In most pairs the true statement is less surprising, because true statements are written more often. But GPT-2 prefers "Sydney" (a city mentioned far more often than Canberra) and the Kilimanjaro sentence. Frequency and plausibility, not truth, drive the preference. Big modern models get all of these right, yet the same effect appears at the edge of their knowledge: rare facts, recent events, specific numbers, names and citations. This is why answers that must be correct should be grounded : give the model the source text and ask it to answer from that text, with citations you can check (retrieval, the Retrieval (RAG) section). Step 3 · Exact work: arithmetic and lookups A language model predicts likely text. A multiplication has exactly one right answer, and "likely-looking digits" are not the same thing. Ask the small model for a product and compare with Python: Copy What you should see Copy GPT-2 small produces nonsense; large models do much better on arithmetic, and reasoning models better still, but exact long calculations, counting characters ( Lesson 5.31 ) and looking up specific records remain jobs for tools. The pattern you will build in the Agents from first principles section looks like this: the model decides which tool to call and with what arguments; ordinary code does the exact work and returns the result to the model. Copy What you should see Copy The regular expression check before eval matters: a tool must never execute arbitrary text that came from a model or a user ( Lesson 5.30 's "rules for format", and the Safety, security and governance section). Step 4 · The other limits Knowledge cutoff . A model knows only what was in its training data, which ends at some date. Ask about later events and it may say it does not know, or confidently describe an older state of the world. Retrieval and search tools supply current information. Context limits. Everything the model works with must fit in its context window later · 10.42 , and attention over long contexts costs compute ( Lesson 7.18 ). Models also tend to use information at the start and end of a long context better than information in the middle (" lost in the middle later · 11.27 ", 2023). Good context design ( Lesson 11.27 ) and retrieval matter even with million-token windows. Prompt injection later · 15.24 . A model reads instructions and data as one stream of tokens ( Lesson 10.36 's chat template ). A web page, email or document that contains "ignore your previous instructions and ..." can steer a model that reads it, especially an agent with tools. There is no complete fix; defences combine separation of roles, permissions and checks (the Safety, security and governance section). Sycophancy . Preference-tuned models tend to agree with the user and soften bad news ( Lesson 10.36 ). Ask for critique explicitly, and do not treat agreement as confirmation. Run-to-run variation. With sampling, the same question can get different answers; even at temperature 0, hosted models are not perfectly repeatable ( Lesson 7.21 ). Systems need evaluations over many runs, not one good demo ( Lesson 14.143 ). Bias. Models absorb associations from their training text ( Lesson 5.33 ) and can reproduce stereotypes in subtle ways ( Lesson 10.41 ). Here is what prompt injection looks like from the inside. The model receives one combined text, and nothing in its tokens says which part is trusted: Copy What you should see Copy The tags help the model tell the parts apart, and well-trained models resist obvious attempts, but tags are just more tokens; a cleverly written document can still mislead. That is why the real protection is outside the model: the support agent should not have a refund tool it can call without approval (Lessons 15.25 and 14.148 ). Step 5 · Why the rest of this course exists What language models get wrong, and the techniques the rest of this course uses to work around each limit. Most of building with LLMs is surrounding a powerful but fallible text predictor with retrieval, tools, checks and people. The whole argument in one cartoon. Asked about today's weather, a model alone can only produce a plausible guess (left). Given a tool that can look the answer up, the same model answers from real data (right). Figure: Hugging Face, Agents Course , Apache 2.0 . Language models are extraordinarily capable text predictors, and every limit above follows from that nature. The course from here on is about building systems that keep the capability and manage the limits: the How models behave in use section and the Talking to models: APIs, messages, prompts and context section : how models behave in practice, and how to talk to them through APIs and prompts. the Agents from first principles section : agents, which give models tools and let them act in loops with checks. the Retrieval (RAG) section : retrieval, which grounds answers in your documents. the sections from Safety, security and governance to Production engineering and AI system design : safety, evaluation and production engineering. The same idea as a formula a model scores statements by p(text) = Π p(xₜ | x₍<ₜ₎); a false statement can have higher probability than a true one if it is more typical of the training text grounded answering: generate y from p(y | question, retrieved sources) and check that each claim in y is supported by the sources Check your mental model ✗ "Hallucinations are rare glitches that the next model version will remove." ✓ They follow from training models to produce plausible text. They become less frequent with better models and training, but systems must still be designed for them. ✗ "If the model sounds confident, it is probably right." ✓ Fluency and confidence are not evidence of truth; made-up facts are written in the same tone. ✗ "A good enough system prompt later · 11.20 prevents prompt injection." ✓ Prompts help, but instructions and data share one token stream. Limit what the model is allowed to do, and check its actions. Exercises Predict before you run What will GPT-2 continue after "The 2031 Olympic Games were held in"? (Solution P1.) Make it your own Add three true/false pairs of your own to Step 2, including one about a rare fact and one where the false version uses a more famous name. How often does GPT-2 prefer the true statement? (Solution M1.) Practice Apply it For each problem, name the remedy from the diagram: (a) a support bot quotes an old returns policy; (b) a finance assistant adds up invoice totals wrongly; (c) an email-reading agent forwards confidential files after reading a malicious email; (d) a bot gives different answers to the same question on different days. (Solution X1.) Solutions Solution P1 · An event that has not happened A city name, stated as fact. No 2031 Olympics had happened when GPT-2 was trained (nor have they now), but the prompt is phrased like a fact and the model completes it plausibly. Modern assistants are trained to notice such false premises more often, but not reliably; a system that needs correct answers about events should search or retrieve current sources. Solution M1 · Your own pairs GPT-2 usually prefers the true statement for very well-known facts and does much worse on rare ones, especially when the false version contains a more frequent or famous word. Larger models shift this boundary further out but do not remove it. This is a simple way to probe what a model "knows", though serious evaluation uses many examples and careful scoring ( Lesson 10.47 ). Solution X1 · Matching remedies (a) retrieval: answer from the current policy document, with a citation; (b) a calculator or code tool for the arithmetic, and a check that totals add up; (c) prompt-injection defences: the agent should not be able to send files externally without approval, and untrusted email content should be handled with limited permissions (the Safety, security and governance section); (d) evaluation and lower temperature, plus monitoring of answers over time ( Lesson 14.143 ). Recap Models are trained to produce plausible continuations, so they can state falsehoods fluently and confidently, including about things that do not exist. Plausibility tracks how often things are written, not whether they are true; grounding answers in sources is the main remedy. Exact arithmetic, counting and lookups belong to tools; the model decides which tool to call and code does the work. Knowledge cutoffs, context limits, prompt injection, sycophancy, variation and bias are the other main limits. Retrieval, tools, agents, evaluation, permissions and human review, the subjects of the rest of this course, exist to manage these limits. Check your understanding Q1 Why do language models hallucinate? A Their training data is mostly false B They are trained to produce plausible text, and nothing in that objective stops them guessing when unsure C They have too few parameters D Temperature is set too high Plausible continuation, not verified truth, is the training goal. Q2 A model must report today's stock levels from your warehouse system. What is the right design? A Fine-tune it on last year's stock levels B Ask it to think step by step C Give it a tool that queries the warehouse system and have it answer from the result D Raise the temperature Current, exact data comes from tools or retrieval. Q3 What makes prompt injection possible? A Bugs in the tokenizer B Instructions and untrusted data reach the model as one stream of tokens C Low temperature D Missing chat templates The model cannot reliably tell which text to obey. Depth : Core. Lesson 10.43 surveys today's model kinds, Lesson 14.137 covers serving and self-hosting in production, and Lesson 14.142 cost engineering. Time : about 55 minutes. Next : Lesson 10.40 goes beyond text, to images, audio and diffusion. Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Open weights A model whose parameters you can download and run yourself Choosing models GGUF The file format for quantised models used by llama.cpp and tools built on it Local models llama.cpp A program that runs quantised language models on ordinary computers Local models Ollama A tool that downloads and serves local models with one command Local models Mentioned here, taught later 4 Frontier model, Prompt caching, vLLM, System prompt This lesson mentions the ideas below before the lesson that teaches them. The one-line meaning is all you need for now; each is marked later where it first appears. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Frontier model The largest, most capable hosted models at a given time Lesson 10.43 Prompt caching Paying much less for a prompt prefix the provider has already processed recently Lesson 11.23 vLLM An open-source server for running language models with high throughput Lesson 3.25 System prompt The instructions given to the model before the conversation, which set its role and rules Lesson 11.20 Why this came about Until 2022, using a strong language model meant calling one company's API. In February 2023 Meta released LLaMA's weights to researchers; they leaked within a week, and a wave of open-weight models followed: Llama 2 and 3, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma, DeepSeek and many more, some close to the best closed models. At the same time, tools like llama.cpp (2023) and Ollama made it easy to run quantised models on ordinary laptops. Teams now choose among hosted frontier models later · 10.43 , cheaper hosted small models, and open models they run themselves, and often use several at once. In plain words first Renting a chef or hiring one Using a hosted API is like ordering from a top restaurant: excellent food, no kitchen to run, you pay per dish, and the recipe is theirs. Running an open model is like hiring a cook for your own kitchen: you pay for the kitchen whether it is busy or not, you control everything, and nothing leaves the building, but quality depends on the cook you can afford. For most dishes the restaurant is simpler; at very high volume, or when the ingredients must not leave your premises, your own kitchen can make sense. Step 1 · The main options Hosted API (closed model) Hosted open-weight model Self-hosted open-weight model Local (laptop, phone) Examples the frontier models of Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Llama, Qwen, Mistral, DeepSeek served by cloud providers the same models on your own GPUs small quantised models via Ollama, llama.cpp Quality the best available very good, a step behind the frontier at the top same as the hosted version limited by small size Cost model per token per token, usually cheaper per GPU-hour, whether used or not your hardware Data leaves your systems? yes (under the provider's terms) yes no no Effort to run none none significant ( Lesson 14.137 ) low Can you fine-tune or inspect weights? limited sometimes fully fully Model names and prices change every few months, so this lesson teaches how to compare rather than which model to pick. Lesson 10.43 describes the current landscape. Step 2 · Estimating cost APIs charge per million tokens, with output tokens usually several times more expensive than input tokens. A support assistant's monthly bill, with example prices (check each provider's current pricing page): Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output With 3,000 input tokens per request (instructions, retrieved documents and conversation history) and 400 output tokens, input dominates the bill for the small model and is a large share for the big one. Context design ( Lesson 11.27 ) and prompt caching later · 11.23 ( Lesson 11.23 ) are often the biggest cost levers. A twelvefold price difference between models is common. Routing easy requests to a small model and hard ones to a large model ( Lesson 14.136 ) can cut costs a lot. Self-hosting changes the shape of the cost: you pay for GPUs by the hour, so the cost per token depends on how busy they are: Copy What you should see Copy A server handling many requests in parallel can produce thousands of tokens per second (the figure above is an assumption for a mid-sized model on one data-centre GPU). Busy, it can be cheap; mostly idle, it is expensive. Add engineering time, monitoring and spare capacity, and self-hosting usually pays off only at high, steady volume or when data rules require it. Step 3 · Will it fit? From Lesson 3.20 : weights need parameters × bytes per parameter, plus room for the KV cache and the runtime. Copy What you should see Copy On a laptop, models up to about 8 billion parameters in 4-bit run comfortably (unified-memory Macs can go further); 70B models need serious hardware even when quantised. Speed matters as much as fit: generation speed is limited by how fast memory can be read ( Lesson 3.20 ), so the same model runs much faster on a GPU than from laptop RAM. Step 4 · Running a small model locally in Python The instruction-tuned SmolLM2 from Lesson 10.36 runs on any laptop CPU. Here is a minimal chat loop that keeps the conversation history, so the model sees earlier turns: Copy What you should see Copy The second answer recalls the name and the order number, though with a small slip ("My name is Ravi" instead of "Your name is Ravi"), and the first answer asks for an order number the customer already gave: a 360-million-parameter model is easily confused. The important part is how it could recall anything: the model has no memory of its own, and "remembering" the first message works only because the whole history is sent again every turn. That is also why long conversations cost more ( Lesson 14.64 covers memory in agents). The same code works with any chat model from the Hub, given enough memory. Step 5 · Ollama and llama.cpp For everyday local use, Ollama downloads quantised models and runs a local server with one command (install it from ollama.com first): Copy The server listens on localhost:11434 and also offers an OpenAI-compatible endpoint , so code written for hosted APIs (the Talking to models: APIs, messages, prompts and context section) can point at it by changing the base URL: Copy llama.cpp is the engine underneath many such tools; its GGUF files hold quantised weights ( Lesson 3.20 ) in variants such as Q4_K_M (about 4.8 bits per weight) and Q8_0. LM Studio and similar desktop apps put a graphical interface on the same engine. For serving many users, engines such as vLLM later · 3.25 and SGLang are used instead ( Lesson 14.137 ). Step 6 · How to actually choose A simple way to choose. Start from what the task needs, then pick the smallest, cheapest option that passes your own evaluation. Most teams use a hosted API first and move parts of the work to smaller or self-hosted models when volume, cost, latency or data rules justify it. Write down what good looks like : 20 to 100 real examples of the task with expected answers or grading rules. Try a strong model first to learn whether the task is solvable at all. Try cheaper and smaller candidates on the same examples; keep the cheapest that passes. Check the non-quality needs : latency, data rules, cost at your volume, licence (for open weights ). Re-test when models change. Providers update and retire models; your examples become your regression test ( Lesson 14.143 ). Public leaderboards and benchmarks are a useful first filter, but your own examples decide. The same idea as a formula API cost per request = (input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price) / 10⁶ self-hosted cost per million tokens = (GPU cost per hour) / (tokens per second × 3,600 × utilisation) × 10⁶ memory needed ≈ parameters × bytes per parameter + KV cache + runtime overhead Check your mental model ✗ "Open-weight models are free." ✓ The weights are free to download (under their licence); running them costs hardware, energy and engineering time. ✗ "A chat model remembers earlier conversations." ✓ It sees only what is sent in the current request; memory is built by your code resending history or retrieving it. ✗ "The best model on a public leaderboard is the best model for my task." ✓ Leaderboards measure general tasks. Your own examples, costs and constraints decide. Exercises Predict before you run In Step 2, if the system prompt later · 11.20 and retrieved documents grow from 3,000 to 12,000 input tokens per request, by roughly how much does the small model's monthly cost grow? (Solution P1.) Make it your own In Step 4, add a third turn asking "Can you summarise our conversation in one sentence?" and print len(tok.apply_chat_template(history, return_dict=False)) after each turn. How fast does the token count of the history grow? (Solution M1.) Practice Apply it Your team handles 2,000 requests a day, each with 1,500 input and 300 output tokens. Using the example prices, compare the large and small models' monthly costs. If the small model passes your tests on 85% of requests and the rest are routed to the large model, what is the blended monthly cost? (Solution X1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Bigger prompts For the small model, input cost per request rises from 3,000 × 0.25 / 10⁶ = $0.00075 to 12,000 × 0.25 / 10⁶ = $0.003, while output stays at $0.0005. The total per request goes from $0.00125 to $0.0035, about 2.8 times as much: from about $188 to about $525 a month. Prompt size is often the biggest cost driver. Solution M1 · A growing history Each turn adds the user's message and the reply, so the history grows by tens of tokens per turn here, and every request resends all of it. Over a long conversation this adds up quickly, which is why chat products summarise or trim older turns (Lessons 11.27 and 14.64 ). Solution X1 · Routing Large model only: (1,500 × 3 + 300 × 15) / 10⁶ = $0.009 per request, × 2,000 × 30 = $540 a month. Small model only: (1,500 × 0.25 + 300 × 1.25) / 10⁶ = $0.00075, about $45 a month. Blended: 85% small and 15% large = 0.85 × 45 + 0.15 × 540 ≈ $38 + $81 = $119 a month, plus the cost of deciding which requests to route ( Lesson 14.136 ). Recap Options range from hosted frontier APIs to hosted open models, self-hosted open models and local quantised models; each trades quality, cost, privacy, control and effort differently. API cost is tokens × price; input tokens often dominate, so context size matters. Self-hosting pays per GPU-hour and is only cheap when busy. Memory needed is parameters × bytes per parameter plus cache and overhead; 4-bit quantisation brings 8B models to laptops. Local models run through transformers in Python, or through Ollama and llama.cpp with OpenAI-compatible servers. Choose by testing candidates on your own examples and keeping the cheapest that passes. Check your understanding Q1 A request has 4,000 input and 200 output tokens. Input costs $1 and output $5 per million tokens. What does one request cost? A $0.0010 B $0.0050 C $0.0210 D $5.00 (4,000 × 1 + 200 × 5) / 1,000,000 = $0.005. Q2 Why does a self-hosted model's cost per token rise when traffic is low? A The GPUs cost the same per hour whether busy or idle B Open models charge more at night C Quantisation stops working D The KV cache grows Fixed hourly cost divided by fewer tokens. Q3 How does a chat model "remember" earlier turns of a conversation? A It updates its weights after each message B The application sends the earlier messages again with every request C The tokenizer stores them D It does not; chat models cannot handle multiple turns Memory lives in the request, not in the model.
