Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Frontier model The largest, most capable hosted models at a given time Lesson 10.43 Speech-to-speech model One model that hears and speaks audio, with tools Lesson 6.18 Context window The most input plus output, counted in tokens, that a model can handle in one call Lesson 10.42 Why this came about For years, images, sound and text each had their own kind of network: convolutional networks for images, recurrent ones for speech. In 2020 the Vision Transformer ( ViT ) showed that a plain transformer works on images if you cut them into patches and treat each patch as a token. In 2021 OpenAI's CLIP trained an image encoder and a text encoder together on 400 million image-caption pairs, so pictures and words landed in one shared embedding space. Image generation took a different path: diffusion models (2020) learned to turn random noise into images step by step, leading to DALL·E 2, Stable Diffusion and Midjourney in 2022. Whisper (2022) applied the encoder-decoder transformer to speech. By 2024, frontier models later · 10.43 read images, audio and documents natively, and the same transformer ideas from the Transformers, step by step section sit underneath all of it. In plain words first Everything becomes a sequence of vectors A transformer does not care where its vectors come from. Cut a photo into small squares and turn each into a vector: now it is a "sentence" of patches. Cut a sound recording into short slices and describe each slice's pitch content: another sequence. Once everything is a sequence of vectors, the same attention machinery can relate image patches, sound slices and words to each other. Generating images works differently: start from pure static and remove a little noise at a time, guided by a network that has learned what images look like. Step 1 · Images as tokens An image is a grid of numbers: brightness per pixel (or three numbers, red, green and blue, for colour). A Vision Transformer cuts it into fixed-size patches, flattens each patch into a vector, and projects it to the model's width, exactly like a token embedding ( Lesson 3.19 ): Copy What you should see Copy Real models use larger images and patches: a 224 × 224 colour image cut into 16 × 16 patches gives 196 patches of 768 numbers (16 × 16 × 3), a "sentence" of 196 tokens. A position embedding tells the model where each patch was ( Lesson 7.19 ), and from there it is an ordinary transformer encoder. Step 2 · Linking pictures and words: contrastive learning CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder so that a picture and its caption get similar vectors, and mismatched pairs get dissimilar ones. In a batch of n image-caption pairs, every image is compared with every caption; the training target is the diagonal: image i should match caption i. With small made-up embeddings: Copy What you should see Copy Training on hundreds of millions of pairs gives encoders that place "a cracked phone screen" near photos of cracked phones, without anyone labelling categories. Such models power image search ("find photos of damaged parcels"), zero-shot image classification (compare an image with the captions "a photo of a dog", "a photo of a cat"), and the image side of many multimodal systems ( Lesson 4.31 ). Step 3 · How a multimodal language model reads an image How a multimodal language model sees an image. The image is cut into patches; a vision encoder turns each patch into a vector; a small projection maps those vectors into the language model's embedding space, where they sit alongside text tokens. The language model then attends to image and text tokens alike. Most multimodal LLMs connect a vision encoder (often CLIP-like) to a language model through a small projection layer, then fine-tune on image-text conversations. The image becomes a few hundred "image tokens" placed in the context alongside the text, and attention does the rest. That is why images count towards a model's context and cost ( Lesson 4.30 ), and why models can misread small text in an image: detail is limited by the patch resolution. Step 4 · Generating images: diffusion A diffusion model learns to reverse a gradual noising process: Forward process (fixed, no learning): take a real example and add a little random noise, step after step, until nothing but noise remains. Reverse process (learned): train a network to look at a noisy example and the step number, and predict the noise that was added. Start from pure noise, repeatedly subtract the predicted noise, and an example emerges. Here is a complete diffusion model on two-dimensional points (two interlocking moons), small enough to train in seconds: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Reading this code After 50 steps almost none of the original point survives (0.5%): the forward process really does end in pure noise. Training never runs the 50 steps one by one: a formula jumps straight to any step t, so each training example is a random point at a random noise level. The loss is just mean squared error between the true noise and the predicted noise ( Lesson 2.23 ). The network sees the step number (scaled to 0 to 1) so it knows how noisy its input is. Image models condition on the step in a similar way, and on the text prompt too. Now generate: start from pure noise and run the reverse steps. Copy What you should see Copy A tiny diffusion model, trained in Lesson 10.40 in a few seconds on a laptop. Left: the training data (two interlocking moons). Middle: pure random noise, where generation starts. Right: what the model produces from that noise after 50 small denoising steps. Image generators do the same with millions of pixel values instead of two coordinates. Most generated points land on the moons, though the model never memorised any training point: it learned the shape of the data. Image generators work the same way, with three differences in scale and design: the "points" are images (often compressed first into a smaller latent space, as in Stable Diffusion), the denoiser is a large network (a U-Net or a transformer), and it is conditioned on a text embedding, so the noise is removed in the direction of "a parcel on a doorstep at sunset". Lesson 4.32 builds each of those pieces in miniature, and Lesson 4.33 covers using such models and the provenance and rights questions they raise. Step 5 · Audio Sound is a sequence of air-pressure measurements, typically 16,000 per second for speech. Models rarely use the raw samples; they use a spectrogram : cut the sound into short frames and measure how much of each frequency each frame contains. Copy What you should see Copy The spectrogram shows the switch from 440 Hz to 880 Hz halfway through. Whisper feeds such spectrograms (on a perceptual "mel" frequency scale) into a transformer encoder, and a decoder writes the transcript token by token: the encoder-decoder design of Lesson 7.22 , with sound in and text out. Text-to-speech runs in the other direction, and speech-to-speech models later · 6.18 used in voice agents ( Lesson 6.18 ) handle both. (Large models can still memorise some heavily repeated images, a known concern for copyright and privacy.) ✗ "A model that reads images sees every pixel in detail." ✓ Images are reduced to a limited number of patch tokens; small text and fine detail can be lost. Exercises Predict before you run In Step 4, what happens to the generated points if you stop the reverse process halfway (run only steps 49 down to 25)? (Solution P1.) Make it your own Replace make_moons with make_circles(n_samples=2000, noise=0.03, factor=0.5, random_state=0) (two rings, one inside the other) and train the diffusion model again. Does it learn both rings? (Solution M1.) Practice Apply it A colour image of 448 × 448 pixels is cut into 14 × 14 patches. How many patch tokens does it produce, and how many numbers does each patch hold before projection? (Solution X1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Stopping halfway The points are still noisy: they have moved towards the moons but are spread in a blurry cloud around them, because the remaining noise (about 28% of the signal survives at step 25, so most of the variation is still noise) has not been removed. Image generators show the same thing: intermediate steps look like blurry blobs that sharpen in the last steps. Solution M1 · Two rings Yes: with the same model and training, most samples land on one of the two rings. The denoiser learns whatever shape the data has; nothing in the code is specific to moons. Thinner or more complex shapes need more training, a bigger network or more steps. Solution X1 · Counting patches 448 ÷ 14 = 32 patches along each side, so 32 × 32 = 1,024 patches. Each holds 14 × 14 × 3 = 588 numbers. 1,024 image tokens is a large share of a context window later · 10.42 , which is why many models resize images or compress image tokens. Recap Vision transformers cut images into patches and treat each patch as a token; CLIP-style training links images and captions in one embedding space. Multimodal language models feed image tokens from a vision encoder, through a projection, into the language model's context. Diffusion models learn to predict the noise added to data; generation starts from pure noise and removes it step by step, guided by text in image generators. Audio is usually turned into spectrograms; Whisper is an encoder-decoder from spectrogram to text. The same transformer and embedding ideas from the sections from Neural networks and deep learning to Transformers, step by step underlie all of these. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Prompt injection Text that tricks a model into following an attacker's instructions instead of yours Lesson 15.24 EU AI Act The EU's risk-based AI regulation Lesson 15.26 Structured output Getting a model's reply as data in a fixed shape, usually JSON that matches a schema, instead of free text Lesson 11.21 Tool calling The model replies with a structured request to run a named function; your code runs it and sends the result back Lesson 14.56 Frontier model The largest, most capable hosted models at a given time Lesson 10.43 Equal opportunity Qualified people are selected at similar rates across groups Lesson 15.26 Why this came about As machine learning moved into hiring, lending, policing and healthcare in the 2010s, its failures became public: a recruiting model that downgraded CVs mentioning women's organisations (reported in 2018), commercial face analysis that was far less accurate for darker-skinned women (the Gender Shades study, 2018), and risk scores whose errors fell unevenly across groups. Generative AI added new problems: convincing misinformation, leaked personal data, prompt injection later · 15.24 , and questions about the text and images models were trained on. Governments responded with rules (the EU AI Act later · 15.26 , adopted in 2024 with obligations phasing in over the following years) and frameworks (such as the US NIST AI Risk Management Framework, 2023). Responsible practice is now part of normal engineering, like security and testing. In plain words first The model is not the whole system A model is a component. Whether it treats people fairly, keeps their data safe and stays under control depends mostly on the system around it: what data goes in, what it is allowed to do, who checks its outputs, and what happens when something goes wrong. Responsible AI is the habit of asking, before and after launch: who could this hurt, how would we know, and what would we do? The main risks of AI systems, grouped by who or what they affect, with the habits that reduce each. Most are managed by how a system is designed, tested and operated, not by the model alone. Step 1 · Measuring fairness Suppose a model scores job applicants and the top scorers are invited to interview. Here are 1,000 simulated applicants from two groups. Half of each group is genuinely qualified, but the model's scores for group B run slightly lower, as happens when the training data or features carry historical patterns ( Lesson 5.33 showed how such associations get into embeddings ): Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Both groups are equally qualified (about 49% and 50%), yet group A is invited 51% of the time and group B only 36%. The selection rate differs. Among qualified people, 90% of group A are invited but only 72% of group B. This is a gap in recall ( Lesson 2.25 ), also called the true positive rate : qualified people in group B are missed much more often. Overall accuracy could look fine and hide all of this. Fairness problems only show up when you break results down by group . There are several definitions of fairness (equal selection rates, equal true positive rates, equal precision), and when groups differ in reality they cannot all be satisfied at once. Choosing which matters is a decision for the organisation, with legal advice in regulated areas such as hiring and lending, not something the model can decide. Generative models need the same habit: test prompts that differ only in a name, gender, dialect or language, and compare the outputs (quality, tone, refusals). Lesson 15.26 covers such evaluations. Step 2 · Privacy: keep personal data out of places it should not be Text sent to a hosted model, written to logs or used for training can contain names, emails, phone numbers and payment details. A common first defence is to redact obvious personal data before the text leaves your system or is stored: Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The email, phone number and card number are replaced; the order number and the tracking number survive. The tracking number has the right length for a card but fails the Luhn checksum , so it is kept: checksums cut down false alarms. The name "Asha" is not redacted. Names, addresses and free-text details are much harder to catch with rules; production systems add named-entity recognition models ( Lesson 5.30 's token labelling) or dedicated PII services, and still treat redaction as one layer among several. Better than redacting is not collecting: send a model only the fields it needs, keep logs for a limited time, and check what your provider does with your data (retention, training use, region). Go deeper (optional) Privacy techniques you will hear named Redaction and data minimisation cover most day-to-day needs. Four more techniques come up when models are trained on sensitive data: Differential privacy : add carefully measured noise during training (or to query results) so that the output would be almost the same whether or not any one person's record was included. It gives a mathematical privacy guarantee at some cost in accuracy. Federated learning : train on data where it lives (phones, hospitals, branches) and send only weight updates to a central server, never the raw data. Usually combined with differential privacy, because updates can leak too. Synthetic data : generate artificial records with the statistical shape of the real ones, for testing and sometimes training. It is only as private as the generator: a model that memorised real records can reproduce them. Machine unlearning : removing the influence of specific data from a trained model without retraining from scratch. It matters for deletion requests and is still an open research problem; the reliable approach today is to keep personal data out of training sets, or to retrain. A related infrastructure idea is confidential computing : running the model inside hardware-protected memory so that even the cloud operator cannot read the data in use. Step 3 · Security and control Lesson 10.38 showed that any text a model reads can try to instruct it. The defences that work are mostly outside the model: Principle In practice Least privilege an assistant that answers questions has no tool that can issue refunds or delete data Human approval for consequential actions payments, sending emails to customers, changing records go to a person first ( Lesson 14.148 ) Separate trusted and untrusted text mark retrieved documents and user uploads as data, never as instructions ( Lesson 15.25 ) Validate outputs check structured outputs later · 11.21 against schemas ( Lesson 11.21 ); check generated code and queries before running them Log and monitor keep records of inputs, outputs and tool calls later · 14.56 , with personal data redacted, so problems can be found and investigated ( Lesson 14.145 ) Step 4 · Other responsibilities Honesty with users : tell people when they are talking to an AI or reading AI-generated content, and make it easy to reach a person. Intellectual property : check the licences of models and datasets you use, and your provider's terms on the outputs. Some open-weight licences restrict commercial use or very large deployments. Energy and cost : training and serving large models uses significant electricity. A training run of 500,000 GPU -hours at about 0.7 kW per GPU uses roughly 350 MWh before cooling overheads. For everyday use, the most effective step is right-sizing: do not use a frontier model later · 10.43 where a small one passes your tests ( Lesson 10.39 ). Over-reliance : people tend to trust fluent answers. Show sources, signal uncertainty, and design workflows where a human stays responsible for important decisions. Step 5 · A checklist before launch The ideas in this lesson, as questions to answer before a system meets real users. It is written as data so that a team can keep it in the repository, record the answers next to each question, and refuse to launch while any answer is missing. Copy What you should see Copy the Safety, security and governance section turns these questions into concrete guardrails , security testing and governance processes, and the Production engineering and AI system design section into production practice. The same idea as a formula selection rate for group g: P(selected | group = g); demographic parity asks these to be equal true positive rate for group g: P(selected | qualified, group = g); equal opportunity later · 15.26 asks these to be equal disparate impact ratio: selection rate of the lower group ÷ selection rate of the higher group (a common rule of thumb flags ratios below 0.8) Check your mental model ✗ "If we remove the group column from the data, the model cannot be biased." ✓ Other features (postcode, school, wording) can carry the same information. Measure outcomes by group to find out. ✗ "Redacting emails and phone numbers makes text anonymous." ✓ Names, addresses and details in free text can still identify people. Redaction is one layer; collecting less is better. ✗ "Responsible AI is the model provider's job." ✓ Providers make models safer, but most risks depend on how you deploy them: your data, your tools, your users. Exercises Predict before you run In Step 1, what happens to the gap between groups if you lower THRESHOLD to 0.4? Will both groups' invitation rates rise, and will the gap close? (Solution P1.) Make it your own Add a rule to redact for twelve-digit numbers written in groups of four (for example "1234 5678 9012"), replacing them with "[ID]". Test that order numbers like "SK-48213" and the card number still behave as before. (Solution M1.) Practice Apply it Compute the disparate impact ratio for Step 1's results (selection rate of B ÷ selection rate of A). Is it below the common 0.8 rule of thumb? (Solution X1.) Solutions Solution P1 · A lower threshold Both groups' invitation rates rise (group A to 66%, group B to 51%), but the gap stays at about 15 percentage points: the scores themselves are shifted, so moving one threshold for everyone moves both groups together. The ratio between the rates improves (from 0.71 to 0.78) only because both are higher. Moving one threshold for everyone trades more invitations for more unqualified invitations; fixing the cause (the features or data that shift group B's scores) is the better path. Some organisations use group-specific thresholds, which raises its own legal and ethical questions. Solution M1 · Another identifier For example, add text = re.sub(r"\b\d{4} \d{4} \d{4}\b", "[ID]", text) after the card rule, so that 16-digit card numbers are handled first. Test with several strings: each new rule can catch things it should not, so keep a small set of test sentences and check them whenever the rules change. Solution X1 · Disparate impact 0.36 ÷ 0.51 ≈ 0.71, below 0.8, so this screening model would be flagged for review under that rule of thumb. The ratio is a warning sign, not a verdict; what to do about it is a legal and organisational question. Recap Risks fall on people (bias, privacy, over-reliance), information (falsehoods, misinformation), security (injection, leakage, misuse) and organisations and society (IP, energy, accountability). Fairness problems only appear when results are broken down by group; selection rates and true positive rates can differ even when groups are equally qualified. Redact personal data before logging or sending it on, using rules with checks such as Luhn, but collect less in the first place. Least privilege, human approval, separation of trusted and untrusted text, output validation and monitoring keep systems under control. A short launch checklist turns these into habits; the Safety, security and governance section goes deeper. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Prompt caching Paying much less for a prompt prefix the provider has already processed recently Lesson 11.23 Tool definition The name, description and JSON Schema the model reads to decide how to call a tool Lesson 14.56 System prompt The instructions given to the model before the conversation, which set its role and rules Lesson 11.20 Why this came about Language models did not start as chat assistants. They grew out of models trained to predict the next piece of text, and that origin explains their units: everything is measured in tokens , and every request has a fixed reading limit. When companies started paying for models through APIs from 2020 onward, tokens also became the unit of cost, so understanding them is the first step to understanding both what a model can do and what it costs. In plain words first Words are cut into pieces, and you pay per piece A model does not read letters or whole words. It reads tokens : pieces of text, often a word or part of one ("refund" might be one token , "unrefundable" three). Everything is measured in tokens: the context window is how many tokens fit in one request, counting the input and the answer, and providers charge per token, with output tokens usually costing several times more than input tokens. Because the API remembers nothing between calls, a chat resends its whole history every turn, so the input grows with every message. That single fact explains most of an agent's bill. Tokens: the unit of everything Models read and write tokens , chunks of text produced by a tokenizer (most use byte-pair encoding , BPE). In English one token is roughly four characters, or three-quarters of a word. Other scripts often need more tokens for the same meaning: the same sentence in Hindi or Tamil can cost two to three times as many tokens as in English, depending on the tokenizer. Code, JSON and numbers are also token-hungry. How a model writes one token: text becomes token IDs, IDs become vectors, the transformer turns the last position into a score for every token in the vocabulary, and one token is sampled. Tokens drive three things you care about: What How tokens drive it Cost Providers charge per million input tokens and per million output tokens. Output usually costs several times more than input. Cached input costs much less. Latency Reading input ( prefill ) is fast and parallel. Writing output ( decode ) happens one token at a time, so long answers are slow. Lesson 11.18 measures both. Limits The context window caps input plus output together. A separate max output tokens setting caps the answer. Estimate before you build. This function is all you need for a first budget: Copy What you should see Copy Agents multiply calls, and every call re-reads the history. That is why prompt caching later · 11.23 and short histories are the first cost levers ( Lesson 14.142 ). In production Token surprises in production Languages cost differently : Hindi, Tamil and other Indic scripts, code and long numbers often take several times more tokens per word than English. Estimate cost and context limits with your real traffic, not English samples. The invisible tokens : tool definitions later · 14.56 , system prompts later · 11.20 and retrieved chunks are input on every call. An agent with 40 tools can spend thousands of tokens before the user's question. Silent truncation : a response cut off at max_tokens looks like a complete but wrong answer, and an input over the limit may be trimmed by the framework. Check the stop reason on every call and alert on length stops. Count with the provider's usage field , not word counts or a different model's tokenizer. This section is a compact version of the same algorithm, used here for one engineering question: why does the same message cost more tokens in some languages than in others? If you did Lesson 5.31 , read the output and the paragraph under it, and skip the code. If you skipped the foundations, the code below is short enough to follow on its own. Models read tokens , produced by a tokenizer trained with byte-pair encoding (BPE) : start from characters, and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token. Frequent words become single tokens; rare words and scripts the tokenizer saw less often split into many pieces. Copy What you should see Copy The English sentences the tokenizer was trained on compress to about one token per word; the Hindi sentence, never seen in training, falls apart into single characters. Production tokenizers are trained on far more languages, but the effect is the same in degree: text in Indian languages often costs noticeably more tokens than the same message in English, so measure token counts per language when you budget (most providers expose a count-tokens endpoint, and tiktoken counts OpenAI tokens locally). Check your mental model ✗ "A token is a word." ✓ It is a piece of text from the model's vocabulary; on average about three quarters of an English word, and more pieces per word in many other languages. ✗ "The model remembers earlier messages, so only the new one is sent." ✓ The whole conversation is sent every time; input tokens grow turn by turn. ✗ "A bigger context window means I can stop worrying about context." ✓ Long inputs cost more, answer more slowly, and models use the middle of a long context less well. How a model becomes a chat model How this connects A four-line recap of the From language model to assistant section Lessons 10.35 to 10.37 cover these four stages in full, with code. They are repeated here in four lines because the two consequences below them matter for every design decision in the rest of the course. Later, the Models: training, evaluation and fine-tuning section returns to training in depth, and its workshop (Lessons 7.25 to 3.25 ) has you fine-tune a model yourself. Pretraining : predict the next token over a huge text corpus. The result knows a lot but does not follow instructions. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) : train on example conversations so it answers like an assistant. Preference tuning : reinforcement learning from human feedback ( RLHF ) or AI feedback (RLAIF) teaches it which answers people prefer. Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) : train on tasks with checkable answers (math, code, tool use). This is what produced today's reasoning models and much of their agent skill. How a modern assistant is made. Pretraining on trillions of tokens produces a base model that continues text. Supervised fine-tuning on example conversations teaches it to answer. Preference tuning (RLHF or DPO) makes its answers more helpful and safe. Reinforcement learning on checkable problems teaches step-by-step reasoning. Most of the compute goes into pretraining; most of the behaviour people notice comes from the later stages. Two consequences for engineers: the model's knowledge stops at a knowledge cutoff , so anything current must come from tools or retrieval. And models are trained on particular tool-calling formats, so the provider's native tool calling usually works better than an improvised JSON format in the prompt. Check your mental model ✗ "A reasoning model is better at everything." ✓ It is better at hard multi-step problems and slower and costlier everywhere; simple steps rarely need it. ✗ "Open-weight means free." ✓ The weights are free; the GPUs , serving and operations are not. ✗ "A system should use one model." ✓ Routing simple steps to small models and hard ones to strong models is common and cheaper. In plain words first How to use these questions These questions check whether the chapter's ideas have really landed. Read each question, then answer it in your own words (out loud, on paper, or to a colleague) before opening the model answer: a one-sentence definition, then how it works, then what it means in practice. Compare with the model answer and the plausible wrong answer, and note any follow-up you could not answer. If a question feels unfamiliar, go back to the lesson that teaches it. Teams can also use these as discussion prompts in a study group. LLM fundamentals Junior What is a token, and why do engineers care about tokenization? A token is the unit a model reads and writes: usually a word piece produced by byte-pair encoding ( BPE ) or a similar algorithm. English averages roughly four characters per token; Hindi, code and numbers often take more tokens per word. Engineers care because tokens set the price, the context limit and the latency, and because tokenization explains odd failures such as miscounting letters or mangling long numbers. Always measure with the provider's tokenizer or the usage field rather than counting words. Junior What do temperature and top-p control? Both shape how the next token is sampled from the model's probability distribution. Temperature rescales the distribution: low values make the most likely token dominate (more deterministic), high values flatten it (more varied). Top-p ( nucleus sampling ) keeps only the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p. For extraction, classification and tool calling later · 14.56 , use low temperature; for brainstorming, higher. Some reasoning models fix or ignore these settings, so check the model's documentation. Mid Why do LLMs hallucinate, and what actually reduces it? The model is trained to produce plausible continuations, not verified facts, so when it lacks knowledge it still produces fluent text. Training also rewards guessing over saying "I don't know" in many benchmarks. What reduces it in products: grounding answers in retrieved sources and requiring citations, giving the model permission and a format to say it does not know, tools for facts that change (prices, order status), structured output later · 11.21 with validation, and a faithfulness later · 14.72 check before answering. Measure the hallucination rate on your own eval set ; it varies a lot by task. Mid What is the KV cache, and why does it matter for cost and latency? During generation, each layer stores the attention keys and values of every previous token so they are not recomputed for each new token. It makes generation fast but uses GPU memory proportional to context length times concurrent users, which is what limits how many conversations one GPU serves. Providers expose its benefit as prompt caching later · 11.23 : a repeated prefix is billed at a discount and returns its first token faster. Keep prompts' stable parts first to exploit it. Mid What are reasoning models, and when are they worth the cost? Models trained (often with reinforcement learning ) to produce an internal chain of thought later · 11.26 before answering, with a controllable effort or thinking budget. They do much better on multi-step problems: maths, planning, debugging, complex tool use. They cost more tokens and add latency, sometimes many seconds. Use them for hard steps such as planning or root-cause analysis, and fast non-reasoning models for routing, extraction and formatting. Decide per step with evals, not per application. Deep learning and transformer internals Junior Explain gradient descent and backpropagation in two minutes. Training needs one number to reduce, the loss (for LLMs , cross-entropy on the next token). The gradient says how the loss changes as each weight changes. Gradient descent repeatedly moves every weight a small step against its gradient, scaled by the learning rate. Backpropagation is how the gradient is computed cheaply: run the network forward, keep intermediate values, then apply the chain rule backward from the loss, layer by layer, reusing each result. A backward pass costs about twice a forward pass regardless of the number of weights. In practice gradients come from mini-batches , and the optimizer is usually AdamW with warmup and cosine decay ( Lesson 3.18 ). Junior Why do neural networks need activation functions, and which ones do LLMs use? Without a non-linearity, stacked layers collapse into one linear map, so depth adds nothing. ReLU was the long-time default; GPT-2 and BERT use GELU, a smooth ReLU; Llama, Mistral, Qwen and most current LLMs use SwiGLU, a gated unit in the feed-forward layers. Softmax at the output turns scores over the vocabulary into probabilities. Mid How do you detect and fix overfitting? The sign is a gap: training loss keeps falling while validation loss stalls or rises. Fixes: more or cleaner data, weight decay, dropout , early stopping at the best validation step, a smaller model or fewer epochs, and for fine-tuning a lower learning rate or LoRA later · 3.24 . Keep a test set you touch once. The same logic applies to prompts: a prompt tuned on 20 examples overfits them, so keep a held-out eval set. Mid Walk through scaled dot-product attention. Why divide by √d_k? Each token's vector is projected into a query, a key and a value. Scores are query-key dot products ; a softmax turns each row into weights; the output is the weighted sum of values: softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V. A causal mask blocks future tokens in decoders. Dot products of d-dimensional vectors grow like √d, so without the division the softmax saturates onto one token and its gradients vanish; scaling keeps it soft and trainable. Multi-head attention runs several of these in parallel subspaces and concatenates the results. Mid Why does attention cost O(n²), and what do production systems do about it? Every token is compared with every other, so the score matrix is n × n. For prefill, compute and memory grow with the square of the context; during generation the KV cache grows linearly with context and concurrency. Remedies: the KV cache itself, grouped-query or multi-query attention to shrink it, FlashAttention to compute exact attention in fast on-chip memory, sliding-window or local attention layers, PagedAttention later · 14.137 for memory management, KV-cache quantization , and hybrid architectures with state-space layers. At the application level: retrieval and context engineering later · 11.27 instead of stuffing the window. Mid How do transformers know word order? Explain RoPE. Attention alone is order-blind, so position must be injected. The original transformer added fixed sinusoids; BERT and GPT-2 learned one vector per position. RoPE , used by Llama, Mistral, Qwen and Gemma, rotates each pair of dimensions in the query and key by an angle proportional to the position. The dot product of a rotated query and key then depends only on the distance between them, so attention sees relative position. Context-extension methods such as position interpolation and YaRN rescale the rotation frequencies so a model can be fine-tuned to longer windows. ALiBi instead subtracts a distance penalty from scores. Mid Encoder-only, decoder-only, encoder-decoder: what is the difference and when do you use each? Encoders (BERT) see the whole input in both directions and are trained by masked-word prediction; they suit embeddings , classification, rerankers later · 5.38 and entity extraction, and they are small and fast. Decoders (GPT, Llama, Claude) see only earlier tokens and predict the next one; they generate, and they are what chat and agent models are. Encoder-decoders (T5, Whisper, the original transformer) encode input fully and decode output with cross-attention ; they suit translation, summarization and speech recognition. Decoder-only won general-purpose LLMs because one objective scales to all text and every task can be phrased as continuation. Mid What are the residual stream, LayerNorm and RMSNorm for? Each sublayer adds its output to its input (x = x + sublayer(norm(x))), so a per-token vector, the residual stream , flows through every layer. It lets gradients reach early layers and makes deep stacks trainable. Normalization keeps activations in a stable range: LayerNorm centers and scales; RMSNorm only scales by the root mean square, which is cheaper and works as well, so Llama-family models use it. Modern models normalize before each sublayer ( pre-norm ), which trains more stably than post-norm. Senior Estimate the memory to serve an 8B model with 50 concurrent 16,000-token conversations. Weights in bf16: about 2 bytes per parameter, so 16 GB. KV cache per token is 2 (key and value) × layers × KV heads × head dimension × bytes: for Llama 3 8B, 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 128 KiB. 50 × 16,000 tokens × 128 KiB is about 98 GiB. Total around 115 GB plus activations and overhead, so two 80 GB GPUs, or one with an 8-bit KV cache and 8-bit weights. Without GQA (32 KV heads) the cache would be four times larger. Then say what you would measure: real context lengths are usually far below the maximum, and PagedAttention allocates only what is used. Senior How does a mixture-of-experts model work, and what are its trade-offs? Each feed-forward layer is replaced by many experts and a router that sends each token to the top few (often 2 of 8, or 8 of 256). Total parameters store knowledge; only active parameters cost compute per token: Mixtral 8x7B has 46.7B total and about 12.9B active, DeepSeek-V3 671B and 37B. Trade-offs: all experts must sit in memory, so memory cost follows the total; routing needs a load-balancing loss ; serving needs expert parallelism and can be uneven across GPUs; fine-tuning is trickier. The win is quality per unit of compute, which is why most large open models are MoE . Senior What is speculative decoding, and does it change the output? A small draft model (or extra prediction heads, or n-gram lookup from the prompt) proposes several tokens; the large model scores all of them in one forward pass and accepts the longest run consistent with its own distribution, then adds one token. With acceptance rate α and k draft tokens, each large-model pass yields (1 − α^(k+1)) / (1 − α) tokens on average, over three at α = 0.8 and k = 4. With the standard acceptance rule the output distribution is exactly the large model's, so quality is unchanged; only latency improves. It helps most when decode is memory-bound and drafts are often right, such as code and structured output. Senior What are state-space models such as Mamba, and will they replace transformers? They process a sequence with a fixed-size running state updated per token, so cost grows linearly with length and there is no growing KV cache; Mamba makes the state update depend on the input (selective). Pure SSMs are weaker at exact recall of something far back in context, which attention does well. The practical direction is hybrids that interleave a few attention layers with many SSM or linear-attention layers (Jamba, IBM Granite 4, NVIDIA Nemotron-H), trading a little recall for much cheaper long context. For agent builders the impact is on serving cost and context length, not on how you build. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Cache-augmented generation (CAG) Putting a whole small corpus in a cached prompt instead of retrieving Lesson 14.75 Vector database A store that finds the vectors nearest to a query vector quickly Lesson 14.71 Agentic RAG Retrieval where an agent decides whether, where and how many times to search Lesson 14.76 Why this came about Models know only what they saw in training, which ends at a cutoff date and never includes your private documents, and they fill gaps with plausible guesses. The 2020 retrieval-augmented generation paper proposed fetching relevant passages and giving them to the model, and after ChatGPT (2022) it became the most common way to build company assistants. In plain words first An open-book exam A model only knows what it was trained on, which stops at a date and never includes your company's private documents. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) turns a closed-book exam into an open-book one: for each question, find the few passages that matter in your own documents and put them in the prompt, then ask the model to answer from them and cite them. Most of the work, and most of the failures, are in the finding. Why RAG exists A model knows only what was in its training data, up to its knowledge cutoff , and nothing about your company. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) fixes that at question time: find the relevant passages in your own content, put them in the prompt, and have the model answer from them, with citations. It is the most deployed pattern in enterprise AI because it is cheaper than fine-tuning , updates as soon as documents change, and can respect who is allowed to see what. How this connects Lesson 10.38 showed why language models state wrong things confidently and named retrieval as the first remedy; Lesson 0.15 ran a five-line version. Lesson 5.32 built a word-matching search engine, and Lesson 7.22 built search by meaning with sentence embeddings . This chapter puts those pieces together into a system and takes each part to production depth. A RAG system is two pipelines: indexing runs ahead of time; the query path runs on every question. Read the figure as two separate pipelines. The indexing pipeline (top) runs ahead of time, whenever documents change: load each document, split it into passages, and store each passage in a form that can be searched quickly. The query pipeline (bottom) runs on every question: search the stored passages, put the best few into the prompt, and have the model answer from them. The lab: ShopKart's help center The whole chapter works on one small knowledge base: six pages from the help centre of ShopKart, the online shop used throughout the course. It is small enough to read in a minute, which matters, because you can check every search result by eye. Everything in the chapter runs offline with uv add rank- bm25 scikit-learn numpy . Run the blocks in order. Copy RAG in thirty lines Before the chapter takes each part seriously, here is the whole thing working, so that every later lesson has a place to fit. It uses two things you already have: the TF-IDF search of Lesson 5.32 to find a document, and the small open model of Lessons 10.36 and 11.25 to write the answer. Nothing here is a stand-in; the outputs are real. The four steps are numbered in the code: index the documents ahead of time, retrieve the best match for a question, augment the prompt with it, and generate the answer. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Without retrieval the model does what Lesson 10.38 predicted. It has never seen ShopKart's policy, so it offers general advice about broken kettles. Retrieved shows what the search found: the refund policy, with a similarity score of 0.34. The question and that document share the word "refund", and no other document contains that exact word. With retrieval the answer is right, and it is right because the policy text was in the prompt: "damaged or defective items are always refundable ... if reported within 30 days", and two weeks is inside 30 days. The model is the same in both runs. The only difference is 60 words of context. That is the whole idea of RAG. Three ways it fails, on the same thirty lines A working demo on one question proves little. Ask three more, and each one breaks in a different place. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Reading this output: which half failed? A RAG system has two halves, retrieval and generation, and they fail separately. Always ask which one failed before changing anything. "How much is express delivery?" Retrieval was right; generation was wrong. The shipping document was found, and it says "Express delivery costs INR 99". The model answered "free for orders above INR 499", blending two neighbouring sentences. The fix is on the generation side: a stronger model, a shorter and more focused passage ( chunking , Lesson 14.70 ), and an answer that quotes its source so the mistake is visible (citations, Lesson 14.72 ). "Do you ship to Nepal?" The answer is not in the documents at all. Retrieval returned the closest thing it had (shipping, at a weak 0.19), and the model, to its credit, declined instead of inventing an answer. This is the behaviour you want, and you have to test for it, because many models will guess. "How do I get my money back?" Retrieval failed. Look at the score: 0.0. The question says "money back"; the policy says "refund". They share no words, so word-matching search found nothing and returned an arbitrary document (account and login). The model then improvised from text that had nothing to do with the question. No prompt can fix this, because the right passage never reached the model. The third failure is the most common one in real systems, and it is why this chapter spends six lessons on search: keyword search done properly ( Lesson 5.37 ), embeddings that match "money back" to "refund" by meaning ( Lesson 14.71 ), both together with a reranker ( Lesson 5.38 ), and then a way to measure retrieval so you know which questions it fails on ( Lesson 14.72 ). Why not just put everything in the prompt? For six short documents, you could. The case for retrieval appears as the knowledge base grows: Paste every document into every prompt Retrieve a few passages per question Six help pages (about 500 tokens) Works, and is simpler Unnecessary A help centre of 2,000 pages (about 1.5 million tokens) Does not fit most context windows A few hundred tokens per question Cost per question at $3 per million input tokens About $4.50 with 1.5 million tokens of context, where it fits at all Well under one cent Speed Slow: every token is read on every call ( Lesson 11.18 ) Fast Accuracy Falls as context grows: facts in the middle get missed ( Lesson 11.27 ) The model reads only what is relevant Permissions Everyone's prompt contains everything Filter per user before the model sees anything ( Lesson 14.73 ) Long context windows and prompt caching have moved the line: for a knowledge base that fits comfortably and rarely changes, pasting it all in (sometimes called cache-augmented generation later · 14.75 , Lesson 14.75 ) is a reasonable design. Past that size, or when permissions differ per user, retrieval is not optional. RAG, fine-tuning, or both? Newcomers often ask why the model is not simply trained on the company's documents. They solve different problems: You want the model to Use Why Know facts that change, or that are private RAG Update a document and the next answer changes. Nothing is retrained, and sources can be cited Follow a format, tone or narrow task more reliably Fine-tuning (the Models: training, evaluation and fine-tuning section) Behaviour is learned from examples; facts learned this way go stale and cannot be cited Do both RAG for the facts, and a fine-tuned or well-prompted model for the behaviour They combine without conflict The map of this chapter The RAG pipeline as a map of this chapter. Exercises Predict before you run A customer asks "Do you deliver on Sundays?" and the help center has no page about it. What does a model do without retrieval, and what should a RAG system do? (Solution P1.) Break it on purpose Paste the whole help center into every prompt instead of retrieving. It fits today. What breaks as the help center grows to 3,000 pages? (Solution B1.) Debugging exercise ShopKart updated its refund window from 7 to 10 days, but the assistant still says 7. The model was not changed. Where do you look first? (Solution D1.) Make it your own Write five questions about ShopKart policies, and for each, the help-center document that answers it. This is the start of the eval set used through the Retrieval (RAG) section. (Solution M1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Not in the corpus Without retrieval, the model answers from its general training, which may be plausible and wrong for ShopKart. A RAG system retrieves nothing relevant and should say it does not know and offer a next step, which requires instructing the model to answer only from the context and testing that case. Solution B1 · Stuffing does not scale Cost and latency grow with every page on every request, the context limit is eventually exceeded, and answers get worse as the relevant page is buried among irrelevant ones ( Lesson 11.27 ). Retrieval sends only what the question needs, and its results can be cited. Solution D1 · Freshness, not the model At the index: the updated page was not re-ingested, or the old chunk is still there next to the new one. Check what the retriever returned for the question. Every change to the source needs an indexing path, and old chunks must be deleted ( Lesson 14.73 ). Solution M1 · A first eval set Pairs like ("How long does a UPI refund take?", refund-policy) are what Lesson 14.72 scores retrieval against. Include one question with no answer in the corpus and one phrased in Hinglish, because those are where RAG systems fail first. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism What problem does RAG solve, and what does it not solve? Worked answer. RAG gives a model access to information it was not trained on, such as private or recent documents, by retrieving relevant passages at question time and putting them in the context, so answers can be grounded and cited and updated by updating documents. It does not make the model reason better, fix bad or contradictory documents, or guarantee the model uses the context; those need good data, prompts and evaluation. A plausible wrong answer. "RAG stops hallucinations ." It reduces them when retrieval is good and the model is told to stay within the context; it does not eliminate them. Follow-ups. When would you fine-tune instead of using RAG? Debug a failure A RAG assistant gives a confident answer that is not in any document. How do you investigate? Worked answer. Separate the halves: check what was retrieved for that question. If the right passage was missing, it is a retrieval problem (Lessons 5.37 to 5.38 ). If it was there, the model ignored or misread it, so check the prompt's instruction to answer only from the context, the order of passages, and whether citations are checked ( Lesson 14.72 ). A plausible wrong answer. "The model hallucinated; try another model." First find which half failed. Follow-ups. How would you catch this automatically? Defend a design RAG, long context, or fine-tuning for a company help assistant? Worked answer. RAG first: the knowledge changes often, answers must cite sources, and access may differ by user. Long context works for a small, stable corpus and for one-off analysis of a long document. Fine-tuning teaches style and formats, not facts that change. Often the answer is RAG with caching of stable context. A plausible wrong answer. "Fine-tune the model on the help center." It would memorize unevenly, could not cite, and would need retraining for every update. Follow-ups. What would make you switch to long context? A To embed every chunk at index time B On the top 50 to 100 candidates, to reorder them precisely C To generate the final answer D To split documents into chunks It is accurate but too slow for the whole corpus. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in LoRA Low-rank adaptation: freeze the model and train two small matrices added to chosen layers Lesson 3.24 Lesson 10.43 gave the four-step recipe for a chat model in a list. This lesson and the next work through each step, because the way a model was trained explains most of its behavior: why it knows things up to a cutoff, why it follows formats, why it sometimes flatters you, why reasoning models think out loud, and why it states wrong facts with confidence. How a chat or reasoning model is made, drawn: pretraining on trillions of tokens gives a base model ; supervised fine-tuning teaches the assistant format; preference tuning teaches which answers people prefer; reinforcement learning on checkable tasks builds reasoning and agent skill. How this connects the From language model to assistant section taught these stages for the first time, slowly, on a real small model: pretraining data and scaling laws in Lesson 10.35 , instruction tuning and preference tuning in Lesson 10.36 , and reasoning models in Lesson 10.37 . This lesson and Lesson 9.13 are the compact reference version of the same story: each stage with the loss it optimises, a few lines of code that compute it, and the papers and names you will hear. If you did the From language model to assistant section, treat these two lessons as a consolidating read before the hands-on workshop that follows (Lessons 7.25 to 3.25 ). If you skipped the foundations, read these two carefully; the workshop assumes them. Why this came about GPT-style models are first pretrained on vast text to predict the next token, which gives knowledge but not helpfulness. InstructGPT (2022) showed that further training on examples of good instruction-following made models far more useful, establishing the pretraining-then-fine-tuning recipe. In plain words first Reading the internet, then learning to be helpful A model is trained in stages. Pretraining reads a huge amount of text and learns to predict the next token, which gives broad knowledge and language skill but not helpfulness. Supervised fine-tuning then trains it on examples of good responses to instructions, turning a text predictor into an assistant. Later stages ( Lesson 9.13 ) refine behaviour with feedback. Pretraining: next-token prediction at scale Pretraining runs the cross-entropy loss of Lesson 2.24 over trillions of tokens of text and code. The data pipeline matters as much as the model: crawl the web (Common Crawl), extract text from HTML, filter for quality with classifiers and heuristics, remove duplicates and personal data, then mix in code, math, books, papers and multilingual text in chosen proportions. Datasets such as FineWeb document this process in the open. Late in pretraining, labs often anneal on a smaller set of high-quality data, and many run mid-training (also called continued pretraining) to add long-context ability, a language or a domain before post-training. Scaling laws describe how loss falls predictably as parameters (N), data tokens (D) and compute (C ≈ 6ND) grow. Kaplan et al. (OpenAI, 2020) found smooth power laws; Hoffmann et al. (DeepMind, 2022, " Chinchilla ") showed that for a fixed compute budget, models had been too big and undertrained, and that the compute-optimal ratio is roughly 20 tokens per parameter . Copy What you should see Copy The middle line reproduces Chinchilla itself: 70B parameters on 1.4T tokens. Compute-optimal is about training cost only, though. A model is trained once and served billions of times, so labs now train small models far past 20 tokens per parameter, accepting a more expensive training run for a cheaper, faster model. The standard measure of a language model's raw quality is perplexity : the exponential of the average cross-entropy on held-out text. Lower is better; a perplexity of 8 means the model is, on average, as uncertain as if it were choosing among 8 equally likely tokens. Copy What you should see Copy Perplexity compares models with the same tokenizer on the same text; it says little about whether a chat model is helpful, which is why later stages are judged differently. Supervised fine-tuning: learning to be an assistant A pretrained base model continues text; asked a question, it may write more questions. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) , also called instruction tuning , trains it on example conversations written or curated by people (and increasingly by stronger models), formatted with a chat template of special tokens marking system, user and assistant turns. The loss is the same next-token loss, but computed only on the assistant's tokens: the model should learn to write answers, not to imitate users. Copy What you should see Copy Quality beats quantity here: the LIMA paper (Meta, 2023) got strong assistant behavior from just 1,000 carefully chosen examples, evidence that SFT mostly teaches format and style on top of knowledge learned in pretraining. The same is true when you fine-tune: a few thousand clean, consistent examples beat a large noisy set ( Lesson 14.131 ). Check your mental model ✗ "Models look facts up in their training data." ✓ Knowledge is compressed into weights; recall is imperfect and can be wrong. ✗ "Fine-tuning teaches new knowledge reliably." ✓ It mostly teaches behaviour and format; use retrieval for facts. ✗ "Bigger training data is always better." ✓ Quality and mix matter as much as quantity. Exercises Predict before you run A base model and its chat-tuned version are asked "What is the capital of France?". How does each typically respond, and why? (Solution P1.) Break it on purpose Fine-tune a model on 200 ShopKart support replies to teach it the refund policy. A month later the policy changes. What is the problem? (Solution B1.) Debugging exercise After fine-tuning on support replies, the model got worse at general questions. What happened, and how do you limit it? (Solution D1.) Make it your own Write the data spec for a supervised fine-tuning set that teaches ShopKart's reply format: sources, size, quality checks and a held-out set. (Solution M1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Pretraining against fine-tuning The base model continues text, perhaps with more quiz questions, because it learned to predict the next token of web text. The chat model answers, because supervised fine-tuning on instruction-response pairs taught it to follow instructions. Solution B1 · Fine-tuning is the wrong tool for facts The old policy is baked into the weights, and changing it needs another training run; the model may also mix old and new. Put facts in retrieval or the prompt; fine-tune for style, format and behavior. Solution D1 · Catastrophic forgetting Training on a narrow set shifted the weights away from general skills. Use parameter-efficient methods ( LoRA later · 3.24 ), mix in general data, lower the learning rate or epochs, and evaluate on general benchmarks before and after. Solution M1 · A data spec Real replies rated good by reviewers, cleaned of personal data, a few thousand examples covering intents and languages, deduplicated, with a held-out set of conversations not used for training and an eval of format and correctness. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism How is an LLM trained, from pretraining to a chat model? Worked answer. Pretraining on large text corpora with next-token prediction builds knowledge and language skill; supervised fine-tuning on instruction-response examples teaches it to follow instructions; preference training ( RLHF , DPO ) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards align behavior and improve reasoning. Each stage changes behavior more than knowledge. A plausible wrong answer. "Fine-tuning teaches the model new facts reliably." It teaches facts unevenly; behavior is what it changes well. Follow-ups. Where does tokenization fit? Debug a failure A fine-tuned model outputs the training format even when asked for something else. Why? Worked answer. Overfitting to one format: training examples all had it, and no examples showed other requests. Add diverse examples, train for fewer steps, and evaluate instruction following on held-out requests. A plausible wrong answer. "The model is broken." It learned exactly what the data showed. Follow-ups. How many epochs would you start with? Defend a design Should a company pretrain its own LLM? Worked answer. Almost never: pretraining costs are enormous and frontier and open models are strong. Fine-tuning or retrieval on top of an existing model covers almost every need. Exceptions are organizations with unique data at large scale and strategic reasons to own the model. A plausible wrong answer. "Yes, to own the IP." Fine-tuned open models give most of the control at a fraction of the cost. Follow-ups. When would you fine-tune an open model instead of using an API? A The model is right 8% of the time B On average the model is as uncertain as choosing among 8 equally likely tokens C It needs 8 attempts per answer D The loss is 8 Perplexity is exp(average cross-entropy). Q3 During SFT, why is the loss usually computed only on the assistant's tokens? A To save memory B The model should learn to write answers, not to imitate user messages C User tokens cannot be tokenized D To speed up inference The prompt is context; the response is what is being taught. l1103: Course home / Phase 10 · Build Your Own Language Model Evaluating models: benchmarks, metrics and hallucination From Zero to Agents Lesson 10.47 35 min Core Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Explain why models hallucinate and what reduces it Read benchmarks critically: saturation, contamination and misleading metrics Before you start Needs : Lesson 7.24 Depth : Core Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up Hallucination Fluent, confident, false output Why models hallucinate Calibration Whether stated confidence matches actual accuracy Why models hallucinate In-context learning Learning a task from examples in the prompt, with no weight updates In-context learning Emergent abilities Skills that seem to appear suddenly with scale In-context learning BLEU / ROUGE N-gram overlap metrics for translation and summarization Evaluating models BERTScore Similarity of contextual embeddings between output and reference Evaluating models Contamination Benchmark items leaking into training data Evaluating models Why this came about As models multiplied, benchmarks became the way to compare them, then grew saturated and contaminated. At the same time, hallucination emerged as the most visible weakness of language models. Understanding both is necessary to judge models for real tasks. In plain words first Exam scores, and why they mislead Benchmarks are standard exams for models. They help compare models, but scores can mislead: the exam may not resemble your task, questions may have leaked into training data ( contamination ), top models may all score near the ceiling, and small differences may be noise. Hallucination , a fluent but unsupported answer, comes from how models are trained to always produce plausible text. Your own evaluation set on your task is the score that matters. Why models hallucinate A hallucination is fluent, confident text that is false. OpenAI's 2025 paper "Why Language Models Hallucinate" (Kalai, Nachum, Vempala and Zhang) gives a clear statistical account with two parts. In pretraining , the model learns from patterns, and some facts have no pattern: an obscure person's birthday seen once in the data cannot be inferred, so errors on such arbitrary facts are unavoidable. In post-training, the problem is how models are graded: most benchmarks score a right answer 1 and both a wrong answer and "I don't know" 0, so guessing always pays. Copy What you should see Copy Under binary grading, guessing beats abstaining at any confidence, so models trained and selected on such benchmarks learn to bluff. Penalize wrong answers and abstaining becomes the right move below the break-even confidence. The paper's proposal is to state a confidence threshold in evaluation instructions and score accordingly. The engineering mitigations follow from the causes: ground answers in retrieved sources and require citations (the Retrieval (RAG) section), let the model say it does not know and reward that in your evals, check claims against tools, and measure calibration (does 80% confidence mean right 80% of the time?). Hallucination in agents also includes invented tool names, arguments and results, which schema validation and tool-result checks catch ( Lesson 14.139 ). In-context learning and emergent abilities In-context learning is a model learning a task from examples in the prompt, with no weight updates: give three labeled tickets and it classifies the fourth. It was the headline finding of GPT-3 (2020) and is why few-shot prompting works ( Lesson 11.25 ). Emergent abilities are skills that seem to appear suddenly above some model size (Wei et al., 2022). Schaeffer et al. (2023, "Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?") showed that many such jumps come from all-or-nothing metrics such as exact match: measured with a smooth metric, ability improves gradually. Both views are worth knowing; the practical lesson is that metric choice shapes what you see. Evaluating models: benchmarks and metrics Three reasons a public benchmark score can mislead you, and the one measurement that does not: your own questions, scored your way. Benchmark Measures Note MMLU, MMLU-Pro Knowledge across 57 subjects, multiple choice MMLU is saturated near 90%; Pro is harder GPQA Diamond Graduate-level science questions written to defeat web search A standard reasoning test Humanity's Last Exam Very hard expert questions across fields Built because older tests saturated HumanEval, LiveCodeBench Writing functions that pass tests LiveCodeBench uses new problems to limit contamination SWE-bench Verified Fixing real GitHub issues in real repositories The common agentic coding test ( Lesson 14.144 ) τ-bench, Terminal-Bench Tool-using agents in simulated customer service, or a terminal Agent reliability, including pass^k ARC-AGI Novel visual puzzles from few examples Tests generalization rather than knowledge LMArena People vote between two anonymous answers; ratings by Elo-style scores Measures preference, which style can sway Text-overlap metrics are still common for summarization and translation. BLEU measures n-gram precision against a reference (translation); ROUGE measures overlap, often via the longest common subsequence (summarization); BERTScore compares contextual embeddings instead of exact words, so paraphrases score better. Their blind spot is meaning: Copy What you should see Copy A correct paraphrase scores zero and an answer saying the opposite scores well. That is why LLM output is judged with task checks, rubric-based LLM judges calibrated against people, and human review ( Lesson 14.143 ), and overlap metrics are used only as a rough signal. Contamination is benchmark questions leaking into training data, which inflates scores. The usual check is n-gram overlap between test items and the training corpus (GPT-3's paper used 13-word windows): Copy What you should see Copy For your own evals the defense is the same: keep a private test set , refresh it from recent production traffic, and be suspicious of a model that scores far better on public benchmarks than on your cases. Check your mental model ✗ "The model with the highest benchmark score is best for me." ✓ Shortlist with benchmarks; decide with your own evaluation set. ✗ "Hallucination is a bug that will be fixed soon." ✓ It follows from how models generate; reduce it with grounding, checks and permission to abstain. ✗ "BLEU and ROUGE measure answer quality." ✓ They measure word overlap; correct answers in different words score low. Exercises Predict before you run Model A scores 2 points higher than model B on a public benchmark. Should ShopKart switch? (Solution P1.) Break it on purpose Evaluate a summarizer only with ROUGE overlap against reference summaries. What failure goes unnoticed? (Solution B1.) Debugging exercise Hallucination rate looks low in the eval but high in production. Using the lesson's ideas, what differs? (Solution D1.) Make it your own Define three metrics for ShopKart's support model: one for correctness, one for faithfulness to retrieved policy, one for abstention, with how each is measured. (Solution M1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Benchmarks are a filter Not on that alone: benchmarks may be contaminated, may not match the task, and 2 points can be noise. Shortlist with benchmarks, decide with your own eval set, cost and latency. Solution B1 · Overlap is not truth A summary can share words with the reference and still state wrong facts, or be correct with different words. Add faithfulness checks and human or calibrated-judge review. Solution D1 · Eval set mismatch Production questions are harder, rarer or outside the knowledge the eval covers, or the eval's judge misses certain errors. Sample production answers, label them, and update the eval. Solution M1 · Metrics with methods Correctness against labeled answers, faithfulness with a calibrated judge comparing claims to sources, abstention rate on unanswerable questions. Report each with intervals and segments. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism How do you evaluate an LLM for a specific application? Worked answer. Build a task-specific eval set from real inputs with labels or rubrics, choose metrics that match the goal (exact match, rubric scores, faithfulness, abstention), use human labels to calibrate any LLM judge, report intervals and segments, and track cost and latency. Public benchmarks only help shortlist models. A plausible wrong answer. "Use the leaderboard." It measures other tasks. Follow-ups. How big should the eval set be? Debug a failure An LLM judge rates a new model higher, but humans prefer the old one. Why? Worked answer. Judge biases: preference for longer answers, for its own model family, or for confident style. Check agreement with human labels, control for length, randomize order in pairwise comparisons, and use a different judge model. A plausible wrong answer. "Humans are inconsistent." Check the judge first. Follow-ups. How would you calibrate the judge? Defend a design Human evaluation or LLM-as-judge? Worked answer. Humans for the core labeled set, rubrics and calibration; LLM judges for scale and fast iteration, with measured agreement. High-stakes decisions keep human review on samples. A plausible wrong answer. "LLM judges are as good as humans." Sometimes close, but only measured agreement tells you. Follow-ups. What agreement level would you require?
